snippets: On the remaining set of  l  learning examples the classifier’s performance is estimated. Note that  l  may vary between classifiers as the probability distributions may be considerably different. When classifying new examples, classifications are either weighted with their local performance, or only the best local classifier is used. In practice, the most frequently used combination method is weighted voting. However, some studies show that the best results are obtained by using the naive Bayesian combination. Regression In regression, a straightforward approach for combining regressional predictors is to average their predictions. Usually, a weighted average is used. For each predictor, its weight is either a reliability of a particular prediction estimated with some method (e.g. transduction ( Section 3.5.4 )), or an overall predictor’s reliability is estimated. As in classification, meta learning of a combination function (stacking) can also be used in regression. 3.5.2 Combining algorithms In the previous section we have reviewed how learning algorithms can be combined in parallel. They are run independently; only their predictions are somehow combined. A combination function may be fixed, or learned by a meta learner from algorithms’ predictions on a validation set. Learning algorithms can also be combined sequentially: the first algorithm learns the target function, the second learns to predict errors of the first, and so on. An ordered chain of hypotheses is built; each (except the first one) predicts errors of the previous hypothesis. Because of possible overfitting, chains of length 2 are mostly used in practice: an algorithm that predicts the target values and an algorithm that tries to correct its errors. It is important to supply the correction algorithm with learning examples from a separate (validation) set; otherwise overfitting may quickly occur. In principle, sequential, parallel and meta learning can be arbitrarily combined. Thus we can get algorithm networks with different topologies. A well known approach to combine a multitude of simple base algorithms (threshold functions) into a complex structure are  artificial neural networks  ( Chapter 11 ). Because of dangers of overfitting,  and preferences for simple and transparent hypotheses, complex combinations of different base learning algorithms are rarely used in practice. 3.5.3 Bagging, boosting and random forests Bagging, boosting and random forests are  ensemble learning algorithms . Their common property is that they generate ensembles of base classifiers and ensure their diversity by providing them with different sets of learning examples. Bagging.

snippets: 3.5 COMBINING SEVERAL MACHINE LEARNING ALGORITHMS More than with friends we learn tolerance with our enemies . —  Dalai Lama The  minimum description length principle  ( Section 3.1.2 ) requires from the learning algorithm to find a trade-off between the hypothesis’ complexity and its accuracy. A hypothesis needs to be as simple as possible and yet provide a good data model. On the other hand, the  principle of multiple explanations  ( Section 3.1.4 ) requires the prediction algorithm to use many considerably different hypotheses consistent with the data. A learning algorithm should consider both criteria and generate several different hypotheses (models) during the learning phase. There are two possibilities: • Hypotheses are generated by different learning algorithms on the same data. In a classification problem we could, for example, learn a naive Bayesian classifier and a multi-layered neural network, store learning examples for a  k -nearest neighbors algorithm, and calculate a discriminant function using the SVM method. • Hypotheses are generated by the same algorithm either by running it with different parameter settings or by variating its learning set. Popular general methods from this group are  bagging  and  boosting;  for decision trees frequently  random forests  are used. When several hypotheses are built they need to be combined into the final hypothesis (classifier or regressor) by the principle of multiple explanations. As the conditional hypothesis probabilities  P ( H|E, B ) from  Equation (3.9)  are usually not known, some suitable method for combining hypotheses needs to be used. In the following sections we review some popular approaches to hypothesis combination. 3.5.1 Combining predictions of several hypotheses Combining predictions of several hypotheses has gained considerable popularity in machine learning, especially in classification problems. As the approaches used in classification and regression are considerably different, they are reviewed separately. Classification In classification, predictions of different classifiers can be combined in several ways: Voting:  each classifier gives a vote for a particular class; the example is labelled with the class label that has received most votes. Weighted voting:  each classifier contributes a class probability distribution (or normalized scores). A class probability acts as a weight; the example is labelled with the class label that has the greatest sum of weights.

snippets: 10.2.2 Combination learners Combination learning refers to the process of combining multiple models or learners to improve the overall performance of a machine-learning system. The goal of combination learning is to leverage the strengths of multiple models to compensate for their individual weaknesses, leading to a more accurate and robust prediction or classification. A combination learner is a type of machine-learning algorithm that combines the outputs of multiple base learners, which are usually simpler or weaker models, to form a more powerful or complex model. The combination learner can be used in both supervised and unsupervised learning problems. In supervised learning, combination learners are typically used for ensemble methods, such as random forests, boosting, or bagging, which combine the predictions of multiple base classifiers to improve classification accuracy or reduce overfitting. The base classifiers can be different types of algorithms, such as decision trees, support-vector machines, or neural networks. In unsupervised learning, combination learners are often used for clustering or anomaly-detection problems, where the goal is to identify hidden patterns or anomalies in the data. Ensemble-clustering methods, such as consensus  clustering or cluster-level ensemble methods, can be used to combine the results of multiple base-clustering algorithms to improve the clustering performance and robustness. A combination function tries to aggregate the outputs of learning models participating in the ensemble process. The outputs to be combined can be in class label form or continuous outputs. Depending on the type of output of the learning model, the combination function must be chosen. 10.2.2.1 Class-label combination To combine the class-label outputs of learning models, two simple strategies that can be used are  Majority voting  and  Weighted majority voting , as discussed below. 1. Majority voting : According to this technique, the ensemble chooses the class label with the most votes. That is, all the learning models have equal opportunities to choose their respective class labels (these are counted as votes), and the label with the most votes is chosen as the winner by the ensemble. For example, let us say we have ten learning models, and six learning models say that a particular instance, say  X 1  belongs to class A and four models say  X 1  belongs to class B. Then, the final output will be class A. This technique can have three different cases: (a) Case 1: All learning models agree unanimously without any conflicts in predicting a single class label. This is a  consensus voting  decision.

snippets: 5.1.3 Learning strategies Different learning paradigms have been proposed to enhance generalization performances. These learning techniques include: ensemble learning, test-time augmentation, incremental learning, self-supervised learning, meta-learning, gradient-operation, distributionally robust optimization, and multi-task learning. 5.1.3.1 Ensemble learning In machine learning, ensemble methods are very common to boost generalization performance. The principle of ensemble learning is to derive a prediction given predictions from multiple models (i.e., an ensemble). This is typically implemented as a simple averaging over the ensemble predictions. In DG, more generally, ensemble learning refers to combining multiple models to enhance generalization. In the context of surgical instrument localization, Philipp et al.    proposed an uncertainty-based dynamic CNN which combines two modalities (image and optic flow modality). Their CNN dynamics were guided using pixel level uncertainty estimated separately for each modality. It comprises two ensemble network, one for each modality. The outputs for each ensemble is fused using the mean of the prediction maps. Next, pixel-wise uncertainty map is estimated using the standard deviation across the ensemble individuals. Uncertainty masks are then computed by normalizing these pixel-wise uncertainty maps. Finally, these uncertainty masks are used to fuse the ensemble for the two modalities by weighting the predictions from each modality based on their respective uncertainties. This method showed good generalization performances when evaluated on heterogeneous surgical datasets coming from different domains including eye, laparoscopic and neurosurgeries. Wang and Xia    proposed  domain-ensemble learning with cross-domain mixup . Their model comprised a shared backbone for all source domains and a domain-specific classifier. After training their domain specific model, they used ensemble learning to expose the model optimization to domain distribution discrepancy. They enforced the consistency between the predictions obtained by all non-domain specific model (ensemble of predictions) and a pseudo label generated by a domain-specific model (i.e., prediction from a domain-specific model). This method was applied for thoracic disease classification in unseen domains and showed that it outperformed the state-of-the-art DG methods on unseen datasets. In their Federated Learning (FL) framework, Shen et al.    and Andreux et al.    addressed the non-IID data across different clients.

concept: Randomization techniques, such as the Random Subspace method, enhance the diversity of classifiers in ensemble learning, particularly for stable algorithms that are less sensitive to input changes, unlike bagging which may not be effective in such cases.
The Random Subspace method mitigates overfitting by training classifiers on distinct subsets of features, thus preventing reliance on any single feature and improving adaptability to new data.
The Rotation Forest (RotF) method further diversifies classifiers by applying feature transformations to randomly selected subsets of features, enhancing overall ensemble performance.
Resampling techniques are crucial for addressing imbalanced datasets, with methods categorized into undersampling, oversampling, and hybrid techniques, each with its own advantages and limitations.

Adaptive synthetic sampling (ADASYN) improves classification performance on imbalanced datasets by generating synthetic samples around hard-to-classify instances, thus increasing minority class diversity.
Image resampling techniques augment image datasets by applying various transformations, which helps in generating new perspectives of important features for better model training.

The popularity of resampling techniques is evident, with a significant number of studies employing these methods, indicating their effectiveness in improving classifier performance in imbalanced scenarios.

The choice between undersampling and oversampling methods depends on the dataset size and the number of minority instances, with specific recommendations for optimal sampling strategies based on empirical studies.

AdaBoost and MultiBoosting are ensemble learning techniques that aim to improve classification accuracy, with MultiBoosting combining the strengths of AdaBoost and bagging to enhance bias and variance reduction.

The Random Subspace Method (RSM) introduces diversity among classifiers by training them on random subsets of features, which helps mitigate overfitting and improves performance, especially in high-dimensional datasets.

Rotation Forest (RoF) enhances classifier diversity through feature transformation techniques, specifically using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to create rotated feature subsets for training, leading to improved accuracy and resilience of the ensemble.
Both RSM and RoF are particularly effective in scenarios with small sample sizes or high-dimensional data, as they allow classifiers to focus on relevant features while reducing noise and redundancy.
The final predictions in these ensemble methods are typically made through majority voting, which aggregates the outputs of individual classifiers to produce a more robust decision.

Regularization techniques, such as those mentioned in the context of pruning decision trees, are essential for maintaining model accuracy and preventing overfitting by controlling the complexity of the model.

snippets: While AdaBoost minimizes potential for parallel computation due to its sequential nature, each classifier learned with wagging is independent, enabling parallel computation—a trait inherited by MultiBoost at the subcommittee level   . Random Subspace Method:  The Random Subspace Method (RSM) is a fusion technique introduced by Ho   . In RSM, adjustments are made to the training data, but these modifications occur within the feature space. Consequently, a random subspace of dimensionality r is derived from the original p-dimensional feature space. This results in a modified training set consisting of r-dimensional training objects. Classifiers are then constructed within these random subspaces and aggregated using simple majority voting in the final decision rule. Utilizing random subspaces for both classifier construction and aggregation can be advantageous. Specifically, when the number of training objects is relatively small compared to the data dimensionality, constructing classifiers in random subspaces can address the issue of small sample size. By reducing the subspace dimensionality while maintaining the same number of training objects, the relative training sample size increases. Moreover, in cases where data exhibit numerous redundant features, classifiers developed in random subspaces may outperform those constructed in the original feature space. Consequently, the combined decision of such classifiers may surpass that of a single classifier developed on the original training set in the complete feature space   . Rotation Forest (RoF):  Rotation Forest is an ensemble learning technique that uses feature extraction techniques to improve the accuracy and variety of individual base classifiers. It builds a collection of decision trees by using feature extraction and modification to produce a variety of training subsets. Every tree in the group receives training on a distinct rotated copy of the initial feature space. High variety among the classifiers is ensured by using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to choose subsets of features to accomplish the rotation randomly   . The provided set of features is first divided in a random fashion in subsets. It uses the training data to create a bootstrap sample for every feature subset. The PCA is then applied to every bootstrap sample of the feature subsets. The subset of characteristics is transformed using PCA into a group of uncorrelated principal components. In this stage, a rotation matrix for every feature subset is produced. To create a complete rotation matrix for all features in the initially supplied feature set, the rotation matrices from each subgroup are combined in the following step.

For every base classifier, a random subset of characteristics is chosen rather than all of the features. It is usual practice to perform this randomization separately for every base classifier. Improving the basic classifiers’ variety is essential to enhancing the ensemble's capacity to adapt successfully to new scenarios and sets of data. Because the Random Subspace method keeps the ensemble from becoming overly reliant on any one feature, it helps decrease overfitting. Because each base classifier only sees a portion of the data, they are unable to learn unnecessary or noisy aspects from the data. The final prediction is produced during the prediction phase by combining the unique predictions of each base classifier. Most commonly, techniques like majority voting are used to accomplish this combination. High-dimensional datasets are a special case for Random Subspace-based ensembles. The technique mitigates the curse of high volume of data by choosing subsets of features at random, making it suitable for handling enormous feature counts. Random Subspace sampling introduces diversity, which adds to the ensemble's resilience. The model is more likely to function successfully in a variety of circumstances and is less susceptible to changes in the input data   . 14.2.5.2 Rotation Forest (RotF) The RotF is an ensemble learning method that belongs to the family of feature transformation-based ensemble classifiers. The key idea behind the RotF is to use feature transformation techniques to create diverse views of the input data   . In this manner it enhances the diversity among base classifiers by applying potential transformations to the input features. The transformation is applied to randomly selected subsets of features. This selection is also based on the concept of orthogonality. A variety of base classifiers are trained using various perspectives on the input data that were acquired throughout the transformation. The main goal is to use various feature subsets and transformations to create diverse base classifiers. Enhancing the ensemble's overall performance and resilience needs this diversity.

MultiBoosting:  MultiBoosting is a decision committee method that combines AdaBoost with wagging, a variation of bagging deemed more suitable for the task than direct bagging. Experimental findings suggest that it generally surpasses its individual components in error reduction. Wagging, initially proposed by Bauer and Kohavi   , diverges from bagging by assigning random weights to cases in each training set instead of using random bootstrap samples. However, their original formulation of wagging utilized Gaussian noise to vary instance weights, which could lead to some weights being reduced to zero, effectively eliminating them from the training set. Observations that bagging and AdaBoost operate via distinct mechanisms and have different impacts, with the most significant effects achieved by the initial committee members, suggest the potential benefits of combining the two. Bagging primarily targets variance reduction, whereas AdaBoost addresses both bias and variance reduction, although evidence suggests bagging is more effective than AdaBoost at reducing variance   . By combining them, MultiBoosting aims to retain AdaBoost's bias reduction while adding bagging's variance reduction to AdaBoost's existing benefits. MultiBoosting can be conceptualized as wagging committees formed by AdaBoost. In addition to inheriting bias and variance reduction properties from each constituent committee learning algorithm, MultiBoost may offer computational advantages over AdaBoost. Subcommittees in MultiBoost can be learned in parallel, unlike AdaBoost's inherently sequential process. While AdaBoost minimizes potential for parallel computation due to its sequential nature, each classifier learned with wagging is independent, enabling parallel computation—a trait inherited by MultiBoost at the subcommittee level   . snippets: Finally, in    visual analytic tools are presented to support a specialist user in interpreting the behaviour of an ensemble of classifiers and its underlying models. 2.2 Selecting the members of the ensemble A key point in the design of an ensemble of classifiers is the generation of the pool of classifiers that make up the ensemble. As was noted before, a necessary condition to obtain an accurate ensemble is that the base learners are both accurate and diverse. Although most of the proposed models ensure diversity among base classifiers in an implicit way   , there are some research works where diversity plays a key role in the design of the ensemble. In    a method for generating ensembles of classifiers that emphasizes diversity among the ensemble members is proposed. In that research, the experimental results prove that accuracy of those ensembles based on diversity is higher than those ensembles based on the error rate. However, unlike our approach, the diversity in that study derives from using different feature subsets. In   , it is described an approach in which the members of the ensemble are selected based not only on the accuracy but also on diversity. For that purpose, the authors use a Multi Objective Evolutionary Algorithm in which the base learners are generated using  Bagging  and manipulating the input features. snippets: 20.2.2 When and why bagging works The success of bagging depends on its base learning algorithm being  unstable , where unstable means that a small change in the training sample can result in a large change in the predictions given by the resulting base model. It has been shown that bagging is able to improve the performance of good but unstable base learning algorithms. On the other hand, bagging could even slightly degrade the performance of stable base learning algorithms [ 46 ]. It has been pointed out that classification and RTs, neural networks, and subset selection in linear regression are typically unstable, whereas  k -nearest neighbor is stable [ 46 ,  47 ]. The reason why bagging needs good but unstable base learning algorithms is related to accuracy and diversity ( Section 20.1 ). If a stable base learning algorithm is used, then the predictions given by different base models created with different bootstrap samples of the training set will be very similar. A good but unstable base learning algorithm will create accurate but diverse base models, making bagging successful. In terms of the ambiguity decomposition explained in  Section 20.1.2 , good but unstable base learning algorithms would increase the ambiguity term, helping to reduce the error of the ensemble. Even if each of the base models is slightly less accurate than a single model trained on the whole training set, the reduction of the error caused by the ambiguity term would compensate for that. On the other hand, bagging using a stable base learning algorithm would not get its error reduced because the ambiguity term would be very small—in the extreme case, zero. At the same time, its base models may be slightly less accurate than single models trained on the whole data set would be. So, the error of the bagging ensemble could be slightly worse than single models trained on the  whole  training set if its base learners are stable. 20.2.3 Potential advantages of bagging for SEE Bagging is a simple and well-known ensemble learning approach that has three main features that make it potentially beneficial for SEE: (1) several ready implementations of bagging can be easily found on the Web, (2) it does not require extensive human participation in the process of building ensembles, and (3) it has theoretically and empirically shown to improve performance in comparison to the base learning algorithm provided that its base learning algorithm is unstable enough [ 46 ].

snippets: Indeed, these algorithms aim to provide higher accuracy in the minority class. To this end, the techniques such as cost-sensitive learning   , threshold-based methods ( e.g.,  threshold-moving)   , and one-class classification    have been proposed. 5.3 Stability–plasticity dilemma Another well-known challenge for OL algorithms is the  stability–plasticity dilemma     . More specifically, the stability–plasticity dilemma refers to the situation in which the learner should make a trade-off between plasticity—the incorporation of new instances—and stability—trying not to forget the previously learned knowledge. If the learner increases its plasticity, it might forget the previously learned knowledge. On the other hand, if the learner increases its stability, it might decrease the reactivity of the learner. The stability–plasticity dilemma is a serious problem in noisy environments, such as IIoT systems, where concept drift is most likely to occur. OL algorithms that are specially designed for dealing with concept drift may provide a solution to this dilemma only during a specific period of time when concept drift happens. The situation will be much worse for OL algorithms that are not equipped with mechanisms to handle concept drift due to catastrophic forgetting   . 5.4 Model complexity estimation The  model complexity estimation  is another frequently mentioned challenge in OL. The model complexity of an algorithm is often measured by the number of parameters ( e.g.,  window size and number of hidden nodes) needed for the representation. This is mainly due to the fact that algorithms may be written in different programming languages, and also these algorithms may differ in efficiency   . In OL, model complexity should be considered as a variable measure due to the fact that it is extraordinarily difficult to provide an estimation of the model complexity in advance of the availability of all data. Since the incoming data of OL algorithms is unknown, the model complexity may increase, if a concept drift happens. When one uses OL algorithms in resource-constrained environments, such as IoT systems, intelligent resources reallocation should be considered as the degree of model complexity is limited by the available restricted resources. From all challenges considered, the concept drift and the imbalance of the classes are the most critical challenges in OL. Hence, in the next section, we discuss these challenges in greater detail.

concept: Feature selection is crucial in high-dimensional data classification, especially in imbalanced scenarios where minority class samples may be overlooked. Effective feature selection can enhance classifier performance by identifying relevant features while discarding irrelevant ones.

There are various methods for feature selection, including filter, wrapper, and embedded methods, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. Filter methods rank features based on metrics, while wrapper methods evaluate subsets through model training, and embedded methods integrate feature selection within the model training process.

Feature extraction, distinct from feature selection, involves creating new features from existing ones to reduce dimensionality. Techniques like PCA and SVD are commonly used for this purpose, particularly with unstructured data.

Recent advancements in feature selection have focused on using data complexity measures and meta-learning frameworks to improve the selection process, especially in imbalanced datasets. These approaches aim to enhance class separability and optimize feature selection algorithms.

Algorithm adaptation strategies are being developed to modify existing classification algorithms for multi-label problems, allowing for more effective handling of complex data structures without prior transformation steps.

The need for adaptive forecasting models in applications like wind energy is highlighted, emphasizing the importance of self-adaptive parameters and transfer learning to improve model universality and interpretability.

The review indicates a preference for using publicly accessible datasets in research, while also recognizing the potential of synthetic data and data fusion techniques to enhance model training and evaluation.

snippets: Under imbalanced scenarios, minority class samples can easily be discarded as noise; however, if the irrelevant features in the feature space are removed, this risk is reduced ( Li et al., 2016c ). The goal of feature selection, in general, is to select a subset of k features from the entire feature space that allows a classifier to achieve optimal performance, where k is a user-specified or adaptively selected parameter. Feature selection can be divided into filters, wrappers, and embedded methods ( Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003 ). The advantages and disadvantages of these methods can be found in  Saeys et al. (2007) . Another way to deal with dimensionality is feature extraction. Feature extraction is related to dimensionality reduction, which transforms data into a low-dimensional space. It should be noted, however, that feature selection techniques are different from feature extraction. Feature extraction creates new features from the original features using functional mapping, whereas feature selection returns a subset of the original features ( Motoda and Liu, 2002 ). There are a variety of techniques for feature extraction, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and f Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) (see  Hartmann, 2004 ). Feature extraction methods tend to be employed more frequently for unstructured data such as images, text and speech. Table 2  shows 31 reviewed articles employed feature selection or feature extraction. It was found that filter and wrapper feature selection methods were most regularly used. For filter methods, various metrics were used to rank the features, and for wrapper methods, heuristic search was a common choice.

snippets: 4.2.2 Feature selection Feature Selection is an important preprocessing step when handling high-dimensional data in every standard classification domain, given that a large number of features can be problematic for some classifiers   . In imbalanced and overlapped domains, it becomes a more strenuous task since it is more difficult to discriminate certain concepts in data and consequently determine the features that increase class separability. Past work has already discerned on the challenges of feature selection in imbalanced domains   , whereas the use of complexity measures for the recommendation of feature selection methods has become a hot topic in the last couple of years. Okimoto et al.    show the suitability of using data complexity measures for univariate feature selection, where F1, F3 and N1 were successful in selecting the most relevant features. F1, associated with class separability was the most effective. In a later work, F1 is coupled with N2 to produce a univariate–multivariate feature selection approach   , combining both feature-based and neighbourhood-based information. Parmezan et al.    proposed a new framework for the recommendation of feature selection algorithms based on meta-learning, considering both the characteristics of the feature selection methods and the intrinsic characteristics of the datasets. Information theoretic and complexity meta-features have shown promising results in the characterisation of datasets   . In particular, the ratio signal/noise, dispersion of the data set and average mutual information between classes and attributes were frequently selected as decision nodes in the meta-models. Similarly, F2 was also present in the all the constructed meta-models. Seijo-Pardo et al.    use a combination of feature overlap measures (F1, F2, F3) to guide the definition of thresholds regarding a suitable number of features to keep by feature selection methods. Dong and Khosla    show that the performance of feature selection methods is correlated with N3. A few emergent approaches have attempted to handle class imbalance and overlap in synergy. Fernández et al. propose a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm to handle class imbalance and overlap   . Both feature and instance selection are considered while evolving solutions, to simultaneously compensate for the class distributions, remove complicated examples, and remove features with high overlap degrees.

snippets: To perform feature selection requires that data contain redundant or irrelevant features, so as to avoid excessive information loss. Feature selection can be accomplished in several ways. • Manual selection. Whether to remove a feature is manually determined. See, for example,  Zhang et al. (2018) . • Exhaustive search. To test every possible subset of features to find the subset with the lowest error rate can be computationally intensive ( Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003 ). • Embedded method. Feature selection is performed during model construction. The Bolasso algorithm ( Bach, 2008 ) reduces many regression coefficients to zero by constructing a linear model and combining the L1 penalty with the L2 penalty of ridge regression. FeaLect ( Zare et al., 2013 ) scores and selects features based on the combinatorial analysis of regression coefficients. • Wrapper approach. A prediction model is trained with each subset and tested on a holdout set. The score of a subset is obtained from the error rate of the model test. This is computationally intensive, and usually used only to find the best subset of features. • Filtering method. Methods such as mutual information ( Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003 ), Pearson correlation coefficients, and significance scores, such as inter- or intra-class distances ( Yang and Pedersen, 1997 ), can be used to score a subset of features, which can rank features but does not produce the best subset. e ) Feature extraction Unlike feature selection ( Sarangi et al., 2020 ), feature extraction, i.e., the creation of new features to facilitate learning, is considered a key factor in building a model. This can be performed by the following algorithms. • Principal Component Analysis (PCA). One of the most used linear dimensionality reduction methods, PCA changes the basis of data according to principal components, which are essentially eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix. De la Hoz et al. (2015) , used PCA for feature extraction, while  Xiao et al. (2019)  combined PCA with autoencoders to compress high-dimensional features for input to CNNs. Variants include probability PCA (PPCA), which utilizes probability distributions; kernel PCA, which uses kernel functions to map low-dimensional spaces to high-dimensional spaces before using PCA to reduce the dimensions; and independent component analysis (ICA), which requires no hidden variables to obey Gaussian distributions.

snippets: Algorithm Adaptation Methods Algorithm Adaptation is a strategy that involves the direct modification or refinement of widely-used single-label multi-class algorithms to address multi-label problems effectively. Classification algorithms are adapted, i.e., adjusted in such a way they can be applied directly to multi-label data, and no prior problem transformation step is actually required. Popular adapted algorithms are Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbors, Multi-Label Decision Trees, and Multi-Label Support Vector Machines. More complex methods have also been proposed and built on top of other models for multi-class classification, including Neural Networks. Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbors The Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbor (ML-KNN) algorithm, proposed in  Zhang and Zhou (2007) , is a multi-label extension of the popular KNN algorithm. The KNN model is a lazy learning algorithm in which there is no explicit training phase, as generalization of the training data takes place directly at test time. The ML-KNN algorithm starts by identifying, in the training set, the  k  nearest neighbors of each new test instance under exam. Once the  k  neighbors have been selected, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) rule returns the label subset associated with the test instance based on the label subsets of the neighboring training samples. Considering a training set  D  and the label space  L , for an unseen test instance  x , the ML-KNN algorithm works as follows. It first defines the training set  D x k  of the  k  nearest neighbors of  x  in  D . Euclidean and Manhattan distances are commonly used to measure the distance between instances. Other popular measures frequently employed in bioinformatics and computational biology applications are Pearson correlation, cosine similarity, and other correlation-based distances. The algorithm then calculates the membership counting vector  C x  based on the label subsets of all training samples in  D x k . Each element  C x ( l j ) , with  l j ∈ L , represents the count of neighbors of  x  being associated with the label  l j .

concept: Resampling techniques are essential for addressing imbalanced data classification, focusing on improving sample distribution through undersampling, oversampling, or hybrid methods.
Undersampling techniques, while effective in reducing training time, risk discarding valuable information from majority class samples, potentially harming classifier performance.

Various undersampling methods, such as Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) and Tomek Links, attempt to refine the selection of majority class samples but have limitations in handling noise and class imbalances.

Oversampling techniques, like random oversampling and SMOTE, aim to enhance minority class representation without losing majority class information, though they may lead to overfitting and noise amplification.
Hybrid sampling techniques combine the strengths of both undersampling and oversampling to mitigate their individual drawbacks, but they can be complex and challenging to implement effectively.

Each method has specific limitations, including difficulties in addressing noise, multi-class imbalances, and time series data, necessitating careful selection and application of techniques based on the dataset characteristics.

snippets: 3.1 Resampling techniques When addressing the issue of imbalanced data classification, one of the most widely used methods in data preprocessing is resampling techniques ( Fan et al., 2021 ). Resampling methods aim to improve the distribution of samples by either replicating or synthesizing minority class samples, or by removing majority class samples. The advantage of resampling techniques is that they do not alter the structure of subsequent classifiers and can be applied independently before the learning and training of classification algorithms ( Xing et al., 2022 ). Resampling techniques can be broadly categorized into three types: undersampling techniques, oversampling techniques, and hybrid sampling techniques. 3.1.1 Undersampling technique Undersampling techniques aim to maintain the minority class samples while extracting a subset of majority class samples based on certain rules to achieve class balance. Random undersampling is the simplest undersampling technique, which balances the dataset by randomly removing majority class samples. Although this method is straightforward and can effectively reduce training time, it runs the risk of discarding important information contained in the majority class samples, leading to a decrease in classifier performance. To address the limitations of random undersampling ( Tahir et al., 2012 ), researchers have made improvements to the deletion criteria. Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) ( Wilson, 1972 ) removes majority class samples by examining the distribution of nearest neighbors from the majority class. If a majority class sample has a predominantly different class in its neighborhood, it is removed. However, ENN has a limited capability to eliminate majority class samples and may not fundamentally address the issue of data imbalance. The Neighborhood Cleaning Rule (NCL) ( Agustianto and Destarianto, 2019 ), based on ENN, considers the distribution of minority class neighbors to remove more majority class samples. This method not only removes noisy majority samples around the minority class but also eliminates noisy majority class samples around the minority class. The Tomek-Links undersampling method ( Xu et al., 2020 ) identifies Tomek Links pairs (if the Euclidean distance between samples a and b from different classes is smaller than the distance between any two samples from the same class, the pair (a,b) is considered a Tomek Links pair) between samples of different classes and removes majority class samples. However, the Tomek-Links algorithm only considers the nearest boundary instances between global samples and ignores potential local overlapping instances.

snippets: Although undersampling techniques can alleviate the imbalance characteristics of a dataset to some extent and have low algorithmic complexity, they have several limitations when addressing noise, between-class and within-class imbalance, multi-class imbalance, and time series imbalance issues: (1) Noise problem:  Undersampling methods may face difficulties in addressing noise. Noise instances are often outliers or mislabeled samples within the minority class. Undersampling may struggle to accurately differentiate between noise and normal samples. Removing noise instances may result in the loss of useful information from normal samples, leading to a decline in model performance. (2) between-class and within-class imbalance problem:  Undersampling methods may have limited effectiveness in handling between-class and within-class imbalance issues. Undersampling typically operates based on the number of samples per class and may not fully address imbalances within each class. If there are uneven or overlapping sample distributions within classes, undersampling may not adequately consider these characteristics, posing challenges in handling within-class imbalance. (3) Multi-class imbalance problem:  Undersampling methods may face difficulties in addressing multi-class imbalance. Multi-class imbalance problems involve imbalances between multiple classes, with some classes having fewer instances. Undersampling may struggle to effectively handle multiple minority or majority classes, and removing majority class samples may further imbalance the dataset. (4) Time series imbalance problem:  Undersampling methods may have limitations in dealing with time series imbalance. Time series data has temporal dependency and continuity, requiring consideration of the temporal order of samples during undersampling. Traditional undersampling methods may not effectively preserve important information and patterns in the time series. 3.1.2 Oversampling techniques Oversampling techniques aim to improve classification performance by increasing the number of instances in the minority class according to certain rules. Unlike undersampling techniques, oversampling does not involve the removal of a large number of samples that may contain important information. The simplest oversampling technique is random oversampling ( Mohammed et al., 2020 ), which randomly duplicates instances from the minority class to match the number of instances in the majority class. However, this random duplication approach can lead to overfitting ( Huang et al., 2020 ) and does not provide additional useful information.

snippets: 3 A review of imbalanced data classification methods Real-world data often exhibits imbalanced characteristics, where the sample sizes of certain classes are significantly smaller than others. Consequently, designing classification methods that ensure accuracy for both majority and minority classes has become a research focus in fields such as data mining and artificial intelligence. This has led to the emergence of numerous methods for addressing imbalanced classification, as depicted in  Fig. 7 . These methods primarily focus on three levels: data preprocessing ( Lin et al., 2018 ), feature extraction ( Maldonado et al., 2014a ), and classifier improvement ( Batuwita and Palade, 2010 ). In this section, we review and analyze these methods and their applications in imbalanced classification in industrial settings. Additionally, we provide a brief overview of a novel classification method called Generating Adversarial Networks (GANs), which addresses imbalanced data. 3.1 Resampling techniques When addressing the issue of imbalanced data classification, one of the most widely used methods in data preprocessing is resampling techniques ( Fan et al., 2021 ). Resampling methods aim to improve the distribution of samples by either replicating or synthesizing minority class samples, or by removing majority class samples. The advantage of resampling techniques is that they do not alter the structure of subsequent classifiers and can be applied independently before the learning and training of classification algorithms ( Xing et al., 2022 ). Resampling techniques can be broadly categorized into three types: undersampling techniques, oversampling techniques, and hybrid sampling techniques. 3.1.1 Undersampling technique Undersampling techniques aim to maintain the minority class samples while extracting a subset of majority class samples based on certain rules to achieve class balance. Random undersampling is the simplest undersampling technique, which balances the dataset by randomly removing majority class samples. Although this method is straightforward and can effectively reduce training time, it runs the risk of discarding important information contained in the majority class samples, leading to a decrease in classifier performance. To address the limitations of random undersampling ( Tahir et al., 2012 ), researchers have made improvements to the deletion criteria. Edited Nearest Neighbor (ENN) ( Wilson, 1972 ) removes majority class samples by examining the distribution of nearest neighbors from the majority class. If a majority class sample has a predominantly different class in its neighborhood, it is removed.

snippets: Oversampling methods increase the quantity of minority class samples, effectively addressing issues such as noise, between-class and within-class imbalances, multi-class imbalances, time series imbalances, and class overlap, thereby improving the classifier's ability to recognize the minority class. However, oversampling methods also have certain drawbacks and limitations. For instance, they may lead to overfitting, increase computational costs and time expenses, and introduce redundant information and noisy samples. Therefore, when applying oversampling methods, it is important to carefully select appropriate algorithms and parameter settings to balance the increase in sample quantity with maintaining the accuracy of data features. 3.1.3 Hybrid sampling technique Both undersampling and oversampling techniques have certain disadvantages and advantages. In order to achieve better sampling results, many researchers combine oversampling and undersampling techniques, i.e., hybrid resampling ( Zhang et al., 2021 ). 3.1.3.1 For the noise effect problem Batista et al. ( Batista et al. ) proposed a hybrid sampling technique called SMOTE-Tome Link, which combines SMOTE with Tome Link and demonstrates improved handling of noise issues compared to standard SMOTE. Tao et al. (2011)  introduced a hybrid sampling technique called ODR-BSMOTE, which combines ODR (Optimization-Driven Undersampling) with BSMOTE oversampling. ODR-BSMOTE first eliminates a significant amount of redundant and noisy samples using ODR to preserve more useful feature information. Subsequently, BSMOTE is applied to synthetically generate new samples only at the boundary to balance the dataset. However, due to the complexity of data distribution, it can be challenging to accurately identify real noise instances. Therefore,  Zhang et al. (2022a)  proposed a hybrid resampling method based on SMOTE and reverse k-nearest neighbors (SMOTE-RKnn). SMOTE-RKnn utilizes the RkNN method to provide probability density information for each instance, and then identifies and removes noise instances based on the density information. However, this approach only works well for binary class imbalance problems and is not effective for multi-class imbalance issues. 3.1.3.2 For the between-class and within-class problems Song et al. ( Song et al. ) proposed a bi-directional sampling method based on the K-means algorithm.

snippets: (4) Time series imbalance problem:  Undersampling methods may have limitations in dealing with time series imbalance. Time series data has temporal dependency and continuity, requiring consideration of the temporal order of samples during undersampling. Traditional undersampling methods may not effectively preserve important information and patterns in the time series. 3.1.2 Oversampling techniques Oversampling techniques aim to improve classification performance by increasing the number of instances in the minority class according to certain rules. Unlike undersampling techniques, oversampling does not involve the removal of a large number of samples that may contain important information. The simplest oversampling technique is random oversampling ( Mohammed et al., 2020 ), which randomly duplicates instances from the minority class to match the number of instances in the majority class. However, this random duplication approach can lead to overfitting ( Huang et al., 2020 ) and does not provide additional useful information. To address this,  Chawla et al. (2002)  proposed a synthetic minority oversampling technique known as SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique). SMOTE synthesizes new instances in the minority class by using interpolation within the k-nearest neighbor region of a minority sample. As shown in  Fig. 8 , SMOTE first selects a sample ( x ) from the minority class. Then, it randomly selects another sample ( y ) from the k-nearest neighbor set of the same class. Finally, it generates a new instance ( g ) by applying linear interpolation using Equation  (1) . (1) g = x + ( y − x ) × α , α ∈ [ 0,1 ] The SMOTE technique generates new instances that are different from the original data, which mitigates the overfitting issue of random oversampling. However, the  k -NN interpolation approach to synthesizing new samples may introduce the following problems ( Su et al., 2023 ): (1) Noise amplification:  When noise is chosen as an interpolation object, the synthesized sample may also be a noise sample, which can amplify the effect of noise. (2) Increased class overlap:  Interpolating in the class overlap area may exacerbate the problem of class overlap, leading to a decrease in classification accuracy of the classifier and the problem of overgeneralization.

concept: Borderline-SMOTE is effective for various applications, including debris flow susceptibility assessment, bankruptcy prediction, and protein residue analysis, demonstrating its versatility in enhancing classification accuracy.

Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) improves upon traditional SMOTE by generating synthetic samples based on the difficulty of learning from minority class samples, thus addressing class imbalance more effectively.
Random sampling methods, while simple, can lead to overfitting and information loss, highlighting the need for more sophisticated techniques in imbalanced datasets.
Hybrid methods that combine oversampling and undersampling techniques, such as SMOTE-Tomek and ODR-BSMOTE, show promise in addressing noise and improving classification performance.
Ensemble learning techniques, like RUSBoost, enhance classification accuracy by integrating multiple classifiers, but the optimal balance of sampling methods remains a challenge.

The exploration of hybrid sampling techniques, such as FCMSMT and bi-directional sampling, indicates a growing trend towards more nuanced approaches to tackle both between-class and within-class imbalances.
Overall, the integration of various data manipulation techniques, including adaptive methods and hybrid strategies, is crucial for improving model performance in the face of class imbalance.

snippets: In terms of applications,  Li et al. (2021)  used borderline-SMOTE for susceptibility assessment of debris flow, and found that using borderline SMOTE resulted in high accuracy of the susceptibility map. Smiti and Soui (2020)  presented an approach combining borderline SMOTE and stacked autoencoder based on the softmax classifier for bankruptcy prediction. Ning, Zhao, and Ma (2021)  used borderline SMOTE with  Tomek Links  for the detection of glutarylation sites on protein residues. Tomek Links ( Tomek, 1976 ) is a modification from the  condensed nearest neighbour  undersampling technique. 3.2 Other data augmentation methods 3.2.1 Adaptive synthetic sampling Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) ( He, Bai, Garcia, & Li, 2008 ) adaptively generates minority data samples according to their distributions. In ADASYN, more synthetic data is generated for minority class samples that are harder to learn when compared to the minority samples that are easier to learn. This means that the bias introduced by class imbalance is reduced, and the decision boundary of the classifier has shifted towards the more difficult training examples. ADASYN has been used to address the CI problems in areas such as recreational water quality modelling ( Xu, Coco and Neale, 2020 ), warning systems for harmful algae blooms ( Kim et al., 2021 ) and design of wireless intrusion detection systems ( Hu, Wang, Qi, Li, & Yang, 2020 ). 3.2.2 Random sampling methods Random over-sampling  (ROS) ( Moreo, Esuli, & Sebastiani, 2016 ) and  random under-sampling  (RUS) ( Hasanin & Khoshgoftaar, 2018; Mohammed, Rawashdeh, & Abdullah, 2020 ) are naive approaches to combat imbalanced dataset in order to balance the class distribution. These are defined as naive techniques, as they simply duplicate the training samples. Random oversampling duplicates the samples from the minority class, while random undersampling deletes training samples from the majority class. However, these techniques often run into problems of overfitting when used with conventional machine learning models ( Mohammed et al., 2020 ). In terms of applications, ROS has been used for malware detection ( Pang et al., 2019 ) and finite element methods ( Calo, Efendiev, Galvis, & Li, 2016 ).

snippets: 5 Summary of results 5.1 Most used data manipulation algorithms In  Table 8 , we report the seven DM algorithms, among the 37 found, that are most applied in manufacturing and we summarize them in the following subsections. The criterion for this selection is that the algorithm is applied at least in two of the reviewed articles. 5.1.1 Adaptive synthetic sampling Adaptive synthetic sampling (ADASYN)    is an extension of SMOTE, an oversampling technique. It aims to balance the class distribution in imbalanced datasets by generating synthetic samples of the minority class. In regard to that, ADASYN uses a density-based approach to oversampling, which means that it generates more synthetic samples around the hard-to-classify samples, which are closer to the decision boundary and therefore more likely to be misclassified. This helps to improve the classification performance of the model on imbalanced datasets by increasing the diversity of the minority class samples and reducing the overfitting to the majority class. 5.1.2 Image resampling Image resampling (IRS) is a form of data manipulation applicable to pre-processing of image data. To the best of our knowledge, there is no scientific article that classifies all the possible methods, thus we listed the major findings from the articles reviewed. In particular, Saqlain et al.    (see Article 8 in  Table 6 ) performed random rotation of 10-degree, horizontal flipping, width shift, height shift, shearing range, channel shifting, and zooming on the input images; Park et al.    (see Article 11 in  Table 6 ) randomly transformed and distorted raw image samples before feeding them to a CNN; Liang et al.    (see Article 23 in  Table 6 ) applied region translation, random patch cropping, small angle image rotation, horizontal flipping, random contrast change, random brightness change and image resizing. The goal in IRS is to augment the number of images containing variations of the important features. The advantage is that images contain a good amount of information that can be easily manipulated to generate new perspectives of the same features. 5.1.3 Random oversampling Random oversampling (ROS)    is a technique used in imbalanced data classification problems, where a minority class has fewer instances compared to the majority class. The method increases the number of samples in the minority class by randomly replicating instances from it.

snippets: A balanced dataset usually provides better overall classification performance ( Estabrooks et al., 2004; Weiss and Provost, 2001 ), and to obtain the same proportion of positive and negative examples is the most common imbalanced learning method. The simplest method, to undersample the majority class, obviously leads to information loss. Liu et al. (2008)  introduced the EasyEnsemble and BalanceCascade algorithms, combining a subset of majority classes with minority classes and performing ensemble learning on the classifiers. NearMiss uses a KNN classifier to select the majority class with the smallest average distance from the minority class ( Mani and Zhang, 2003 ). Oversampling of minority examples is usually accomplished by synthetic sampling. The synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) synthesizes data based on feature space similarity between minority examples ( Chawla et al., 2002 ). Modified and extended sampling algorithms ( Fernández et al., 2018 ) have been proposed to address the problem of over-generalization in SMOTE ( Wang and Japkowicz, 2004 ). The adaptive integrated sampling method (ADASYN) ( He et al., 2008 ) adaptively creates synthetic data based on the distribution of minority examples and solves the problem of overlapping between classes. • Cost-sensitive approach. This approach considers the costs associated with misclassification and uses a different cost matrix to describe them when misclassifying data ( Ting, 2002 ). It has been shown to be a viable alternative to sampling methods ( McCarthy et al., 2005 ). • Additional methods. Many algorithms obtain good performance from other perspectives. Based on kernel methods as well as active learning, Ertekin et al. proposed an SVM-based active learning method ( Ertekin et al., 2007 ) that restricts the query process in each iteration of active learning to the data pool rather than the entire dataset. The SVM is trained during this process, and the most informative instances are extracted from the hyperplane to form a new training set. One-class learning uses mainly or only single-class samples for recognition, distinguishing it from traditional distinction-based induction, with good results with extremely unbalanced data (especially high feature space dimensions) ( Raskutti and Kowalczyk, 2004 ). c ) Data conversion Training data must often be transformed and mapped before being fed to the model to accommodate requirements, and to improve detection speed and accuracy. This affects two types of data in IDS datasets.

snippets: 4.3 Hybrid methods A hybrid technique for tackling class imbalance is consists of a couple of methods, which can be used for dealing with imbalance issues or applied several approaches for a particular part of the general solution. These techniques have a burden on the confidence that the variations in the methods rightly complement each other. Hybrid techniques mix strategies of various types and attempt to get the advantage of their best characteristics. The main disadvantages of these approaches are: (1) Perfectly balanced data may not be optimal, (2) It is difficult to determine the appropriate number of over/under-sample to utilize in this system. 4.3.1 Hybrid methods for classification (i) Re-sampling with learning methods:  The ensemble of classifiers in machine learning is well-known to improve the accuracy of individual classifiers by mixing some of them. But none of those learning methods cannot lonely fix the class imbalance issue. To deal with that issue, we need to design ensemble learning algorithms   . The initial hybrid techniques were proposed by   . The motivation for those papers is to describe that which classifier is mixed. Also, in which way we can mix them. The mixture-of-experts method assumes that mixing several re-sampling techniques with the mixing of the expert framework is an effective presentation in the tuning problem   . A new hybrid technique is a combination of boosting and data sampling, which is named RUSBoost   . This technique tackles two overall kinds of re-sampling techniques: (1) Over-sample the minority samples to achieve a size almost similar to the majority samples, (2) Under-sample the majority instance to achieve a size almost similar to the minority samples. They proposed a technique for mixing several classifiers that is under and over-sample the dataset at various rates in a combination of a professional’s framework. The authors claimed, it was unknown that under-sampling was more efficient than over-sampling and which rate of under-sampling or over-sampling should be studied. An ensemble learning technique on multi-class imbalance sample sets is proposed in   . This technique produces one-versus-others classifiers that can learn over multi-class samples under the skewed normal distribution of the training samples. Another ensemble learning technique is ensemble knowledge for imbalance sample sets (eKISS), which mixes the rules of the basic classifiers to produce new classifiers for the last decision-making.

concept: Data augmentation is crucial for improving machine learning model performance, especially in cases of class imbalance, by synthetically increasing the dataset size through techniques like SMOTE.

Test-time augmentation methods enhance model robustness and uncertainty estimation by generating multiple predictions from augmented test data, leading to improved accuracy and reliability in predictions.
Knowledge distillation simplifies the model training process by transferring knowledge from multiple teacher models to a single student model, enhancing computational efficiency.
Self-supervised learning approaches in robotics can reduce reliance on manual annotations and improve sample efficiency, although challenges remain in dealing with noisy real-world data.

Transfer learning has shown promise in applying machine learning techniques to complex problems in physics, such as fluid turbulence, demonstrating the versatility of these methods across different domains.

Problem transformation methods, particularly Binary Relevance, allow for the decomposition of multi-label problems into simpler binary classification tasks, though they may overlook label correlations, which can affect performance.

snippets: 3 Data augmentation for CI problems If the dataset for training the machine learning model is sufficiently balanced, the model performs better and more accurately. Data augmentation has the potential to improve the model performance of such models ( Van Dyk & Meng, 2001 ). Data augmentation provides a set of techniques to synthetically increase the amount of data by generating new data points from existing data to address imbalance in classes. A simple strategy to artificially generate data would require minor alterations such as flip, transformation, or rotations in the case of image data. Data augmentation methods have been prominent for image data in deep learning ( Shorten & Khoshgoftaar, 2019 ) and graph-based data ( Ding, Xu, Tong and Liu, 2022 ). It has also been used for natural language processing problems ( Feng et al., 2021; Li, Hou and Che, 2022 ) such as text classification ( Bayer et al., 2022 ). Data augmentation methods have also been used for time series ( Wen et al., 2020 ) and tabular datasets for a wide range of applications. 3.1 SMOTE-based methods The focus of this paper is the CI problem and the combination of data augmentation and ensemble learning for tabular datasets. The most prominent approach in using data augmentation for CI datasets is generating examples in the minority class using  synthetic minority oversampling technique  (SMOTE) ( Chawla, Bowyer, Hall, & Kegelmeyer, 2002 ) that uses the  k-nearest neighbour  (KNN) model ( Cover & Hart, 1967 ). SMOTE generates synthetic examples in a less application-specific manner, by operating in “feature space” rather than “data space”. We can increase the minority class by taking each minority class sample and introducing synthetic examples along the line segments joining any or all of the nearest neighbours of the minority class. We can choose neighbours for KNN depending on the amount of oversampling required. Although SMOTE was developed for classification problems, it can also be extended to regression problems ( Torgo, Ribeiro, Pfahringer, & Branco, 2013 ). SMOTE has made an impact in various domains over the decade with a diverse set of applications ( Fernández, Garcia, Herrera, & Chawla, 2018 ).

snippets: 3.2.4 Related works based on test-time augmentation methods Test-time data augmentation methods involve predicting and quantifying uncertainty at inference based on multiple predictions generated from various augmentations of the primary input data. Typically, multiple test data are created from each input data by applying data augmentation methods; then, the entire set of test data is used to calculate the predictive distribution for the estimation of uncertainty [ 4 ]. Greedy policy search [ 190 ] is an example of an augmentation policy where each stage of the search selects a sub-policy that provides the most significant improvement in the ensemble predictions, which is added to the existing policy. These methods can improve model robustness and generalization by generating a diverse set of augmented data for testing and prediction. In their study, Wang et al., [ 191 ] introduced a unique approach by using a CNN model with a bounding box for the segmentation of fetal and brain tumor images. They further explored scribble-based segmentation and image-specific fine-tuning during testing. The authors concluded that the proposed fine-tuning technique significantly improved segmentation accuracy while reducing user time and interactions required for the process. Ayhan et al., [ 192 ] developed a CNN model and incorporated a conventional geometric and color transformation technique as an uncertainty measure during testing on fundus images. The aim was to analyze the variations in the network's output. Based on their findings, the authors reported that their test-time augmentation approach provides valuable approximations for predicting uncertainties in deep models. Wang et al. [ 193 ] investigated aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties by incorporating test-time augmentation and test-time dropout methods into their CNN model. The authors' analysis revealed that the aleatoric uncertainty estimation technique yielded superior advantages compared to the test-time dropout technique. Specifically, it effectively mitigated the issue of overconfident predictions, resulting in more accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates. Zhang et al. [ 194 ] introduced a novel method for MRI reconstruction, where measurements are dynamically selected, and the prediction is iteratively refined during inference to achieve optimal reconstruction. The authors found that this technique effectively reduces reconstruction uncertainty in the resulting images. Athanasiadis et al., [ 195 ] developed a generative adversarial network to explore the relationship between visual and audio emotional expressions. They employed conformal prediction to obtain calibration error and confidence values during testing.

snippets: Problem Transformation Methods Learning algorithms belonging to the Problem Transformation category decompose the multi-label problem into multiple single-label problems. Any single-label classification algorithm can be used as a base learner, such as logistic regression, support vector machines (SVMs), or decision trees. Single-label sub-problems are solved as binary classification tasks. If such binary tasks learn how to assign a label independently from all the others, the adopted strategy is called Binary Relevance (BR). Yet, the decomposition approach into binary tasks can be further modified as in Calibrated Label Ranking and in Classifier Chains to also account for second-order and high-order relations among labels. The Problem Transformation paradigm also includes the Label Powerset strategy, which transforms the multi-label problem into a multi-class problem considering as a class any different combination of labels, and the Ensemble methods, which turn the multi-label problem into an ensemble of multi-class classification problems. Binary Relevance Binary Relevance ( Boutell  et al ., 2004 ) is a MLC method that trains a separate binary classifier for each label such that each classifier then predicts whether the instance belongs to the corresponding class under exam or not. The method trains  q  binary classifiers  C 1 , … , C q , where each classifier  C j  predicts the  0 / 1  association for the corresponding label  l j ∈ L . This implies that all training instances are used in the learning process: the training instance ( x i ,  y i ) is considered a positive sample for each relevant label  l j ∈ y i  and a negative instance for each irrelevant, not assigned label  l k ∉ y i . The Binary Relevance method is a first-order strategy; therefore, it ignores correlations among labels. The label independence assumptions might result in information loss and low performance if labels are correlated, with the Binary Relevance model predicting either too few or too many labels for new instances, or even combinations of labels that do not actually occur. However, there are also scenarios in which this assumption can be advantageous. Binary Relevance is quite suitable when test data, as well as the corresponding label combinations, might be different from those used for training or when the label space changes dynamically, as for online learning applications. The wide use of Binary Relevance relies on the simplicity of the algorithm itself: it is straightforward and generally has low computational complexity. The algorithm scales linearly with the size of the label space  L , also allowing for parallel implementation since the binary problems are independent and separate.

snippets: 3.4 Classification, optimization, and performance evaluation Machine learning (ML) algorithms have demonstrated their utility across a wide spectrum of applications, including but not limited to email filtering, computer vision, speech recognition, and medicine. These applications often involve tasks for which designing conventional algorithms is impractical or unfeasible [ 69 ]. ML techniques are increasingly at the forefront of data mining, enabling the recognition of historical trends and the development of predictive models for the future. Deep learning (DL), a subset of ML, is characterized by artificial neural networks that learn from vast volumes of data [ 70 ]. DL algorithms are particularly well-suited for addressing intricate problems where datasets are diverse, unstructured, and interlinked. It is worth noting that DL algorithms tend to excel as they encounter more data, continually improving their performance [ 71 ]. Several types of DL algorithms have been developed, with notable examples being Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). CNN algorithms are specifically designed for tasks such as object detection and image processing. The core feature of CNNs is convolution, a unique filtering process that systematically assesses each element within an image to extract meaningful patterns and features [ 72 ]. RNNs are equipped with built-in feedback loops that enable them to retain memory of past data points. This ability to remember and reference historical data enables RNNs to enhance their comprehension of current events and sequences, making them highly effective in tasks that involve sequential data. 3.4.1 Machine learning classifiers In the realm of classification, a variety of classifiers are available, ranging from simpler models to more complex ensemble techniques. Simple classifiers encompass methods such  as Naive Bayes, Decision Trees, Logistic Regression, and K-Nearest Neighbor [ 73 ]. In contrast, ensemble classifiers refer to algorithms that consolidate predictions from two or more individual models. The appeal of ensemble classifiers lies in their ease of implementation and their remarkable success across a wide range of predictive modeling problems [ 74 ]. Within the context of this chapter, we employ five ensemble classifiers: − Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM) Classifier:  LGBM is a distributed gradient boosting framework primarily developed by Microsoft for applications in machine learning. It builds upon decision tree algorithms and is particularly well-suited for tasks involving classification, ranking, and more. LightGBM places a strong emphasis on scalability and performance.

First, each selected article will be summarized with a focus on the developed techniques. The datasets are then analyzed, with a focus on their sizes, types, sources, and distinctive characteristics that may have an impact on model performance. The features employed in these models and their influence on the outcomes are categorized and assessed using a thematic analysis. To give a comprehensive overview of the present status of research in evaluating predictive models, this synthesis attempts to integrate techniques, model accuracy, dataset characteristics, features analysis, gaps, and future directions for further investigation.

snippets: Randomization Versus Bagging Randomization demands more work than bagging because the learning algorithm must be modified, but it can profitably be applied to a greater variety of learners. We noted earlier that bagging fails with stable learning algorithms whose output is insensitive to small changes in the input. For example, it is pointless to bag nearest-neighbor classifiers because their output changes very little if the training data is perturbed by sampling. But randomization can be applied even to stable learners: the trick is to randomize in a way that makes the classifiers diverse without sacrificing too much performance. A nearest-neighbor classifier’s predictions depend on the distances between instances, which in turn depend heavily on which attributes are used to compute them, so nearest-neighbor classifiers can be randomized by using different, randomly chosen subsets of attributes. In fact, this approach is called the  random subspaces  method for constructing an ensemble of classifiers and was proposed as a method for learning a random forest. As with bagging, it does not require any modification to the learning algorithm. Of course, random subspaces can be used in conjunction with bagging in order to introduce randomness to the learning process in terms of both instances and attributes. Returning to plain bagging, the idea is to exploit instability in the learning algorithm in order to create diversity amongst the ensemble members—but the degree of diversity achieved is less than that of other ensemble learning methods such as random forests, because of randomization built in to the learning algorithm, or boosting (discussed in  Section 12.4 ). This is because bootstrap sampling creates training datasets whose distribution resembles that of the original data. Consequently, the classifiers learned by bagging are individually quite accurate, but their low diversity can detract from the overall accuracy of the ensemble.  Introducing randomness in the learning algorithm increases diversity but sacrifices accuracy of the individual classifiers. If it were possible for ensemble members to be both diverse and individually accurate, smaller ensembles could be used. Of course, this would have computational benefits.

An additional method could be to evaluate the learners’ accuracy on a different validation set and use the results to determine the weights, giving greater weights to learners who are more accurate   . 14.2.5.1 Random subspace By training each base classifier on a distinct subset of data, the Random Subspace-based ensemble classification approach introduces variety among the classifiers   . For every base classifier, a random subset of characteristics is chosen rather than all of the features. It is usual practice to perform this randomization separately for every base classifier. Improving the basic classifiers’ variety is essential to enhancing the ensemble's capacity to adapt successfully to new scenarios and sets of data. Because the Random Subspace method keeps the ensemble from becoming overly reliant on any one feature, it helps decrease overfitting. Because each base classifier only sees a portion of the data, they are unable to learn unnecessary or noisy aspects from the data. The final prediction is produced during the prediction phase by combining the unique predictions of each base classifier. Most commonly, techniques like majority voting are used to accomplish this combination. High-dimensional datasets are a special case for Random Subspace-based ensembles. The technique mitigates the curse of high volume of data by choosing subsets of features at random, making it suitable for handling enormous feature counts. Random Subspace sampling introduces diversity, which adds to the ensemble's resilience. The model is more likely to function successfully in a variety of circumstances and is less susceptible to changes in the input data   . 14.2.5.2 Rotation Forest (RotF) The RotF is an ensemble learning method that belongs to the family of feature transformation-based ensemble classifiers. The key idea behind the RotF is to use feature transformation techniques to create diverse views of the input data   . In this manner it enhances the diversity among base classifiers by applying potential transformations to the input features. The transformation is applied to randomly selected subsets of features. This selection is also based on the concept of orthogonality. A variety of base classifiers are trained using various perspectives on the input data that were acquired throughout the transformation. The main goal is to use various feature subsets and transformations to create diverse base classifiers. Enhancing the ensemble's overall performance and resilience needs this diversity.
