snippets: 7.4.5 Big Data Techniques and Technologies A wide variety of techniques and technologies has been developed and adapted to aggregate, manipulate, analyze, and visualize big data. These techniques and technologies draw from several fields, including statistics, computer science, applied mathematics, and economics. This means an organization that intends to derive value from big data has to adopt a flexible, multidisciplinary approach. Some techniques and technologies were developed in a world with access to far smaller volumes and variety in data but have been successfully adapted to be applicable to very large sets of more diverse data. Others have been developed more recently, specifically to capture value from big data. Some were developed by academics and others by companies, especially those with online business models predicated on analyzing big data. In this section, we note some of the main techniques and technologies to harness big data. These are not comprehensive—the story of big data is still being written; new methods and tools continue to be developed to solve new problems ( Manyika et al., 2011 ). 7.4.5.1 Techniques for Analyzing Big Data In this section, we list some techniques used to analyze big data across a range of industries. Not all strictly require the use of big data—some can be applied to smaller datasets (e.g., A/B testing, regression analysis). However, all can be applied to big data, and, in general, larger and more diverse datasets can be used to generate more numerous and insightful results than smaller, less diverse ones ( Manyika et al., 2011 ). • A/B testing . A technique in which a control group is compared with a variety of test groups to determine what treatments (i.e., changes) will improve a given objective variable, e.g., marketing response rate. This technique is also known as split testing or bucket testing. An example is determining what copy text, layouts, images, or colors will improve conversion rates on an e-commerce website. Big data enable huge numbers of tests to be executed and analyzed, ensuring that groups are of sufficient size to detect meaningful (i.e., statistically significant) differences between the control and treatment groups. When more than one variable is simultaneously manipulated in the treatment, the multivariate generalization of this technique, which applies statistical modeling, is often called “A/B/N” testing. • Association rule learning .

snippets: Techniques of Big Data Massive data processing includes obtaining useful data related to specific applications, aggregating these data and making them easy to store, analyzing data correlations, and identifying relevant properties; and allowing the results of the data analysis to be properly displayed ( Jagadish et al., 2014 ). This manner of processing is similar to the traditional method. The core techniques that Big Data would solve are related to these corresponding steps: ● Data description: Because of data variety, the first step before processing is a uniform description for different formatted data. Unified data structures not only simplify the system’s processing complexity but also reduce processing data overhead in upper application. In order to deal with large quantities of data, data descriptions based on ontology have become a research hotspot. This description mainly concentrates on the models of consistency, logical consistency, and relation consistency. The present study concentrates on small data sets, and thus far there is no case which can successfully describe data uniformly at PB or above. ● Data storage: Data in quantities of TB or PB are increasing at an incredible speed. In order to meet vast-volume storage, a distributed storage system is  needed, for example the Hadoop distributed platform. When the data amount increases, the data distribution balance and system extensibility are maintained by adding storage nodes. According to the variety of data structures, different storage strategies can be chosen according to the different data formats. Structured, semistructured, and unstructured data can adopt similar shared-nothing distributed and use the parallel database system, distributed storage system for document, and distributed storage system for files. ● Data mining: With the emergence of texts, images, and network data, new machine learning applications for dealing with large data are being put forward and have caused much concern. As the generalization ability is limited, traditional machine learning such as support vector machine, decision tree, Bayesian, and neural network, etc., are not able to adapt to the need for rapid analysis of a large-scale network. Recently, labeled or unlabeled semisupervised learning and ensemble learning with multiple models are new directions of the Big Data research. ● Data display. Data visualization is the process of converting data into graphs. Structured data can be represented through data tables and various statistical graphics; unstructured data are usually shown using a 3D (three dimensions) shape due to the variety and complex relationships of the data.

snippets: Analytic and decision-making tools for big data can allow companies to discover trends and characteristics about their customers that might otherwise remain hidden, in data that were never apparent or intended in the source information. There are many facets of and channels for analytics and decision-making solutions within the realm of big data; see  Fig. 7.36  ( Probst et al., 2013 ). Data that can be exploited by businesses can broadly be classed into the following three categories ( PwC Australia, 2012 ): • Internal data : information that a business collects through its own systems and processes. They can consist of both quantitative and qualitative information and are typically the type of data that provides the greatest insights for a business. For example, Walmart handles more than one million  customer transactions every hour; it imports these into databases estimated to contain more than 2.5 petabytes of data. This information enables the retailer to map out buyer behavior and merchandising and operational strategies. • Structured external data : from third-party sources. These data often require processing to be coupled with existing internal information to yield further insights. Facebook, for example, processes 2.5 billion pieces of content and 500 + terabytes of data each day. The social network also pulls in 2.7 billion likes and 300 million photos per day and scans approximately 105 terabytes of data each half hour. These data provide a significant amount of information about user behavior. • Unstructured external data : from sources outside the control of a business but having a potential impact on it. Like structured external data, these data can provide concise and targeted business insights when coupled with internal data. For example, when a search is conducted on Google, the search engine's algorithm takes into account over 200 factors, such as relevance, social media, geography, advertising, collective popularity, and so forth. This essentially makes sense of unstructured data to deliver the most relevant results to users. The latest developments in data analytics suggest there is great value in capturing and processing information with the appropriate cutting-edge tools. Possible applications areas are business, science, government, and society and draw on both structured data, traditionally collected by organizations internally, and external data, whether structured or unstructured. Future demand for analytics and decision-making solutions will be driven by the continuously increasing volume of data. A 2011 report by the Economist Intelligence Unit suggests there is a strong link between an effective data management strategy and financial performance.

snippets: Big data are high-volume, high-velocity, and high-variety information assets that demand cost-effective, innovative forms of information processing for enhanced insight, and decision-making (Gartner). As a result, efforts have been made to measure variables through ever improving digital sensors, communications, and computational power. snippets: Based on the rapid development of 5G technology and the empowerment of IoT, IoT will be in a state of continuous development in the future, and the security issues and related research will also become a research hotspot in the field of security. 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). Raw data usually contain noisy and unreliable data that can affect training and analysis. Moreover, datasets used in intrusion detection are characterized by high dimensionality, making it more difficult to discover knowledge during training. To build high-performance detectors requires efficient preprocessing. Fig. 4  summarizes the common data preprocessing methods used in intrusion detection, including data cleaning, imbalance learning, data transformation, feature selection, feature extraction, and Visualization ( RQ2(a) ). The above methods preprocess the data from different perspectives to enable the analysis model to better learn useful information from the data. In order to study the technical characteristics of different methods, we summarize their implementation principles and applications to answer  RQ2(b) . a ) Data cleaning Data cleaning corrects corrupt or inaccurate records. Quality criteria may include the following. • Validity. Data might have to be of a certain type, such as Boolean or numeric. • Accuracy. Data must conform to the situation. For example, outliers may exist due to the recording process. Accuracy is difficult to guarantee through data cleaning because real data sources are needed for validation. • Completeness. Some data may have unknown or missing values. Completeness issues are generally resolved through default values, setting zeros, or removal. • Uniformity. Inconsistency occurs when there are conflicts in a dataset. For example, a source IP may differ between two receivers. Fixing this type of problem requires the determination of which datum is most reliable. Data analysis based on means, standard deviations, or clustering algorithms can reveal errors, whose values can sometimes be set to a mean or other statistical measure. b ) Imbalanced learning A sample with different proportions of positive and negative cases will lead to a bias in the learning process toward the higher proportion. For example, in the extreme case of a dataset with 95 %  positive and 5 %  negative cases, the model will have no practical meaning. Since attacks tend to be sparse, datasets in intrusion detection are often unbalanced.

snippets: 8 Research challenges in SDA The discussion of SDA for various application areas in context to data analysis security. Rapid advancements in information technology encourage the process and system automation in almost all the areas such as-smart home, smart city, manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare. This leads to rapid and exponential data growth, i.e., data generated in every millisecond. The devices such as-sensor devices generates a huge amount of real-time data and send it to the cloud for further processing and analysis. Existing systems use fog and mobile edge computing to reduce latency and increases data security. But still, there is an issue of security with the analysis of data being captured from heterogeneous sources such as-sensor devices, Internet, machines, smart grid, and enterprises. Based on the exhaustive literature survey, we identified some issues and challenges in ML-based SDA implementation that need to be addressed, as shown in  Fig. 15 . • Efficient data analysis:  It is a major concern in SDA system design if we look for efficiency, then we need to compromise with the data security. Before sending data to the cloud, it should be encrypted for secure processing. Before the processing and analysis of data, it needs to be decrypted. The encryption–decryption process is time-consuming, which reduces the efficiency of data analysis. It has been observed from the literature that both the data efficiency and security are inversely proportional to each other and can be achieved with the implementation of ML algorithm ( supervised, unsupervised, NN, CNN, and AE ) which helps to detect network intruders and anomalies from network traffic without any cryptographic methods. • Network communication latency:  To reduce delay in network communication is also a challenge in designing the SDA system. More the delay (existing network communication delay), the more the chances of network attacks which may compromise the data security. 5G-enabled Tactile Internet (TI) is a viable solution for the aforementioned issue which ensures  < 1ms latency and  99.999%  reliability, and availability   . Rapid transfer of data makes the data secure and reliable for analysis. • System Reliability:  Reliability of data is also a prime concern to achieve correct processing and analysis results. Input traffic data is categorized into either normal or attack data. Correct classification of input traffic data is important otherwise, analysis results may vary.

snippets: 5.3 Challenge 3: Leveraging multiple sources of data enhances the effectiveness of threat detection In cybersecurity, relevant data can originate from various sources, such as Windows event logs, Sysmon logs, and memory logs. Moreover, data streams from user machines, network infrastructures, and sentinel systems contribute to the rich tapestry of information available for analysis. Integrating and analyzing these diverse data sources cohesively is crucial to improving the effectiveness of threat detection. As different sources of data complement each other by providing both compatible and distinct types of information, integrating multiple modes of data in the learning model will boost the learning process to learn more comprehensive features or indicators to detect malicious event logs. Various multi-source approaches have been developed for the cyber threat detection problem, for example, to enhance an IDS ( Lin et al., 2022 ), or for mining association rules from snort logs, firewall logs, and system logs ( Lou et al., 2021 ). In general, many sources of logs, e.g. from firewalls, web servers, and vulnerability scanners, might be collected and standardized before being incorporated into the learning model ( Lin et al., 2009 ). These approaches highlight the significance of considering multiple sources of data in the learning process. However, these methods typically apply data fusion either early or late during the process of integration. While they aim to enrich the learning model with comprehensive knowledge, such fusion techniques may overlook interactions among multiple sources, potentially being less effective than  intermediate  fusion ( Nayak and Luong, 2023 ). 5.4 Challenge 4: Evolving adversarial techniques limit the effectiveness of retrospective learning The challenge posed by adversarial techniques in cyber threat hunting lies in the ability of adversaries to adapt and evolve their tactics, developing sophisticated strategies to obfuscate their activities and circumvent traditional defense mechanisms. Adversarial techniques employ evasion, manipulation, and vulnerability exploitation to evade detection, including zero-day exploits ( Chen et al., 2022a ), and advanced persistent threats (APTs) ( Mahmoud et al., 2023 ). Evasion Techniques:  Adversaries utilize various evasion tactics to conceal their presence and activities from detection systems, including encryption, obfuscation, and stealthy manipulation of network traffic to evade IDS, IPS (intrusion prevention systems), and antivirus software.

snippets: To improve robustness against evasion techniques, adversarial training involves using adversarial examples to enhance models' robustness against techniques attackers use to bypass security measures ( Jiao et al., 2022 ). Incorporating behavioral analysis techniques detects anomalies in user and system behaviors, indicating sophisticated attacks that evade traditional signature-based detection ( Mahdi et al., 2021 ). Scalability and performance optimization are essential for handling large volumes of data and maintaining system efficiency. Designing detection systems using scalable architectures, such as cloud-based solutions and microservices, ensures scalability ( Liu and Zhao, 2023 ). Continuous performance monitoring helps identify and address bottlenecks, maintaining high reliability and efficiency ( Karimian and Beigy, 2023 ). Advanced threat-hunting capabilities involve proactive techniques to search for indicators of compromise and potential threats within the network rather than relying solely on automated detection ( Gâlmeanu and Andonie, 2021 ). Utilizing User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) identifies deviations from normal behavior patterns, revealing insider threats and advanced persistent threats ( Shao et al., 2021 ). Comprehensive logging and auditing ensure detailed logging of all network and system activities, providing a rich data source for threat detection and forensic analysis ( Nancy, 2020 ). Regular audits of the detection system's performance help update detection rules and models based on audit findings, improving reliability ( Wei et al., 2020 ). Finally, addressing concept drift and feature drift awareness and handling involves implementing continuous monitoring techniques to detect concept drift, where the statistical properties of the target variable change over time ( Xu et al., 2022 ). Techniques such as statistical process control charts or drift detection methods (e.g., DDM, EDDM) are used ( Priya and Uthra, 2023 ). Developing and deploying algorithms to detect and adapt to feature drift, where the relevance of input features changes, involves periodic re-evaluation of feature importance and automated feature selection to ensure the most relevant features are used ( Priya and Uthra, 2023 ). Adaptive learning algorithms adjust to concept and feature drift, with ensemble learning methods weighing models differently over time based on their performance ( Ren et al., 2023 ). Establishing feedback loops continuously updates the models based on new data and detected drifts, ensuring the IDS remains effective even as the threat landscape evolves ( Cheng et al., 2021 ).

snippets: 7 Taxonomy of machine learning-based secure data analytics The detailed taxonomy of ML-based SDA is summarized in  Fig. 10 . The detailed description of each existing approach is discussed in the following subsections. 7.1 Distributed processing-based SDA The volume of the data is exponentially increasing day-by-day, and it is not possible to store it at one single site, which in turn decreases the efficiency of system such as-throughput and delay. One of the best ways to store such a massive volume of data is at distributed locations   . Various possible techniques to store the data at distributed sites are discussed in the subsequent paragraphs. 7.1.1 Cloud-assisted SDA Cloud Computing (CC) is an emerging technology, which stores numerous amount of data at remote servers. It allows anytime and anywhere access to the data. In CC, the data is online, so it is more vulnerable to attacks such as-confidentiality and privacy attacks   . Thus, financial firms are moving towards the development of Cybersecurity Insurance (CSI) procedures to protect their data. The cost of CSI procedures is too high. So, Gai et al.    developed a framework to reduce the CSI cost without compromising the security level of BD. Bothe et al.    presented an eSkyline query interface to process skyline queries on an encrypted data. It answers the queries posted by clients without disclosure of actual data values based on the Attribute-Order-Preserving-Free-SFS (AOPFS) algorithm. It provides security to cloud-based databases. However, the problem with this system is that it is not suitable for large datasets. Later, Cuzzocrea    extended the work presented in    to perform secure BDA based on the same AOPFS algorithm. The author used a skyline operator to perform secure BDA, which becomes effective and reliable using the AOPFS algorithm. It was focused on BD compression with reference to immense data IoT frameworks. It is currently known as an emerging interdisciplinary field that incorporates service-oriented infrastructures, CC, BD management, and analytics. Puthal et al.    proposed a security verification model that considers the security aspects of BDA and provides real-time analysis of CC services.

snippets: Applications in biomedicine Owing to advances in high-throughput technologies, a deluge of biological and medical data has been obtained in recent decades, including data related to medical images, biological sequences, and protein structures. Some successful applications of deep learning in biomedical fields are reviewed in this section and a summary of applications is shown in  Table 1 . Medical image classification and segmentation Machine learning for medical images has long been a powerful tool in the diagnosis or assessment of diseases. Traditionally, discriminative features referring to medical image interpretation are manually designed for classification (detection of lesions or abnormalities) and segmentation of regions of interest (tissues and organs) in different medical applications. This requires the participation of physicians with expertise. Nonetheless, the complexity and ambiguity of medical images, limited knowledge for medical image interpretation, and the requirement of large amounts of annotated data have hindered the wide use of machine learning in the medical image domain. Notably, deep learning methods have attained success in a variety of computer vision tasks such as object recognition, localization, and segmentation in natural images. These have soon brought about an active field of machine learning in medical image analysis. Segmentation of tissues and organs is crucial for qualitative and quantitative assessment of medical images. Pereira et al. used data augmentation, small convolutional kernels, and a pre-processing stage to achieve accurate brain tumor segmentation   . Their CNN-based segmentation method won first place in the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BRATS) Challenge in 2013, and second place in 2015. Havaei et al. presented a fully automatic brain tumor segmentation method based on DNNs in magnetic resonance (MR) images with a two-phase training procedure   , which obtained second place in the 2013 BRATS. Their methodology was tested on the publicly available datasets INbreast    and Digital Database for Screening Mammography (DDSM)   , outperforming in terms of accuracy and efficiency several state-of-the-art methods when tested on DDSM. Additional medical applications employing a deep learning architecture have been demonstrated in segmenting the left ventricle of the heart from the MR data   , the pancreas through computed tomography (CT)   , tibial cartilage through magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)   , the prostate through MRI   , and the hippocampus through MR brain images   .

snippets: By implementing these solutions, patient data can be managed safely and securely, improving patient outcomes  [29–31] . 2.3.2 Biomedical image analysis The study of biomedical image analysis (BIA) focuses on the creation of algorithms and techniques that can be applied to medical images for the purpose of extracting relevant information and insights. This critical component of MI helps to facilitate diagnosis, treatment planning, and research. BIA also involves effective interpretation and utilization of MI data from the field of computer science, mathematics, and engineering. 2.3.3 Why is biomedical image analysis important? BIA is a crucial tool that is used in many fields of medical research and clinical practice. It involves the utilization of computational techniques and methodologies to derive objective and quantitative data using medical images. MI has become an essential tool in modern medicine, allowing doctors to visualize internal organs, tissues, and structures noninvasively   . BIA enables researchers and clinicians to analyze these images in a systematic and efficient manner, for acquiring crucial information on the anatomy and functioning of the body. There are many reasons why BIA is important. First, it allows for more accurate and reliable interpretation of medical images. Human interpretation of images is often subjective and can vary depending on the individual’s experience and training. In contrast, computational methods and algorithms used in BIA provide objective and quantitative measures of image features, which can be reproduced consistently across different imaging modalities and patients   . This enhances the consistency and precision of diagnostic and medical planning. Second, BIA can help to identify specific diseases and conditions by analyzing the image features. For example, in cancer diagnosis, features such as tumor size, shape, and density can be extracted from the images and used to differentiate between benign and malignant tumors   . This helps doctors to diagnose the condition accurately and plan appropriate treatment   . Third, BIA provides valuable information for treatment planning and monitoring. For example, in radiation therapy, image analysis can be used to identify the tumor and its location accurately. This allows radiation oncologists to precisely target the tumor while minimizing damage to healthy tissues   . Similarly, in neurology, image analysis can be used to identify brain regions that are affected by neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease or epilepsy. This helps doctors to plan surgical procedures or other treatments more effectively   . Fourth, BIA is crucial for drug discovery and development.

snippets: 2.3 Challenges in biomedical imaging One of the most significant challenges in BI is the interpretation of images. Medical images can be complex and difficult to read, requiring specialized training and expertise to accurately diagnose and treat patients. Additionally, there can be significant variability in the appearance of normal and abnormal tissues, leading to difficulties in distinguishing between the two. Moreover, the interpretation of images can be a time-consuming and subjective process, with different clinicians potentially coming to different conclusions. Efforts are underway to improve image analysis techniques through advanced computational techniques, like machine learning (ML) and AI   . Another challenge in BI is the cost of imaging procedures. Medical imaging (MI) is often expensive, with some imaging modalities costing thousands of dollars per scan. This can be a significant financial burden on patients, especially those without insurance or with high out-of-pocket costs. As a result, some patients may delay or avoid imaging studies, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment. Efforts are underway to develop more affordable imaging modalities and to reduce the cost of existing imaging technologies  [13–15] . A related challenge in BI is the potential for harm to patients. Some imaging studies, such as CT scans, involve the use of ionizing radiation, which can potentially elevate the chances of cancer and other diseases. Additionally, some patients may experience adverse reactions to contrast agents used in imaging studies, such as allergic reactions or kidney damage. Efforts are underway to develop imaging technologies that minimize the potential for harm to patients, such as low-dose CT scans and noninvasive imaging modalities  [16–18] . Another challenge in BI is the standardization of imaging protocols. Different imaging centers may use different imaging protocols, leading to variability in image quality and potential errors in diagnosis. Efforts are underway to develop standardized imaging protocols that can be used across different centers, allowing for more consistent image quality and better diagnostic accuracy   . Finally, data management and privacy are significant challenges in BI. Medical images can be large and complex, requiring specialized hardware and software to store and manage. Additionally, there are significant concerns around patient privacy and the potential for data breaches. Efforts are underway to develop more secure and efficient methods  of data storage and management, such as cloud-based imaging systems and block chain-based data management systems    ( Fig. 2.3 ). BI is a critical component of modern medicine, but it is not without its challenges.

snippets: 4.3 Methods In the literature, there are numerous methods utilized for user profiling from smartphone apps. The choice or propose of methods depends on the research problem to be solved. User profiling can either be for an individual or a group of users, and this property has to be considered when the suitable method is chosen. For example, a simple clustering method, which depends on the similarity of users in app usage behaviors, is inadequate for extracting one’s key characteristics from the perspective of an individual. Therefore, it is impossible to obtain meaningful results with inappropriate methods. It is not easy to make a thorough analytical comparison of the existing methods, because the performance of the given method also depends heavily on the available data sources. Therefore, some of the models would outperform the others based on a given dataset; but for a different dataset, their performance would deteriorate. Hence, the appropriate method should be chosen by examining beforehand the given dataset and understanding the effect of various parameters. We summarize and roughly divide the methods into four categories: descriptive statistics, regression, clustering and classification. In  Table 3 , we present prominent empirical user profiling approaches often used in the literature. The table includes data type and population size, user information, methods and results, where MDC for mobile data challenge, SVM for Support Vector Machine, GBDT for Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, kNN for k-Nearest Neighbor, GMM for Gaussian Mixture Model, and EER for equal error rate. We also highlight the advantages and disadvantages of the methods. As we can see from  Table 3 , the study scale can vary in a large range from 20 users to more than 100,000 users. The data duration also varies a lot, from 28 days to around 2 years. Among the four types of app data, app usage records have been used the most for user profiling (17 out of 28 tabulated studies). Installed app lists and app installation behaviors have been explored in four studies, respectively. App metadata, especially app categories and app description, has been used in most of the studies, since it can be available from public app store websites. Classification methods are the most used in the studies. Almost half of (13 out of 28 in total) the tabulated studies utilized classification methods to profile users in an individual level. 4.3.1 User profiling with descriptive statistics Descriptive statistics are a fairly simple approach for user profiling from smartphone apps.

snippets: 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). Raw data usually contain noisy and unreliable data that can affect training and analysis. Moreover, datasets used in intrusion detection are characterized by high dimensionality, making it more difficult to discover knowledge during training. To build high-performance detectors requires efficient preprocessing. Fig. 4  summarizes the common data preprocessing methods used in intrusion detection, including data cleaning, imbalance learning, data transformation, feature selection, feature extraction, and Visualization ( RQ2(a) ). The above methods preprocess the data from different perspectives to enable the analysis model to better learn useful information from the data. In order to study the technical characteristics of different methods, we summarize their implementation principles and applications to answer  RQ2(b) . a ) Data cleaning Data cleaning corrects corrupt or inaccurate records. Quality criteria may include the following. • Validity. Data might have to be of a certain type, such as Boolean or numeric. • Accuracy. Data must conform to the situation. For example, outliers may exist due to the recording process. Accuracy is difficult to guarantee through data cleaning because real data sources are needed for validation. • Completeness. Some data may have unknown or missing values. Completeness issues are generally resolved through default values, setting zeros, or removal. • Uniformity. Inconsistency occurs when there are conflicts in a dataset. For example, a source IP may differ between two receivers. Fixing this type of problem requires the determination of which datum is most reliable. Data analysis based on means, standard deviations, or clustering algorithms can reveal errors, whose values can sometimes be set to a mean or other statistical measure. b ) Imbalanced learning A sample with different proportions of positive and negative cases will lead to a bias in the learning process toward the higher proportion. For example, in the extreme case of a dataset with 95 %  positive and 5 %  negative cases, the model will have no practical meaning. Since attacks tend to be sparse, datasets in intrusion detection are often unbalanced. The following methods may improve performance. • Sampling methods.

snippets: Several data preprocessing techniques have been used before feeding data to the BGL prediction models: 23 papers out of 32 used data preprocessing techniques while nine papers did not specify if such methods have been applied. Data preprocessing techniques used in the selected studies can be categorized into three tasks: data cleaning, data reduction and data transformation. Table 6  shows the preprocessing tasks and techniques used by the selected studies as well as the datasets on which they were applied. Data cleaning:  These techniques aim to handle missing data, eliminate outliers, remove noise and correct inconsistencies. Data cleaning preprocessing techniques were used by 50% of the selected papers (16 out of 32) where missing data handling ranked first with 12 papers, followed by noise elimination with seven papers. Several missing data handling techniques have been used where imputation using linear interpolation was the most adopted in seven papers. Forward filling, filling with zeros and simple removal of rows with missing data were used twice each. The remaining missing data handling techniques were all used once each. With regard to noise elimination, simply removing outliers from the dataset was the most common noise elimination technique by defining thresholds and removing any rows with values out of the defined ranges. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD), extreme value analysis, and moving average filter were all used once each. Data reduction:  This category of techniques intends to reduce the data dimensionality by selecting and extracting a minimum set of features to decrease the model computation time without losing the data integrity. Among the selected studies, 12 papers (37.5%) applied data reduction where feature selection was used by seven papers and feature extraction by six papers. Feature selection was performed using different techniques where correlation coefficient method was the most adopted in 3 papers followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with 2 papers. Gini index, information gain, Lasso regression, PCA, Random Forest and Sequential backward selection (SBS) were all used once each. Concerning feature extraction, all the techniques were used once each. Data transformation:  The purpose of these techniques is to transform the data into a suitable form for mining and training the model. 40.625% of the selected studies (13 papers) used these techniques where reframing was used in nine studies, followed by normalization in six papers and categorical data encoding in one paper.

With the help of hidden variables, the incomplete-data log-likelihood shown above can be optimized by using the EM algorithm ( Dempster et al., 1977 ) in which the latent variables or unobserved data ( z 1 , … , z N ) can be estimated in the E-step and the parameters for each Gaussian distribution can be estimated in the M-step ( Amari, 1995 ). Clustering analysis has many applications in medical image segmentation. For example, Chen et al. proposed a robust algorithm for 3D image segmentation by combining adaptive  k -means clustering and knowledge-based morphological operations together ( Chen et al., 1998 ). They applied the proposed method to cardiac CT volumetric images to segment the volumes of the left ventricle chambers. Yao et al. applied fuzzy clustering and deformable models to colonic polyp segmentation in CT colonography ( Yao et al., 2004 ). 2.7 Dimensionality reduction and feature selection With the rapid development of modern measurement and detection instruments, we are able to sample more and more data (regarding both dimension and size of the sample) from real applications. For example, in radiology achievable image resolution has increased significantly compared with 10 years ago. Higher resolution means more voxels in an image which corresponds to more input features if we feed a classifier with all voxels. The increase in dimensionality (number of voxels in radiology images or number of features in feature space that can be extracted from original images) is a significant obstacle to solving optimization problems. This, in turn, complicates machine learning because of the optimization tasks involved in the learning stage. Dimensionality reduction is dedicated to solve this problem by extracting or selecting useful information from the feature space. Classical techniques for dimensionality reduction, such as Principal Components Analysis (PCA), are designed for data whose submanifold is embedded linearly or almost linearly in the observation space ( Jolliffe, 2002 ). Submanifold is a subset of a manifold in space and has its own structure.

snippets: For example, in   , the source data of lists of recent tasks was used to discover smartphone user groups, each list consisting of up to 10 package names that can be used to identify an app. It was unknown which app was used in each hour slot and how much it was used in this source data, and the number of apps in different lists could be different. It was difficult to obviously describe users’ app usage behaviors. Thus, the authors converted the source data into an understandable format, by detecting which app was used and computing how much it was used in each hour slot. In   , in order to detect the app usage records from the internet entries when apps fetch resources from the Internet, Qin et al. used Regular Expression Matching with different key words (“football” refers to a category of “sports”), and matched the corresponding Internet resource to a certain app category. Thus, each Internet entry was converted to a user’s request to an app category. Yu et al.    identified app usage records from the raw data which was cellular data accessing traces obtained by Deep Packet Inspection. (3) Dimensionality reduction  refers to reduce the number of variables input to models to minimize the data amount that is needed for research goals   . Dimensionality reduction improves computation efficiency, especially for the datasets where there exists large number of variables, data redundancy and data sparsity. For example, considering the high number of apps in the datasets, apps were divided into relatively small number of app categories based on their function similarity   . Moreover, compared to apps, app categories have an inherent semantic meaning, e.g., News, Games, and Banking, that allow us to reason more easily about app usage than using the name of the apps alone. In   , if all the apps were used to represent users, user vectors would be dramatically long and very sparse. Thus, important apps for a given user attribute were selected by the method of information gain, since some apps are redundant and not all the apps are useful for describing a user attribute. In this way, the data dimensionality was dramatically reduced, and the computation efficiency was greatly improved. Seneviratne et al.    selected the top-50 words with relatively high information gain from all the app description to represent each user rather than all the words.

concept: Sensor fusion in human activity recognition (HAR) is enhanced through hybrid feature extraction techniques, which combine various methods to optimize performance.

Deep learning methods have revolutionized feature extraction by automatically learning from raw sensor data, significantly reducing the need for manual feature engineering and improving recognition accuracy.
Traditional feature extraction methods like PCA, LDA, and ICA remain relevant, particularly for structured data, while deep learning techniques dominate in unstructured data scenarios.
Feature selection is crucial for improving classification performance by eliminating irrelevant features, with methods categorized into filter, wrapper, and hybrid approaches.
Data preprocessing is essential in machine learning, involving cleaning, transformation, reduction, and integration to prepare raw data for analysis.
Different types of features, including statistical, textual, facial expression, and speech features, are critical for understanding mental health data and enhancing model performance.
Transform domain feature computation, such as using Fourier and Wavelet transforms, is important for real-time visual scene analysis, particularly in dynamic environments.
Compressed domain approaches for video analysis improve computational efficiency by utilizing motion vectors and transform coefficients, which are essential for detecting moving objects.

Data preprocessing is crucial for enhancing the quality and representation of data before it is used in predictive models, particularly in the context of BGL prediction models and intrusion detection systems.

The three main categories of data preprocessing techniques identified are data cleaning, data reduction, and data transformation, each serving distinct purposes to improve data quality and model performance.
Data cleaning techniques, which include handling missing data and eliminating noise, were employed in 50% of the reviewed studies, highlighting the importance of addressing data quality issues.
Data reduction techniques, aimed at reducing dimensionality and improving computational efficiency, were used in 37.5% of the studies, with feature selection and extraction being common methods.

Data transformation techniques, which help in standardizing and preparing data for analysis, were utilized in 40.625% of the studies, indicating their significance in making data suitable for modeling.

The challenges of label noise and subjective annotation in data labeling were acknowledged, leading to the development of deep learning methods that focus on data-centric and model-centric approaches to improve prediction performance.
Data-centric methods emphasize adjusting and transforming data to correct noisy labels, while model-centric methods leverage collaborative learning strategies to enhance model performance.

The integration of advanced techniques such as spatio-temporal regression and Topological Data Analysis (TDA) reflects the evolving landscape of data preprocessing, particularly for complex datasets like sensor data.

snippets: Traditional data cleaning techniques for conventional big data (e.g. data warehousing) do not take into account the strong spatial and temporal correlations typically present in sensor-based data types. Information about an event in sensor data is usually reflected in multiple measurement points due to overlapping areas of coverage. Thus, the inconsistency among multiple sensor measurements serves as an indicator for the data quality. Some useful approaches for data cleaning for sensor data have used techniques like spatio-temporal regression and Kalman filters   . The authors in    proposed three models to detect and identify erroneous data among inconsistent observations based on the inherent structure of various sensor measurements from a group of sensors. The first model used multivariate Gaussian model to explore the correlated data changes of a group of sensors. The second model used principal component analysis (PCA) to capture the sparse geometric relationship among sensors, and the third model used kernel functions to map the original data into a high dimensional feature space prior to using the PCA model (i.e. kernel PCA). Their results demonstrated good detection rates with limited false alarms. 3.3 Data integration, aggregation and representation The authors in    defined two types of sensor-based applications depending on the information that is needed at the sink: (1) functional – where only statistical summary values (e.g. maximum, average, median) are required, and (2) recoverable – where the full dataset is required. For functional applications, data integration and aggregation can be easily performed during the data collection and transmission process as part of a hierarchical data gathering tree. On the other hand, the challenges of recoverable applications pose more difficulty for data aggregation due to the lack of prior knowledge on the spatial data correlation structure. The recent work in    for a functional sensor application, proposed a data aggregation approach based on compressed sensing (CS). The authors showed that their CS scheme based on diffusion wavelets could achieve high fidelity recovery for aggregated sensor data while achieving significant energy savings. 3.4 Data modeling and analysis The aim of data modeling and analysis is to derive value from the big data system and discover new insight or knowledge through analytical and statistical methods. Fig. 3  shows some analytical/statistical methods used for big data systems. In this section, we will discuss some of the techniques, and point to the reviewed case studies in Section  2  when relevant. Recommender systems are arguably the defining analytic method for big data systems.

snippets: Transformations are used to standardize variables, ensuring they are on the same scale, enhancing model flexibility to accommodate diverse data, making the model more interpretable, preventing computational errors, and improving accuracy. Common transformations include binning, rounding, scaling, exponential and logarithmic transformations, as well as power functions [ 52 ]. Feature Extraction:  Feature extraction techniques are employed to identify a smaller set of new variables, each of which is a combination of the input variables, capturing the same underlying information. Feature extraction reduces the data volume to a more manageable set suitable for modeling [ 57 ]. These techniques encompass methods such as text analytics, cluster analysis, principal components analysis, and edge detection algorithms. Feature Selection:  In this phase, only the most relevant variables are retained from the original dataset. Feature selection algorithms are utilized to evaluate, assess, and rank a subset of features from the pool of available features. Selection aids in determining which features are redundant or irrelevant and should be eliminated, and which are the most valuable features for the model and thus prioritized [ 58 ]. These selection methods are broadly categorized into four high-level categories: filter (e.g., ANOVA, Pearson correlation, variance thresholding), wrapper (e.g., forward, backward, and stepwise selection), embedded (e.g., Lasso, Ridge, Decision Tree), and hybrid methods [ 23 ]. 3.2.1 Topological data analysis (TDA) Topology, as defined by mathematicians [ 59 ], is the study of shapes and their inherent properties, often encompassing features such as the number of components and loops within these shapes. A particular approach to analyzing datasets, known as Topological Data Analysis (TDA) [ 60 ], leverages topological techniques to explore the topological and geometrical aspects of data, such as shape and connectivity. The fundamental idea behind TDA is rooted in the belief that geometry and topology provide a robust means to derive strong qualitative insights about data structures [ 61 ]. TDA is particularly valuable for datasets that are incomplete, high-dimensional, and contaminated with noise, as it offers a versatile framework for analysis while ensuring resilience to noise and dimensionality reduction challenges [ 61 ]. Moreover, TDA is enriched with functoriality, a core concept in modern mathematics, which enables it to adapt to emerging mathematical tools [ 62 ].

snippets: Nevertheless, the annotation process can be subjective, and the issue of label noise is sometimes unavoidable. In addition, the quality of annotations can differ among various annotators. To improve prediction performances, DL methods have been proposed to address the problem of noisy labels and concept shift. These methods can be categorized into two main classes:  data-centric  methods and  model-centric  methods. Data-centric methods focus on  data adjustment and transformation  (Section  5.2.1 ). These methods focus on identifying noisy samples and correcting their labels. Model-centric methods include  learning methods  (Section  5.2.2 ) and  collaborative methods  (Section  5.2.3 ). Learning methods propose an optimization framework based on loss functions (i.e., regularization), architecture (e.g., graphs) and learning strategies (active learning, zero-shot learning, meta-learning, etc.). On the other hand, collaborative methods exploit the cooperation between models to boost DL performances. 5.2.1 Data adjustment and transformation Data adjustment and transformation based methods are proposed to mitigate the problem of inconsistency of medical data annotation. These methods focus on adjusting the labels using techniques such as sampling, label correction, data programming, or label propagation. 5.2.1.1 Sampling Sampling-based methods aim to identify samples with inaccurate labels and then proceed to either correct these labels or remove the samples entirely. Given a training dataset, the neural network is designed in such a way that the number of neurons in the input layer is equal to the number of features. Apart from these restrictions, there is no hard and fast rule regarding the number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in a hidden layer. concept: Feature selection is essential in machine learning, particularly in imbalanced scenarios, as it helps to mitigate the risk of minority class samples being discarded as noise by removing irrelevant features.
There are three main categories of feature selection methods: filter, wrapper, and embedded methods, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.
Feature extraction, which transforms data into a lower-dimensional space, is distinct from feature selection; it creates new features rather than selecting from existing ones.
Deep learning methods have revolutionized feature extraction by automatically learning features from raw data, significantly reducing the need for human intervention.
Dimensionality reduction is a two-step process involving feature selection followed by feature projection techniques, which compress data while retaining essential information.

The effectiveness of feature selection techniques can be evaluated using various statistical tests and performance metrics, with wrapper methods often providing better results than filter methods in specific contexts.

The choice of feature selection method can significantly impact the performance of classification and recognition tasks, emphasizing the need for careful selection based on the dataset and problem context.
Best practices in model selection involve testing multiple algorithms and hyperparameters to ensure unbiased results and a deeper understanding of the variables used.

snippets: Under imbalanced scenarios, minority class samples can easily be discarded as noise; however, if the irrelevant features in the feature space are removed, this risk is reduced ( Li et al., 2016c ). The goal of feature selection, in general, is to select a subset of k features from the entire feature space that allows a classifier to achieve optimal performance, where k is a user-specified or adaptively selected parameter. Feature selection can be divided into filters, wrappers, and embedded methods ( Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003 ). The advantages and disadvantages of these methods can be found in  Saeys et al. (2007) . Another way to deal with dimensionality is feature extraction. Feature extraction is related to dimensionality reduction, which transforms data into a low-dimensional space. It should be noted, however, that feature selection techniques are different from feature extraction. Feature extraction creates new features from the original features using functional mapping, whereas feature selection returns a subset of the original features ( Motoda and Liu, 2002 ). There are a variety of techniques for feature extraction, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and f Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) (see  Hartmann, 2004 ). Feature extraction methods tend to be employed more frequently for unstructured data such as images, text and speech. For filter methods, various metrics were used to rank the features, and for wrapper methods, heuristic search was a common choice.

snippets: Filter method: Filtering is used to evaluate the predictive power of each feature. Features are ranked based on their respective correlation to outcome variables on some statistical testing. The feature with the highest correlation is the best. Common statistical tests used with machine learning include Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Pearson’s correlation, and Chi-Square test   . Wrapper method: In this method, the model is trained using a subset of features obtained from the original feature set   . Features can be added or removed further from the subset based on the inference drawn from the previous model. Two types of wrapper methods are commonly used as follows. Forward Feature Selection: This method starts with a null model (having no feature). Then, at each iteration, the model is fitted with an effective new feature. The process repeats until a new feature is added to the set that does not enhance the model’s performance. Backward Feature Elimination: This method starts with a full model (having all features). Then, at each iteration, a less effective feature is removed from the set. The process repeats until the elimination of an existing feature does not enhance the model’s performance. Floating Forward and Backward Selection: This method allows dynamic addition and deletion of features until the current existing feature set enhances the model’s performance up to a certain extent   . Embedded method: This method combines the goodness of filter method and wrapper method. In this method, feature selection is treated as a part of learning   . The learning algorithm uses its own variable selection process and performs feature selection, classification/regression simultaneously. In   , Wi-Fi based localization is discussed where rank correlation computation is performed on fingerprints to rank the APs from strongest to weakest. Co-Training is a method where two classifiers are used in parallel to improve the prediction   . For each classifier, effective features are needed to be selected and ranked according to their effectiveness so that both classifiers work equally well causing an observable accuracy hike. This step can be seen as a sort of data compression, which mainly is realised in two steps. First, the feature selection methods select the most important features. Next, the feature project techniques transform an existing feature space into another one ( Vlachos, 2010 ). Fig. 4  shows the different types of dimensionality reduction. Feature selection The feature selection techniques retain only the most relevant/descriptive features or dimensions and discard the remaining. The standard review approach classifies them into three main groups, namely ( Bellotti, Nouretdinov, Yang, & Gammerman, 2014; Guyon & Elisseeff, 2003; Li, Li, & Liu, 2017b ) filter, wrapper, or embedded feature selection methods. The filter methods utilise a feature ranking function to select the best features. The ranking function assigns a relevance score based on a sequence of examples. Intuitively, a more relevant feature will be higher in rank. Subsequently, the  n -top features are retained or the  n -worst features are removed from the dataset. The wrapper methods are general-purpose algorithms employed for searching the space of feature subsets. Furthermore, the wrapper methods test the performance of each subset using a learning algorithm. Finally, the feature subset that yields the best performance is selected for use. The embedded feature selection methods learn which features contribute most to the accuracy of a model while the model is being created. Some learning algorithms (e.g. decision trees) include an embedded feature selection method so that it becomes an implicit part of their learning process.

snippets: 27.3.3 Feature selection techniques The process of feature selection is crucial to machine learning and data analysis. It entails selecting the most important and useful components from a dataset while eliminating unnecessary or redundant information. In addition to increasing the effectiveness and accuracy of machine learning models, this approach helps to simplify and minimize the dimensionality of the data. Each method for feature selection has advantages and disadvantages of its own. Fig. 2  shows the broad classification of the feature selection techniques. A common method for selecting appropriate features from a dataset is filter-based feature selection. It involves inspecting each feature's characteristics independent of the target variable. This approach often ranks and selects the most informative characteristics using statistical methods or scoring criteria. Another technique for selecting features called “wrapper-based feature selection” includes assessing subsets of features based on how well they perform when applied to a particular machine learning algorithm. It approaches feature selection as a search problem, testing various feature combinations and ranking them using predetermined evaluation criteria. In tree-based feature selection, the algorithm builds ensemble models or decision trees using the dataset, taking different features into account at each split. A feature's significance is measured by how much it contributes to lowering impurities or enhancing the tree's or ensemble's ability to make predictions. The importance of a feature is determined by how frequently it is used for splitting and how much is the impurity or performance improvement. In the proposed work, correlation-based, recursive feature elimination, and tree-based feature selection are used, which are the subcategories of filter-based, wrapper-based, and embedded-based feature selection techniques. The statistical relation between each feature in the dataset and the target feature is measured using correlation-based feature selection. Low correlation features are eliminated while the most significant features with high correlation coefficients are kept. The RFE approach, which recursively eliminates the least significant features based on the performance of the model, is one of the well-known wrapper-based feature selection techniques. There exist several iterations, and in each of them, the features that are less important are eliminated. Random forest ensemble learning machine learning model is used to extract the important features for a tree-based feature selection technique. Random forest is constructed with the help of multiple decision trees, and the results of their predictions help to provide a robust measure of feature importance. In summary, feature selection is a critical stage in enhancing the effectiveness of machine learning models.

Various enhancement techniques like point and line enhancement filters were employed in their study to enhance granular and vein opacities in the lung areas. Also, the influence of ribs was removed by employing the Sobel filter method. 3.1.1.3 Fourier Transform Fourier transform ( Nixon et al., 2019 ;  Gonzalez, 2009 ) is a mathematical technique for decomposing an image from spatial domain to a frequency domain. Fourier transform doesn't actually modify the image, but rather provides a new representation of it in which the features that were obscured in spatial domain are now readily apparent in Fourier domain. The new representation is basically a plot of high and low frequencies (variations). The low frequency components reflect gradual changes in a spatial image and are exhibited close to the Fourier image origin (or center after applying shift), whereas high frequency components represent abrupt changes in a spatial image and are scattered away from the origin. The intuition behind the Fourier transform is that by tinkering with the Fourier representation and then applying inverse Fourier to it, we may more readily extract the features of interest.

snippets: Finally, The PS values from each of the  3  enhanced versions of ROI were then obtained and classified using the rule-based ANN mechanism. 3.1.1.4 Wavelet transform Unlike Fourier transform, which is based on sinusoidal decomposition, wavelet transform ( Nixon et al., 2019 ;  Wirsing, 2020 ;  Toufik et al., 2012 ;  Baaziz et al., 2010 ) decomposes an image into a set of wavelets. The wavelets are represented by wavelet functions and coefficients. The wavelet functions are generated from a single mother wavelet function ( Haar ,  Daubechies , and  Coiflets  etc.) through a series of scale and shift operations and are controlled by scale and shift parameters. The scale parameter controls the frequency band of the wavelet function, while the shift parameter controls the spatial region of the wavelet function. This means that different wavelet functions correspond to different frequency bands and spatial regions of an image. The coefficients are calculated by convolving a set of wavelet functions at different scales and positions. Two types of coefficients are obtained at each application of wavelet function i.e.,  approximations  and  details . The  approximations  are basically low frequency components that represents the overall structure and shape (i.e., coarseness) of an image, whereas  details  are high frequency components that pertain to the fine details or texture. Wavelets overcome the drawback of windowed Fourier transform by allowing the multiresolution analysis via varying window, which offers better spatial resolution for high frequency portions of an image and better frequency resolution for lower frequency portions of an image. Furthermore, because Fourier Transform allows decimation in the frequency domain only, it only provides global information of an image while ignoring local patterns such as irregularities or sharp spikes. On the contrary, wavelets allow simultaneous decimation in both space and frequency. Simultaneous decimation means representing an image in a way that is localized in both frequency and space (i.e., where are specific frequencies positioned in space). The wavelet transform is efficiently implemented with Mallat's tree algorithm ( Mallat, 1999 ), which employs iterative linear filtering (high and low pass) and critical subsampling on the original image to produce  4  sub-bands at each scale level as shown in  Fig. 4 .

By offering a representation of signals in both time and frequency domains, it facilitates the extraction of local and global signal features. In this thorough investigation, we delve into the mathematical underpinnings, characteristics, uses, and advancements of the DWT   . A pivotal attribute of the discrete wavelet transform lies in its capability to localize both time and frequency components. Through the decomposition of signals into various frequency bands, the DWT allows for the detection of transient features and abrupt signal variations. This characteristic renders it especially beneficial in fields where time-varying signal attributes are of significance, such as speech and biomedical signal analysis. Furthermore, the DWT boasts a crucial property of multiresolution analysis. It partitions a signal into approximation and detail coefficients at different scales, enabling a hierarchical representation of the signal. This feature facilitates tasks like signal compression, noise reduction, and feature extraction, rendering the DWT a versatile asset in signal processing endeavors   .

snippets: 2.2.2 Features in a transform domain In order to accomplish some of the real-time demands of visual scene analysis, feature computation in a transform domain has gained importance. – Frequency domain:  The frequency domain offers a good framework to detect periodic processes that appear in dynamics backgrounds such as waving trees and waves in the ocean. For this, there is a need to transform the data values in the pixel domain into the frequency domain via a transformation such as the Fourier Transform (FFT) [ 155,156 ], Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) [ 157 ], Wavelet Transform [ 158–160 ], Curvelet Transform [ 161 ], Walsh Transform [ 162–164 ], Hadamard Transform [ 165 ], Slant Transform [ 166 ] and Gabor Transform [ 167–169 ]. Practically, FTT processes blocks much faster in comparison with DCT. But, DCT outperforms slightly FFT in terms of precision, similarity and  F -measure [ 98 ]. – Video compressed domain:  As videos are usually compressed before transmission and storage, a number of compressed domain approaches have also been developed to improve the computational complexity of feature extraction. To obtain moving objects, the compressed video stream is partially decoded. Thus, the compressed domain data, such as motion vectors (MVs), transform coefficients, are employed to extract moving objects. Initially, compressed domain algorithms focussed attention on the MPEG standard. According to the classification of moving object detection, those methods can be mainly divided into three groups: MVs based method [ 170 ], coefficients based method [ 171,172 ], and combining MV and coefficients based methods [ 173,174 ]. Typically, more cost will be spent on high motion and/or detailed MBs and less cost for low motion and/or homogeneous MBs, which was verified in the experiments of [ 175 ]. Fourier transform doesn't actually modify the image, but rather provides a new representation of it in which the features that were obscured in spatial domain are now readily apparent in Fourier domain. The new representation is basically a plot of high and low frequencies (variations). The low frequency components reflect gradual changes in a spatial image and are exhibited close to the Fourier image origin (or center after applying shift), whereas high frequency components represent abrupt changes in a spatial image and are scattered away from the origin. The intuition behind the Fourier transform is that by tinkering with the Fourier representation and then applying inverse Fourier to it, we may more readily extract the features of interest.

snippets: Under imbalanced scenarios, minority class samples can easily be discarded as noise; however, if the irrelevant features in the feature space are removed, this risk is reduced ( Li et al., 2016c ). The goal of feature selection, in general, is to select a subset of k features from the entire feature space that allows a classifier to achieve optimal performance, where k is a user-specified or adaptively selected parameter. Feature selection can be divided into filters, wrappers, and embedded methods ( Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003 ). The advantages and disadvantages of these methods can be found in  Saeys et al. (2007) . Another way to deal with dimensionality is feature extraction. Feature extraction is related to dimensionality reduction, which transforms data into a low-dimensional space. It should be noted, however, that feature selection techniques are different from feature extraction. Feature extraction creates new features from the original features using functional mapping, whereas feature selection returns a subset of the original features ( Motoda and Liu, 2002 ). There are a variety of techniques for feature extraction, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and f Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) (see  Hartmann, 2004 ). Feature extraction methods tend to be employed more frequently for unstructured data such as images, text and speech. Table 2  shows 31 reviewed articles employed feature selection or feature extraction. It was found that filter and wrapper feature selection methods were most regularly used. For filter methods, various metrics were used to rank the features, and for wrapper methods, heuristic search was a common choice.

Therefore, the original collection of characteristics is largely summarized by the new reduced set of features. Common transformations include binning, rounding, scaling, exponential and logarithmic transformations, as well as power functions [ 52 ]. Feature Extraction:  Feature extraction techniques are employed to identify a smaller set of new variables, each of which is a combination of the input variables, capturing the same underlying information. Feature extraction reduces the data volume to a more manageable set suitable for modeling [ 57 ]. These techniques encompass methods such as text analytics, cluster analysis, principal components analysis, and edge detection algorithms. Feature Selection:  In this phase, only the most relevant variables are retained from the original dataset. Feature selection algorithms are utilized to evaluate, assess, and rank a subset of features from the pool of available features. Selection aids in determining which features are redundant or irrelevant and should be eliminated, and which are the most valuable features for the model and thus prioritized [ 58 ]. A particular approach to analyzing datasets, known as Topological Data Analysis (TDA) [ 60 ], leverages topological techniques to explore the topological and geometrical aspects of data, such as shape and connectivity. The fundamental idea behind TDA is rooted in the belief that geometry and topology provide a robust means to derive strong qualitative insights about data structures [ 61 ]. TDA is particularly valuable for datasets that are incomplete, high-dimensional, and contaminated with noise, as it offers a versatile framework for analysis while ensuring resilience to noise and dimensionality reduction challenges [ 61 ]. Moreover, TDA is enriched with functoriality, a core concept in modern mathematics, which enables it to adapt to emerging mathematical tools [ 62 ].

snippets: Mobile apps and digital platforms • Digital platform is an online resource that facilitates user interactions through which the data related to mental health is collected using mobile phones. 3.2 Preprocessing techniques Once the data is collected, the collected raw data is converted into an ML-understandable format using data preprocessing. Statistical features • Statistical features are the measurable features that can be computed from the raw mental health data using statistical analysis. The terms that are used to describe the characteristics of statistical data are mean, range, variance, skewness, median, mode, minimum, maximum, summation, and kurtosis. 2. Textual features • Textual feature is a feature that is generated in written communication. snippets: 2.2.2 Features in a transform domain In order to accomplish some of the real-time demands of visual scene analysis, feature computation in a transform domain has gained importance. – Frequency domain:  The frequency domain offers a good framework to detect periodic processes that appear in dynamics backgrounds such as waving trees and waves in the ocean. For this, there is a need to transform the data values in the pixel domain into the frequency domain via a transformation such as the Fourier Transform (FFT) [ 155,156 ], Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) [ 157 ], Wavelet Transform [ 158–160 ], Curvelet Transform [ 161 ], Walsh Transform [ 162–164 ], Hadamard Transform [ 165 ], Slant Transform [ 166 ] and Gabor Transform [ 167–169 ]. Practically, FTT processes blocks much faster in comparison with DCT. To obtain moving objects, the compressed video stream is partially decoded. Thus, the compressed domain data, such as motion vectors (MVs), transform coefficients, are employed to extract moving objects. Initially, compressed domain algorithms focussed attention on the MPEG standard. snippets: 9 Machine learning tasks in cyber security Machine learning (ML) is typically considered as a branch of “Artificial Intelligence,” which is closely related to computational statistics, data mining and analytics, data science, particularly focusing on making the computers to learn from data. Thus, machine learning models typically comprise of a set of rules, methods, or complex “transfer functions” that can be applied to find interesting data patterns, or to recognize or predict behavior, which could play an important role in the area of cyber security. In the following, we discuss different methods that can be used to solve machine learning tasks and how they are related to cyber security tasks. 9.1 Supervised learning Supervised learning is performed when specific targets are defined to reach from a certain set of inputs, i.e., task-driven approach. In the area of machine learning, the most popular supervised learning techniques are known as classification and regression methods. These techniques are popular to classify or predict the future for a particular security problem. For instance, to predict denial-of-service attack (yes, no) or to identify different classes of network attacks such as scanning and spoofing, classification techniques can be used in the cyber security domain. ZeroR, OneR, Navies Bayes, Decision Tree, K-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, adaptive boosting, and logistic regression are the well-known classification techniques. In addition, recently Sarker et al. have proposed BehavDT, and IntruDtree classification techniques that are able to effectively build a data-driven predictive model. On the other hand, to predict the continuous or numeric value, e.g., total phishing attacks in a certain period or predicting the network packet parameters, regression techniques are useful. Regression analyses can also be used to detect the root causes of cybercrime and other types of fraud. Linear regression, support vector regression are the popular regression techniques. The main difference between classification and regression is that the output variable in the regression is numerical or continuous, while the predicted output for classification is categorical or discrete. Ensemble learning is an extension of supervised learning while mixing different simple models, e.g., Random Forest learning that generates multiple decision trees to solve a particular security task. 9.2 Unsupervised learning In unsupervised learning problems, the main task is to find patterns, structures, or knowledge in unlabeled data, i.e., data-driven approach.

snippets: 1.6 Cyberattacks Detection Using ML Algorithm The cyberattacks in the SG-CPS can be detected by analyzing the sensor and smart meter data and the associated power system events. Using an ML algorithm to detect cyberattacks involves data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, selection of appropriate ML models, model training, model validation, and deployment. The first step is the collection of historical data from the SG-CPS, such as smart meter data, PMU and RTU data, communication network traffic, and renewable energy sensors data. The second step is to preprocess the collected data to remove outliers and missing values and convert the data into an appropriate format for the ML algorithm. The next step is to extract relevant features from the preprocessed data. This is followed by selecting a suitable ML model from the range of algorithms described in the previous section. After that, the selected ML model is trained using the historical dataset, which contains both standard and malicious data. During training, the model's hyperparameters are fine-tuned to optimize its performance on the training dataset. The next step is to evaluate (test) the performance of the trained model on a separate dataset that was not utilized for training. Finally, the evaluated model can be deployed in the SG-CPS for cyberattack detection if its results are satisfactory. This section discussed studies that applied ML algorithms for cyberattack detection in SG-CPS, focusing on advanced ML techniques. The ensemble of KNN and SVM was proposed by  Tabar et al. (2022 ). to detect FDI attacks (FDIA) on the wind on solar sensor data in renewable energy-integrated SG-CPS. The model is evaluated using simulated attack data on the IEEE 33-bus system. However, the model’s detection success rate is susceptible to data uncertainties associated with the nature of renewable resources and the false data threshold values. Ahmed et al. (2019)  proposed an ensemble of binary DTs using an unsupervised iForest algorithm to detect covert data integrity attacks (CDIA) on RTUs. The model is evaluated by simulating and detecting a DC load flow attack on IEEE 14-bus, 39-bus, 57-bus and 118-bus systems. However, the study assumed that the attacker had complete knowledge of the power network.
