snippets: 1.9 Advancements, Constraints, and Recommendations The previous subsections analyzed advancements in using ML algorithms for cyberattack detection, localization, and mitigation in SG-CPS. Table 6  summarizes some of the most noteworthy contributions. Several studies applied advanced ML techniques for cyberattack detection in SG-CPS. These studies employed different algorithms, such as an ensemble of stand-alone classifiers like SVM, KNN, DT, MLP, and NB, and ensemble classifiers like XGBoost, RF, extra-trees, iForest, and DL. Different types of attacks, including FDIA, DoS attacks, MITM attacks, and replay attacks, are considered in these studies. It is noteworthy that the majority of the studies considered FDIAs, that is because FDIA is the most popular type of cyberattack on the SG-CPS ( Cardenas and Tippenhauer, 2021 ). The performance of the models is evaluated using simulated attack data on various power system setups, including Oak Ridge Laboratories testbed and IEEE standard bus systems. To comprehensively evaluate and compare the effectiveness of ML and DL techniques in SG-CPS cybersecurity countermeasures, researchers commonly utilize a range of performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, area under the ROC curve (AUC), and F1-score. A detailed description of the performance metrics can be found in ( Radoglou-Grammatikis and Sarigiannidis, 2019 ). The challenges faced in using ensemble learning models include the handling of high-dimensional data and the need for additional feature extraction stages. DL algorithms such as CNN, RNN, LSTM, RBM, and autoencoders (AE) were identified as potential solutions for automatically extracting salient features from heterogeneous and high-dimensional data involved in SG-CPS. Moreover, while most studies focus on detection, localization is essential to cybersecurity countermeasures for effective mitigation. ML models, including SVM, XGBoost, and QDA, and several DL algorithms, including CNN, LSTM, transformer, and hybrid models, have been utilized to detect and localize cyberattacks in the SG-CPS simultaneously. The review also points out that most studies focus on detection, and research on mitigation using ML algorithms is still in its early stages.

snippets: 1.5 cybersecurity countermeasures using machine learning algorithms In the SG-CPS, the SCADA system receives a huge amount of data from smart meters and sensors that are used for wide-area network monitoring, protection, and control. The data is stored in the historical databases located at the control center. Recent literature studies have demonstrated that these data can be used through data-driven modelling techniques to develop security countermeasures, including cyberattack detection, localization, and mitigation to achieve a secured SG-CPS ( Habib et al., 2023 ), ( Narayanan et al., 2018 ), ( Mahi-Al-rashid et al., 2022 ), ( Hossain et al., 2019 ). Data-driven modelling methods refer to extracting and analyzing useful information, relationships, and patterns from datasets. These methods leverage algorithms, statistical tools and ML models to make predictions, classifications, pattern recognition, decisions, or recommendations. One of the significant advantages of data-driven methods is their ability to learn directly from data without prior knowledge of the underlying processes ( Baul et al., 2023a ). ML techniques are an important category of data-driven modelling methods that involve training computer algorithms on historical data to learn relationships and patterns and make predictions on new, previously unobserved data ( Usman et al., 2021 ). ML models are classified based on the input data used during their training and their architecture into supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised ensemble, deep, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning is the most commonly used ML technique, which involves training a model using previously labeled or annotated data, with inputs paired with corresponding target outputs. Support vector machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), linear and logistic regressions, Naïve Bayes (NB), and decision trees (DT) are examples of supervised learning algorithms that are used for regression and classification tasks ( Ahmad Fauzi et al., 2022; Alloghani et al., 2020; Sarker, 2021a ). In the unsupervised learning technique, the model is trained using unlabeled data to find patterns or structures within the dataset.

An important part of knowledge mining is rule mining, which is used to find interesting relationships between variables in large datasets. Using discovered knowledge or rules and expert systems in cybersecurity modeling allows for enhanced threat detection and mitigation. In rule mining, patterns, and correlations are automatically discovered in vast datasets, which can be used to identify vulnerabilities and malicious behavior. Based on these rules, an expert system can be constructed that emulates the decision-making capabilities of human cybersecurity experts. To discover rules, Sarker et al.    explored a taxonomy of diverse methods such as knowledge-based approach,  i.e. , based on human expertise, data-driven approach,  i.e. , extracting insights or useful knowledge from data, and their ensembles. Different types of rules can be discovered depending on the data nature and the target cyber solution. For example, association rules    can be employed to identify a correlation between certain user behaviors and the likelihood of a security breach. Similarly, classification rules    can be used to identify the type of malware that is present on a network and to determine the appropriate action to take to mitigate the threat. In addition, fuzzy rules    and belief rules    based modeling can be used to handle uncertainty and imprecision in data. For instance, a fuzzy rule could be used to detect network traffic that is slightly anomalous but not necessarily indicative of a specific attack. Similarly, a belief rule could be used to determine the likelihood that a particular security event is a false positive, based on the level of confidence in the detection algorithm and other relevant factors. By using rule-based modeling, security analysts can detect and respond to threats more effectively and find the root cause of such threats for proactive solutions. Through continuous learning and adaptation, rule mining and expert systems enhance the resilience and security posture against evolving cyber threats. However, a balance between rule complexity and interpretability is crucial to effective cybersecurity decision-making.

concept: Learning Types: There are three primary types of machine learning: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning uses labeled data to learn mappings for classification and regression tasks, while unsupervised learning identifies hidden patterns in unlabeled data through clustering and dimensionality reduction. Reinforcement learning focuses on learning through trial and error, optimizing actions based on feedback from the environment.

Supervised Learning: This approach is effective for problems where labeled data is available, allowing for accurate predictions and classifications. However, it requires a substantial amount of quality training data to avoid costly errors, particularly in dynamic fields like finance.

Unsupervised Learning: This method is advantageous when labeled data is scarce or when the underlying patterns are unknown. It can uncover complex relationships within data, making it suitable for applications like anomaly detection in quality control.

Reinforcement Learning: This technique is essential for complex, dynamic tasks where traditional supervised methods may struggle. It allows models to adapt and learn from real-time interactions, making it valuable in environments like cybersecurity.

Continuous Learning in Cybersecurity: The evolving nature of cyber threats necessitates models that can continuously learn and adapt. Research should focus on developing dynamic algorithms that can respond to new patterns and threats effectively.

Context-Aware Cybersecurity: Incorporating context into decision-making processes enhances the effectiveness of AI in cybersecurity. Understanding the environment and user behavior can lead to more informed responses to potential threats.

Challenges and Future Directions: There are significant advancements in machine learning applications for cybersecurity, but challenges remain. Future research should address constraints in detection and mitigation strategies, focusing on adaptive algorithms and context-aware systems to improve resilience against cyberattacks.

snippets: 3 Types of Learning There are two broad classes of learning: supervised and unsupervised. Supervised learning involves learning from examples, which is a set of associations between inputs and outputs. This is akin to how children learn to read and write—a teacher presents letters of the alphabet and utters the corresponding sounds. Repeating the process with the same examples will gradually train students’ biological neural networks to associate symbols with sounds. Training data is comprised of two parts: input and expected output. Let ( i ,  o ) be an item in the training dataset, which specifies that when the system is presented with input  i , it should output  o . The training data is a set of  n  such pairs: {( i 1 ,  o 1 ), ( i 2 ,  o n ), …, ( i n ,  o n )}. A trained model should work correctly if the examples in the training set are given to the model again. For example, given  i  as input to the trained model, it should produce  o  as the output. A reasonable criterion should be defined to measure the error between the correct output and the outcome generated by the model. The main task of supervised learning is to minimize the error function. This is similar to how the teacher corrects students in their initial attempts to read or write, which gradually minimizes the error function of their biological neural network model. In addition to the error function, other characteristics of the model include the number of model parameters and modeling flexibility ( Battiti et al., 2008 ). Decision trees, neural networks, regression, and Bayesian classification are examples of supervised learning algorithms. Unsupervised learning algorithms draw inferences from datasets consisting of just input data without labeled responses. Unsupervised learning infers a function which describes the hidden structure from unlabeled data. Since the examples given to the learner are unlabeled, there is no error or reward signal to evaluate a potential solution. This distinguishes unsupervised learning from supervised learning and reinforcement learning (see  Section 3.2 ). K-means clustering, genetic algorithms, and simulated annealing are examples of unsupervised learning algorithms. For cognitive analytics, unsupervised algorithms have an edge over the supervised ones. In the big data context, we do not know the patterns in the data  a priori . Furthermore, training data may not be available. Unsupervised learning algorithms are better suited for this scenario.

snippets: 5.1 Types of learning 5.1.1 Supervised learning Supervised learning refers to ML algorithms trained on labeled data (i.e., inputs for which the desired outputs are known) to learn a mapping   . Supervised learning can be used to solve two types of problems, namely: • Classification problems , where the predicted output is a discrete categorical value representing the class to which the input sample belongs. Depending on the number of classes, the classification task can be either  binary  or  multiclass . • Regression problems , rely on ML algorithms that facilitate learning of a continuous mapping function, which can be used to predict the output, e.g., the prediction of the next user’s position based on the previous residing locations. 5.1.2 Unsupervised learning Unlike supervised learning, unsupervised learning operates over unlabeled data by uncovering hidden patterns   . The key problems solved by unsupervised learning include: • Clustering , which groups data into clusters based on their similarity. Samples within the same cluster exhibit high similarity, while samples belonging to different clusters have low similarity. • Dimensionality reduction , which focuses on compressing the data while maintaining its structure and usefulness. Dimensionality reduction is the process of reducing the input’s dimension (i.e., number of features) by retaining salient and informative features, which can decrease the computational complexity. 5.1.3 Semi-Supervised learning Semi-supervised learning exhibits the same usage as supervised learning, but with the key difference of leveraging partially labeled data for training. In real-world applications, labeled data may be scarce or expensive, and a fully labeled data set on large scale may not be feasible   . 5.1.4 Reinforcement learning Reinforcement Learning (RL) allows an agent to learn through trial and error by interacting with its environment   . As illustrated in  Fig. 10 , at each time step, the agent observes the environment’s state and selects an action based on its policy. By executing the selected action, the environment transits from the old state to a new state and generates a feedback in the form of reward. This reward is used by the agent to determine the optimal policy that maximizes the expected cumulative rewards.

snippets: The prediction of a single house price, for instance, might use data that include several properties of individual houses in the dataset, called features. Each house might include features describing earlier sales prices, the neighborhood, square footage, number of bedrooms, and so forth. Another algorithm may be trained on patterns leading up to major shifts in the market to predict major trends in the future. Costly errors can be made when an algorithm, meant to predict stock prices, is trained on data that neglect the potential of dramatic swings in the market due to unique events (e.g. a natural disaster or war). Thus, supervised learning algorithms can have powerful predictive and discriminatory capabilities—provided the availability of enough quality training data that is also sufficiently representative of the targeted population. Unsupervised learning When well-labeled data is unavailable and the task of creating a labeled dataset is neither physically nor financially feasible, or when one is without preconceived categories (or unsure what to even look for), unsupervised learning may be the ideal approach. The unsupervised approach allows the algorithm to detect patterns that may be too complex for a human to recognize. The algorithm reads the unlabeled data and discovers hidden patterns within. For instance, the construction of a commercial airliner involves millions of mechanical parts. Each part of the aircraft will have a degree of error in length, weight, or performance due to simple variation in quality control—all pieces meeting a minimum standard, but not perfect. Even though all parts individually may work without perceivable error, in a complex machine like an aircraft, the accumulated error may be catastrophic. Traditionally, technicians must manually conduct multiple systemic evaluations of the plane, which cost tremendous amounts of time and money. Using an unsupervised approach, such as Anomaly Detection, and data regarding the quality of each part, an algorithm can holistically assess the amount of accumulated error and determine to what extent the accumulated errors affect the quality of the plane's airworthiness before the plane even leaves the warehouse. Reinforcement learning Both supervised and unsupervised learning are powerful approaches, but sometimes real-world problems that are natural to humans can be too complex or dynamic for machines to label or model (e.g. driving a car on a highway). Compared to supervised learning, where the answers are provided upfront, reinforcement learning tackles a task with parameters for successful completion.

snippets: Future research should explore ways to build trust by designing AI models that are not only accurate but also reliable and resilient. This involves addressing concerns related to false positives, false negatives, and the overall robustness of the detection system. Moreover, incorporating mechanisms for users and cybersecurity professionals to provide feedback and contribute to the learning process will contribute to the continuous improvement of these systems, fostering a sense of collaboration between humans and AI in the cybersecurity domain. 7.3 Continuous learning and adaptation Cybersecurity operates in a perpetual state of flux, as malicious actors continuously refine their tactics, particularly in DGAs. One prominent strategy for bolstering AI models against adversarial attacks is adversarial training. While perturbing all inputs during this process enhances robustness and efficiency, it also entails increased computational demands and potentially weaker generalization capabilities. Adaptive adversarial training emerges as a promising solution to this challenge. This technique enables the selective targeting of specific inputs for perturbation, aiming to optimize the training process. For example, Balaji et al. proposed an instance-adaptive adversarial training method that sets individual perturbation margins for each training sample ( Balaji et al., 2019 ). Their findings indicate improved generalization on unperturbed test data with a minimal decrease in robustness. Adaptive adversarial training represents a burgeoning field of research with the potential to significantly enhance the resilience of security models built on ML and DL. We anticipate increasing interest and advancements in this area in the forthcoming years. Recognizing the dynamic nature of cyber threats, the imperative to develop models capable of continuous learning and adaptation has emerged as a cornerstone in fortifying our digital defenses ( Yang et al., 2021a; Bisio et al., 2017; Yilmaz et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020 ). 1. Developing Models that Can Adapt to New DGA Patterns Over Time:  As cyber adversaries evolve their strategies, the ability of detection models to adapt becomes paramount. Traditional static models may falter when faced with novel DGA patterns. Hence, a critical research avenue involves the development of dynamic models that can autonomously learn and adjust to emerging DGA techniques. This necessitates departing static rule-based systems and embracing adaptive algorithms, such as reinforcement learning, which empower models to evolve in response to real-time data and changing threat landscapes.

snippets: • Automatic Rule Generation and Security Policies:  This involves data-driven approaches to generate rules and policies that trigger alerts or response actions when deviations from normal behavior are detected. The discovered patterns from the data collected from the DT environment and relevant features can be used to generate rules and policies to detect any deviations from the normal system behavior that could indicate a potential cyber threat. The major advantages of data-driven approaches are creating evidence-based rules according to data patterns, adapting to new updates as well as reducing manual efforts, discussed briefly in Sarker et al.   , which is very difficult to create and manage rules manually for a large scale DT system. Existing techniques such as association learning    may not be effective due to producing redundant rules which may lead to inefficient decision-making and computationally expensive. Therefore, developing scalable rule discovery algorithms and eventually making dynamic decisions accordingly could be a significant direction in the context of DT research. • Handling Malicious Behavior Changes and Adapting Concept Drift in Cyberspace:  In the real-world scenario in the DT context, concept drift may occur due to changing behavioral patterns over time. Traditional AI algorithms may not be able to adapt to concept drift in cyberspace in DT in real time, which can lead to inaccurate predictions and false alarms. Thus developing adaptive algorithms that can continually learn and adapt to the new types of attacks, could be a promising research direction in this context. Moreover, algorithms that can automatically identify the most relevant features for detecting different types of attacks, could play a key role   . In addition, developing incremental learning   , dynamic updated ensemble learning   , recent pattern-based mining    as well as their hybridization could be a major direction in this context. Investigating how transfer learning    can be used,  e.g. , transferring knowledge from related domains like network traffic analysis, could be another possible domain depending on data availability. • Context-Awareness for Adaptive Cybersecurity:  In cybersecurity, context-aware decision-making involves analyzing the context of a potential threat or attack and making a decision based on that analysis. Thus it can be considered a crucial aspect of AI-based cybersecurity as it enables systems to make informed decisions based on the relevant contextual information such as the spatio-temporal, environment, the user, the device, and other factors to decide on how to respond to a security event.

snippets: DL techniques in cybersecurity are advantageous because they can learn from large volumes of data and identify complex patterns that traditional approaches may overlook. However, much attention might be needed to ensure the effectiveness of the DL model and avoid potential biases or false positives in DT environments. 4.1.3 Rule mining and expert system modeling Typically, knowledge mining involves extracting insights, patterns, and relationships from large volumes of data   . An important part of knowledge mining is rule mining, which is used to find interesting relationships between variables in large datasets. Using discovered knowledge or rules and expert systems in cybersecurity modeling allows for enhanced threat detection and mitigation. In rule mining, patterns, and correlations are automatically discovered in vast datasets, which can be used to identify vulnerabilities and malicious behavior. Based on these rules, an expert system can be constructed that emulates the decision-making capabilities of human cybersecurity experts. To discover rules, Sarker et al.    explored a taxonomy of diverse methods such as knowledge-based approach,  i.e. , based on human expertise, data-driven approach,  i.e. , extracting insights or useful knowledge from data, and their ensembles. Different types of rules can be discovered depending on the data nature and the target cyber solution. For example, association rules    can be employed to identify a correlation between certain user behaviors and the likelihood of a security breach. Similarly, classification rules    can be used to identify the type of malware that is present on a network and to determine the appropriate action to take to mitigate the threat. In addition, fuzzy rules    and belief rules    based modeling can be used to handle uncertainty and imprecision in data. For instance, a fuzzy rule could be used to detect network traffic that is slightly anomalous but not necessarily indicative of a specific attack. Similarly, a belief rule could be used to determine the likelihood that a particular security event is a false positive, based on the level of confidence in the detection algorithm and other relevant factors. By using rule-based modeling, security analysts can detect and respond to threats more effectively and find the root cause of such threats for proactive solutions. Through continuous learning and adaptation, rule mining and expert systems enhance the resilience and security posture against evolving cyber threats. However, a balance between rule complexity and interpretability is crucial to effective cybersecurity decision-making.

The use of NLP typically facilitates the identification of potential vulnerabilities and suspicious activities by extracting valuable insights from unstructured text data, such as security logs, incident reports, and threat intelligence feeds. The use of LLMs can allow cybersecurity systems to efficiently sift through vast amounts of unstructured data, identify subtle indicators of malicious activities, and make better-informed decisions in real time. However, much attention is needed to take into account diverse issues,  e.g. , data poisoning, fine-tuning, and trustworthiness in different phases, such as pre-modeling, in-modeling, and post-modeling summarized by Sarker et al.   . To generate a comprehensive understanding of potential threats, multimodal intelligence refers to the ability to process and integrate cyber information from various modalities in DT environments, such as text, images, audio, and sensors, rather than relying solely on one type of data. For example, a cybersecurity model may analyze network traffic data,  e.g. , text, and detect patterns of suspicious activities in DT. It may also analyze images from security cameras and detect unusual behavior or identify individuals who are not authorized to be on the premises.

Many computationally intensive security operations such as homomorphic encryption and attribute-based access control can be deployed in EDC to collect and store data from many terminal devices IEDs. Thus it can be considered a crucial aspect of AI-based cybersecurity as it enables systems to make informed decisions based on the relevant contextual information such as the spatio-temporal, environment, the user, the device, and other factors to decide on how to respond to a security event.

snippets: Context-aware decision-making is also highly human-interpretable and can help security experts understand and trust the decisions made by the models. For instance, context awareness can play a significant role in classifying software vulnerabilities   , user behavior modeling   , and so on. Thus developing context-awareness cybersecurity models that can behave according to the current contexts, could be a significant research direction in this domain. Researchers also need to explore new approaches to human–AI collaboration, where AI systems can work together with human experts to make context-aware decisions that are more effective than either system could achieve alone. • Enhancing Semantic Knowledge with Extracted Cyber Insights:  The knowledge-driven system such as cybersecurity knowledge graph or ontology-based knowledge representation can represent the complex knowledge of heterogeneous systems with the semantic capabilities   . However, it would not be able to detect anomalies since it fails to handle large amounts of raw data and human experts lack the knowledge to manually confirm which patterns in the raw data might indicate potential threats   . Thus a hybridization of semantic knowledge representation techniques with machine-learning and knowledge or rule mining methods    could be useful in terms of automation, scalability, performance and interpretability in the context of large scale cybersecurity systems. By analyzing data from security logs, incident reports, threat intelligence feeds, and other sources, AI and machine learning algorithms    can automatically identify patterns, correlations, and anomalies that can be used to construct a comprehensive and dynamic knowledge graph. For instance, NLP can be used to extract information from unstructured data sources such as text-based logs and reports, and RL can be used to optimize the graph structure based on feedback from SOC analysts. Thus designing ML-enhanced dynamic knowledge graphs that can help security teams better understand their network and quickly respond to potential threats of an organization, could be a significant research direction. • AI Model Interpretability and Trustworthiness:  Ensuring the interpretability and trustworthiness of AI models is paramount for effective cybersecurity modeling within digital twin systems. As digital twin systems become increasingly complex, understanding the decisions that AI algorithms make becomes increasingly important for cyber defense strategies.

snippets: 4.5.5 Threat mitigation in a general context Unfortunately, state-of-the-art regarding automated approaches to countermeasure executions in fog computing and IoT is still in its infancy. In this way, we look for some alternatives that already exist in other paradigms. The authors Nespoli et al.    presented a study on several approaches to automated countermeasure and reaction frameworks against attacks in general contexts. These approaches may have their feasibility in the context of IoT studied. One of the approaches was proposed by Chung et al.   , they proposed a mechanism for protecting cloud infrastructures. The framework can detect and neutralize potential attacks against cloud infrastructure, taking advantage of SDN network control approach. When a vulnerability is discovered, or some virtual machines are identified as suspicious, various countermeasures can be taken to limit the attacker’s capabilities. Based on patterns and vulnerability catalogs, the system can calculate the score of each vulnerability and use it to build an Attack Graph (AG). A pool of countermeasures based on a virtual network is built, where each countermeasure is presented with (I) cost, (II) intrusiveness, (III) condition to enable the implementation of the countermeasure, and (IV) effectiveness. Optimal countermeasure selection is modeled as a multiple objective optimization problem, minimizing cost and impact while maximizing benefit. Zonouz and Haghani    introduced a framework called EliMet that combines expert knowledge and reinforcement learning to support decision making against intrusive incidents. The system passively observes administrator reactions against offensive incidents to calculate security measures and uses a reverse reinforcement learning algorithm to incorporate expert response policy and a Competitive Markov Decision Process (CMDP) model to target iteratively refining security measures converge with expert knowledge. In this way, after learning, the system can respond autonomously. Singh and Kaushik    proposed an approach based on Fuzzy ELECTRE (ELimination and Choice Expressing Reality) to accurately measure the weight of the importance of each response selection criterion and also solve the problem of prioritizing the response set to intrusion. Fuzzy ELECTRE is a method for multi-criteria decision-making. Shameli-Sendi et al.    presented a model called ORCEF, capable of dynamically evaluating the positive and negative effects of defense actions in a system under attack.

concept: Feature selection is a vital process in machine learning and data analysis, aimed at identifying the most relevant features while discarding irrelevant or redundant data, thereby enhancing model performance and reducing dimensionality.

Various feature selection techniques exist, including filter-based, wrapper-based, and tree-based methods, each with unique advantages and disadvantages. Filter methods assess features independently of the target variable, while wrapper methods evaluate subsets based on model performance, and tree-based methods utilize decision trees to gauge feature importance.

Correlation-based feature selection, recursive feature elimination (RFE), and tree-based selection are highlighted as effective techniques for identifying significant features, with RFE being particularly noted for its iterative elimination of less important features.

The importance of feature selection is underscored in the context of building balanced machine learning models that avoid overfitting and underfitting, emphasizing the need for optimal feature extraction to achieve low bias and variance.

A comprehensive review of past surveys on feature selection reveals a rich history of research, with significant contributions from various authors over the decades, yet a gap remains in detailed studies on recent metaheuristic approaches.

The effectiveness of feature selection is further validated by its impact on classification model efficiency and result generation time, with numerous strategies employed in early studies, including correlation-based methods, genetic algorithms, and principal component analysis.

Evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are essential for assessing the performance of classifiers with and without feature selection, indicating the critical role of feature selection in improving predictive outcomes.

snippets: 27.3.3 Feature selection techniques The process of feature selection is crucial to machine learning and data analysis. It entails selecting the most important and useful components from a dataset while eliminating unnecessary or redundant information. In addition to increasing the effectiveness and accuracy of machine learning models, this approach helps to simplify and minimize the dimensionality of the data. Each method for feature selection has advantages and disadvantages of its own. Fig. 2  shows the broad classification of the feature selection techniques. A common method for selecting appropriate features from a dataset is filter-based feature selection. It involves inspecting each feature's characteristics independent of the target variable. This approach often ranks and selects the most informative characteristics using statistical methods or scoring criteria. Another technique for selecting features called “wrapper-based feature selection” includes assessing subsets of features based on how well they perform when applied to a particular machine learning algorithm. It approaches feature selection as a search problem, testing various feature combinations and ranking them using predetermined evaluation criteria. In tree-based feature selection, the algorithm builds ensemble models or decision trees using the dataset, taking different features into account at each split. A feature's significance is measured by how much it contributes to lowering impurities or enhancing the tree's or ensemble's ability to make predictions. The importance of a feature is determined by how frequently it is used for splitting and how much is the impurity or performance improvement. In the proposed work, correlation-based, recursive feature elimination, and tree-based feature selection are used, which are the subcategories of filter-based, wrapper-based, and embedded-based feature selection techniques. The statistical relation between each feature in the dataset and the target feature is measured using correlation-based feature selection. Low correlation features are eliminated while the most significant features with high correlation coefficients are kept. The RFE approach, which recursively eliminates the least significant features based on the performance of the model, is one of the well-known wrapper-based feature selection techniques. There exist several iterations, and in each of them, the features that are less important are eliminated. Random forest ensemble learning machine learning model is used to extract the important features for a tree-based feature selection technique. Random forest is constructed with the help of multiple decision trees, and the results of their predictions help to provide a robust measure of feature importance. In summary, feature selection is a critical stage in enhancing the effectiveness of machine learning models.

snippets: 5.3 Feature selection/ranking As described in  Chapter 5 , there are many ways of feature extraction and they are based on time-domain, frequency-domain, time-frequency domain, or signal decomposition approaches. It is difficult for practitioners and researchers to know whether an optimal set of features has been extracted. There is very little theoretical advancement in understanding which features are important. Typically, the importance of features is evaluated  experimentally or using statistical approaches. Understanding the important features could help in building balanced ML models that do not underfit or overfit   . Also, by knowing the contribution of features, one could try to provide an explainable framework for an ML outcome. These features become even more important in building ML models for on-device and/or local computing applications that could be a requirement in many IoT-based healthcare applications. Feature selection techniques are primarily based on one or more of the following attributes: maximizing relevance, minimizing redundancy, and maximizing dependency. Common Feature Selection methods include Fisher Methods, Mutual Information methods, and Graph-based methods   . In general, feature selection methods are easy to implement for supervised ML when compared to unsupervised ML. The presence of label information in supervised ML makes it easier to adjust the feature selection process in real time, and this is also sometimes referred to as RFE (recursive feature elimination). Filter and wrapper methods are ways commonly referred for feature selection. Main considerations to keep in mind while training the system include bias and variance trade-offs. In order for a model to generalize well and avoid overfitting and underfitting, optimal curve fitting would be needed to achieve such separation. Linear curve fitting is the best possible solution, but if features were not extracted optimally or the model does not fit fully, then polynomial curve fitting needs to be performed. This involves some sort of convex and nonconvex optimizations   . The goal of building ML models would be to provide a low bias, which is commonly referred as training error and low variance, which is commonly referred as error in testing. A model is said to have overfitted if it has low bias and high variance, underfitted if it has high bias and low variance, and an optimal model would be the one that provides a low bias and a low variance.

snippets: 2 Previous surveys for feature selection In this part of our survey, we aimed to summarize the previous reviews of feature selection in the last 30 years. More than 40 most-cited and recent surveys in the literature are listed chronologically. We believe that it will be a good resource for interested readers. There are many surveys in this area, and they contain good information on the subject. However, there is no detailed research like our review on recent state-of-the-art metaheuristics used for feature selection. Although the first papers about feature selection date back to the 1970s, the best survey papers of this area started appearing in 1992. Kira et al. analyzed the strengths and weaknesses of feature selection and introduced a new statistical algorithm (Relief) in 1992   . The Relief works in linear time complexity according to the number of given features and training instances. The authors reported the comparison results of Relief and other algorithms, which supports their theoretical analysis. Siedlecki & Sklansky analyzed the feature selection methods, branch-and-bound search, and beam search for multidimensional pattern classification in 1993   . They reported the benefits of using GA and SA. Dash & Liu focused on a set of methods used for the feature selection between 1970 to 1997   . They grouped existing methods in terms of evaluation functions and generation. The advantages and disadvantages of the methods were explained, and research areas were investigated. Martin-Bautista & Vila reviewed data mining and knowledge discovery issues of feature selection   . A comprehensive survey about GA to select the most relevant features was presented. Different fitness values and parameters used by this evolutionary algorithm were reviewed. Philippe & Gallinari prepared a review of neural network approaches to feature selection   . The authors introduced baseline statistical methods used in regression and classification in their study. The methods were compared using benchmark problem instances. Molina et al. evaluated the fundamental algorithms in the literature using a controlled scenario, and they developed a scoring framework to analyze the amount of relevancy and redundancy of datasets   . Liu & Yu wrote a comprehensive survey on the main approaches and algorithms of feature selection for classification and clustering   . A new framework was proposed for search evaluation, strategies, and data mining. They built an integrated method for intelligent feature selection. Examples were given on feature selection to integrate a meta-algorithm. The authors identified the challenges and main trends in feature selection.

concept: Machine learning (ML) is a subfield of artificial intelligence that enables machines to learn from data and improve their performance on specific tasks over time, drawing parallels to human cognitive processes of pattern recognition.

ML encompasses various approaches, primarily categorized into supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and ensemble learning, each suited for different types of tasks and data availability.

The effectiveness of ML in applications like voice recognition is enhanced through pre-training on diverse datasets and continuous learning from user interactions, exemplified by personalized devices like smartwatches.

In physiological computing, ML is crucial for decoding physiological signals, facing challenges such as variability in data and the need for labeled samples, which can be addressed through techniques like transfer learning, active learning, and deep learning.

Model performance in ML is evaluated using metrics like accuracy and area under the curve (AUC), with variations in predictive accuracy observed across different studies and input parameters, highlighting the importance of feature selection in model development.

Research indicates that combining human and environmental factors can optimize model performance, with specific parameters like skin temperature and heart rate showing significant influence on predictive accuracy in thermal comfort models.

The analysis of feature importance is essential for understanding model performance and guiding data collection efforts, as different features can have varying impacts on the effectiveness of ML models in real-world applications.

snippets: What is machine learning? Think of Pavlov's dogs. When he would ring a bell, they started to salivate. Pavlov taught them this pattern: every time the bell rings, food is on the way. The dogs soon learned the pattern and eventually began to respond to the bell  before  the food appeared. To cognitive psychologists, human brains are also natural pattern matchers. Since birth, we are constantly trying to find patterns in what we perceive, then associate new patterns with existing patterns in our memory. This pattern-matching process happens automatically. Through our everyday experiences, our brains are constantly collecting new patterns and adding them to memory. These patterns then influence the inferences and decisions we make in the future. Inspired by an understanding of how the human brain works, researchers in the field of ML draw on connections to psychology, neuroscience, and the learning sciences. These connections are evident in the use of shared or similar terminology (e.g. reinforcement learning). Tom  Mitchell (1997)  wrote a widely quoted definition of ML: “A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T and some performance measure P, if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience E” (p. 2). Machine learning focuses on developing algorithms that allow machines to improve their performance on a certain task over time through accumulating experiences. Going back to Beverly, her watch implements an ML algorithm to understand her voiced instructions. Although the initial performance is not fully satisfying (i.e. she had to repeat herself several times), the watch becomes better over time as it experiences more instances of Beverly's voice. Modern companies that build these voice-recognition systems often pre-train the algorithm with massive amounts of voice recordings covering a wide range of accents, volumes, and acoustic environments prior to selling them to the customers. The initial accuracy of the watch's voice recognition should be acceptable, but it is further improved by specifically learning its owner's voice. Approaches to training Although all ML approaches share the goal of automatically improving performance on a task based on accumulated experiences, they differ largely on the target task, the nature and availability of training data, and the measure of performance. Given the complexity and variability of typical problems addressed with ML, there is no one-size-fits-all approach to training. Although not a comprehensive list, the three largest categories are: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.

snippets: Machine learning Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence, where data is acquired to let machines learn or train machines. By designing a model using the learned ability, we try to find an answer to a problem or predict the result of events. Learning is done by algorithms, which typically receive data and generate output using mathematics and logic. This learning process studies algorithms to automatically find rules from given data without having to program them one by one. We call this machine learning because it allows the machine to learn from the data. Machine learning is closely related to the field of statistics and optimization. This field is showing high interest and rapid development with the support of the computing power of computers. In connection with the geographic information system, this field is applied to satellite and aerial photographic image processing, industry spatial distribution and trends, and optimal transportation routes. Even a very good algorithm calculates the accuracy of results that are more than necessary, or if the complexity increases, it results in high-performance inefficiency. On the contrary, if the accuracy is low and there are many errors in the result prediction, the error in the prediction leads to incorrect results. Machine learning uses the following different approaches to learn based on datasets and problems being solved. 1. Supervised learning 2. Unsupervised learning 3. Reinforcement learning 4. Ensemble learning Supervised learning allows artificial intelligence to infer answers by putting answers that are already known by algorithm participants into the algorithm. Therefore, this participant sets the input data to a specific labeled output and creates a pair of inputs and outputs to determine the correlation. Thus, artificial intelligence trained with this pair generates an output value by attaching a label suitable for the new input data. On the other hand, there is no labeled pair in the input value of unsupervised learning. It is just creating a group of similar data. Then, the clustered input data features are extracted to generate an output value for a new input value. Reinforcement learning is a learning process in which agents and environments interact through information such as action, state, and reward to achieve a given goal. In this process, feedback may be delayed as the reward signal is the only guide without a supervisor who determines the result. Therefore, time differences should be considered due to delayed feedback. A function of receiving a state as an input and outputting an action to be taken is called a policy. In other words, the policy is an algorithm used by an agent to determine an action.

snippets: 2.2 Machine learning Machine learning is an essential component in physiological computing as it is used to decode physiological signals. There challenges in physiological computing are abound including, cross-subject/device/task variations, non-stationarity of physiological signals, difficulty acquiring many labelled samples, lack of domain knowledge in extracting informative features, and difficulty selecting the most appropriate model. Different machine learning approaches, or combinations thereof, can be used to mitigate these challenges as denoted in  Fig. 2 . Noteworthy, transfer learning can be used to cope with cross-subject/device/task variations and non-stationarity of physiological signals, active learning can reduce the number of labelled samples, deep learning can eliminate the manual feature extraction and feature selection process, and ensemble learning aggregates multiple machine learning models to increase the generalization. 2.2.1 Transfer learning Transfer learning uses data/knowledge in auxiliary tasks (source domains) to facilitate the learning in a new task (target domain)   . For example, a model developed from a source domain is reused as the starting point for a new model in the target domain. Transfer learning can effectively reduce the labelled data requirement in the target domain and thus facilitate the calibration of a physiological computing system. It has been extensively used in brain-computer interfaces    and affective computing   . For example, domain adaptation, a special case of transfer learning, has been used for EEG-based driver drowsiness estimation   . 2.2.2 Active learning Active learning selects the most beneficial unlabelled samples to label so that good learning performance can be achieved from a small number of labelled samples   . It can be used for both classification and regression tasks, for example, EEG-based rapid serial visual presentation classification   , driver drowsiness estimation   , and emotion recognition   . Additionally, active learning and transfer learning can be integrated to reduce further the training data required in physiological computing (e.g., EEG-based image classification)   . 2.2.3 Deep learning Deep learning uses a single neural network to perform feature engineering and classification/regression   . It has been demonstrated to provide accurate and reliable results in computer vision, image processing, speech recognition, and natural language processing. It has also started to find applications in physiological computing   .

snippets: 1.5 cybersecurity countermeasures using machine learning algorithms In the SG-CPS, the SCADA system receives a huge amount of data from smart meters and sensors that are used for wide-area network monitoring, protection, and control. The data is stored in the historical databases located at the control center. Recent literature studies have demonstrated that these data can be used through data-driven modelling techniques to develop security countermeasures, including cyberattack detection, localization, and mitigation to achieve a secured SG-CPS ( Habib et al., 2023 ), ( Narayanan et al., 2018 ), ( Mahi-Al-rashid et al., 2022 ), ( Hossain et al., 2019 ). Data-driven modelling methods refer to extracting and analyzing useful information, relationships, and patterns from datasets. These methods leverage algorithms, statistical tools and ML models to make predictions, classifications, pattern recognition, decisions, or recommendations. One of the significant advantages of data-driven methods is their ability to learn directly from data without prior knowledge of the underlying processes ( Baul et al., 2023a ). ML techniques are an important category of data-driven modelling methods that involve training computer algorithms on historical data to learn relationships and patterns and make predictions on new, previously unobserved data ( Usman et al., 2021 ). ML models are classified based on the input data used during their training and their architecture into supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised ensemble, deep, and reinforcement learning. Supervised learning is the most commonly used ML technique, which involves training a model using previously labeled or annotated data, with inputs paired with corresponding target outputs. Support vector machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), linear and logistic regressions, Naïve Bayes (NB), and decision trees (DT) are examples of supervised learning algorithms that are used for regression and classification tasks ( Ahmad Fauzi et al., 2022; Alloghani et al., 2020; Sarker, 2021a ). In the unsupervised learning technique, the model is trained using unlabeled data to find patterns or structures within the dataset.

snippets: • Automatic Rule Generation and Security Policies:  This involves data-driven approaches to generate rules and policies that trigger alerts or response actions when deviations from normal behavior are detected. The discovered patterns from the data collected from the DT environment and relevant features can be used to generate rules and policies to detect any deviations from the normal system behavior that could indicate a potential cyber threat. The major advantages of data-driven approaches are creating evidence-based rules according to data patterns, adapting to new updates as well as reducing manual efforts, discussed briefly in Sarker et al.   , which is very difficult to create and manage rules manually for a large scale DT system. Existing techniques such as association learning    may not be effective due to producing redundant rules which may lead to inefficient decision-making and computationally expensive. Therefore, developing scalable rule discovery algorithms and eventually making dynamic decisions accordingly could be a significant direction in the context of DT research. • Handling Malicious Behavior Changes and Adapting Concept Drift in Cyberspace:  In the real-world scenario in the DT context, concept drift may occur due to changing behavioral patterns over time. Traditional AI algorithms may not be able to adapt to concept drift in cyberspace in DT in real time, which can lead to inaccurate predictions and false alarms. Thus developing adaptive algorithms that can continually learn and adapt to the new types of attacks, could be a promising research direction in this context. Moreover, algorithms that can automatically identify the most relevant features for detecting different types of attacks, could play a key role   . In addition, developing incremental learning   , dynamic updated ensemble learning   , recent pattern-based mining    as well as their hybridization could be a major direction in this context. Investigating how transfer learning    can be used,  e.g. , transferring knowledge from related domains like network traffic analysis, could be another possible domain depending on data availability. • Context-Awareness for Adaptive Cybersecurity:  In cybersecurity, context-aware decision-making involves analyzing the context of a potential threat or attack and making a decision based on that analysis. Thus it can be considered a crucial aspect of AI-based cybersecurity as it enables systems to make informed decisions based on the relevant contextual information such as the spatio-temporal, environment, the user, the device, and other factors to decide on how to respond to a security event.

snippets: 3.1.2 Data-driven approaches arise (2000–2009) Even though rule-based approaches had been extensively used so far, data-driven approaches started to be used from this point onwards, including the EBMT and the SMT. This part starts with a new transfer MT approach in which ( Zhao et al., 2000 ) proposed a text-to-video translation system with two steps: (i) building an intermediate representation using syntactical, grammatical and morphological information and (ii) producing motion from that representation. The chosen intermediate representation was based on glosses and they mapped all the necessary cues to obtain them using a Synchronous Tree Adjoining Grammar (STAG) ( Shieber, 1994; Shieber & Schabes, 1991 ). To generate signs, they employed a sign synthesiser that took glosses as keys for a lookup table to retrieve their associated motion. Some errors could be given in the translation pipeline, or even some decisions that needed to be taken and there was not a direct solution for them. That is why introducing human feedback within the translation pipeline was also often seen. For instance,  Sáfár and Marshall (2001)  presented a two-phase system: (i) the transformation of the English input text into a semantic representation and (ii) the production of a graphical representation from the previous step. The system was prepared to be able to receive feedback from users in any step, e.g. the user can intervene to manually correct an assignation or a link between two items. Going into details, first the text was parsed through the CMU link grammar parser ( Sleator & Temperley, 1995 ). From that, an intermediate representation was composed in the form of a Discourse Representation Structure (DRS) ( Kamp & Reyle, 1993 ). For the morphology and syntax of the generation of signs, the Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG) framework was employed. Another transfer MT approach, and this time limited to the health domain, was proposed by  Szmal and Suszczańska (2001) , in a text-to-SL setting, performing a morphological, syntactic and semantic analysis of the input sentences. The translation was also limited to a set of semantic relations.

snippets: We can interestingly mention five papers which compared a feature-based method with a fully data-driven method. First, for STN localisation using MER's, Khosravi et al. [ 37 , 68 ] compared the utilization of state-of-the-art features versus the raw signal's Fourier coefficients, and Hosny et al. [ 76 ] compared the utilization of state-of-the-art features versus the raw signal directly. Second, Baumgarten et al. [ 29 ] compared two methods for predicting the occurrence of Pyramidal Tract Side Effect (PTSE) during the stimulation: a Volume of Tissue Activated (VTA)-based method versus a method using the raw information straightforwardly, which is the three-dimensional location of the contact and the stimulation voltage. All of the four papers showed a superiority of the fully data-driven paradigm which outperformed the feature-engineering approaches. Lastly, Yao et al. [ 71 ] compared the utilization of handcrafted features versus a CNN for LFP signals classification, and got better results with handcrafted features, likely due to overfitting. Feature engineering could be thought of as a particular, very involved type of pre-processing, that is, the modification of the input data before it is presented to the machine learning algorithm. From this perspective, pre-processing can be seen as a matter of degree. For example, for machine learning methods that process MERs as input, some use a spectral representation of the entire signal [ 37 , 63 ], whereas others use a spectrogram [ 61 ] or Haar wavelets [ 10 ], i.e. a mixed temporal/frequential representation, and others process the temporal signal directly without explicitly representing the frequency components [ 14 ]. These can be interpreted as a gradation between methods that require a large amount of pre-processing in order to make the informative components more accessible to the machine learning algorithm and others that rely more heavily on the algorithm itself. That being said, some amount of pre-processing appears to always be necessary, even for complex machine learning approaches, to ensure that the input data is meaningful to the particular algorithm or adheres to some pre-defined scope, however that scope has appeared to get broader as newer methods are developed, which is evidenced by half of the feature-selection-free methods being published in the last two years.

snippets: 27.3.3 Feature selection techniques The process of feature selection is crucial to machine learning and data analysis. It entails selecting the most important and useful components from a dataset while eliminating unnecessary or redundant information. In addition to increasing the effectiveness and accuracy of machine learning models, this approach helps to simplify and minimize the dimensionality of the data. Each method for feature selection has advantages and disadvantages of its own. Fig. 2  shows the broad classification of the feature selection techniques. A common method for selecting appropriate features from a dataset is filter-based feature selection. It involves inspecting each feature's characteristics independent of the target variable. This approach often ranks and selects the most informative characteristics using statistical methods or scoring criteria. Another technique for selecting features called “wrapper-based feature selection” includes assessing subsets of features based on how well they perform when applied to a particular machine learning algorithm. It approaches feature selection as a search problem, testing various feature combinations and ranking them using predetermined evaluation criteria. In tree-based feature selection, the algorithm builds ensemble models or decision trees using the dataset, taking different features into account at each split. A feature's significance is measured by how much it contributes to lowering impurities or enhancing the tree's or ensemble's ability to make predictions. The importance of a feature is determined by how frequently it is used for splitting and how much is the impurity or performance improvement. In the proposed work, correlation-based, recursive feature elimination, and tree-based feature selection are used, which are the subcategories of filter-based, wrapper-based, and embedded-based feature selection techniques. The statistical relation between each feature in the dataset and the target feature is measured using correlation-based feature selection. Low correlation features are eliminated while the most significant features with high correlation coefficients are kept. The RFE approach, which recursively eliminates the least significant features based on the performance of the model, is one of the well-known wrapper-based feature selection techniques. There exist several iterations, and in each of them, the features that are less important are eliminated. Random forest ensemble learning machine learning model is used to extract the important features for a tree-based feature selection technique. Random forest is constructed with the help of multiple decision trees, and the results of their predictions help to provide a robust measure of feature importance. In summary, feature selection is a critical stage in enhancing the effectiveness of machine learning models.

snippets: A typical supervised approach is to first construct or develop a set of dedicated features or filters, then to build a statistical model based on the features as sufficient statistics, with model parameters being estimated (i.e., learned) from a set of training examples. Martin et al. [ 73 ] devise gray-level and moment invariants-based features for segmenting the retinal vessels using neural networks. Ricci et al. concept: Data pre-processing is essential in machine learning (ML) as it significantly impacts the quality and effectiveness of models. Proper handling of raw data, including cleaning, transformation, and reduction, is crucial for achieving high performance and accuracy.
Different studies highlight varying opinions on the relationship between training set size and model performance, indicating that larger datasets do not always guarantee better results.

Techniques such as data cleaning, which involves managing missing data and eliminating noise, are commonly employed to enhance dataset quality. Various methods, including imputation and outlier removal, are frequently used in practice.

Data transformation techniques, such as normalization and feature selection, are vital for preparing data for ML algorithms, especially in heterogeneous datasets where variable scales can hinder performance.

The challenge of imbalanced datasets is addressed through data pre-processing strategies, which modify data distributions to improve model training and explainability, although these methods come with their own set of difficulties.

A significant portion of research emphasizes the importance of data pre-processing, with many studies applying various techniques to ensure data integrity and model reliability, underscoring its role in the overall ML pipeline.

Data preprocessing is crucial for enhancing the quality and representation of data before it is used in predictive models, particularly in the context of BGL (Big Graph Learning) and intrusion detection systems.

The majority of studies (23 out of 32) employed various data preprocessing techniques, which can be categorized into data cleaning, data reduction, and data transformation, highlighting the importance of these methods in improving model performance.
Data cleaning techniques, such as handling missing data and eliminating noise, were the most commonly used, with linear interpolation being the preferred method for missing data.

Data reduction techniques, aimed at reducing dimensionality and improving computational efficiency, were applied in 37.5% of the studies, with feature selection being more prevalent than feature extraction.
Data transformation techniques, which prepare data for analysis, were utilized in 40.625% of the studies, indicating a significant focus on making data suitable for model training.
The challenges of high dimensionality and noise in datasets, particularly in intrusion detection, necessitate effective preprocessing methods to ensure accurate model training and analysis.
Advanced noise removal techniques and robust feature extraction methods are essential for improving the accuracy of models in noisy environments, as demonstrated by various studies.
The integration of spatio-temporal data cleaning methods for sensor data highlights the need for specialized approaches that consider the unique characteristics of different data types.
Overall, the synthesis of these preprocessing techniques is vital for developing high-performance predictive models, as they directly influence the quality of insights derived from the data.

snippets: Several data preprocessing techniques have been used before feeding data to the BGL prediction models: 23 papers out of 32 used data preprocessing techniques while nine papers did not specify if such methods have been applied. Data preprocessing techniques used in the selected studies can be categorized into three tasks: data cleaning, data reduction and data transformation. Table 6  shows the preprocessing tasks and techniques used by the selected studies as well as the datasets on which they were applied. Data cleaning:  These techniques aim to handle missing data, eliminate outliers, remove noise and correct inconsistencies. Data cleaning preprocessing techniques were used by 50% of the selected papers (16 out of 32) where missing data handling ranked first with 12 papers, followed by noise elimination with seven papers. Several missing data handling techniques have been used where imputation using linear interpolation was the most adopted in seven papers. Forward filling, filling with zeros and simple removal of rows with missing data were used twice each. The remaining missing data handling techniques were all used once each. With regard to noise elimination, simply removing outliers from the dataset was the most common noise elimination technique by defining thresholds and removing any rows with values out of the defined ranges. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD), extreme value analysis, and moving average filter were all used once each. Data reduction:  This category of techniques intends to reduce the data dimensionality by selecting and extracting a minimum set of features to decrease the model computation time without losing the data integrity. Among the selected studies, 12 papers (37.5%) applied data reduction where feature selection was used by seven papers and feature extraction by six papers. Feature selection was performed using different techniques where correlation coefficient method was the most adopted in 3 papers followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with 2 papers. Gini index, information gain, Lasso regression, PCA, Random Forest and Sequential backward selection (SBS) were all used once each. Concerning feature extraction, all the techniques were used once each. Data transformation:  The purpose of these techniques is to transform the data into a suitable form for mining and training the model. 40.625% of the selected studies (13 papers) used these techniques where reframing was used in nine studies, followed by normalization in six papers and categorical data encoding in one paper.

snippets: 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). Raw data usually contain noisy and unreliable data that can affect training and analysis. Moreover, datasets used in intrusion detection are characterized by high dimensionality, making it more difficult to discover knowledge during training. To build high-performance detectors requires efficient preprocessing. Fig. 4  summarizes the common data preprocessing methods used in intrusion detection, including data cleaning, imbalance learning, data transformation, feature selection, feature extraction, and Visualization ( RQ2(a) ). The above methods preprocess the data from different perspectives to enable the analysis model to better learn useful information from the data. In order to study the technical characteristics of different methods, we summarize their implementation principles and applications to answer  RQ2(b) . a ) Data cleaning Data cleaning corrects corrupt or inaccurate records. Quality criteria may include the following. • Validity. Data might have to be of a certain type, such as Boolean or numeric. • Accuracy. Data must conform to the situation. For example, outliers may exist due to the recording process. Accuracy is difficult to guarantee through data cleaning because real data sources are needed for validation. • Completeness. Some data may have unknown or missing values. Completeness issues are generally resolved through default values, setting zeros, or removal. • Uniformity. Inconsistency occurs when there are conflicts in a dataset. For example, a source IP may differ between two receivers. Fixing this type of problem requires the determination of which datum is most reliable. Data analysis based on means, standard deviations, or clustering algorithms can reveal errors, whose values can sometimes be set to a mean or other statistical measure. b ) Imbalanced learning A sample with different proportions of positive and negative cases will lead to a bias in the learning process toward the higher proportion. For example, in the extreme case of a dataset with 95 %  positive and 5 %  negative cases, the model will have no practical meaning. Since attacks tend to be sparse, datasets in intrusion detection are often unbalanced. The following methods may improve performance. • Sampling methods.

snippets: Traditional data cleaning techniques for conventional big data (e.g. data warehousing) do not take into account the strong spatial and temporal correlations typically present in sensor-based data types. Information about an event in sensor data is usually reflected in multiple measurement points due to overlapping areas of coverage. Thus, the inconsistency among multiple sensor measurements serves as an indicator for the data quality. Some useful approaches for data cleaning for sensor data have used techniques like spatio-temporal regression and Kalman filters   . The authors in    proposed three models to detect and identify erroneous data among inconsistent observations based on the inherent structure of various sensor measurements from a group of sensors. The first model used multivariate Gaussian model to explore the correlated data changes of a group of sensors. The second model used principal component analysis (PCA) to capture the sparse geometric relationship among sensors, and the third model used kernel functions to map the original data into a high dimensional feature space prior to using the PCA model (i.e. kernel PCA). Their results demonstrated good detection rates with limited false alarms. 3.3 Data integration, aggregation and representation The authors in    defined two types of sensor-based applications depending on the information that is needed at the sink: (1) functional – where only statistical summary values (e.g. maximum, average, median) are required, and (2) recoverable – where the full dataset is required. For functional applications, data integration and aggregation can be easily performed during the data collection and transmission process as part of a hierarchical data gathering tree. On the other hand, the challenges of recoverable applications pose more difficulty for data aggregation due to the lack of prior knowledge on the spatial data correlation structure. The recent work in    for a functional sensor application, proposed a data aggregation approach based on compressed sensing (CS). The authors showed that their CS scheme based on diffusion wavelets could achieve high fidelity recovery for aggregated sensor data while achieving significant energy savings. 3.4 Data modeling and analysis The aim of data modeling and analysis is to derive value from the big data system and discover new insight or knowledge through analytical and statistical methods. Fig. 3  shows some analytical/statistical methods used for big data systems. In this section, we will discuss some of the techniques, and point to the reviewed case studies in Section  2  when relevant. Recommender systems are arguably the defining analytic method for big data systems.

snippets: Noise removal techniques:  Some popular techniques for noise removal are: logMMSE   , Karnuhen-Loeve transform (KLT) decomposition   , spectral subtraction   , and wiener filter    for speech enhancement. Vasquez-Correa et al.    evaluated logMMSE and KLT decomposition for SER. These techniques need the silence regions of fixed duration for characterizing the background noise. Their experiments did not produce any improvement in FAU-Aibo database due to the absence of such silence regions. The WPT and SSWT-based features improved the results after applying logMMSE algorithm for white, street, and cafeteria noises. Chenchah and Lachiri    used speech enhancement techniques such as spectral subtraction, wiener filter, and MMSE for real-world speech signals (airport, babble, and cafeteria). The spectral subtraction and MMSE methods are robust against airport and babble noises for emotion recognition. 2. Robust features:  Recently, some works    have focused on extracting robust features that are not affected by noise. Chenchah and Lachiri    proposed power normalized cepstral coefficients (PNCC) features and its variants for SER. The PNCC features are robust against the car, train, airport, and babble noises. The authors compared PNCC and its variants with the well-known MFCC and perceptual linear prediction (PLP) coefficients. The PNCC features differ from the MFFC features for the following reasons. First, PNCC simulates cochlea behavior based on equivalent rectangular bandwidth by gammatone auditory filters. Second, PNCC utilizes an extra step that is the subtraction of the medium-magnitude bias from the output of the gammatone auditory filters. The bias level was computed based on the ratio of the arithmetic to geometric mean (AM-GM ratio) of the medium-time magnitude. Finally, the power function non-linearity was achieved with 1/15 exponent. Mansour and Lachiri    showed the robustness of the MFCC-shifted-delta-cepstral (SDC) coefficients features for airport noise. The author claimed that MFCC-SDC outperformed the traditional MFCC and LPCC features in both the clean and noisy environments.

(2021)  introduced a noise-adaptive synthetic oversampling technique based on the concept of data noise ratio, which determines the number of synthetic samples generated for each sample in the minority class based on the sum of distances to its k-nearest neighbors within the same class. Our research team (Wei et al.) proposed an improving noise-immunity majority weighted minority oversampling technique (NI-MWMOTE), which incorporates a noise-adaptive processing strategy. First, the “suspected” noise is identified using the k-nearest neighbors approach. The distinction between suspected noise is illustrated in  Fig. 9 , where we can observe that suspected noise with a greater distance from the minority class center and a smaller distance from the majority class center is more likely to be actual noise. Additionally, suspected noise with a lower density in the neighborhood of the minority class and a higher density in the neighborhood of the majority class is also more likely to be actual noise. Next, a noise probability set is obtained by ranking the likelihood of suspected noise being true noise based on the weighted value of Euclidean distance between samples and neighborhood density. Finally, the best noise processing strategy is adaptively selected based on the noise probability set, misclassification errors, and an iterative approach. This overcomes the limitations of the k-nearest neighbors noise removal method, particularly in cases of sparse and insufficient data.
