snippets: The detection of the presence of voiced speech among various unvoiced speech and silence is called endpoint detection, speech detection or voice activity detection. The performance of the endpoint detection algorithm affects the accuracy of the system. It’s hard to model silence and noise accurately in a dynamic environment; if voice and noise frames are removed, it will be easier to model speech. In addition, speech consists of many silent and noisy frames which increase the computational complexity. Removal of these frames decreases the complexity and increases accuracy. Most widely used methods for voice activity detection are zero crossing rate, short time energy, and auto-correlation method. Zero crossing rate is the rate at which a signal changes its sign from positive to negative or vice versa within a given time frame. In voiced speech, the zero crossing count is low whereas it has a high count in unvoiced speech ( Bachu et al., 2010 ). The voiced speech has high energy due to its periodicity while low energy is observed in the unvoiced speech. The auto-correlation method provides a measure of similarity between a signal and itself as a function of delay. It is used to find repeating patterns. Because of its periodic nature, voiced signals can be detected using the auto-correlation method. 5.1.4 Normalization Feature normalization is an important step which is used to reduce speaker and recording variability without losing the discriminative strength of the features. By using feature normalization, the generalization ability of features are increased. Normalization can be done at different levels, such as function level and corpus level. Most widely used normalization method is z-normalization (standard score). If mean  μ  and standard deviation  σ  of the data is known, z-normalization is calculated as  z = x − μ σ . 5.1.5 Noise reduction In real life, the noise present in the environment is captured along with the speech signal. This affects the recognition rate, hence some noise reduction techniques must be used to eliminate or reduce the noise. Minimum mean square error (MMSE) and log-spectral amplitude MMSE (LogMMSE) estimators are most successfully applied methods for noise reduction ( Pohjalainen et al., 2016 ). In MMSE, the clean signal is estimated from a given sample function of the noisy signal. It needs apriori information of speech and noise spectrum. It is based on the assumption that the additive noise spectrum and estimate of the speech spectrum is available.

concept: The importance of using large, high-dimensional datasets in classifier comparisons is emphasized to ensure the external validity of empirical results. Many studies rely on smaller datasets, which may limit generalization and lead to biased outcomes due to poor-quality data.

The methodology for training, testing, and evaluating machine learning models is generally consistent, but there is a lack of standardized guidelines for data partitioning, leading to varied practices among researchers.

Overfitting is a significant concern when using small training datasets, as it can lead to models that do not generalize well. Techniques such as data augmentation, dropout, transfer learning, and ensemble learning are commonly employed to mitigate this issue.

The "curse of dimensionality" highlights the challenges faced in machine learning, particularly in civil engineering applications, where available datasets are often limited due to confidentiality, exacerbating the risk of overfitting.

Data scarcity and class imbalance are critical issues that affect the robustness of machine learning algorithms. Strategies to address these challenges include data augmentation and the use of ensemble methods, although they may require more computational resources.

snippets: Real credit datasets are typically large and high-dimensional, and so should be the datasets used in classifier comparisons, ensuring the external validity of empirical results ( Finlay, 2011 ;  Hand, 2000 ). snippets: Training, testing, and evaluation are generally done as prescribed in the ML literature, and the methods are generally evaluated using metrics such as the Mean Square Error (MSE), accuracy, and so on. For example, to learn objective functions in  Biggs et al. (2018) , the data is split in a 70:30 ratio between training and test sets, and prediction accuracy used as the evaluation metric. See Chapter 2 of  James et al. (2013)  for more information on training and testing ML models. In terms of the size of the ANNs, with the exception of  Yang & Bequette (2021)  who use a network with six hidden layers, most networks used in constraint learning are generally small. One reason for this could be to reduce the burden of embedding large networks as constraints — it will be seen from (5a) to (5e) in  Section 4.4  that the number of binary variables required is proportional to the size of the network. Also, as the input of a current layer is the output of a previous one, using multiple layers results in nested activation functions in the final model. This could lead to issues regarding convexity and/or differentiability, therefore smaller networks are used. Another reason for small neural network sizes is that using larger networks provides no benefit in some cases. Lombardi et al. (2017)  for example use a network with one hidden layer (with two neurons) as increasing the network size did not improve the solution quality of the optimization problem. To view the effect of network size on computation times,  Schweidtmann & Mitsos (2019)  vary both the number of neurons and the number of layers. Results showed that the solution time increases approximately exponentially with the number of layers used to learn the constraints. Deep neural networks required more processing time than shallow neural networks for the same total number of neurons. An alternative to using small networks could be to use sparsification. Murzakhanov et al. (2020)  use a network with three hidden layers and fifty neurons in each layer to learn constraints, however they reduce the size of the network by enforcing  70 %  of the weights to be zero. This sparsification procedure ensures that the network was not too large and also avoided over-fitting during training. Say et al. (2017)  use a similar technique to remove connections to and from neurons with very small weights in order to strengthen the MILP formulation.

snippets: The need of large training datasets can be reconnected to the  curse of dimensionality  concept introduced in [ 39 ] explaining the exponential growth of learning complexity with the linear growth of dimensionality in classification approaches. Especially in civil engineering ML applications, this growth is not reflected by the volume of available datasets which, are often limited by confidentiality issues with the client. One of the possible consequences of small training dataset is overfitting. It means that the statistical model contains more parameters than can be justified by the data. Even if in specific circumstances the overfitting phenomena doesn't negatively affect or even increases the prediction performance of the algorithm [ 40 ], it will result in a poor prediction ability of the network in more general cases. Data augmentation [ 41–43 ] is the most common approach to tackle the issue of small datasets. It consists in minor geometric and/or appearance alteration of the images. The benefit is that, applying the same geometric alterations to the target mask, the data volume enlarges without any extra work. Dropout [ 44 ] is one of the regularization methods to avoid overfitting. Sometimes, it is also seen as an additional augmentation approach [ 24 ]. The value of its hyperparameter  ρ , representing the probability of disconnecting neurons at each training step, is usually set to 0.5 for crack detection [ 8 , 18 , 21 , 45 ]. Another very popular approach for the same problem is so called transfer learning. It represents the possibility to apply to the target task knowledge leveraged from a source task [ 46 ]. Avoiding overtraining with a cross validation approach [ 26 ] or avoiding overfitting by undercomputing [ 47 ] are two other solutions to face this problem. Finally, a less popular approach to reduce the risk of overfitting is ensemble learning. This approach consists in combining predictions from two or more models with statistics approaches [ 32 , 48 , 49 ]. The drawback of such an approach, especially for semantic segmentation, is the higher computational power required for both training and prediction phases. Apart from small datasets, another detrimental data related performance issue is  class imbalance  [ 50–52 ]. With this term we refer to the case when the number of samples belonging to one class (minority class) are outnumbered by the samples of another class (majority class).

concept: Data scaling methods, including min-max normalization and standardization, are crucial for improving machine learning model performance by ensuring that all features contribute equally to the learning process.

Feature selection is a vital step in data preparation, aimed at enhancing model performance by reducing overfitting, increasing interpretability, and decreasing training time through the careful selection of relevant features.

Various feature selection techniques exist, such as filter methods, wrapper methods, and embedded methods, each with its own advantages and suited for different types of datasets and machine learning algorithms.

The study emphasizes the importance of using appropriate feature scaling and selection techniques to improve classification efficiency and reduce the risk of overfitting, particularly in complex datasets.

Feature extraction, while related to feature selection, involves creating new features from existing ones and is often used for unstructured data, highlighting the need for different approaches depending on the data type.

The effectiveness of machine learning models can be significantly enhanced by employing robust feature selection techniques, which help in identifying the most relevant features while discarding irrelevant ones, thus optimizing model performance.

snippets: For example, in understanding cardiac conditions, the gold standard of echocardiography or exercise ECG information would be used in annotating the signal for regions of interest. 5.2 Feature normalization Feature normalization helps in controlling overfitting by scaling the feature vectors to a uniform dynamic range and thereby avoiding any bias. The common ways of feature normalization involve min–max normalization and standardization approaches. In min–max normalization, the rescaling is done in such a way that the features take a range of 0 to 1 or −1 to 1. The formula for min–max is given by x ′ = x − min ( x ) max ( x ) − min ( x ) Certain ML algorithms provide a better performance if the features are standardized in a way that they have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of unity. The standardization could be achieved by using Z-score formula, which is defined as x ′ = x − mean ( x ) standard deviation ( x ) ML algorithms that are based on distance measures benefit from feature normalization, and specifically, they include linear discriminant analysis (LDA), logistic regression, k-nearest neighbor (k-NN), and neural networks. Approaches that are non-distance based such as Naïve Bayes, Decision Trees (DTs), Random Forest, etc., do not need feature normalization, but nevertheless there is no downside in normalizing or standardizing features for these classifiers. 5.3 Feature selection/ranking As described in  Chapter 5 , there are many ways of feature extraction and they are based on time-domain, frequency-domain, time-frequency domain, or signal decomposition approaches. It is difficult for practitioners and researchers to know whether an optimal set of features has been extracted. There is very little theoretical advancement in understanding which features are important. Typically, the importance of features is evaluated  experimentally or using statistical approaches. Understanding the important features could help in building balanced ML models that do not underfit or overfit   . Also, by knowing the contribution of features, one could try to provide an explainable framework for an ML outcome. These features become even more important in building ML models for on-device and/or local computing applications that could be a requirement in many IoT-based healthcare applications. Feature selection techniques are primarily based on one or more of the following attributes: maximizing relevance, minimizing redundancy, and maximizing dependency.

snippets: In this study, we employ five of the most commonly used feature scaling techniques [ 68 ]: − Absolute Maximum (Max-Abs) Scaling:  This technique involves computing the absolute maximum value of the feature within the dataset and then dividing all the  values in the column by this computed maximum. As a result, the output values fall within the range of 1 to −1. − Minimum Maximum (Min-Max) Scaling:  Min-Max Scaling is accomplished by subtracting the minimum value from all the values in the dataset and subsequently dividing the output value by the dataset's range, which is calculated as the maximum value minus the minimum value. − Normalization:  Normalization employs the maximum value to perform the scaling. Unlike the previous techniques that change the data range, normalization adjusts the distribution shape of the data. − Standardization (Z-Score Normalization):  In the case of Z-Score Normalization, a Z-score is calculated for each data point, replacing the original data value with the calculated Z-score. Consequently, all features are centered around the mean value, with a standard deviation of 1. − Robust Scaling:  This scaling method is resilient to outliers. It begins by subtracting the median value from all data points and subsequently divides the output values by the Interquartile Range (IQR). The IQR represents the range between the 25th and 75th percentile data points, thereby centering the median value at zero. 3.4 Classification, optimization, and performance evaluation Machine learning (ML) algorithms have demonstrated their utility across a wide spectrum of applications, including but not limited to email filtering, computer vision, speech recognition, and medicine. snippets: Under imbalanced scenarios, minority class samples can easily be discarded as noise; however, if the irrelevant features in the feature space are removed, this risk is reduced ( Li et al., 2016c ). The goal of feature selection, in general, is to select a subset of k features from the entire feature space that allows a classifier to achieve optimal performance, where k is a user-specified or adaptively selected parameter. Feature selection can be divided into filters, wrappers, and embedded methods ( Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003 ). The advantages and disadvantages of these methods can be found in  Saeys et al. (2007) . Another way to deal with dimensionality is feature extraction. Feature extraction is related to dimensionality reduction, which transforms data into a low-dimensional space. It should be noted, however, that feature selection techniques are different from feature extraction. Feature extraction creates new features from the original features using functional mapping, whereas feature selection returns a subset of the original features ( Motoda and Liu, 2002 ). There are a variety of techniques for feature extraction, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and f Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) (see  Hartmann, 2004 ). Feature extraction methods tend to be employed more frequently for unstructured data such as images, text and speech. Table 2  shows 31 reviewed articles employed feature selection or feature extraction. It was found that filter and wrapper feature selection methods were most regularly used. For filter methods, various metrics were used to rank the features, and for wrapper methods, heuristic search was a common choice.

snippets: 27.3.3 Feature selection techniques The process of feature selection is crucial to machine learning and data analysis. It entails selecting the most important and useful components from a dataset while eliminating unnecessary or redundant information. In addition to increasing the effectiveness and accuracy of machine learning models, this approach helps to simplify and minimize the dimensionality of the data. Each method for feature selection has advantages and disadvantages of its own. Fig. 2  shows the broad classification of the feature selection techniques. A common method for selecting appropriate features from a dataset is filter-based feature selection. It involves inspecting each feature's characteristics independent of the target variable. This approach often ranks and selects the most informative characteristics using statistical methods or scoring criteria. Another technique for selecting features called “wrapper-based feature selection” includes assessing subsets of features based on how well they perform when applied to a particular machine learning algorithm. It approaches feature selection as a search problem, testing various feature combinations and ranking them using predetermined evaluation criteria. In tree-based feature selection, the algorithm builds ensemble models or decision trees using the dataset, taking different features into account at each split. A feature's significance is measured by how much it contributes to lowering impurities or enhancing the tree's or ensemble's ability to make predictions. The importance of a feature is determined by how frequently it is used for splitting and how much is the impurity or performance improvement. In the proposed work, correlation-based, recursive feature elimination, and tree-based feature selection are used, which are the subcategories of filter-based, wrapper-based, and embedded-based feature selection techniques. The statistical relation between each feature in the dataset and the target feature is measured using correlation-based feature selection. Low correlation features are eliminated while the most significant features with high correlation coefficients are kept. The RFE approach, which recursively eliminates the least significant features based on the performance of the model, is one of the well-known wrapper-based feature selection techniques. There exist several iterations, and in each of them, the features that are less important are eliminated. Random forest ensemble learning machine learning model is used to extract the important features for a tree-based feature selection technique. Random forest is constructed with the help of multiple decision trees, and the results of their predictions help to provide a robust measure of feature importance. In summary, feature selection is a critical stage in enhancing the effectiveness of machine learning models.

concept: Modifying the target model is a viable strategy to defend against adversarial attacks, with various methods focusing on reducing model complexity and enhancing robustness.
Techniques such as model regularization, defensive distillation, and feature squeezing aim to simplify decision boundaries and reduce the search space for adversarial samples.
Advanced methods like deep contractive networks and DeepCloak introduce architectural changes to increase the difficulty of generating adversarial samples.
Ensemble learning and model diversity are emphasized as effective strategies to improve model robustness against adversarial attacks.
Data pre-processing is crucial for addressing class imbalance, with techniques like random sampling and variable elimination being essential for effective model training.
Model tuning and ensemble learning are key to improving model performance, particularly in complex datasets, by combining the strengths of multiple algorithms.
The choice of modeling techniques is critical, with a trend towards using advanced machine learning methods and ensemble approaches to capture complex patterns in data.
The integration of various machine learning models through stacking and tools like Super Learner demonstrates the growing importance of ensemble methods in achieving better predictive performance.

snippets: 4.2.2 Modifying the target model Besides modifying data, another solution to defend adversarial attacks is to directly modify the target classification model. Commonly used methods include: (1) model regularization   , which reduces the complexity of decision boundaries. Therefore, models can be well generalized on those adversarial samples which need to be carefully designed according to the landscape (usually complex) of the decision boundaries; (2) defensive distillation   , which was originally designed to transfer knowledge from a large model with high complexity to a small one, and was also proved powerful in defending adversarial attacks by substantially reducing the gradients used in generating adversarial samples; (3) feature squeezing   , which reduces the available search space to generate adversarial samples by coalescing multiple samples into a single one; (4) deep contractive network   , an end-to-end architecture based on contractive penalty in each layer, which significantly increases the amplitude of required perturbation to generate adversarial samples; (5) highly non-linear activations, which employ highly nonlinear and saturated neural networks, biologically inspired by the principles underlying nonlinear dendritic computation in neurons   ; (6) DeepCloak   , a defensive mechanism with an additional masking layer to remove those unnecessary features in a deep network, through which the effects of adding perturbations on irrelevant feature dimensions to generate adversarial samples were largely reduced; (7) ensemble of diverse models, which encourages diversity among individual models to improve the robustness of the ensemble model; (8) constraining the Lipschitz constant  [141–143] , a measure of the maximum gradient around a data point, which is the most important metric used in generating adversarial samples; and (9) model pruning   , which makes the pruning techniques aware of the training objective to enhance the model robustness so that both compressed and robust models can be trained effectively. A common concept of most methods listed above is to reduce the model complexity, by simplifying either the distribution in the feature space or the landscape of decision boundary. That is because a main factor to generate adversarial samples is the extremely complex manifold distribution of high-dimensional natural samples and a small perturbation to certain dimensions would largely change the location of a sample along the manifold surface.

snippets: 4.1 Data pre-processing The strategy of data pre-processing techniques is to pre-process the given imbalanced dataset and modify the data distribution to make use of the standard algorithms. We pre-process the datasets to modify the distribution, instead of directly using learning techniques to the presented datasets. These techniques have the following benefits: (1) This strategy can be utilized for any existing learning methods, (2) Selected models are biased to the targets of the researcher because the data distribution was already modified to fix these targets, and it is expected the models are most explainable in the circumstances of these targets. These techniques have the following drawbacks: 1- It is tough to connect the data distribution with the target loss function because mapping the data distribution into the proper new one is not easy, 2- The initial algorithm is based on the information presented by the user concerning which class value is usually known as the minority or positive class. So, It is tough to define which are the relevant observations and the “normal” samples, 3- It is tough to produce new synthetic samples, 4- For the generation of new synthetic samples, the target value of each synthetic sample was calculated as a weighted average of the target variable values of the two samples. So, it is tough to determine the value of the target variable in the synthetic samples. 4.1.1 Data pre-processing for classification (i) Random Sampling:  The available re-sampling techniques are designed based on different strategies, such as random over-sampling, random under-sampling, clustering algorithms, data cleaning approaches, and evolutionary algorithms. Under-sampling and over-sampling  [6,43–47]  are two main re-sampling techniques that can be used for data distribution. These techniques can be decreased and increased the influence of one class in the dataset to track-back the optimal misclassification costs, respectively. By eliminating samples from the dataset, it prevents the increase of the imbalance ratio. On the other hand, it has a bad influence on our performance because it can raise the likelihood of over-fitting (particularly for high over-sampling scores). Random over-sampling and under-sampling are two straightforward techniques for dealing with the issue of class imbalance learning  [43–47] . The additional computational cost of using over-sampling is unjustified as the performance obtained by under-sampling  [48–53] .

Finally, it is important, generally speaking, that the variables are not correlated between them; it usually adds more noise than knowledge to the learning process. Although there are models that take advantage of this correlation between variables, the number of them that do this is smaller. For this reason, during the preprocessing of the data, variables that have a very low variance or that are highly correlated within the datasets are eliminated. This part of the experimental design is critical as it is considered that to obtain satisfactory results it would be necessary to invest at least 80% of the time in data analysis in order to generate it and check that everything is correct. Model training Perhaps this is the most important part of the experimental design when using machine learning techniques. The first thing that should be done, even before the starting of this phase, is to check in the state of the art if there are previous results with the same dataset or if someone have already obtained good results with the algorithms that we plan to use. If the plan is to use a newly created dataset, it will be the researchers themselves the ones who must use simple machine learning models that allow them to evaluate, on the one hand, the performance of the most complex techniques and, on the other hand, the difficulty of the problem they are facing. As the machine learning algorithms learn by examples, it is necessary to train them with a set of samples and to validate the training phase with unknown examples. Therefore we can evaluate the predictive as well as the generalization capacities of the model. This can be done using cross-validation techniques that allow us to measure the degree of generalization of the algorithms during the training phase while predicting the performance of the techniques when new examples are passed. The most used technique is the 10-fold cross validation in which the data are divided into 10 subsets and 9 of them are used to train and the remaining one is used to validate iteratively, but without repeating the validation set. Each machine learning technique has different hyperparameters that must be optimized for each studied problem. An important point is that we should not mix the search process of the best hyperparameters of the models with the training process itself.

snippets: 4.7 Improving Model Performance Many learning algorithms include parameters that have to be specified by the user, where the user does not know, which set of parameters will give the best result. Finding this set of parameters is called  model tuning . Typically, the tuning of a model is performed by an inner cross validation or bootstrap loop; that is, each training dataset by resampling is further split into training and test sets, and the set of parameters giving the best performance in this inner loop are selected ( Kuhn and Johnson, 2013 ). Another very popular approach that aims at improving model performance is  model averaging  or  ensemble learning  ( Yang et al., 2010 ). Instead of just using the result of one learning algorithm, the results of multiple learning algorithms are combined to a so-called ensemble model. Ensemble classifiers were shown to perform better than any of the single ones ( Freund and Schapire, 1995 ). This is of particular interest when working with medical datasets that often have high dimensionality but may only have a few strongly predictive features of the target response and many weak ones. In this case, the effects of weak features may have to be combined to achieve good predictions. Averaging the predictions of a number of models that contain different sets of features aggregates the predictive power of their possibly weak features in the final prediction ( Schapire, 1990 ).

snippets: 3.2.5 Model building techniques Table 5  presents the machine learning modeling techniques used in the 38 articles. It is undeniable that traditional regression techniques are still the most widely used predictive model construction techniques. In 2009, the Menza team established the first HIV infection risk prediction model for men who have sex with men using Cox regression techniques. However, due to the complexity of medical data, traditional regression approaches fall short in accurately modeling its complexity [ 50 ]. In response, researchers have extensively utilized fully supervised machine learning methods such as random forest, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM). In recent years, medical models based on deep learning techniques exhibit the ability to capture intricate details and patterns within the data [ 51 ], researchers can harness the power of unlabeled data and delve deeper into the complex interplay of factors influencing HIV infection risk. There are a wide variety of machine learning modeling techniques, and choosing the best modeling technique has become a new problem. The first type of researchers choose to use multiple modeling techniques at the same time and select the model with the best predictive effect. For instance, Bao Y et al. and others used logistic regression, random forests, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) at the same time, and ultimately GBM showed the best predictive effect. The second type of researchers opts for stacking ensemble learning (an ensemble learning method that trains a new model based on the combined predictions of 2 or more previous machine learning models) has also been explored in the latest studies to generate better performs than individual machine learning techniques.  Fig. 4  depicts the twenty-six ensemble learning models developed by Xu X et al. These models are derived from various combinations of the five base learner models. Specifically, there are ten models that result from combinations of two distinct base learner models, ten additional models that incorporate combinations of three distinct base learner models, five models that are formed by combining four distinct base learner models, and one model that integrates all five base learner models. What's more, some scholars have established a tool called Super Learner which is an R-based tool that applies ensemble learning by integrating multiple weighted classifiers, leveraging cross-validation techniques. snippets: 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). Raw data usually contain noisy and unreliable data that can affect training and analysis. Moreover, datasets used in intrusion detection are characterized by high dimensionality, making it more difficult to discover knowledge during training. To build high-performance detectors requires efficient preprocessing. Fig. 4  summarizes the common data preprocessing methods used in intrusion detection, including data cleaning, imbalance learning, data transformation, feature selection, feature extraction, and Visualization ( RQ2(a) ). The above methods preprocess the data from different perspectives to enable the analysis model to better learn useful information from the data. In order to study the technical characteristics of different methods, we summarize their implementation principles and applications to answer  RQ2(b) . a ) Data cleaning Data cleaning corrects corrupt or inaccurate records. Quality criteria may include the following. • Validity. Data might have to be of a certain type, such as Boolean or numeric. • Accuracy. Data must conform to the situation. For example, outliers may exist due to the recording process. Accuracy is difficult to guarantee through data cleaning because real data sources are needed for validation. • Completeness. Some data may have unknown or missing values. Completeness issues are generally resolved through default values, setting zeros, or removal. • Uniformity. Inconsistency occurs when there are conflicts in a dataset. For example, a source IP may differ between two receivers. Fixing this type of problem requires the determination of which datum is most reliable. Data analysis based on means, standard deviations, or clustering algorithms can reveal errors, whose values can sometimes be set to a mean or other statistical measure. b ) Imbalanced learning A sample with different proportions of positive and negative cases will lead to a bias in the learning process toward the higher proportion. For example, in the extreme case of a dataset with 95 %  positive and 5 %  negative cases, the model will have no practical meaning. Since attacks tend to be sparse, datasets in intrusion detection are often unbalanced. The following methods may improve performance. • Sampling methods.

snippets: 4.2 Detecting false data attacks on state estimation Data integrity attacks have become one major threat to the power control system and the SE process. It becomes more likely for attackers to make control centers do wrong decisions through manipulations of various SG measurements ( Pan et al., 2018 ). According to the reviewed papers, we classify the ML-based detection algorithms on SE into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning methods. Supervised learning:  Similar to NTL detection methods, there are many supervised algorithms that have been used for detecting FDI in SE, such as  Ozay et al. (2015), Yan et al. (2016) . A recent work by  Jacob Sakhnini (2019)  analyzed the performance of several popular supervised ML algorithms combined with different heuristic feature selection techniques. Through testing and comparisons on these algorithms in FDI detection, the authors concluded that SVM and KNN algorithms can achieve better accuracy than ANN. The authors also indicated that ANN is expected to have better performance in larger systems. Unsupervised learning:  Considering a more realistic scenario, where supervised methods are not useful to detect compromised unlabeled data. Ahmed et al. (2019)  recently proposed an isolation forest-based unsupervised detection method. Because the compromised data points are much fewer than normal data points, they can be easily isolated. Evaluations on standard IEEE test systems ( Zimmerman et al., 2010 ) show that the developed approach shows better performance than other existing detection schemes, such as SVM and KNN. Recently, some works investigate the anomaly detection method for PMUs data. As it is difficult to get the real labels over the fast data streams of PMUs,  Zhou et al. (2018)  adopted unsupervised ensemble learning as a detector. Wang et al. (2018b)  developed a distributed detection framework by using a deep auto-encoder model. The reliabilities of these methods were verified through case studies on real world and simulated data. However, it is impractical to make use of entire historical PMUs data to train the model. Further studies are required to discover valuable measurements from the massive historical records efficiently. Reinforcement learning:  In reality, some smart attackers may have the ability to adjust their strategies according to actions and gains. Recent studies have shown that some FDI methods developed based on certain data-driven strategies are unidentifiable ( Yu and Chin, 2015; Kim et al., 2014 ).

snippets: 3.2.1 Conventional machine learning Integrity attacks are recognized most familiar types for attacks treated by ML experts. This reflects the fact that this type is the most important one in guaranteeing secure connectivity. Bhusal  et al .   made a study on attacks detection in voltage regulation that could disturb voltage control algorithm (i.e. malicious control). They, therefore, investigated the training of small-scale ML architecture that includes RF and LR algorithms for diagnosing transmission lines in a SG network. Two datasets/systems have been involved in this work. Accordingly, a 240-node real distribution system located in Midwest USA    and the IEEE 123-node simulation model were chosen for the process of ML model reconstruction and evaluation   . The first system contains sets of three feeders supplied by a 69 kV substation. This system has a total of 23 miles of main power conductors, which provides power to over 1100 customers. The second system features are overhead and underground lines, four voltage regulators, four shunt capacitor banks, multiple sectioning and coupling switches, and an unbalanced load with constant current, power, and impedance patterns that allow total active and reactive loads of 3490 kW and 1925 kV, respectively. This makes their data support their conclusion of ML model explainability based on realistic results. Soltan  et al .   investigated two types of attacks on a SG, which can remotely activate switches (i.e., tripping), namely, disconnection of lines and blocking measurements that attempt to reach the control center. The investigated ML model is, in this case, a Probabilistic Bayesian Regression (PBR) model used to detect different classes. In their study, they followed a similar methodology of attack deployment using the DC power flow model as in their previous work in   . More specifically, a linearized DC power flow model was used. It is typically used as an approximation for a nonlinear AC power flow model when studying electrical network vulnerabilities. Their PBR approach achieves great performance, especially when it fits into the analysis of malicious controls, which is a very important aspect of data integrity. An integrity attack detection-based Denial of Service (DoS) is discussed in the work of Wang  et al .  . SVM and DT are used to train an ML model as a particular agent. Many agents have thereafter been cloned to make sure that several combinations of hyperparameters have been scanned.

snippets: ML can detect and prevent intrusions by analyzing network patterns and anomalies before they can cause harm. 3. Predictive maintenance for EnFV components: ML can be used to analyze historical data on EnFV components, such as battery health, motor performance, and wear and tear indicators, to predict when these components are likely to fail ( Theissler et al., 2021; Zahra et al., 2021 ). This predictive maintenance capability allows for proactive replacement of components before they lead to malfunctions or safety hazards. 4. Secure vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication: ML can play a crucial role in securing V2X communication, which enables EnFVs to exchange information with other vehicles, infrastructure, and pedestrians ( Lipu et al., 2022 ). ML models can analyze V2X messages to detect malicious data injections, spoofing attempts, or attempts to disrupt communication channels. 5. User behavior analysis for EnFV security: ML can analyze user behavior patterns, such as driving habits, access patterns, and interaction with vehicle systems, to identify anomalies that may indicate unauthorized usage or compromised user accounts ( Xiao et al., 2019 ). This behavioral analysis can help prevent unauthorized access and misuse of EnFVs. These examples illustrate how ML improves EnFV security by providing real-time threat detection, predictive maintenance, and enhanced secure communication. As ML techniques advance, their impact on EnFV security will grow. 4.1.2 Factors affecting ML-based EnFV security solutions Several factors can impact the effectiveness, reliability, and acceptability of ML-based security solutions as below ( Rasool et al., 2022; Shaukat et al., 2020d ). 1. Data Quality: Data quality is a critical factor in ML, as it directly affects the performance and generalizability of ML models. In the context of EnFV security, data quality issues can manifest in various forms:  • Incompleteness: Missing or incomplete data can lead to biased or inaccurate models, potentially overlooking important patterns or anomalies. • Inaccuracy: Errors or inconsistencies in data can introduce noise into the training process, resulting in less reliable models for detecting genuine threats. • Bias: Bias in the underlying data can lead to biased models that unfairly discriminate against certain groups or conditions. Addressing data quality issues requires careful data collection, cleaning, and preprocessing.

Data Pre-processing : Pre-Processing is a crucial step in ML pipelines to ensure data quality for model effectiveness. It involves various tasks, including handling missing data by substituting with median, mean, or mode; identifying and removing duplicate entries to prevent bias, dropping unnecessary features, and encoding categorical variables using one hot or label encoding. ML Models : The pre-processed dataset, obtained after pre-processing the raw data, undergoes evaluation using various ML models. The results, encompassing accuracy, True Positive (TP) rate, False Positive (FP) rate, mean absolute error, and Model Build-up Time (MBT), are assessed. To outperform others, a model should exhibit high accuracy and TP rate, along with low FP rate, mean absolute error, and MBT. The data is classified into Binary and multiclass, which includes Six-class and Fifteen-class classification. Various models from different model categories are applied and tested. The model category defines the specific algorithm or methodology utilized for evaluation. The ML model categories and their respective models utilized in our study are: 1. Rule Based models : The field of Rule-Based Machine Learning (RBML) includes techniques for identifying, learning, and evolving ‘rules’ for the storage, processing, and application of information. These interpretable and transparent models are appropriate for jobs that need rationality. In contrast to conventional rule-based systems, RBML uses learning algorithms in place of manual rule creation to automatically find rules from data [ 11 ]. • Decision Table: This decision backing tool depicts decision logic using a table of conditions and corresponding actions. The table lists the associated action or result for each row, which represents a distinct set of criteria. • JRip (Java RIPper): It uses the RIPPER algorithm—Repeated Incremental Pruning to Produce Error Reduction—as its foundation. JRip classifies instances by repeatedly developing rules, which are subsequently pruned to increase precision and simplify the algorithm. • OneR (One Rule): This method chooses a single rule based on a single data set attribute, usually the one that yields the greatest accuracy when applied alone. Next, new instances are categorized using the chosen rule and the attribute value. • PART (Partial Rule-Based Classifier): It combines the advantages of decision tree and rule-based methodologies.

Data preprocessing Since machine learning algorithms are expected to be able to achieve results with a high degree of performance and accuracy, they should be able to extract meaningful information from the available data. In addition to this, as far as possible, a subset of examples should always be safeguarded in order to validate the performance of the algorithm, data unknown by the model. Until now, we know that machine learning techniques are capable of obtaining the same results as clinical ones, even being able to improve them in some cases, especially when complex and large heterogeneous datasets are integrated that escape the human understanding. It is critical therefore to take care of the preprocessing phase of the data and to take into account that, in biomedical computing, it is quite common to find incomplete or simply missing data, as well as uncertainty and errors ( Dasu and Johnson, 2003 ). In heterogeneous datasets it is also quite common to have very different dimensions between datasets. It is necessary to normalize between the variables of each subset as well as between subsets in order to mitigate the differences of scales that could make machine learning algorithms focus on the variables with a higher dimension during the knowledge extraction. In biomedical informatics in particular, it is very conventional that the data present different scales and sizes, making the learning process difficult on equality of conditions. Although there are many different approaches, the most used are normalization and standardization of data. Both approaches have their advantages and disadvantages and none is the only solution for any type of problem. Therefore it is necessary to analyze the data before applying any preprocess to understand what needs have each particular data type. In case we have outliers in the data if we preprocess the data by making a normalization between zero and one, we would reduce to a very small scale the useful data, losing capacity of generalization by the algorithms. Obviously this is an unwanted behavior that we should try not to reproduce. In the case of choosing to standardize the data, each variable will have a mean of zero and a standard deviation equal to one at the end of the process. During this phase the number of cases could also be balanced in a classification problem.

snippets: Several data preprocessing techniques have been used before feeding data to the BGL prediction models: 23 papers out of 32 used data preprocessing techniques while nine papers did not specify if such methods have been applied. Data preprocessing techniques used in the selected studies can be categorized into three tasks: data cleaning, data reduction and data transformation. Table 6  shows the preprocessing tasks and techniques used by the selected studies as well as the datasets on which they were applied. Data cleaning:  These techniques aim to handle missing data, eliminate outliers, remove noise and correct inconsistencies. Data cleaning preprocessing techniques were used by 50% of the selected papers (16 out of 32) where missing data handling ranked first with 12 papers, followed by noise elimination with seven papers. Several missing data handling techniques have been used where imputation using linear interpolation was the most adopted in seven papers. Forward filling, filling with zeros and simple removal of rows with missing data were used twice each. The remaining missing data handling techniques were all used once each. With regard to noise elimination, simply removing outliers from the dataset was the most common noise elimination technique by defining thresholds and removing any rows with values out of the defined ranges. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD), extreme value analysis, and moving average filter were all used once each. Data reduction:  This category of techniques intends to reduce the data dimensionality by selecting and extracting a minimum set of features to decrease the model computation time without losing the data integrity. Among the selected studies, 12 papers (37.5%) applied data reduction where feature selection was used by seven papers and feature extraction by six papers. Feature selection was performed using different techniques where correlation coefficient method was the most adopted in 3 papers followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with 2 papers. Gini index, information gain, Lasso regression, PCA, Random Forest and Sequential backward selection (SBS) were all used once each. Concerning feature extraction, all the techniques were used once each. Data transformation:  The purpose of these techniques is to transform the data into a suitable form for mining and training the model. 40.625% of the selected studies (13 papers) used these techniques where reframing was used in nine studies, followed by normalization in six papers and categorical data encoding in one paper.

snippets: 1 Introduction Speech signals have been widely used in developing intelligent automated systems. It refers to the ability of the system to understand the spoken input and extract information from it by identifying the essential features of the underlying speech signal. The research directions in this domain envisions smart systems that can respond to audio and visual inputs of their surroundings and provide meaningful inferences. Speech analysis and modelling can be viewed as a combination of time-series and sequence processing task   , as the speech signal is essentially a continuous distribution of energy that varies with time. On an abstract level, when grouped for a particular period of time, this energy forms an utterance that basically represents a word or a phonetic sound. A salient feature of the speech signals is that they cannot be defined completely using a rule-based approach since it is impossible to account for the variations in phonetics that are unique to every person   . Another challenging aspect in the processing of speech signals is the presence of noise and other unwanted background signals    that are often interlaced with the primary speech signal. Due to this aspect, it becomes important to design effective denoising systems that can separate the primary signals from the noise. The review study    presents an overview of deep learning methods that are used for speech denoising. Due to the complexity and variations that arise in the analysis of speech signals, machine learning (ML) has been seen as an effective tool to counter these issues. Multiple studies have been carried out to use ML for creating smart denoising and sequence processing systems  [5–7] , which can separate the noise from the base signal and extract meaningful linguistic elements from the same. Nonetheless, as speech signals are essentially a sequence of utterances, the models used for their analysis comprise of well-known memory elements such as long short term memory (LSTMs), recurrent neural network (RNNs) and gated recurrent unit (GRUs)   . As of recent, advanced sequence-to-sequence architectures have been applied to this task, which includes the widely accepted transformer architecture    for achieving state-of-the-art results. Another novel approach that has been adopted is to use the techniques defined in the domain of computer vision to process the speech signals directly through their spectrogram representation.

snippets: 2 Background This section discusses fundamentals of speech signals and the tasks that can be attributed involving speech signals. 2.1 Speech Signals Speech signals are one dimensional functions of pressure. They can be viewed as a continuous distribution of energy varying with time. Speech signals are characterized by a high variability between different individuals due to the differences in accents, dialects and native language   . Due to this property, speech signals serve as important markers for uniquely identifying different attributes among individuals, apart from serving an important means of information transfer between them. Speech signal has multiple characteristic features which help humans in many aspects. There are wide variety of tasks that can be accomplished with the help of speech signal analysis   . Most typical of these tasks are discussed below: • Emotion Recognition:  Emotion recognition has gained importance in recent times to analyze the emotional state of an individual. Using speech signals, one can automatically detect the emotional state (i.e, happy, angry, sad, surprise, etc.) of a speaker and utilize this information to achieve a number of objectives such as generating personalized responses according to a person’s mood or analyzing reception towards a certain item. The domain of emotion recognition is further divided into two categories, i.e., emotion identification and emotion verification  [77–79] . The surveys    review the existing deep learning architectures for speech emotion recognition task. • Speaker Recognition:  The process of recognizing a speaker from his/her speech falls under the purview of automatic speaker recognition. Speaker identification is one part of speech recognition where the task is to determine the speaker belonging to a set of known voices or speakers. On the other hand, speaker authentication/verification task involves determining the authenticity of a speaker’s claim of who he/she is. There are several applications with speaker recognition techniques in the literature such as transaction authentication, speech data management and access control   . • Age and Gender Recognition:  The task of determining the age (child, adult, etc) of the speaker via his/her voice is applied in many domains such as security   , age group classification    and others   . • Language Recognition:  The aim of this task is to determine under what category (English, French and German, etc.) a given language can be placed. One major challenge in language recognition is to discriminate between two closely related languages, such as Serbian and Croatian.

snippets: 5 Speech emotion recognition 5.1 Preprocessing Preprocessing is the very first step after collecting data that will be used to train the classifier in a SER system. Some of these preprocessing techniques are used for feature extraction, while others are used to normalize the features so that variations of speakers and recordings would not affect the recognition process. 5.1.1 Framing Signal framing, also known as speech segmentation, is the process of partitioning continuous speech signals into fixed length segments to overcome several challenges in SER. Emotion can change in the course of speech since the signals are non-stationary. However, speech remains invariant for a sufficiently short period, such as 20 to 30 ms. By framing the speech signal, this quasi-stationary state can be approximated, and local features can be obtained. Additionally, the relation and information between the frames can be retained by deliberately overlapping 30% to 50% of these segments. Continuous speech signals restrain the usage of processing techniques such as Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for feature extraction in applications such as SER. Consequently, fixed size frames are suitable for classifiers, such as Artificial Neural Networks, while retaining the emotion information in speech. 5.1.2 Windowing After framing the speech signal, the next phase is generally applying a window function to frames. The windowing function is used to reduce the effects of leakages that occurs during Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) of data caused by discontinuities at the edge of the signals. Typically a Hamming window is used, as given in  Eq.  1 , where the window size is  M  for the frame  w ( n ). (1) w ( n ) = 0.54 − 0.46 cos ( 2 π n M − 1 ) 0 ≤ n ≤ M − 1 5.1.3 Voice activity detection An utterance consists of three parts; voiced speech, unvoiced speech, and silence. Voiced speech is generated with the vibration of vocal folds that creates periodic excitation to the vocal tract during the pronunciation of phonemes which are perceptually distinct units of sound that distinguish one word from another; such as bag, tag, tab. On the other hand, unvoiced speech is the result of air passing through a constriction in the vocal tract, producing transient and turbulent noises that are aperiodic excitations of the vocal tract. Due to its periodic nature, voiced speech can be identified and extracted.

snippets: Noise removal techniques:  Some popular techniques for noise removal are: logMMSE   , Karnuhen-Loeve transform (KLT) decomposition   , spectral subtraction   , and wiener filter    for speech enhancement. Vasquez-Correa et al.    evaluated logMMSE and KLT decomposition for SER. These techniques need the silence regions of fixed duration for characterizing the background noise. Their experiments did not produce any improvement in FAU-Aibo database due to the absence of such silence regions. The WPT and SSWT-based features improved the results after applying logMMSE algorithm for white, street, and cafeteria noises. Chenchah and Lachiri    used speech enhancement techniques such as spectral subtraction, wiener filter, and MMSE for real-world speech signals (airport, babble, and cafeteria). The spectral subtraction and MMSE methods are robust against airport and babble noises for emotion recognition. 2. Robust features:  Recently, some works    have focused on extracting robust features that are not affected by noise. Chenchah and Lachiri    proposed power normalized cepstral coefficients (PNCC) features and its variants for SER. The PNCC features are robust against the car, train, airport, and babble noises. The authors compared PNCC and its variants with the well-known MFCC and perceptual linear prediction (PLP) coefficients. The PNCC features differ from the MFFC features for the following reasons. First, PNCC simulates cochlea behavior based on equivalent rectangular bandwidth by gammatone auditory filters. Second, PNCC utilizes an extra step that is the subtraction of the medium-magnitude bias from the output of the gammatone auditory filters. The bias level was computed based on the ratio of the arithmetic to geometric mean (AM-GM ratio) of the medium-time magnitude. Finally, the power function non-linearity was achieved with 1/15 exponent. Mansour and Lachiri    showed the robustness of the MFCC-shifted-delta-cepstral (SDC) coefficients features for airport noise. The author claimed that MFCC-SDC outperformed the traditional MFCC and LPCC features in both the clean and noisy environments.

snippets: (1) Noise cleaning  removes the noise from the app data that is irrelevant or meaningless to research goals. There are several approaches to remove noisy data, and here we summarize three ones, including observation-based, distribution-based, and clustering-based approach. First, the observation-based approach removes noisy data based on researchers’ observation and experiences, especially for incomplete and abnormal data samples that are not difficult to identify. For example, the data of the users who did not complete the questionnaires were removed   , and only the users with complete questionnaires were taken into consideration. Pre-installed apps were manually identified and removed from users’ installed app lists, since they cannot reflect users’ needs and interests and would bias the correlation between users and apps   . Although the observation-based approach is fairly simple to conduct, it is difficult to find the noisy data samples that are hidden in the normal data samples. Second, the distribution-based approach is based on the distribution of a statistical dataset, such as normal distribution and long-tail distribution, to detect the noisy data samples that are far away from most data samples in the dataset. For example, Malmi et al.    focused on the apps frequently used by users and discarded the ones used by less than ten users to remove all personally identifiable information. In   , the users who used their smartphones less frequently were taken as outliers and removed, and the ones that used fewer than 5 or more than 80 apps in total over the month of data collection were also removed. In spite of the simplicity to implement, it is not easy for the distribution-based approach to determine the boundary to separate out the noisy data samples. Third, clustering-based approach identifies noisy data samples as a by-product of the clustering process, where small clusters, that are far away from other major clusters, are taken as sets of noisy samples. Although it can detect more complex outliers, the clustering-based approach is not so frequently used in this field compared with the other two approaches, since it is sensitive to the choice of clustering algorithms and has difficulties in deciding which clusters should be identified as outliers   . (2) App data transformation  converts the raw data into understandable, unified, and ready-to-use form. Some app datasets were collected in a complex form which make it difficult to use for profiling.

concept: Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a powerful supervised learning technique used for classification and regression tasks, focusing on finding the optimal hyperplane that separates different classes of data. It effectively handles both linear and non-linear data through the use of kernel functions, making it suitable for complex datasets, including those with imbalanced classes.

Bayesian Networks utilize probabilistic graphical models to represent variables and their conditional dependencies, making them effective for modeling uncertainty and integrating information from various sources. They are particularly useful in anomaly detection by categorizing probabilistic independencies among variables.

Decision Trees (DTs) are straightforward to construct and interpret, allowing for quick classification of unknown data. However, they are prone to overfitting and can be sensitive to small changes in training data, which may affect the decision rules significantly.

Neural Networks, including Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), are designed to mimic biological neural networks, enabling them to process complex data inputs and learn from them. ANNs consist of interconnected processing units (neurons) that can model intricate functions, while CNNs are specialized for tasks like image recognition and computer vision.

The integration of various machine learning techniques, such as SVM, Bayesian Networks, and Neural Networks, highlights the versatility and adaptability of these models in addressing complex problems, including anomaly detection and classification in diverse fields.

snippets: b. Support Vector Machine Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a statistical learning theory that classifies data by establishing a set of support vectors that are part of the labeled training data. Standard SVM is a supervised learning approach. However, it can be adapted to unsupervised learning as well. The major objective of SVM is to find the optimal hyper-plane for the classification of the unseen data points. A set of hyper-planes are generated to separate the feature vectors ensuring a maximum separation. The classification problem is considered as a quadratic optimization problem by SVM. They integrate the generalization control by placing an upper bound on the margin among the various classes in order to avoid the “curse of dimensionality” which makes it suitable for dynamic and big data   . SVM can be implemented in the classification of linear, non-linear data and single and multi-class classification. Various classifiers such as OC-SVM, multi-class SVM, radial SVM, and least-square SVM are employed to enhance the ability of the classifier to discriminate the non-linear and linear data. Non-linear data are usually classified using kernel function by mapping data to higher dimensions for better classification. Fan et al.    proposed magnetic anomaly detection using SVM. A model is designed using SVM with kernel function (radial basis function). The input of the model is analyzed and determined by using features, such as magnetic entropy and orthonormal basis function energy, as the magnetic anomaly. Using the dataset with magnetic signals, model is trained and applied to the raw magnetic signal for anomaly detection. In   , discusses the detection of anomaly and intrusion in depth. c. Bayesian Network Bayesian Network represents a set of variables using the probabilistic graphical model and probabilistic independencies. The information from various variables is integrated and estimated based on the expectancy of an event that belongs to the specific class. They are efficient techniques to model uncertainty using probability. A directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is represented in a discrete random variable containing a Conditional Probability Table (CPT) where every node reflects the state of random variables. The probability of the node existing in a particular state is determined by CPT. According to the degree of probabilistic independencies between variables, Bayesian networks for anomaly detection are categorized into three groups as summarized in  Table 3 .

The culmination of this process yields a potent model derived from the collective results of all individual weak models. RUSBoost has exhibited proficiency in addressing CI quandaries, particularly in scenarios where the minority class is scanty and the majority class is voluminous. 5.2.13 Support Vector Machine Support Vector Machine (SVM)    is a supervised learning technique tailored for both classification and regression challenges. In its essence, SVM identifies a hyperplane – a linear demarcation – in a multidimensional space to optimally segregate data into distinct classes. Notably, the data points in closest proximity to this hyperplane are termed ‘support vectors’ and play a pivotal role in delineating the class boundaries. Once this boundary is established, classifying new data becomes straightforward, contingent on which side of the hyperplane the data resides. For regression tasks, SVM strives to pinpoint a hyperplane that most congruently aligns with the data. In scenarios riddled with CI, SVM proves invaluable. It excels at discerning the spatial region inhabited by the minority class, facilitating the synthesis of new samples essential for dataset equilibration. SVM seamlessly collaborates with other Data Manipulation (DM) techniques in this endeavor. Additionally, its binary incarnation, the one-class SVM (1-SVM), serves as a potent outlier detection tool, enhancing the classification of minority class instances.

snippets: • DTs are easy to construct, they are fast in classifying unknown data, provide interpretation in many applications, they can handle both numerical and categorical data, the accuracy rates  are generally comparable to other popular ML techniques, and as they do not include distance measure, they may not need feature normalization or standardization. • Some disadvantages include the following: they easily overfit, large trees may be difficult to interpret, and small changes in the training data can drastically change the decision rule. 6.5 Support vector machine 6.5.1 General concept Support vector machine (SVM) belong to the group of linear classifiers, where a hyperplane acting like a separator is drawn to separate two classes   . The two classes are labeled as positive and negative, and sometimes as 1 and 0. If separation is linear, the hyperplane is used, and if separation is nonlinear, kernel functions are used to fit the criteria. It is a supervised method of classification. The linear SVM is shown in  Fig. 6.13 . The diagram shows two classes here, C1 and C2. The dotted line here represents the hyperplane which is trying to separate two classes. The solid blue (black in print version) lines are passing through the features lying closest to the hyperplane. The distance between the dotted hyperplane and solid blue (black in print version) line is represented as “d,” and the distance between two solid blue (black in print version) lines is called as margin. The margin is twice the distance “d” of the hyperplane. The features lying on the hyperplane are called as “support vectors”. W  is the weight vector of the hyperplane. The main aim of SVM is to increase the margin as big as possible. If that margin is big, it becomes easy for a machine to discriminate between two classes and the accuracy rate becomes high. Mathematically, let us have  T  sets of training samples as follows:  [ ( x 1 , y 1 ) , ( x 2 , y 2 ) , ( x 3 , y 3 ) … ( x T , y T ) ]  where  x i = ( x 1 , x 2 , … , x T )  is an input vector in a real values space and  y i  is the class label or output value which could be either −1 or +1.  +1 shows the positive class and −1 shows the negative class.

snippets: 4.2.1 Neural network A neural network is a computational learning system that uses a network of functions to understand and translate a data input of one form into the desired output, usually in another form     . Neural networks, in this context, refer to a set of neurons that could be artificial. Several layers of linked nodes make up a neural network. Each node is a perceptron, which works similarly to multiple linear regression. The perceptron converts the signal from a multiple linear regression into a non-linear activation function   . snippets: 2.2 Artificial neural networks (ANNs) Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are parallel calculation algorithms, which consist of many linked processing units. These processing units have a very simple structure and are able to convert an input signal to an output signal with an activation function in correspondence with the biological neurons. Parallel processing of a large number of inputs simultaneously in a hierarchical structure enables the simulation of several complex functions based on input data. The Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) term has been established earlier than the term of Artificial Intelligence (AI). First attempts on utilizing ANNs was in the form of simplified neuron models and date back to the early 1940s ( McCulloch & Pitts, 1943 ). The concept of ANN learning ( Bergenti, Giezes, & Zambonelli, 2004 , Wiener, 1948 ) and more specifically, the idea of developing different types of computing systems with intelligence ability comparable to that of biological organisms starts circa 1950 ( Von Neumann, 1958 ). The term “artificial” is used to indicate the effort of simulating the structure of biological neural networks. This trend is justified by the particular ability of Biological Neural Networks to process large amounts of data and to draw conclusions in a really short period of time. The benefits of applying those Biological Neural Networks make them ideal for predictive computing and data processing architectures. Particular features related to the structure of neural networks are their ability to learn, store information, generalize to new data, and group concepts. The human brain comprises of at least one hundred billion neurons that are interconnected by dense network elongated structures ( Fig. 2.1 ). Stimulations emanating from specialized cell structures that can transduce environmental signals to electrical current (sensory cells) are intercepted by dendrites that transmit the information through induction of electrical impulses. The signals transmitted from one to another neuron in such a way that the information is passing quickly through the whole neural assembly allowing the attention to critical signals or deciding to overlook if it is not critical ( Fig. 2.1 ). The term, ANN models refers often to the MultiLayer Perceptron (MLP), as a biomimetic model trying to reverse engineer biological network systems for constructing neural computing particles. The simplest structure of an ANN includes only one hidden layer, however, it demonstrates strong similarity to the network of neurons in a brain due to its vast interconnections between the neurons in consecutive layers.

snippets: 5.2 Summary of existing efforts (Machine learning techniques) 5.2.1 Artificial neural network (ANN) An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model consisting of various processing elements known as neurons and a scaled connection between them called weights [ 94 ]. Various forms of artificial neural networks are used, but the network topology could be generally categorized as feed-forward networks (SLP, MLP, and radial basis function) and recurrent/feedback networks (Elman net, Kohonen’s SOM, and Hopfield Networks). The feed- forward network is the most common topology, where it consists of a connection between different neurons that are directed only in one direction (forward) from the earlier stage to the next level. Recurrent or feedback network topology involves at least one feedback loop in the architecture [ 94 ]. Both of these network topologies have been successfully employed in modeling and for the prediction of BG levels in type 1 diabetes patients. Regarding the feed-forward network, for example, Allam et al. and others [ 18 , 44 , 45 ] have developed a feed-forward neural network from CGM data using the back propagation Levenberg-Marquardt optimization training algorithm. Pappada et al. and others [ 46 , 47 , 65 ] have also proposed time-lagged feed-forward neural networks trained through a back-propagation gradient descent algorithm, which is capable of storing previous values of data within the network. Zainuddin et al. [ 29 ] have proposed a wavelet neural network, integrating different wavelet families as an activation function for modeling BG dynamics trained through pseudo-inverse with fixed parameter initialization. Zarkogianni et al. [ 27 ] developed a seven-layer neuro-fuzzy network using wavelets as an activation function and Gaussian function as a membership function trained through a gradient-based algorithm with an adaptive learning rate. Compared to these shallow networks, Mhaskar et al. [ 52 ] proposed a semi-supervised deep learning neural network with a judge predictor based on the function approximation on data-defined manifolds, using diffusion polynomials. Baghdadi et al. [ 19 ] implemented a radial basis function network using Gaussian function in the hidden layer neuron.

concept: Regression algorithms are essential for predicting continuous outcomes based on independent variables, with various types including Decision Trees (DT), Linear Regression (LR), and Neural Networks (NN).
Decision Trees are effective for classification and regression but are unstable and struggle with continuous variables. They are widely used in IoT security applications.
Linear Regression is straightforward and less complex but assumes a linear relationship, making it less effective in the presence of outliers and not suitable for all practical applications.
Neural Networks can handle complex, nonlinear data and consist of interconnected layers, making them versatile for various tasks.
Ridge and Lasso regression are specialized forms of linear regression that help prevent overfitting through regularization.
Classification techniques, including clustering and decision tree-based methods, are crucial for labeling datasets, with algorithms like K-NN and Random Forest being prominent.
Logistic Regression is a binary classification method that predicts probabilities using the sigmoid function, applicable in various fields such as healthcare and image processing.
Support Vector Machines (SVM) are powerful binary classifiers that maximize the decision boundary for improved classification confidence.

The choice of regression or classification technique depends on the nature of the data and the specific requirements of the task, with simpler models often outperforming complex ones in certain scenarios.

snippets: 4.1.2 Regression algorithms Regression algorithms investigate the relationship between independent features (variables) and a dependent variable for predicting the output. The output can either be a continuous value or a real number based on the input. DTs, NNs, and ELs are the types of regression algorithms which are discussed in below points: • Decision Trees (DT):  DTs are better classifiers which can also perform regression tasks similar to SVM. DTs can predict the value of a target variable by learning simple decision based rules. These rules are derived from the extracted features. For a given sample, initially an individual decision tree will perform a random selection process through the bootstrap resampling mechanism and the obtained samples will be employed for constructing a decision tree. In a decision tree, each leaf node is provided with a class label and the non terminal nodes which consists of internal and root nodes, are incorporated with certain feature test constraints to distinguish different features with different characteristics. DTs are widely used in IoT security to classify different types of attacks such as intrusion detection   , user centric security solutions    and interference recognition   . One of the prominent drawbacks of DTs is associated with its stability. DTs are highly unstable and they fail to handle continuous variables and hence generate less effective results. • Linear Regression:  Linear regression (LR) is used for analyzing the relationship between different input and output variables. LR models predict a target value based on independent variables. One of the prominent prerequisites for LR algorithm is the Markov property which states that the present instance is dependent on the previous instances. The preliminary aim of the LR model is to achieve an accurate estimation of the LR parameters by reducing the error between the estimated value and the actual value   . LR algorithms are simple to implement and are less complex compared to other ML models. However, the performance of LR models is affected by the presence of outliers. Besides, LR models assume a linear relationship between the input and output variables, which is not suitable for practical applications. • Neural Networks:  The architecture of NNs resembles the structure of the neurons in the human brain. NNs can handle complex and nonlinear data without affecting the performance efficiency   . Neural network models are either connected in a hierarchical manner or are interconnected with other layers in the network. In general, NNs consist of three main layers namely an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer.
