snippets: Ridge regression  is another special regression type that performs normal regression and generalizes the model  by regularizing to prevent the model overfitting. Generalized linear models are basic implementations that can be used to model data that forecasts various types of output responses ( Sarkar et al., 2018 ). 3.5.3 Linear models In machine learning,  linear models  are of particular relevance since they are simple. Linear models are  parametric , which means that they have a fixed form with a small number of numeric parameters that can be learned from data. Since linear models are stable, small variations in the training data have only limited impact on the learned model. Linear models are less likely to overfit the training data than some other models since they have comparatively few parameters. The reverse of this sometimes results in  underfitting . Moreover, linear models have low variance but high bias. Such models are generally desirable once you have limited data and need to avoid overfitting. Linear models exist for all predictive tasks, including classification, probability estimation, and regression ( Flach, 2012 ). A simple linear regression model assumes that the regression function E(Y |X) is linear in the inputs X 1 ,. . . ,X p . Linear models were developed primarily in the precomputer era of statistics, but there are still good reasons to study and use them even in today’s computer age. These are simple and mostly include a summary of how the inputs influence the output. We can sometimes outperform fancy nonlinear models for predictive purposes, especially in cases with small training instances, poor signal-to-noise ratio, or sparse data. Finally, linear approaches can be extended to input transformations, and this extends their scope considerably. Such generalizations are sometimes referred to as forms of basic function ( Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman, & Franklin, 2005 ). 3.5.4 The perceptron If there is a linear decision boundary dividing the classes, the labeled data is termed  linearly separable . The least-squares classifier can find a dividing decision boundary if any exists, but it is not guaranteed. A linear classifier, which can accomplish exact separation on linearly separable data, is the  perceptron , initially proposed as a simple neural network. The perceptron repeats over the training set, updating the weight vector each time it comes across an incorrectly classified example ( Flach, 2012 ).

snippets: In the case of a medical diagnosis, a wrong decision may result in inappropriate or lack of treatment, and it is preferable for the classifier to reject and defer a decision to a human expert in cases of doubt. Because of variations in gender, age, or accent, several people pronounce the same word in different ways, which makes this task rather difficult. The best way to create a language model is to learn it from a large amount of data. The applications of machine learning to  natural language processing  are continually expanding. Spam filtering  is one in which spam generators on one side and filters on the other side keep generating more and more clever ways to outwit each other. Document analysis is another exciting example, such as analyzing posts or blogs on social networking sites to extract “trending” topics or to determine what to advertise. Biometrics  is the authentication or recognition of people by utilizing their physiological or behavioral characteristics and needs an integration of inputs from diverse modalities. Physiological characteristics might be images of the fingerprint, face, palm, and iris; behavioral characteristics might be dynamics of signature, gait, voice, and keystroke. Machine learning can be utilized to recognize different modalities to obtain an overall accept/reject decision ( Alpaydin, 2014 ). 3.5.2 Forecasting, prediction, and regression Regression  is a machine learning task in which the main aim is the estimation of value. Regression techniques are based on sets of input data and output responses that are continuous numerical values, unlike classification, in which they have distinct classes or categories. Regression models utilize input data features or attributes and their accompanying numerical output values to learn basic relations and associations between inputs and their corresponding outputs. One of the most common real-world examples of regression is stock market forecasting. A  simple regression  model can be built to forecast stock prices based on data related to the previous stock market values. Simple linear regression models attempt to model data relationships with one feature or descriptive variable x and a single response variable y with the goal of predicting y.  Lasso regression  is a special regression type that performs normal regression and generalizes the model well through regularization and selection of features or variables. Lasso is the least complete operator of shrinkage and choice.

snippets: 2.1 Some classification techniques In this subsection, we describe some of the classification techniques used by ML algorithms for classifying and labeling training datasets. 2.1.1 Clustering based classification Clustering is an unsupervised learning method for discovering patterns in unlabeled data and grouping similar data   . There are several algorithms for clustering such as K-nearest neighbors algorithm (K-NN)   , K-means clustering (which originated from signal processing), Mean-Shift Clustering   , Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN)   , Gaussian Mixture Models   , Hierarchical Clustering, and others. For example, basic idea behind K-NN algorithm developed by Fix et al.    and later generalized by Cover et al.    is illustrated in  Fig. 2 . This example illustrates how continuous data can be classified using Euclidean distance. In this example, training data are classified into two types (C-1 and C-2). Data of type C-1 are colored green and data of type C-2 are colored red. When a new data point (colored blue) needs to be classified, K-NN selects  K  neighboring points ( K  is a user defined constant) and calculates the Euclidean distances between the new data point and the chosen  K  neighbors. Then, using some algorithm such as majority voting algorithm, it decides whether to classify the new data point as type C-1 or type C-2 data point. In this example, after applying K-NN, the blue data point is classified to be of type C-1 because it has been determined to be closer to majority of the data points in C-1. For discrete variables, such as in natural language processing, Hamming Distance can be used for text classification. 2.1.2 Decision tree based classification A decision tree is tree structure, in which each leaf node represents a class label and each internal node is a decision node or a chance node. A decision node performs a test on a feature and each branch node of a decision node represents an outcome of the test. Some of the well-known algorithms for building decision trees are ID3   , and C4.5   . Both these algorithms use the concept of information entropy for building decision trees from training datasets for labeling data. Generally, using decision trees result in high classification accuracy.

snippets: 4 Classification techniques Classification is a data analysis process where a model is designed to predict and distinguish the class labels of the data set. From the literature, it can be observed that there are numerous machine learning and data mining classifiers used for classifying data. A decision tree-based classifier has major applications in data classification where a tree-based model distinguishes the class labels of the data. This classifier can be used for classifying various multidimensional data. Random forest is another type of tree-based classifier where multiple decision tree classifiers are combined to classify a specific type of input data. It attempts to construct a set of assumptions and combine them for further decision-making. The final outcome is measured by a voting scheme. A Bayesian classifier is another type of statistical model that works on Bayes' theorem. The probabilistic features are made in it to discover the class label of an input set. The performance of these types of classifiers can be improved by adopting some other types of models that can handle greater amounts of data with improved accuracy. An artificial neural network (ANN) is a generalized mathematical model which is based on biological nervous systems. The fundamental elements of the neural network are artificial neurons interconnected with each other. ANN and its variants have been widely used for classifying the data. Multilayer perceptron (MLP), radial basis function network (RBFN), probabilistic neural network (PNN), generalized regression neural network (GRNN), and block-based neural network (BBNN) are the most commonly used data classification models. These classifiers consist of an input layer, hidden layer, and output layer. concept: Supervised learning is a key area in machine learning (ML) that utilizes labeled data to train models for making predictions, with two main tasks: regression (predicting continuous values) and classification (categorizing data).
The effectiveness of supervised learning relies heavily on the quality and quantity of training data; larger and more diverse datasets lead to better model accuracy.

Common algorithms for supervised learning include Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Naive Bayes, and Decision Trees, each with unique strengths suited for different applications.
Supervised learning is analogous to a student learning from a teacher, where the model learns to associate inputs with correct outputs, minimizing errors through iterative training.
Active learning is a variant of supervised learning where the model can request labels for specific data points, reducing the need for extensive manual labeling.
Unsupervised learning, in contrast, deals with unlabeled data, focusing on discovering patterns and structures within the data, often used for clustering and anomaly detection.

Semisupervised learning combines both labeled and unlabeled data, enhancing model performance when labeled data is scarce, and is effective in various applications like sentiment analysis and image classification.

Reinforcement learning is a distinct paradigm where agents learn to make decisions through interactions with an environment, optimizing actions based on feedback received in the form of rewards or penalties.

snippets: 2.1 Supervised learning Supervised learning is a fundamental field in ML that involves training predictive models with labeled data to make accurate predictions on missing data. Two core types of supervised learning tasks exist: regression and classification. Regression predicts continuous numeric values, such as state of charge (SoC) for EVs or charging demand forecasts [ 46 ]. Classification, on the other hand, categorizes data into predefined classes. Prevalent classification algorithms include Logistic Regression for binary classification [ 47 ], K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) for assigning data points based on their neighbors [ 48 ], Random Forest (RF) for ensemble learning [ 49 ], Support Vector Machines (SVM) for defining decision boundaries between classes [ 50 ], Naive Bayes for efficient high-dimensional data handling [ 51 ], and Decision Trees for versatile decision-making in both classification and regression tasks. These algorithms have strengths and characteristics, making them suitable for various applications and data types.  Table 2  presents these methods' brief pros and cons [ 13 ].

snippets: Supervised learning In supervised learning, the ML algorithms are trained using large collections of examples that are  labeled  with the correct “answer.” Similar to how one studies for a test by completing endless practice problems, the algorithm “learns” how properly to identify or classify a given input by processing large, labeled datasets until it can do so with an elevated level of confidence—the larger the training set with rich and diverse examples, the more accurate the algorithm. A simple example of supervised learning involves training an algorithm to differentiate between images of cats and dogs. The training dataset consists of a huge selection of different images showing either a cat or dog, along with its correct label. The algorithm “studies” these examples by identifying patterns within the pixels. Then, when provided with a novel (unlabeled) image, the algorithm will look for similar patterns and provide an answer—although “best guess” might be more appropriate—and a level of confidence. Now, what happens when the algorithm, trained on nothing but cats and dogs, is given an image of a rabbit? There are certainly similarities that could be drawn between rabbits, cats, and dogs, but the algorithm can only choose between the latter two animals. It will have to choose whichever category the rabbit image most closely resembles, but the confidence of the result will likely be low. The training data are critical to a successful supervised learning approach, but reliance on the training data is also a limitation. If high-quality training datasets (i.e. containing accurate human coders' labels with unbiased and diverse training examples) are not available, it can take hundreds of hours for humans to collect and label a new training set. Moreover, if humans are doing the labeling, they must be very careful as each error will influence a dataset's quality and the overall performance of any ensuing predictive model. Supervised learning primarily deals with problems of prediction and forecasting. Supervised learning algorithms look at existing data to make an inference about new instances or predict the outcome of a yet-to-be-seen example. And while identifying the species of pet photos on the Internet may be fun, supervised learning can be applied to data beyond images, such as using numerical data for predicting and forecasting. For example, stock prices or real estate trends, due to the potential financial gains and the ample amounts of historical data, are popular real-world examples of supervised learning.

snippets: Supervised Learning Supervised learning takes refined raw data and uses an algorithm to predict the outcome (with the algorithm having derived from previously studying the labeled data in a training set of data in the process described earlier). In other words, the training data help to guide the machine to the right prediction or output via an algorithm so that the model can be used to make predictions of the new data. Active learning is a supervised learning that involves a learning algorithm that can query the user for labels to avoid manually labeling a large number of samples. In short, supervised learning develops a predictive model from both input and output data (the later labeled by humans) and this model is then used to make predictions on a new set of data. These supervised learning methodologies lead to classification (dichotomous or categorical) or regression (to a continuous variable). For classification, the popular methodologies are support vector machines (SVMs), naive Bayes classifier,  k -nearest neighbor, and decision trees (with boosting or bagging); logistic regression is a misnomer and is in fact a classification methodology. For regression, linear and polynomial regression methods are most commonly used, but other types [such as ridge and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression] may become more popular in the future. Classification This methodology leads to predicting or assigning a label or category for an unlabeled sample [e.g., “tumor” vs “not tumor” on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)]. Classification strategy is good for fraud detection and facial recognition. In medicine and health care, classification is good for medical images, phenotyping, and cohort identification. The supervised classification methodologies are listed in  Table 5.3  but only the more popular methods will be described in more detail. Logistic regression (which is a misnomer as it is not a true regression but rather a classification methodology) is included in this classification section. Support vector machine This “maximum-distance” classification methodology is achieved by creating a line or an optimal hyperplane (a decision surface) in a high-dimensional space that represents the largest separation between the two classes (see  Fig. 5.4 ). In general, the larger this separation, the better the SVM performance.

snippets: 3 Types of Learning There are two broad classes of learning: supervised and unsupervised. Supervised learning involves learning from examples, which is a set of associations between inputs and outputs. This is akin to how children learn to read and write—a teacher presents letters of the alphabet and utters the corresponding sounds. Repeating the process with the same examples will gradually train students’ biological neural networks to associate symbols with sounds. Training data is comprised of two parts: input and expected output. Let ( i ,  o ) be an item in the training dataset, which specifies that when the system is presented with input  i , it should output  o . The training data is a set of  n  such pairs: {( i 1 ,  o 1 ), ( i 2 ,  o n ), …, ( i n ,  o n )}. A trained model should work correctly if the examples in the training set are given to the model again. For example, given  i  as input to the trained model, it should produce  o  as the output. A reasonable criterion should be defined to measure the error between the correct output and the outcome generated by the model. The main task of supervised learning is to minimize the error function. This is similar to how the teacher corrects students in their initial attempts to read or write, which gradually minimizes the error function of their biological neural network model. In addition to the error function, other characteristics of the model include the number of model parameters and modeling flexibility ( Battiti et al., 2008 ). Decision trees, neural networks, regression, and Bayesian classification are examples of supervised learning algorithms. Unsupervised learning algorithms draw inferences from datasets consisting of just input data without labeled responses. Unsupervised learning infers a function which describes the hidden structure from unlabeled data. Since the examples given to the learner are unlabeled, there is no error or reward signal to evaluate a potential solution. This distinguishes unsupervised learning from supervised learning and reinforcement learning (see  Section 3.2 ). K-means clustering, genetic algorithms, and simulated annealing are examples of unsupervised learning algorithms. For cognitive analytics, unsupervised algorithms have an edge over the supervised ones. In the big data context, we do not know the patterns in the data  a priori . Furthermore, training data may not be available. Unsupervised learning algorithms are better suited for this scenario.

snippets: 4.7.6 Consensus Unsupervised learning is another group of machine learning techniques. The fundamental difference between it and supervised learning is that unsupervised learning usually handles training samples without corresponding labels. Therefore, the primary usage of unsupervised learning is to do clustering. The reason why ensemble methods are employed is to combine some weak clusters into strong one. To create diverse clusters, several approaches can be applied: using different sampling data, using different subsets of the original features, and employing different clustering methods ( Şenbabaoğlu et al., 2014 ). Sometimes, even some random noise can be added to these base models to increase randomness, which is good for ensemble methods according to  Bian and Wang (2007) . After receiving all the outputs from each cluster, various consensus functions can be chosen to obtain the final output based on the user’s requirement ( Vega-Pons and Ruiz-Shulcloper, 2011 ). The ensemble clustering is also known as consensus clustering  Fig. 7 . Zhou and Tang (2006)  explored ensemble methods for unsupervised learning and developed four different approaches to combine the outputs of these clusters. In recent years, some new ensemble clustering methods have been proposed that illustrated the priority of ensemble learning ( Huang et al., 2017b; Zheng et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2016a ). Most of the clustering ensemble method is based on the co-association matrix solution, which can be regarded as a graph partition problem. Besides, there is some research focus on integrating the deep structure and ensemble clustering method. Liu et al. (2015, 2016)  firstly showed that ensemble unsupervised representation learning with deep structure can be applied in large scale data. Then the author combined the method with auto-encoder and extends it to the vision field. Shaham et al. (2016)  first demonstrated that some crowdsourcing algorithms can be replaced by a Restricted Boltzmann Machine with a single hidden neuron, then propose an RBM-based Deep Neural Net (DNN) used for unsupervised ensemble learning. The unsupervised ensemble method also makes some contribution to the field of Natural Language Processing. Alami et al. (2019)  demonstrated that the ensemble of unsupervised deep neural network models that use Sentence2Vec representation as the input has the best performance according to the experiments.

snippets: Unsupervised learning plays a crucial role in various applications, such as customer segmentation, anomaly detection, topic modeling, and data preprocessing. By autonomously identifying patterns within data, unsupervised learning contributes to a deeper understanding of complex datasets and informs decision-making processes ( Boray, 2023 ;  Schumacher & LaBounty Jr., 2023 ). 2.2.3 Semisupervised learning Semisupervised learning is a hybrid approach that combines elements of both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. In this method, the algorithm leverages a limited amount of labeled data along with a larger pool of unlabeled data to train a model. The underlying idea is that incorporating the labeled data helps guide the learning process while also benefiting from the wealth of information present in the unlabeled data. Semisupervised learning is particularly useful when obtaining labeled data is expensive or time-consuming, which is often the case in real-world scenarios. The algorithm can learn from a small labeled dataset and generalize its knowledge to the unlabeled data, effectively improving its performance through a process known as self-training. This approach is especially effective when there is a significant overlap between the distribution of labeled and unlabeled data. Semisupervised learning finds application in various domains, such as sentiment analysis, speech recognition, and image classification, where labeled data might be limited but unlabeled data are more abundant. By harnessing the power of both labeled and unlabeled data, semisupervised learning offers a pragmatic solution to enhancing model performance and expanding the scope of machine learning applications ( Boray, 2023 ;  Schumacher & LaBounty Jr., 2023 ). 2.2.4 Reinforcement learning Reinforcement learning is a paradigm within machine learning that focuses on training intelligent agents to make a sequence of decisions in an environment to maximize a cumulative reward. Unlike supervised learning, where explicit labels guide the learning process, and unsupervised learning, which seeks patterns in unlabeled data, reinforcement learning involves learning by interaction. The agent interacts with an environment and learns to take actions that lead to favorable outcomes. The environment responds with feedback in the form of rewards or penalties, guiding the agent's future actions. The core challenge in reinforcement learning is to find an optimal policy—the sequence of actions—that maximizes the long-term cumulative reward.

concept: Computational decision-making employs techniques like machine learning, optimization, and computational intelligence to transform complex data into actionable insights, enabling businesses to make informed decisions in the big data era.

The process of data analysis involves several steps: data collection and preparation, exploratory data analysis, feature selection, machine learning application, optimization, and continuous improvement, all while addressing challenges such as bias and complexity.

Real-time decision-making leverages analytics to select optimal actions for business operations, requiring well-defined operational rules to ensure timely and accurate responses to changing conditions.

Big data techniques and technologies are multidisciplinary, drawing from statistics, computer science, and economics, necessitating organizations to adopt flexible approaches to derive value from large and diverse datasets.

Ensemble reinforcement learning (ERL) methods enhance decision-making performance by improving Q-functions, reward mechanisms, and overall algorithm efficiency, demonstrating superior results in various applications, including financial trading and drug design.

The integration of reinforcement learning with deep learning techniques has shown promise in generating novel compounds for drug design, although further refinement is necessary to ensure specificity and reliability in outcomes.

snippets: 3 Techniques in computational decision making To convert complex data into useful insights, computational decision making uses a variety of approaches including machine learning, optimization, and CI. In addition to identifying and extracting useful patterns using statistical techniques, data mining, and pattern recognition, machine learning allows systems to adapt and perform better. While fuzzy logic, evolutionary algorithms, and neural networks (NNs)  [14–16]  handle ambiguity, optimization approaches discover the best answers. Effective data management is ensured by DBMS and AI integration. Managing assumptions, minimizing biases, and achieving a balance between complexity and performance are challenges. These cutting-edge methods enable businesses to make informed, data-driven decisions in the big data era for the best results. 3.1 Algorithm for data analysis using computational decision-making techniques 1. Data Collection and Preparation: Gather relevant raw data; clean by handling missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies; normalize, standardize, and scale features. 2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA): Visualize data through graphs, histograms, scatter plots; calculate summary statistics; identify trends and patterns. 3. Feature Selection and Engineering: Identify relevant features; use domain knowledge and correlations for selection; create new features via transformations. 4. Machine Learning and Pattern Recognition: Select suitable algorithms; split data into train/test sets; train models; evaluate using performance metrics. 5. Computational Intelligence Techniques: Apply methods like NNs   , evolutionary algorithms; adjust parameters for better results. 6. Optimization and Decision Making: Use optimization to find the best solutions within constraints; make decisions based on outcomes. 7. Challenges and Biases: Address data/model biases; minimize bias, ensure fairness in decisions. 8. Balancing Complexity and Performance: Optimize model complexity and performance trade-off; regularize to prevent overfitting. 9. Informed Decision Making: Align decisions with goals based on analysis; communicate insights to stakeholders. 10. Continuous Improvement: Monitor solution performance; adapt models as data/business requirements evolve. 3.2 Machine learning techniques AI techniques such as machine learning allow computers to improve their performance on particular tasks without having to be explicitly programmed. Due to these techniques’ prowess in analyzing and deciphering complicated information, finding patterns, and making predictions, they have become incredibly prominent in computational decision making. Fig. 2  depicts the various machine-learning techniques that are employed in computational decision making   .

snippets: 7.4.4.4 Real-Time Decision-Making Based on the results of the real-time analytics, it is possible to select the best option for improving the present business operations or profitability and determine the most appropriate actions to respond to the business or operational environment. Various configurations of decision-making can be created by defining business or operational rules developed by domain experts and derived from strategic decisions. These rules help to interactively and intelligently respond to evolving business and operational situations. A decision process checks for predefined business and operational rules to take specific business or operational actions based on the options provided by the real-time analytics modules. It can also notify responsible individuals or trigger other processes to conduct further actions. The biggest challenge is defining business and operational rules that facilitate correct and timely decision-making ( Mohamed and Al-Jaroodi, 2014 ). 7.4.4.5 Real-Time Responses This involves initiating, executing, and monitoring an action defined by the real-time decision-making process. For example, a company decides to buy a specific stock quantity; the real-time response process will initiate a stock buying transaction, send the transaction request, and monitor its execution. In another example, in wild fires, if the real-time big data application determines a prospective fire expansion pattern, fire fighters and all relevant resources need to be informed and actions taken to contain the expansion area before the fire spreads too far. The process usually needs to interact with various different distributed systems to perform its tasks. The interactions should be reliable and achieved in real time ( Mohamed and Al-Jaroodi, 2014 ). 7.4.5 Big Data Techniques and Technologies A wide variety of techniques and technologies has been developed and adapted to aggregate, manipulate, analyze, and visualize big data. These techniques and technologies draw from several fields, including statistics, computer science, applied mathematics, and economics. This means an organization that intends to derive value from big data has to adopt a flexible, multidisciplinary approach. Some techniques and technologies were developed in a world with access to far smaller volumes and variety in data but have been successfully adapted to be applicable to very large sets of more diverse data. Others have been developed more recently, specifically to capture value from big data. Some were developed by academics and others by companies, especially those with online business models predicated on analyzing big data. In this section, we note some of the main techniques and technologies to harness big data.

snippets: 3 Strategies for ensemble reinforcement learning Previous studies have shown that the ERL method demonstrates superior average performance and sampling efficiency compared to RL methods, as evidenced by results obtained from public RL test sets and practical tasks   . By using ERL, the performance improvement can reach up to 20%  [31–33] . Moreover, for classification tasks, the ERL method achieves the best accuracy scores across multiple benchmarks in the UCI online data repository   . The strategies employed by ERL to outperform other solution methods in various problems are closely interconnected. These strategies are categorized based on the diverse improvements made to the ERL. The ensemble strategies for ERL encompass Q-function, reward, and loss function ensembles, as well as model combinations, combination training algorithms, and decision strategies. In this section, we will introduce these strategies individually. 3.1 Ensemble strategies for Q-functions In most RL methods, the Q-function reflects how good the agent is in any given state   . A “good state” refers to a state that can achieve a high expected return, which is contingent upon the action taken by the agent. The background section provides the Q-function formula, which is applicable to ERL methods. Additionally, tailoring Q-functions specifically for ERL methods can further enhance the algorithm performance  [15,36–38] . A Max–min Q-learning algorithm using multiple Q-functions was proposed by Lan et al.    to evaluate the performance. The max–min mechanism integrates multiple predicted values as a reference for agent decision-making. Specifically, the prediction term in the original Q-value calculation formula is determined by selecting the smallest value among multiple Q functions. The efficacy of this algorithm is demonstrated using the Mountain Car environment. It can be observed from the results that enhancing the Q-function positively impacts both the convergence performance and search efficiency of the algorithm. The Q-function can also be enhanced through the utilization of Bayesian optimization. Chen et al. incorporated this concept into the design of the ERL method to update  Q ∗  using Bayesian optimization, which proves particularly effective in addressing high-dimensional ERL problems and especially valuable when dealing with ultra-large solution spaces   . In this study, an upper-confidence bounds (UCB) based strategy for exploring the solution space is employed for action selection by the agent.

snippets: 8.1 Machine Learning for Source Separation Source separation is seen as a joint framework of signal processing and machine learning, which ranges from front-end processing of signal inputs with the mixed signals to back-end learning of regression outputs for the demixed signals. The number of accepted papers and attendees in the areas of speech enhancement, audio and source separation are comparable with those of speech recognition. Source separation and speech recognition have been recognized as two of the most popular research directions in ICASSP and INTERSPEECH. In the activities of the IEEE Signal Processing Society, source separation papers have been intensively proposed in recent years in three technical directions, including  Speech and Language Processing  (SLP),  Machine Learning for Signal Processing  (MLSP) and  Audio and Acoustic Signal Processing  (AASP). snippets: 1 Introduction Speech signals have been widely used in developing intelligent automated systems. It refers to the ability of the system to understand the spoken input and extract information from it by identifying the essential features of the underlying speech signal. The research directions in this domain envisions smart systems that can respond to audio and visual inputs of their surroundings and provide meaningful inferences. Speech analysis and modelling can be viewed as a combination of time-series and sequence processing task   , as the speech signal is essentially a continuous distribution of energy that varies with time. On an abstract level, when grouped for a particular period of time, this energy forms an utterance that basically represents a word or a phonetic sound. A salient feature of the speech signals is that they cannot be defined completely using a rule-based approach since it is impossible to account for the variations in phonetics that are unique to every person   . Another challenging aspect in the processing of speech signals is the presence of noise and other unwanted background signals    that are often interlaced with the primary speech signal. Due to this aspect, it becomes important to design effective denoising systems that can separate the primary signals from the noise. The review study    presents an overview of deep learning methods that are used for speech denoising. Due to the complexity and variations that arise in the analysis of speech signals, machine learning (ML) has been seen as an effective tool to counter these issues. Multiple studies have been carried out to use ML for creating smart denoising and sequence processing systems  [5–7] , which can separate the noise from the base signal and extract meaningful linguistic elements from the same. Nonetheless, as speech signals are essentially a sequence of utterances, the models used for their analysis comprise of well-known memory elements such as long short term memory (LSTMs), recurrent neural network (RNNs) and gated recurrent unit (GRUs)   . As of recent, advanced sequence-to-sequence architectures have been applied to this task, which includes the widely accepted transformer architecture    for achieving state-of-the-art results. Another novel approach that has been adopted is to use the techniques defined in the domain of computer vision to process the speech signals directly through their spectrogram representation.

Naive Bayes: A probabilistic method that implements Bayes’ theorem with an understanding of feature-independent. Given the feature values, it computes the likelihood of each class label and assigns the data point to the class with the greatest probability of occurring. Naive Bayes is a highly computationally effective method for dealing with data with high dimensions. Neural networks: In recent years, neural networks, particularly deep learning models, have received a lot of attention. snippets: 3 Task prediction In this section, task prediction is explained. The obtained feature descriptor of the input from the previous step is fed as input into the task prediction. In a machine learning problem, a task is a type of prediction or inference which is being asked in the problem. Each problem could have many types of tasks. Based on the literature, we have divided different tasks into four categories: (1) regression, (2) classification, (3) ranking, and (4) structural output prediction. Regression assigns a continuous label to each sample. For example, in compound-target prediction, a real binding affinity value is assigned to a pair of compound and protein targets, which states the strength of the binding interaction of a biomolecule target (e.g., protein, enzyme, or DNA) with the ligand of the compound. In classification, a discrete label is assigned to each input sample, which states the class label of the input data. The classification task is divided into two categories: binary classification and multiclass classification. In binary classification, the number of classes is two, and in multiclass classification, the number of classes is more than two. Prediction of drug-likeness is an example of binary classification in which the input drug compound is divided into drug-like/non-drug-like class labels. Ranking assigns a partial order for each item by giving a numerical or ordinal score, which states the relevance degree of each item match. Gerdes et al. (2021)  utilize omics data to assign a numerical score to lists of drugs based on their antiproliferative efficacy in the cancer cell. In the structural output prediction task, a structured object is predicted as output compared to classification and regression, which produce, respectively, scalar discrete or real values as an output. For example, protein 3D structure prediction ( Jumper et al., 2021 ) takes the protein sequence as input, then produces the 3D structure of the protein as output. In this chapter, we focus on regression and classification tasks. 3.1 Classic approaches In this section, the classic approaches for regression and classification tasks are investigated. In classic machine learning algorithms, to extract features from the raw input data, the hand-crafted feature extractor algorithms are utilized, and then, it is fed into the task predictor. In this section, to explain the introduced algorithms in a practical way, we take the molecular property prediction problem as an application.

snippets: 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). Raw data usually contain noisy and unreliable data that can affect training and analysis. Moreover, datasets used in intrusion detection are characterized by high dimensionality, making it more difficult to discover knowledge during training. To build high-performance detectors requires efficient preprocessing. Fig. 4  summarizes the common data preprocessing methods used in intrusion detection, including data cleaning, imbalance learning, data transformation, feature selection, feature extraction, and Visualization ( RQ2(a) ). The above methods preprocess the data from different perspectives to enable the analysis model to better learn useful information from the data. In order to study the technical characteristics of different methods, we summarize their implementation principles and applications to answer  RQ2(b) . a ) Data cleaning Data cleaning corrects corrupt or inaccurate records. Quality criteria may include the following. • Validity. Data might have to be of a certain type, such as Boolean or numeric. • Accuracy. Data must conform to the situation. For example, outliers may exist due to the recording process. Accuracy is difficult to guarantee through data cleaning because real data sources are needed for validation. • Completeness. Some data may have unknown or missing values. Completeness issues are generally resolved through default values, setting zeros, or removal. • Uniformity. Inconsistency occurs when there are conflicts in a dataset. For example, a source IP may differ between two receivers. Fixing this type of problem requires the determination of which datum is most reliable. Data analysis based on means, standard deviations, or clustering algorithms can reveal errors, whose values can sometimes be set to a mean or other statistical measure. b ) Imbalanced learning A sample with different proportions of positive and negative cases will lead to a bias in the learning process toward the higher proportion. For example, in the extreme case of a dataset with 95 %  positive and 5 %  negative cases, the model will have no practical meaning. Since attacks tend to be sparse, datasets in intrusion detection are often unbalanced. The following methods may improve performance. • Sampling methods.

Data pre-processing is a critical step in ML classification. In the preparation phase, before model development, it is mandatory to handle the raw data correctly, so it can be appropriately used to train the classifier, considering the quality of a model's results is dependent on the quality of the data ( García et al., 2016 ;  Frénay and Verleysen, 2014 ). The process of handling noisy data and missing parts of raw data is known as data cleaning. Fortunately, while missing data can be directly removed or replaced, both supervised ( e . g . NN or KNN) and unsupervised ( e . g . clustering) ML approaches can be useful in dealing with noisy data, eliminating mislabeled samples and/or outliers, and even balancing datasets, as we will further discuss. When it comes to data mining algorithms, it's also often necessary to transform the data. Data transformation includes rescaling, normalization (scaling data values within a predefined range), merging attributes (attribute selection), and discretization (replacing raw numeric values with intervals or conceptual levels). Finally, data reduction is essential when it comes to huge amounts of data ( Li and Chen, 2022 ). Reduction techniques aim to reduce data storage and analysis costs by compression encoding mechanisms, storing a model of the data instead of all data, and by attribute subset selection (feature selection performed at the data-level). According to  García et al. (2016) , pre-processing raw data might also avoid overfitting and poor generalization. Additionally, model interpretability can also be improved. Therefore, to ensure better results, it is important to consider the necessary pre-processing steps. Data pre-processing methods were addressed in a total of 35.82% of all articles. This, however, does not mean most models weren't prepared appropriately, given some of these methods are so commonplace, they often go unmentioned.

snippets: Among these categories, the COM and CSM are related to classification tasks, while CRM and CFM are related to regression tasks in most cases. The classification metrics applied in the existing studies for performance evaluation include accuracy, precision, F1-score, recall (or sensitivity), area under the receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curve (AUC), specificity, false positive rate (FPR), geometric mean (G-Mean), average precision-recall score (APR score), Matthews’ correlation coefficient (MCC), loss, negative predictive value (NPV), and positive predictive value (PPV). Specifically, the most notable metrics include accuracy (44 studies), precision (33 studies), F1-score (29 studies), recall (28 studies), and AUC (16 studies). These metrics are usually measured with the support of 4 elements, namely the true positive ( TP ), false positive (FP), true negative (TN), and false negative ( FN ). • Accuracy:  The accuracy of a model evaluates the model's ability to classify the inputs into their respective class categories correctly. It is often applied for CSM and COM where the accuracy is measured based on the ratio between the number of correctly classified data in terms of severity level or crash occurrence and the total number of instances. • Precision:  The precision of a model describes the quality, or level of relevancy when the input is classified as a TP. snippets: 3.4 Validation Fig. 7 a  presents the validation strategy with respect to how data was split between the training set and the testing set. A patient-wise validation strategy, employed by 36 papers, implies that data collected from a single patient is not simultaneously included in the training set and the testing set, reducing bias. 37 papers (i.e. more than half) did not employ such a strategy, possibly containing information from a single patient in both the training and testing sets, or did not specify how such splitting was achieved which leaves them open to potential data leakage. Three different strategies were mainly used to split datapoints between training and testing sets. Hold-out , arguably the most common technique in the broader machine learning community, corresponds to separating a portion of the datapoints in a testing set at the beginning of the experiment in order to isolate it entirely from the training process, and was used 30 times in total, which makes it the most regularly used strategy. k -fold Cross-Validation (CV) ( k -CV) comes second, with 26 occurrences in total. This strategy consists in partitioning the datapoints into  k  different disjoint sets. An independent training procedure is then performed  k  times, each using a different set as testing data and the remaining  k  − 1 as training data. When performed correctly (i.e. ensuring that the training procedures are completely independent and isolating from each other) this has the benefit of evaluating the algorithm on all the data possible although at the expense of re-training the algorithm several times. Leave-one-out CV (LOOCV) is a specific case  k -CV for very small datasets, in which  k  is equal to the number of datapoints (or the number of patients, if the validation was done patient-wise) in the database. LOOCV is beneficial in that it also ensures that a maximum amount of data is present in the training set at any given time. LOOCV has been used 13 times. Two papers did not validate their method on a separated testing set, and one did not specify the validation method employed. Finally,  bootstrapping  refers to evaluation procedures in which the algorithm is trained once, but the effect of any individual datapoint can be isolated and removed from the model, thus allowing for said datapoint to be used in evaluating the reduced model.

snippets: 4 State-of-the-art of basic and hybrid approaches This section presents state-of-the-art basic and hybrid CI techniques used for various medical diagnostic tasks. Basic approaches use single CI techniques (e.g. Information theory (IT), Rough set theory (RST), Fuzzy logic (FL)-based, Z-number, Naïve bayes classifier (NBC), Artificial neural network (ANN), Support vector machine (SVM), etc.). However, hybrid approaches are a combination of two or more CI techniques (e.g. Neuro-fuzzy (N-F), Casebased reasoning (CBR) & Rule-based reasoning (RBR), SVM-ensemble method, etc.). 4.1 Basic approaches This section reviews the basic approaches applied for diverse tasks (diagnosis, prediction, classification, severity assessment, the correlation between disease and attributes, etc.) in medical diagnosis and prognosis. 4.1.1 Information theory IT is particularly useful in the diagnosis of age-related diseases   . For the 21st century, aging is a big challenge in medical science   . Aging is a decline in the physiological activity required for survival and fertility   . The various aging-related diseases are neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and nutritional and metabolic diseases  [20–22] . These diseases involve both the continuous and discrete parameters and there is a non-linear relationship among the parameters. The three information theoretical measures are: (i) entropy and normalized Shannon entropy measures the degree of uncertainty of random variables, (ii) mutual information (MI) and normalized mutual information (NMI) measures the correlation between random variables, and (iii) auto-mutual information (AMI)/normalized auto-mutual information and cross-mutual information (CMI)/normalized cross-mutual information for time-series analysis. The usefulness of information theory in medical diagnosis lies in its ability to describe both the isolated and unified systems. This is due to the additive property of entropy obtained from the property of logarithm (entropy of the unified system can be equated by the sum of entropies of the individual isolated systems). AMI measures the (non-linear) relationship between preceding and succeeding values of a certain time series. This helps in estimating and even predicting the dynamic processes by taking measurements at numerous successive time points.

For the 21st century, aging is a big challenge in medical science   . Aging is a decline in the physiological activity required for survival and fertility   . The various aging-related diseases are neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and nutritional and metabolic diseases  [20–22] . These diseases involve both the continuous and discrete parameters and there is a non-linear relationship among the parameters. The three information theoretical measures are: (i) entropy and normalized Shannon entropy measures the degree of uncertainty of random variables, (ii) mutual information (MI) and normalized mutual information (NMI) measures the correlation between random variables, and (iii) auto-mutual information (AMI)/normalized auto-mutual information and cross-mutual information (CMI)/normalized cross-mutual information for time-series analysis. The usefulness of information theory in medical diagnosis lies in its ability to describe both the isolated and unified systems. This is due to the additive property of entropy obtained from the property of logarithm (entropy of the unified system can be equated by the sum of entropies of the individual isolated systems). AMI measures the (non-linear) relationship between preceding and succeeding values of a certain time series. This helps in estimating and even predicting the dynamic processes by taking measurements at numerous successive time points. However, CMI correlates between values of dissimilar time series. This will allow for establishing the relations between different dynamic processes. In general, the requirement for modeling the medical diagnosis is twofold: (i) finding the cumulative impact of the various factors on the disease and (ii) ranking the parameters according to their importance. Also, the ability to analyze the model which consists of both the continuous and discrete parameters is very important. Information theoretical approach provides good theoretical ground to address these requirements   . Blokh and Stambler    used NMI to find the weight of the several attributes that assess the risk of heart disease (HD), particularly, the weight of age as a risk attribute singly and in combination with other attributes.

snippets: Liu et al.    first revealed the reasons for being under-performed by revisiting existing modality-specific feature compensation based models and then accordingly presented a new two-stage GAN based model, achieving new state-of-the-art performance. Instead of image-level compensation, Lu et al.    modeled the affinities of different modality samples according to their shared features and then transferred both shared and specific features among/across modalities, thus achieving feature-level compensation. Differently, Zhang    presented a novel feature-level modality compensation network (FMCNet), which, instead of generating images of missing modalities, directly generated those missing modality-specific features of one modality from existing modality-shared features of the other modality. For that, a single-modality feature decomposition module was first designed to decompose single-modality features into modality-specific ones and modality-shared ones. Then, a feature-level modality compensation module was presented to generate those missing modality-specific features from existing modality-shared ones. 4.3 Auxiliary information    Table 6  shows most existing auxiliary information based models, which mainly explore the ways of using person masks, person postures or auxiliary modalities for the extraction of those discriminative person features. We will detail them in the following content. Person mask:  In order to enhance the contour information of input images and reduce the impact of background clutters, Qi et al.    proposed a novel mask-guided dual network (MDAN) by introducing the foreground person as the emphasized information for enriching those representations. Based on the human parsing masks, Zhao et al.    proposed a novel color-irrelevant consistency learning method for VI-ReID, which learned color-irrelevant features with high discriminability by imposing color-irrelevant consistency constraints on random clothing color transformation. Person posture:  Miao et al.    exploited pose estimation as an auxiliary learning task to assist the VI-ReID task in an end-to-end framework. By jointly training the two tasks in a mutually beneficial manner, their model learned higher quality modality-shared and ID-related features.

Ensuring the data collection covers diverse and comprehensive groups not only helps in mitigating bias but also promotes relevant research on the impacts of the attributes. Another critical aspect is the potential for algorithmic bias, where ML models may inadvertently perpetuate or amplify existing biases present in the data, leading to unfair or discriminatory outcomes. Moreover, models that are overly complex or fitted too closely to the training data may capture noise or spurious correlations, leading to overfitting. Overfit models may perform well on the training data but fail to generalize to new data, leading to biased predictions. Moreover, researchers may have preconceived notions or hypotheses about the mechanisms of autophagy, which can influence the interpretation of machine learning model outputs or the selection of features and experimental designs. To mitigate these biases, it is essential to employ strategies such as ensuring diverse and representative data collection, rigorous experiments and validation, collaborating with domain experts, and conducting independent validation experiments.

snippets: The umbrella for the detection of rare variants is the method of  CMC (Combined Multivariate and Collapsing),  which brings together all the variants pooled in a genetic pool for the identification of both common and rare variants in a  ROI (Region of Interest)  alongside  RVT1 (Rare Variant Test 1 ). Similar to CMAT, the CMC method checks for at least one MAF (Minor Allele Frequency) position in the genetic pool . RVT2 (Rare Variant Test 2)  investigates the genetic pool while searching for a proportion of at least one MAF as a weight to detect a potential phenotype increase. A more flexible method is  VT (Variable Threshold)  which uses a maximum number of tests to detect MAF variants, the maximum test implementation encompasses the complete set of MAFs to detect optimal rare variants in the genetic pool. The method of  WS (Weighted Sum)  gives more weighting to rare variants leading to stronger nominated effects for rare rather than common variants. Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA)  is used to reduce the analysis complexity   . The FPCA (Functional Principal Component Analysis) considers the mean squared average distance of PCs (Principal Component) to score between cases and controls and is utilised to investigate the dominant variations of the functional data. Further studies of collapsing methods include  KBAC (Kernel Based Adaptive Cluster)  which is a kernel based adaptive method used to enable the use of adaptive weights within the sample risk of ROI. KBAC can be used for different MAF effect directions, thus having a varied potential to detect numerous rare variants in the genetic pool. The problem of rareness of an allele is another prevailing problem, which is addressed with alternative collapsing methods by combining multiple rare variants within a gene. The method of  CAST(Cohort Allelic Sum Test)  has been investigated alongside RVT2, arguing that regression models are less efficient whilst analysing rare variants accumulated from derived data with VT and CMC methods. KBAT (Kernel Based Association Test)      is another technique which helps to reduce the degree of freedom in multiple variants while studying for dichotomised traits. Association analysis has been carried out for analysing the effects of rare variants on conventional factors, with the motivation of designing algorithms to determine genetic variant significance in a single nucleotide. KBAC    has been largely used for the analysis of entire genome associations using collapsing methods of WS and CMC.

concept: Data preprocessing is a crucial step in machine learning (ML) that significantly impacts the quality of model outcomes. It encompasses three main tasks: data cleaning, data reduction, and data transformation.

Data cleaning techniques are essential for addressing issues such as missing data, outliers, and noise, with the most common methods being linear interpolation for missing data and threshold-based outlier removal.

Data reduction aims to minimize dimensionality and enhance computational efficiency, with feature selection and extraction being the primary techniques employed. The correlation coefficient method and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) are frequently used for feature selection.
Data transformation prepares data for analysis by normalizing, reframing, and encoding categorical data, which is vital for effective model training.
The effectiveness of ML models is influenced by the quality of the training data, and proper preprocessing can prevent overfitting and improve model interpretability.

Performance evaluation metrics are varied, with accuracy being the most commonly used, but reliance solely on accuracy can be misleading. Other metrics like precision, recall, and AUC provide a more comprehensive assessment of model performance.
The literature indicates a need for standardized evaluation procedures, as many studies utilize different metrics, making comparisons challenging.
The choice of evaluation metrics should align with the specific characteristics of the dataset and the classification problem to ensure meaningful performance assessment.

snippets: 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). snippets: Techniques and Applications of Big Data Characteristics of Big Data Big Data is not a definite concept and many people are confused about how to understand and define it. “BIG” is insufficient to accurately describe all the features of data mining. It has four main characteristics: 1. Vast volume. The data order of magnitude ranges from terabyte (TB) to PB even to EB; as the volume is so vast that it cannot be expressed in gigabytes or TB,  the starting measurement unit of Big Data is at least a PB (2 40  bytes), EB (2 50  bytes), or a zetabyte (2 60  bytes). 2. Various types. Data from different applications and different equipment determine its diversity. There are three types: ● Structured: data produced by a financial system, information management system, medical system, etc. These are characterized by a strong causal relationship between the data. ● Unstructured: videos, images, audio, etc. These data are typified as exhibiting no causal relationship between the data. ● Semistructured: HTML documents, posts, webpages. This type is distinguished by a weak causal relationship between the data. Multitype data have higher requirements for data processing ability. 3. Low-value density. The amount of irrelevant information is phenomenal which, in turn, requires us to mine deeper for useful information. The diverse application of the Internet in the modern world means that information acquisition is everywhere. The amount of information is massive but its value density is low. A pressing question which needs to be resolved in the era of Big Data is how to maximize value more quickly with a powerful machine algorithm. 4. Fast processing velocity. The cycle of processing data has evolved from weeks, days, and hours into the realm of minutes and seconds. The improvement in velocity is closely related to a reduction in cost and an increase in efficiency, helped along by cloud computing (the Internet of Things). Greater time efficiency is the most notable feature of Big Data and distinguishes it from traditional data mining. Techniques of Big Data Massive data processing includes obtaining useful data related to specific applications, aggregating these data and making them easy to store, analyzing data correlations, and identifying relevant properties; and allowing the results of the data analysis to be properly displayed ( Jagadish et al., 2014 ). This manner of processing is similar to the traditional method.

snippets: Transformations are used to standardize variables, ensuring they are on the same scale, enhancing model flexibility to accommodate diverse data, making the model more interpretable, preventing computational errors, and improving accuracy. Common transformations include binning, rounding, scaling, exponential and logarithmic transformations, as well as power functions [ 52 ]. Feature Extraction:  Feature extraction techniques are employed to identify a smaller set of new variables, each of which is a combination of the input variables, capturing the same underlying information. Feature extraction reduces the data volume to a more manageable set suitable for modeling [ 57 ]. These techniques encompass methods such as text analytics, cluster analysis, principal components analysis, and edge detection algorithms. Feature Selection:  In this phase, only the most relevant variables are retained from the original dataset. Feature selection algorithms are utilized to evaluate, assess, and rank a subset of features from the pool of available features. Selection aids in determining which features are redundant or irrelevant and should be eliminated, and which are the most valuable features for the model and thus prioritized [ 58 ]. These selection methods are broadly categorized into four high-level categories: filter (e.g., ANOVA, Pearson correlation, variance thresholding), wrapper (e.g., forward, backward, and stepwise selection), embedded (e.g., Lasso, Ridge, Decision Tree), and hybrid methods [ 23 ]. 3.2.1 Topological data analysis (TDA) Topology, as defined by mathematicians [ 59 ], is the study of shapes and their inherent properties, often encompassing features such as the number of components and loops within these shapes. A particular approach to analyzing datasets, known as Topological Data Analysis (TDA) [ 60 ], leverages topological techniques to explore the topological and geometrical aspects of data, such as shape and connectivity. The fundamental idea behind TDA is rooted in the belief that geometry and topology provide a robust means to derive strong qualitative insights about data structures [ 61 ]. TDA is particularly valuable for datasets that are incomplete, high-dimensional, and contaminated with noise, as it offers a versatile framework for analysis while ensuring resilience to noise and dimensionality reduction challenges [ 61 ]. Moreover, TDA is enriched with functoriality, a core concept in modern mathematics, which enables it to adapt to emerging mathematical tools [ 62 ].

snippets: 4.2 Data quality traits Data quality traits refer to the validity of the data, which can be directly carried out in the next model construction, and the quality traits include data missing and data noise. For data missing, it is only necessary to observe the number of missing values to clarify the extent of the missing dataset. As for noise data is different to identify, and it requires some specific methods to find values that are similar to but inconsistent with the correct values. Generally speaking, in the classic credit risk control system, data preprocessing and exploratory data analysis are the key technologies to test data quality. Missing data traits:  According to the literature research on the mechanism of missing, missing data traits can be divided into three types ( Florez-Lopez, 2010; Rubin, 1976 ): missing completely at random (MCAR), missing at random(MAR), and missing not at random (MNAR). In general, according to the composition of the data, the data set can be divided into attributes and labels. To subdivide missing data, it can be divided into missing attribute data and missing class labels. Finally, considering fusing the three missing types with missing attribute data and missing labels, the corresponding summary is as follows. • MCAR  indicates that missing data is independent of each other and is not related to any other variable. In this sense, the influence of the data processing method on data distribution is not at risk. The number of completely random missing samples is small and is a factor of chance, labels can be removed directly when they are missing. • MAR  means that the missingness is related to some other observed variables. At this time, direct deletion or partial processing methods may lead to biased results. If the attribute data is missing randomly, the missing data is completely random, does not depend on any incomplete variable or complete variable, and does not affect the unbiased sample. In short, the probability of data loss is completely independent of the value of its hypothesis and the value of other variables.

concept: Algorithm adaptation methods are essential for effectively addressing multi-label problems by modifying existing single-label multi-class algorithms, allowing for direct application to multi-label data without prior transformation.

The Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbors (ML-KNN) algorithm exemplifies this adaptation, utilizing a lazy learning approach to classify instances based on the label subsets of their nearest neighbors, employing various distance measures for accuracy.
Ensemble learning techniques, such as AdaBoost and XGBoost, enhance model performance by combining multiple classifiers, although they may sacrifice interpretability and increase training time.

Evolutionary algorithms, inspired by biological processes, offer global optimization solutions through iterative refinement of candidate solutions, but their effectiveness is highly dependent on the chosen evaluation functions and parameters.

Feature extraction techniques, including PCA and MDS, are crucial for visualizing data complexity and classifier performance, enabling the identification of challenging datasets and improving interpretability.

Big Data processing involves several core techniques: uniform data description, efficient storage solutions like distributed systems, advanced data mining methods, and effective data visualization strategies to handle the vast amounts of diverse data generated today.

snippets: Algorithm Adaptation Methods Algorithm Adaptation is a strategy that involves the direct modification or refinement of widely-used single-label multi-class algorithms to address multi-label problems effectively. Classification algorithms are adapted, i.e., adjusted in such a way they can be applied directly to multi-label data, and no prior problem transformation step is actually required. Popular adapted algorithms are Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbors, Multi-Label Decision Trees, and Multi-Label Support Vector Machines. More complex methods have also been proposed and built on top of other models for multi-class classification, including Neural Networks. Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbors The Multi-Label K-Nearest Neighbor (ML-KNN) algorithm, proposed in  Zhang and Zhou (2007) , is a multi-label extension of the popular KNN algorithm. The KNN model is a lazy learning algorithm in which there is no explicit training phase, as generalization of the training data takes place directly at test time. The ML-KNN algorithm starts by identifying, in the training set, the  k  nearest neighbors of each new test instance under exam. Once the  k  neighbors have been selected, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) rule returns the label subset associated with the test instance based on the label subsets of the neighboring training samples. Considering a training set  D  and the label space  L , for an unseen test instance  x , the ML-KNN algorithm works as follows. It first defines the training set  D x k  of the  k  nearest neighbors of  x  in  D . Euclidean and Manhattan distances are commonly used to measure the distance between instances. Other popular measures frequently employed in bioinformatics and computational biology applications are Pearson correlation, cosine similarity, and other correlation-based distances. The algorithm then calculates the membership counting vector  C x  based on the label subsets of all training samples in  D x k . Each element  C x ( l j ) , with  l j ∈ L , represents the count of neighbors of  x  being associated with the label  l j .

In order to deal with large quantities of data, data descriptions based on ontology have become a research hotspot. snippets: 5.4 Model selection The process of choosing the best machine learning model from a group of potential models for a particular task is known  as model selection. It involves choosing the appropriate algorithm and its hyperparameters that can best represent the underlying data distribution and make accurate predictions on unseen data ( Dasari et al., 2023; Ghai et al., 2022; Prasanna & Tripathi, 2022 ). Model selection aims to reduce the danger of overfitting, which happens when a model becomes overly complicated and starts to train noise in training data rather than underlying patterns. There are various techniques for model selection, including cross-validation, grid search, and Bayesian optimization. The selected model should have good predictive performance on unseen data, and it should also have a good generalization ability to work well on new data that is not used for training. Choosing the right model for a given problem can significantly impact the accuracy and efficiency of the prediction or classification task. A poorly chosen model may lead to poor performance on the test set, resulting in suboptimal outcomes for the problem at hand. Additionally, the complexity of the model should be taken into consideration to avoid overfitting or underfitting, which can lead to poor generalization ability. Therefore, model selection plays a critical role in ML, and it is essential to consider different evaluation metrics, algorithmic performance, and computational efficiency while selecting the best model for a given problem. Audio model selection is an important step in the process of developing an audio classification or recognition system. The algorithm for audio model selection typically involves the following steps: • Data preprocessing:  In this step, the audio data is preprocessed to remove any noise or artifacts that could interfere with the model training process. This may involve filtering the data, applying noise reduction techniques, or normalizing the data to a standard scale. • Feature extraction:  The preprocessed audio data is then subjected to feature extraction, where the relevant features of the audio signal are extracted. This step involves applying various signal processing techniques such as Fourier Transform, MelFrequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), and wavelet transform to extract features such as pitch, timbre, and amplitude. • Model selection:  In this step, various ML models are trained and tested on the extracted audio features to determine the most accurate and effective model for the given task. The particular application and the kind of data being used will determine which model is best.

In order for a model to generalize well and avoid overfitting and underfitting, optimal curve fitting would be needed to achieve such separation. Linear curve fitting is the best possible solution, but if features were not extracted optimally or the model does not fit fully, then polynomial curve fitting needs to be performed. This involves some sort of convex and nonconvex optimizations   . The goal of building ML models would be to provide a low bias, which is commonly referred as training error and low variance, which is commonly referred as error in testing. A model is said to have overfitted if it has low bias and high variance, underfitted if it has high bias and low variance, and an optimal model would be the one that provides a low bias and a low variance. Some common approaches in building optimal ML models that generalize well include (1) Regularization, (2) Bagging, (3) Boosting, (4) Data augmentation, (5) Randomization approaches, (6) Proper modeling (Ensemble learning), and (7) Cross-validation (k-fold, leave-one-out for small dataset).

snippets: 6.3 Applications The predictive modeling tools described in this chapter provide an idea of the commonly used tools in regression modeling. There are numerous other predictive modeling approaches that have been developed (sometimes specific to application scenarios) and it is beyond the scope of this book to review all such possibilities. For application purposes, there is usually no single tool that always works best and often the associated steps of data preprocessing, feature selection, and error estimation play significant roles along with model selection in the final model performance. The various steps involved in predictive model generation can be broadly categorized as (A) Data Preprocessing, (B) Feature Selection, (C) Model Selection, and (D) Performance Evaluation, as shown in  Fig. 6.3 . Step A involves processing the genetic and epigenetic data to numerical or categorical form that can be utilized to train the predictive model. These steps have been described in  Chapter 2 . A specific form of model may require a particular form of data processing; for instance, a logistic regression model will require the output response to be categorical. Normalization can allow use of data collected from different platforms to be used in the model training. Step B involves feature selection, which has been discussed in detail in the chapter on  Feature Selection . This step may require the use of the specific model in step C if wrapper or embedded form of feature selection is used. Often, prior biological knowledge can provide information on selecting the important features. Step C involves the selection and training of the specific predictive model. Data type can sometimes guide the selection of the model class, such as when we are certain that the output response is linearly related to the input features, a linear regression form of model will likely be a good choice. Note that a complex model-to-model data that can be represented by a linear relationship might result in overfitting and will be going against the idea of  Occam’s Razor . Step D involves performance evaluation which was discussed in detail in  Chapter 4 . For performance evaluation, we select a performance measure, such as mean square error and the approach, such as cross-validation to measure it based on the available samples. If we are planning to select a model from competing models in part C, step D becomes even more crucial. The error estimation techniques are not guaranteed to generalize well over the real population distribution and the estimated errors may be significantly different from the true error.

In the context of imbalanced and overlapped datasets, a common strategy is to incorporate information regarding both these problems in the development of approaches. Such information might appear in the form of an heuristic based on complexity measures and/or other observed characteristics of datasets, leading to the development of specialised approaches. Alternatively, it can also be based on the tuning of hyperparameters. In this case, the main objective is to maximise the classification performance by choosing optimal hyperparameters for classifying or preprocessing each dataset. Whereas some strategies for specialised approaches have been applied in the literature, hyperparameter tuning remains an understudied topic in what concerns the design of approaches sensitive to the peculiarities of data suffering simultaneously from class imbalance and overlap. 11 11 Note that hyperparameter tuning,  per se , constitutes a topic of interest across several fields beyond traditional Supervised Learning, such as Deep Learning, and Meta-learning   . Accordingly, some intersections between terms, trends, and solutions are likely to arise. Notwithstanding, in this paper, we detach from that intersection and overall considerations on hyperparameter tuning regarding the Deep Learning and Meta-leaning fields specifically. In alternative, we focus particularly on hyperparameter tuning with respect to imbalanced and overlapped domains, highlighting existing limitations which are yet to be addressed by all communities. In what follows, we discuss some existing approaches in this regard. 4.3.1 Specialised approaches Depending on the category of class overlap based-approaches (please refer to Section  4.2.1 ), different strategies may arise for the development of specialised approaches.
