snippets: 3.4 Interpretability through probabilistic modeling A repeatedly cited drawback of interpretable load forecasting algorithms is that uncertainties are neither sufficiently quantified nor made visible to the end user. Probabilistic Load Forecasting (PLF) aims to quantify and integrate uncertainties into the forecast. This can be done by estimating quantiles on the predictions or some level of additional confidence boundaries. Fig. 6  shows a visualization example of a probabilistic prediction by plotting selected quantiles. We recognize that the class of probabilistic models cannot be fully classified as interpretable as defined in Section  1.1 , and we see PLF at the far edge of the interpretability spectrum. While the additional modeling helps to better understand the prediction without requiring additional information for the user, the underlying models can be very complex, and the design depends on how the PLF is made. For the classification of interpretability, first, the different modeling techniques are described. According to   , three approaches for calculating a PLF can be distinguished in general: (1) deterministic models that become ensemble learners by passing in different input scenarios, (2) novel PLF models that implicitly learn a posterior probability by definition and (3) post-processing of a point forecast model by integrating the residual likelihood function or combining multiple models. Models created according to approaches (1) and (3) inherit the interpretability properties of their deterministic models. The easy-to-interpret concept of a SVM, for example, was augmented by an ensemble-learning setup in the work done by Li et al.   . For this purpose, SVMs were trained on subsamples of the entire training set, and the hyperparameters of each model were determined using swarm optimization. The SVMs were then sampled using Monte Carlo simulation to obtain both final forecasts and confidence intervals. Models following approach (2) internally model the probabilities, that yield inherent interpretability in the sense that likelihoods are modeled directly. A popular base class are State-Space Model (SSM), i.e. classical statistical models that allow interpretable statements to be made about trends and seasonality by construction, which are then extended.  , for example, achieve interpretability by using a Bayesian Structural Time Series Model (BSTS), which combines a SSM at its core with quantifying the posterior uncertainties of the model components.

A fifth method is developed by combining the models with the highest accuracy. Ensemble learning is an approach that combines several algorithms into a single predictive model in order to decrease variance (bagging), reduce bias (boosting) or improve predictions (stacking) ( Witten et al., 2011 ). To combine models, a stacking technique ( Wolpert, 1992 ) is used. Unlike bagging and boosting (used, e.g., in RF), stacking is used to merge models of different type. Roughly, stacking discovers how best to combine the output of base models by using another learning algorithm (the metalearner). For this purpose, a meta-model is trained with the outputs of the base classifiers as input features. In this work, SVM and ANN are selected as base classifiers for stacking, since it will be shown later that they provide higher accuracy.

snippets: To maximize accuracy in practical applications, advantage can often be gained by combining multiple models. snippets: The rules governing the behavior of ML systems, conversely, are often encoded within complex mathematical architectures that the conscious mind is incapable of interpreting. A visualization of a rudimentary artificial neural network (ANN) algorithm (the most sophisticated genre of ML algorithm, which underpins deep-learning applications) is shown in  Fig. 1 . There have been many attempts to explain the rules encoded within such algorithms using saliency maps,  deconvolution of convolutional networks, etc. Such approaches can offer useful insights into certain aspects of a system’s functionality but the wider internal logic remains overwhelmingly opaque. The importance of this in the clinical setting is that even if an ML system has been extensively informed by and validated upon high-quality data, it is extremely difficult to anticipate when and how it will defy an operator’s expectations. Any parent is well placed to grasp this concept: one may develop and validate a predictive model of a child’s behavior based on enormous quantities of observational data, and the model may be reliable the vast majority of the time. However, the opaque nature of the internal logic that governs a child’s behavioral impulses means it is impossible to foresee when and how a child will confound expectations. How many of us, for example, have anticipated that our children will continue to play nicely if we leave the room for a few moments—based, in all likelihood, on this pattern having been observed countless times before—only to find the walls covered in crayon on our return? For real-world examples, consider the Google algorithm that labeled a photograph of an Afro-Caribbean couple as gorillas or the Tesla whose autopilot caused a fatal collision by failing to detect a truck pulling out on to the road, despite the accident report concluding that the truck would have been visible to the car for a full 7 seconds prior to impact   . The former example is sobering because if Google cannot exert enough control over their ML algorithms to avoid a public relations disaster, one must wonder how smaller companies in the digital health space will fare. The latter is even more concerning from a healthcare perspective, as it exemplifies the potentially grave consequences of reliance on opaque technology in a high stakes setting. Moving forwards The need for transparency in AI is becoming widely acknowledged, though how this is achieved remains an open question for regulatory bodies   .

snippets: Transparency refers to the degree to which the inner workings of an IDS are understandable and interpretable by human operators. Black-box models, such as deep neural networks, often provide high accuracy but lack transparency due to their complex architectures. Techniques like layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) ( Binder et al., 2016 ) and sensitivity analysis ( Pizarroso et al., 2022 ) can be employed to shed light on their decision-making process. On the other hand, white-box models like decision trees or rule-based systems offer higher interpretability by directly exposing their decision rules. However, they may sacrifice some predictive performance. Hybrid approaches, combining the strengths of both black-box and white-box models, can be explored to strike a balance between accuracy and transparency. As pointed out by  Duraz et al. (2023) , evaluation of XAI-based methods is still difficult and often lacking and more work is needed; they also suggest completeness and correctness as quantitative metrics for measuring the quality of explanations by an XAI-based system. Following are some techniques used in XAI-based IDSes to generate explanations for the predictions of black-box models, thereby enhancing interpretability: • RuleFit proposed by  Friedman and Popescu (2008) . • LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) proposed by  Ribeiro et al. (2016) . • SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) proposed by  Lundberg and Lee (2017) . Not many researchers have designed ML models which use XAI for intrusion detection in IoT. In this section, we delve into the few ML-based IDSes developed for intrusion detection in IoT in the last five years. El Houda et al. (2022)  introduce an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)-powered framework based on ML and DL for intrusion detection in IoT. This framework not only identifies intrusions but also provides explanations for the conclusions it draws regarding attacks. The authors construct a DNN architecture for real-time intrusion detection and subsequently develop multiple XAI-models layered on top of the DNN architecture. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of their approach in not only detecting well-known IoT attacks but also elucidating the decision-making process. Khan et al. (2022b)  introduce the XSRU-IoMT model, designed for the prompt detection of sophisticated attacks in IoMT networks.

snippets: Mir et al.    show that interpretability, model complexity, and model performance are not necessarily opposing properties of a predictive model: a linear regression prediction with a strong dependence on the exogenous variable yields good results if further polynomial combinations are added to the input variables in the context of feature engineering. The coefficients of the terms resulting from the training permit interpretable conclusions on the influence of the variables. Another simple but widely used class of models are autoregressive models, i.e., models that make future predictions by a weighted linear combination of past data points and integrated exogenous variables. To evaluate the tradeoff between interpretability and model performance,    compare three autoregressive models with exogenous input with three parameterizations: In the simplest case (linear parameterization), the coefficients correspond precisely to the variable weights. In the second case (black box parameterization), coefficients are trained that weight an unknown nonlinear feature map (box function), similar to the kernel of a Support Vector Machine (SVM). In the last case (Partially Linear Parameterization), weather and calendar information are weighted nonlinearly, while historical values are weighted linearly. The case study for forecasting in a Short-Term load forecasting setting shows that the partial linear variant with partially interpretable coefficients performs just as well as the fully black-box-based variant. 3.2 Interpretability through time series decomposition A recurring pattern as an aid to interpretability is the decomposition of the time series to be forecast into individual partial forecasts, which are then again combined into one global forecast. The decomposition serves several purposes in terms of interpretability. Firstly, the decomposition reduces the forecast complexity of the decomposed signals so that partly less complex models, each of which can be interpreted separately, can be used. Second, the decomposed functions, such as  Trend  and  Season , are based on semantics that the user can inherently understand. The three steps of decomposition, sub-forecasting, and aggregation are the essential components of this procedure, as visualized in  Fig. 3 . The work of Peng et al.    combines simple concepts, each of which can be interpreted individually, to obtain a powerful yet interpretable hybrid model. The load is decomposed into a set of high-frequency signals, and a low-frequency residual is done using an Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) method (namely Differential Empirical Mode Decomposition (DEMD)).

concept: Support Vector Machines (SVM) are powerful supervised learning algorithms used for classification and regression, capable of handling both linear and non-linear data through the use of kernel functions. They are particularly effective in high-dimensional spaces and have applications in various fields, including image and text classification.

Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) consist of autonomous agents that interact to achieve specific goals, showcasing diverse capabilities and perspectives. They are applicable in smart cities, transportation, supply chain management, and healthcare, with models designed for coordination, reasoning, traffic control, and privacy management.

Computer Vision is a critical area that enables machines to interpret visual data, leveraging machine learning techniques to recognize objects and patterns. It plays a vital role in analyzing data from IoT sensors and cameras, enhancing decision-making processes.

Deep Learning, a subset of machine learning, utilizes hierarchical neural networks to learn complex patterns from data. It has transformed fields like image recognition and natural language processing, requiring substantial data and computational resources for training.

Neural Networks, inspired by the human brain, consist of interconnected nodes that process data through layers. They excel in capturing intricate patterns and relationships, making them suitable for tasks such as image analysis and language translation.

The evolution of deep learning has been significantly influenced by advancements in computing power, allowing for the management of large datasets and complex models, thus enhancing the viability of these techniques in practical applications.

Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a powerful supervised learning algorithm used for classification and regression, particularly effective in high-dimensional spaces, making it suitable for tasks like pneumoconiosis detection.

The performance of SVM is heavily influenced by the choice of kernel functions, which transform data into higher dimensions to facilitate better class separation. Common kernels include linear, polynomial, radial basis function (RBF), and sigmoid.
SVM operates by identifying support vectors, which are the data points closest to the decision boundary (hyperplane), and maximizing the margin between classes to enhance classification accuracy.

While SVM is robust and can handle complex nonlinear relationships, it requires significant computational resources and may struggle with larger datasets, making it less suitable for extensive training sets compared to other methods.
The algorithm's complexity can lead to challenges in interpreting the relationships between input features and output classifications, which is a notable disadvantage in practical applications.
SVM has been successfully applied in various fields, including medical imaging, financial analysis, and text classification, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

Decision trees are another supervised learning method that can handle both classification and regression tasks, providing a clear and interpretable model structure, but they may not perform as well in capturing complex relationships compared to SVM.

Feature selection is crucial in SVM applications to avoid the negative impact of irrelevant or noisy features, which can degrade model performance, highlighting the importance of preprocessing in machine learning workflows.

snippets: 3.1.2.1 Support vector machine SVM is a widely used conventional classifier for pneumoconiosis detection, because of its strong generalization capability for high dimensional input space. SVM is a supervised learning algorithm which can be applied for both classification and regression problems. For classification, the basic idea of SVM is to construct a hyper-plane that efficiently segregates the data samples into distinct classes, by maximizing the margin between nearest examples of either class. The performance of SVM greatly depends on the choice of kernels. The kernels are the functions that takes a low-dimensional input space and transforms it into a high-dimensional space (i.e., from inseparable to separable). Some of the commonly used kernel functions include:  linear ,  polynomial ,  radial basis function (RBF) , and  sigmoid  etc.  Zhu et al. (2014a)  investigated  SVM  with  4  different kernels based on the  Energy  features extracted from wavelet transform and found that SVM with a polynomial kernel result in higher diagnostic performance than the rest. Zhu et al. (2014b)  further their study by using an ensemble learning approach and used “SVM with a linear kernel” as a base classifier. First, they extracted the lung fields and divided them into six regions, and then for each region the base classifier is used to perform classification. Second, individual classification results were aggregated based on a weighted voting method, which is based on the AUC value of each region. Several researchers ( Yu et al., 2009a ,  2009b ,  2011 ;  Masumoto et al., 2011 ) have attempted to create a CAD system based on SVM for widespread clinical screening for pneumoconiosis, including  Sundararajan et al. (2010)  and  Xu et al. (2010) . The first step in their research is to segment left and right lung fields. The former aimed to perform lung segmentation using rule-based approaches including  thresholding ,  morphology , and  connected components , while the later attempted to improve it by employing an active shape model (ASM) approach. In both the studies, each lung area is subsequently split into three equal zones namely:  top ,  middle , and  bottom . Multiscale difference filter bank method is utilized to enhance chest abnormalities.

snippets: The points that are closest to the border are termed “support vectors.” SVM can be in two forms: (1) linear SVM: use of linear optimization for linear separation (if possible) and this methodology is relatively fast (and resembles logistic regression) and (2) kernel SVM: use of many different kinds of dividing structures called kernels (Note. The so-called kernel trick is a mathematical trick that adds an extra dimension so that what is not possible in certain number of dimensions can now be possible with more dimensions.) In short, kernels delineate the boundary in a nonlinear fashion (either curved line or an optimal plane). Common usages are spam filtering, sentiment analysis, image classification and segmentation, recognition of handwritten characters, and fraud detection. Advantages and disadvantages This popular but relatively complex ML methodology can be good for complex nonlinear relationships between input features and output. This methodology is often considered one of the most accurate algorithms for classification, especially when there is a high number of features (compared to the number of data points) and is therefore effective in high-dimensional data. SVM is also robust and thus can avoid noise as well as minimize overfitting. SVM is frequently used when one has a small training dataset as it does not scale well to larger datasets (larger training sets may be better suited for other classification methodologies or even DL). While linear SVM is considered relatively fast (but less accurate), kernel SVM is perhaps more accurate (but slower) for classification. Disadvantages include SVM needing high levels of both memory and processing power and difficulty in interpreting the precise relationship between input features and output. An example in the recent biomedical literature is the usage of SVM in CT-based radiomic features to effectively identify high and low grades of clear cell renal cell carcinoma in only 227 patients with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.88–0.91   . Naive Bayes classifiers This supervised learning methodology uses probability to divide or categorize the data and is based on Bayes’ theorem (with its concept of prior probability which selects the outcome with the highest probability). The presumption is that the predictors are independent of each other (hence the term “naive”) so the model becomes essentially a probability table where the presence of a certain feature is not dependent on any other feature.

snippets: This allows a clear separation of data in the data space, thus allow selecting data precisely to one class or the other   . SVM is very useful when the numbers of features are high. It allows mapping the data in the feature space with very less computation in comparison to other classification algorithms. SVM defines a margin or a hyperplane for segregating two classes, where the hyperplane is a subspace having dimensions one less than the dimension required for projecting the data in space. The hyperplane is linear, where there are two features. Fig. 1.10  shows the hyperplane made from the support vectors, which uniquely partitions two classes of data in space. The margin of separation is wide enough, which provides the boundary of separation and thus, confidence in classification   . For high dimensional space, linearly separating the classes is not possible. Appropriate kernel functions are used for defining such hyperplane to separate classes nonlinearly, which otherwise is a nontrivial job. The SVM algorithm thus can be considered as a set of kernel functions. The kernel function transforms the input data into the desired output form. snippets: For a two-class classification problem, given training samples {( x 1 , y 1 ), … , ( x n , y n )},  y i ϵ {−1, +1}, the optimization problem for learning a linear classifier in the feature space is defined as (hard margin):  min w , b 〈 w , w 〉 , subject to  y i 〈 w , Φ ( x i )〉 + b ⩾ 1,  i = 1, … , n , where  Φ  is the mapping from original space to feature space and symbol 〈〉 means the inner product of two vectors. The matrix composed by inner products of samples in feature space (after linear or non-linear mapping) is called the kernel matrix which describes the similarities between samples and serves as evidence when we maximize the margin between two classes of samples. The above problem is a quadratic programming (QP) optimization problem and it is convex. The optimal ( w * , b * ) is a maximal margin classifier with geometric margin  γ = 1/|| w * || 2  if it exists. It can be applied to classify test samples once it is learned from the training set. The concept of the geometric margin learned by the SVM is shown in  Fig. 3  in which samples on the margin are called support vectors. In many real clinical applications, we can extract many features with the help of modern medical test equipment, e.g., lab tests and radiology devices. In addition, with hundreds (or thousands or more) of features from test equipments doctors may also wonder which features are relevant or useful for the diagnosis of certain diseases so they can give better interpretations of the clinical findings. concept: Support Vector Machines (SVM) are effective supervised learning algorithms for classification and regression, widely applied in fields like image and text classification and speech recognition.

Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) consist of autonomous agents that interact to achieve common goals, applicable in diverse areas such as smart cities, transportation, supply chain management, and healthcare.
Specific MAS applications include:
Computer Vision enables machines to interpret visual data, supporting decision-making through analysis of data from IoT sensors and cameras.
Anomaly detection in networks can be enhanced through decentralized methods, utilizing statistical models and behavior analysis to identify malicious agents.
Multi-timescale decision-making is crucial in environments with varying operational frequencies, such as UAV systems, where task offloading and power control are optimized at different time scales.
Clustering techniques, like k-means and fuzzy c-means, are essential for managing large-scale systems by grouping devices for efficient decision-making and communication.
Multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) frameworks facilitate independent decision-making among agents, promoting cooperation and competition in edge computing environments.

This family refers to MAS, which are systems composed of multiple autonomous agents that interact with each other and with the environment to achieve certain goals. MAS can be used in various applications, such as smart cities, transportation systems, supply chain management, and healthcare. Some examples of MAS used in the reviewed articles include:  •  Coordinator Agent: A MAS model was proposed to optimize the coordination between multiple stakeholders in a supply chain management system. The system included a coordinator agent who monitored the supply chain and coordinated the activities of the other agents to achieve the best possible outcomes. •  Reasoning and Belief Knowledge on graphs: Another MAS model was proposed to represent and reason about beliefs and knowledge in a social network. The system used graph theory to represent the social network and the Neo4j tool to store and query the graph. The agents in the system could infer beliefs and knowledge based on the information available in the network. •  Autonomous Agents: A MAS model was proposed to control traffic in a smart city. The system included autonomous agents that could communicate with each other and with the traffic infrastructure to optimize traffic flow and reduce congestion. •  AI-Privacy Agent: In a healthcare application, a MAS model was proposed to manage the privacy of patient data. snippets: Agents conduct detection through operating conditions classed against optimal desired goal states. States are determined from Routing Protocol for Low power and Lossy network (RPL) characteristics and employed within agents. Cluster heads determine malicious nodes based on solicited node information. Inter-device requests are monitored to detect deviation in system behavior interactions within ( Lauf et al., 2007 ). Behavior analysis results are categorized based on statistical features, represented in a list as values. Behaviors are generated based on semi-random Chi-squared probability density functions. Local and global maxima are used to determine malicious agents, with lower tolerance levels yielding improvements. Markov models are used for statistical anomaly detection within a wireless sensor environment ( Paschalidis and Chen, 2010 ). Chains are used to model behavior in comparing activity to known anomaly free behavior with transitions and deviations. First considering node level events of interest, secondly based on connection structures through tree indexing and thirdly, hierarchical state relating to parent/child, also by an index tree. 3.2.3 Utility Lauf et al. (2010)  proposes a decentralized anomaly detection of node behavior, namely application level interactions. Within an ad-hoc environment, identification is achieved through two detection methods,  Maximal Detection System  (MDS), which is then used to calibrate the  Cross-Correlation Detection System  (CCDS). Behavior determination is achieved through a Probability Density Function (PDF) of local and global maxima to help determine the state of the network. Application requests among devices are recorded within a history table to an associated integer; entries are ranked based on most appropriate behavior against defined offline behavior set, with CCDS constructing average nodes scores based on probability density function (PDF). Variance thresholds based on average score results in identification, providing an associated utility regarding operation. Adjustments were made to allow scalable function and threshold calibration. An autonomous Multi-Agent Immune System,  MAIS-ID,S  is presented in  Seresht and Azmi (2014) . The hybrid approach seeks to determine system settings and traffic classification through the use of Immune Network, Negative Selection (NS), Clonal Selection (CS) and Danger Theory (DTh). Implemented within a virtual environment, agents seek to improve their detection goals in collaboration based on an agent's fitness utility. A review of immunity based intruder detection and context mappings can be found at  Liu et al. (2011) .

concept: Machine learning in robotics is categorized into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, each serving distinct purposes in enhancing robotic capabilities such as perception, navigation, and adaptability.

Deep learning and computer vision have significantly advanced, particularly in industrial applications, enabling machines to perform complex tasks like automated disassembly with high accuracy through models like CNNs and YOLO.

Supervised learning relies on labeled data to train algorithms, allowing for predictions based on input-output mappings, while unsupervised learning identifies patterns in unlabeled data, and reinforcement learning focuses on goal-oriented behavior through reward systems.

Machine learning encompasses various algorithms, including support vector machines, decision trees, and neural networks, which are designed to learn from past experiences and make autonomous decisions.

The integration of machine learning with IoT applications is growing, necessitating the development of hybrid approaches to address complex challenges in smart environments, such as energy consumption prediction and travel pattern analysis.

Density-based algorithms have shown superior performance in clustering tasks compared to distance-based methods, particularly in terms of memory efficiency and handling arbitrary shapes, highlighting the need for innovative techniques in data analysis.

snippets: 3.5 Machine learning and AI approaches Machine learning in robotics falls into supervised, unsupervised, and  Reinforcement learning  (RL) categories. Supervised learning leverages labelled data, fuelling advancements in robotic perception, sensing, and navigation (primarily through deep learning and computer vision). Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data, aiding robotics in complex scenarios. RL trains goal-oriented behaviours with reward systems, driving progress in robotic adaptability; a simplified instance of this can be seen  Fig. 6 . 3.5.1 Deep learning and Computer vision Deep learning and computer vision have seen remarkable advancements in recent years, significantly impacting various applications, including automated disassembly   . Machine vision integration, which encompasses object detection, localisation, and segmentation, has become pivotal in industrial applications. These technologies achieved remarkable accuracy and efficiency. Research employing deep learning models such as  Convolutional Neural Networks  (CNNs) and their derivatives, including Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, and  You Only Look Once  (YOLO)   , along with innovative methods for 3D perception   , have showcased the profound impact of AI integration in tasks that were once considered difficult for automation. The deep learning architectures have empowered machines to analyse and interpret visual data with unparallelled precision. The advancement in deep learning, precisely Computer vision, primarily uses two types of input data: 2D RGB images and 3D point clouds, each with distinct methodologies and applications tailored to the challenges of disassembling electronic waste, optimising railway fastener detection and enhancing structural health monitoring, among others. Table 6  presents a concise comparison of 2D RGB image and 3D point cloud processing methods. For 2D RGB images, region proposal-based two-stage methods have been developed to improve the accuracy of object detection tasks, such as screw detection in electronic waste disassembly. Studies like  [42–45,48]  exemplify the use of deep learning models, like Faster R-CNN, combined with techniques such as gamma correction and rotation edge similarity, to achieve high precision in identifying and classifying objects for disassembly. Despite their high accuracy, these methods are noted for their slower inference speeds and higher computational costs, which may limit their suitability for real-time applications.

snippets: 6.4 Introduction to machine learning Artificial intelligence (AI) is growing as a powerful and most promising technology due to the exponential growth of high computing devices. AI is applied almost in all fields wherever human intelligence can be replaceable. The field which is emerging from AI is machine learning. It consists of a set of efficient algorithms based on statistical methods such as regression and correlation. The supremacy of these machine learning algorithms is that they facilitate the power of autonomous working to any system by learning from past experiences without any human intervention. Machine learning algorithms are designed from combinations of computational, mathematical, and statistical methodologies. The principal objective of machine learning is to develop computer programs that can learn themselves from past experiences and making efficient decisions for necessitating further action in any domain. The machine learning comprises of a number of algorithms based on statistical techniques such as regression, classification, and correlation. The commonly used machine learning are support vector machines, decision trees, naïve Bayes, artificial neural networks, K-nearest neighbor. Machine learning is a subfield of computer science derived from the field of artificial intelligence (AI). There are four categories of machine learning methods based on the learning strategy, such as supervised learning algorithms, unsupervised learning algorithms, semisupervised algorithms, and reinforcement learning algorithms, which are explained below. 6.4.1 Categories of machine learning Machine learning algorithms are divided into four categories, as supervised learning, unsupervised learning, semisupervised learning, and reinforcement learning based on their learning pattern. Each category has its unique functionality and limitations, and they are described below. 6.4.1.1 Supervised learning Many of the machine learning algorithms are based on supervised learning strategy. In the supervised learning category, the set of input variables ( X ) and a set of output variables ( Y ) will be provided. The algorithm will learn the mapping function  Y = f ( X ) from the input to the output. The mapping function is designed such that for a new value of  X , the output value  Y  can be predicted. This data is called as training data set as it acts as a supervisor for the learning process. The algorithm makes a number of iterations for predicting the value until it obtains optimum value. The supervised learning method is applied in regression and classification problems. In the supervised machine learning, the set inputs or features are directly associated with a known outcome. This attribute is useful for representing the real-world scenario by appropriately associating the objects with their characteristics.

snippets: Machine learning Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence, where data is acquired to let machines learn or train machines. By designing a model using the learned ability, we try to find an answer to a problem or predict the result of events. Learning is done by algorithms, which typically receive data and generate output using mathematics and logic. This learning process studies algorithms to automatically find rules from given data without having to program them one by one. We call this machine learning because it allows the machine to learn from the data. Machine learning is closely related to the field of statistics and optimization. This field is showing high interest and rapid development with the support of the computing power of computers. In connection with the geographic information system, this field is applied to satellite and aerial photographic image processing, industry spatial distribution and trends, and optimal transportation routes. Even a very good algorithm calculates the accuracy of results that are more than necessary, or if the complexity increases, it results in high-performance inefficiency. On the contrary, if the accuracy is low and there are many errors in the result prediction, the error in the prediction leads to incorrect results. Machine learning uses the following different approaches to learn based on datasets and problems being solved. 1. Supervised learning 2. Unsupervised learning 3. Reinforcement learning 4. Ensemble learning Supervised learning allows artificial intelligence to infer answers by putting answers that are already known by algorithm participants into the algorithm. Therefore, this participant sets the input data to a specific labeled output and creates a pair of inputs and outputs to determine the correlation. Thus, artificial intelligence trained with this pair generates an output value by attaching a label suitable for the new input data. On the other hand, there is no labeled pair in the input value of unsupervised learning. It is just creating a group of similar data. Then, the clustered input data features are extracted to generate an output value for a new input value. Reinforcement learning is a learning process in which agents and environments interact through information such as action, state, and reward to achieve a given goal. In this process, feedback may be delayed as the reward signal is the only guide without a supervisor who determines the result. Therefore, time differences should be considered due to delayed feedback. A function of receiving a state as an input and outputting an action to be taken is called a policy. In other words, the policy is an algorithm used by an agent to determine an action.

snippets: Authors used statistical approaches in power datasets, KNN, and discrete-time warping for distance measures in a smart environment. Ni et al. (2014)  also presented a hybrid technique for sensor data prediction in the IoT. To address this problem, Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD) is employed for non-linear and non-stationary signal sequences. It also applied Support Vector Regression (SVR) after mapping the data to a high-dimensional space using a kernel function. The parameters of SVR are optimized using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Ma et al. (2013)  proposed a model for transit riders’ travel patterns that uses smart card transaction data and employed the DBSCAN algorithm to discover historical travel patterns as well as KMeans with rough set techniques for clustering and classification. Due to the massive amount of data presented on the Internet of Agricultural Things ( Han et al., 2014 ), the bayesian network is used to determine the final product’s trust value. Costa and Santos (2015)  utilized data mining techniques for massive data processing in smart homes to predict future energy consumption. They also used K-means algorithm to detect intra-cluster similarities. Shukla et al. (2015)  proposed outlier detection techniques for stream data mining. They demonstrated that a density-based algorithm produces more purity than a distance-based approach. The density-based technique gives the best results in terms of memory consumption and arbitrary shape. Monekosso and Remagnino (2013)  explored the data-driven approach for validating sensor-generated historical data utilizing Curvilinear Component Analysis (CCA) and Principle Component Analysis (PCA) algorithm to detect intermittent faults and failure masking. This study infers that the key algorithms applied in smart city management are KNN, PSO, DBSCAN, K-means, naive bayes, PCA, CCA, ensemble learning, and DT for classification and clustering. As the IoT sector grows, new and hybrid ML approaches are required to tackle complex problems.

snippets: 8.3 Hierarchical inference Hierarchical (or staged) inference is an application of a  divide et impera  paradigm to DNN execution. An inference task (e.g., a classification) is split into multiple subtasks, with the easiest being the most common. These multiple tasks are then sequentially executed in increasing complexity order, with the chance of stopping earlier to save energy. Optionally, the subinferences can be performed on different devices, such as edge nodes for the simplest tasks and cloud server for the most computationally intensive ones, in a collaborative fashion. The main difficulty in this approach is being able to split a single machine learning task into multiple subinferences, which is a strongly application-dependent problem. Therefore, this is a somewhat less generally applicable method compared to ensemble and conditional systems. One domain where this methodology has been successfully applied is speech recognition for voice assistants such as Apple Siri, and in particular the implementation for the Apple Watch [ 26 ]. In general, speech recognition requires large and power hungry DNNs, unable to fit on a constrained smartwatch. On the other hand, the latency and energy requirements for interacting with a voice assistant are strict, in order to achieve a good user experience, and may not be obtained by a system that constantly transmits to the cloud. The task is then split in two parts: wakeword recognition and speech recognition. A reduced-size RNN is deployed on the edge device (the smart watch), constantly running in the background but with very low-power consumption. This network performs wakeword recognition, which being a much easier task than voice recognition can be handled by simple and low-power models. When a wakeword is detected, the edge device offloads the rest of the audio data to the cloud, where a computationally expensive model is used to interpret them. This division in subtasks permits both a consistent reduction of the data transmitted to the cloud, and a smaller response latency. A similar hierarchical approach is proposed in [ 35 ], where the authors hierarchically split a face recognition task for personal devices such as smartphones.

snippets: 2.2.6 Deep learning Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that focuses on training artificial neural networks to learn and represent complex patterns and relationships in data. Inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain, deep learning involves the use of multiple layers, or “deep” architectures, to progressively learn hierarchical features from raw input data. Each layer in the network extracts higher-level features from the representations learned in the previous layer. Deep learning has revolutionized various domains, such as image recognition, natural language processing, and speech synthesis, achieving remarkable performance improvements compared to traditional machine learning techniques. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at image-related tasks by exploiting spatial hierarchies, while recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are adept at sequential data, like language ( Aggarwal, 2018 ). Deep learning models often require substantial amounts of labeled data and considerable computational resources, making them computationally intensive but capable of learning intricate patterns and representations. The use of deep architectures, in combination with techniques, such as regularization, optimization, and transfer learning, has enabled deep learning to excel across a wide range of applications and significantly advance the capabilities of machine learning systems ( Schmidhuber, 2015 ). 2.2.7 Neural networks Neural networks are computational models inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain's interconnected neurons. These networks consist of layers of interconnected nodes, or artificial neurons, which process and transform input data to produce output ( Aggarwal, 2018 ;  Du & Swamy, 2019 ). Each connection between neurons is associated with a weight, and these weights are learned from data during training. The architecture typically includes an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Information is fed forward through the layers, with each neuron performing a weighted sum of its inputs followed by a nonlinear activation function. This process allows neural networks to capture complex patterns and relationships in data that might be difficult for traditional algorithms. Various types of neural networks exist, such as feedforward neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) ( Ozturk, 2022 ) for image analysis, and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequential data processing. Neural networks have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in tasks like image recognition, language translation, and game playing, leading to their prominence in the fields of machine learning and artificial intelligence.

snippets: According to Geoffrey Hinton (Google) “Deep Learning is an algorithm which has no theoretical limitations of what it can learn; the more data you give and computational time you provide, the better it is.” Due to the Deep Learning popularity during last years, several academic and industry groups (Facebook, Google, Baidu, …) started to develop frameworks to help users to apply easily these techniques to their problems. Maybe the most known software was TensorFlow, from Google, but there are many others such as Theano, Neon, DeepLearning4J, Eblearn, and MXNet. In biomedicine, these techniques offered good results in cancer diagnosis and classification, splicing (one of the major factors that provide biological diversity of proteins in eukaryotic organisms), image processing (microarrays analysis or segmentation, for example), feature extraction, proteomics, drug discovery, and so on. Furthermore, approaches based on Deep Learning techniques have been recently used successfully in fields like Phenotypic automation of embryo development (Deep Learning—Convolutional Neural Networks), predict drug toxicity both at the atomic and molecular level (Deep Learning—Convolutional Neural Networks), prediction of molecular properties, such as aqueous solubility (Deep Learning—Recurrent Neural Networks), biomedicine ( Mamoshina et al., 2016 ), or privacy preserving ( Shokri and Shmatikov, 2015 ). Of course, despite the great results achieved in biomedicine and other many different areas the solutions based on Deep Learning approaches are not free from challenges and limitations. Among them, we can cite the following: ● They act as a black box. This is one of the major limitations of these methods. They take an input and provide an output without any (useful) information about how this association is done giving the final user a lack of transparency. ● The need of large data sets. In biomedicine this is not the main problem, but in other areas it can be a bottleneck. ● The selection problem. There are many types of Deep Learning approaches: convolutional neural networks, feedforward, recurrent or recursive neural networks, extreme learning machines … and the task-appropriate selection is not always straightforward ( Deng, 2014 ).

Geng et al. proposed induction networks for better generalization by leveraging dynamic routing algorithms in meta-learning to implement a more generalized representation of the data in the support set   . Afterwards, they evolved a dynamic routing mechanism on static memory to adapt it to new classes better   . It was also possible to capture language features and understand downstream language tasks better by pre-training the language representation   . In parallel, the textual diversity restricts the application of meta-learning as texts can be expressed in different ways even for the same class   . Existing research augmented the data by generating more samples   , and also enhanced the prototype network with relational and entity descriptions   . snippets: 1 Introduction Deep learning is an exciting paradigm in the pattern recognition and machine learning communities. In essence, the proliferation of high performance computing and large annotated datasets (big data), coupled with the rapid development of deep neural networks (DNNs), has greatly improved the quality of the data learning process   . There has been a rapid shift from shallow learning of hand-crafted features extracted using local descriptors (e.g., HOG, SIFT, etc.) to automatic learning of high-level feature representations derived from raw data, allowing complex features and deep classifiers to be learned together   . In general, this new approach requires little hands-on engineering, as the parameter tuning pipeline can be run directly from the raw data with fewer time-consuming data pre-processing steps. Flexible learning mechanisms and the use of deep networks are key factors that facilitate the use of deep learning methods, along with the development of appropriate frameworks. Many vision-based challenges have been effectively solved by integrating the deep learning paradigm instead of hand-crafted methods. In addition, many computer vision tasks, especially image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, have been introduced, and the latest competitive solutions are based on deep learning methods   . In this paper, we first provide a basic overview of deep learning and explain how deep learning can be used in practice, including a discussion of the most commonly used DNN models and their main properties. Standalone discriminative and generative DNNs, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs)    and generative adversarial networks (GANs)   , are popular deep learning techniques that have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in many real-world applications and use cases   . For example, CNNs are mainly used to process visual cues and have shown better generalization ability than other discriminative networks; RNNs and their variants are another type of DNN that can be trained to extract short- and long-range dependencies between features from continuous data. A model can be classified as a hybrid deep learning model when two deep learning architectures are merged using a bridging network (or fusion method), or when deep learning and machine learning are mixed for prediction purposes. We call this process hybridization. This process, or the act of merging two or more standalone architectures, is often referred to as a hybrid fusion.

snippets: In the context of power systems, which consist of interconnected generators and loads, GCNs are applied to understand the graph structure of the power systems, comprising nodes (buses) and edges (branches)   . Another advanced model of GNNs used in the system inertia monitoring is Graph Attention Networks (GATs). GATs allocate different levels of attention to neighbouring nodes during information diffusion, learning the importance of each node in a graph   . By utilizing attention mechanisms, GATs effectively capture intricate relationships and spatial dependencies, improving their performance in tasks like node classification and link prediction. 3.3.2 Residual neural network Residual neural Network (ResNet) represents a significant advancement in CNN-based architectures, addressing the vanishing gradient problem that tends to occur in deep networks with many layers   . ResNet introduces a “shortcut connections” or “skip connections” to facilitate the training of very deep networks, allowing the gradients to flow more effectively through the network without vanishing or exploding. The ability to train very deep networks with ResNet has led to improved accuracy on various computer vision tasks, such as image classification   , object detection   , and segmentation   . 3.3.3 Long-Term Recurrent Convolutional network Long-term Recurrent Convolutional Network (LRCN) is a hybrid neural network architecture that combines the strengths of CNN and LSTM networks    to integrate spatial and temporal learning. The strength of the LRCN lies in its ability to integrate the spatial features extracted by the CNN with the temporal context captured by the LSTM, making it particularly well-suited for applications like activity recognition   , image captioning   , and video description. 3.4 Physics-Informed neural network Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) represents a novel approach to solving problems with limited data, particularly when dealing with noisy experimental measurements. These networks are designed to seamlessly integrate information from both data measurements and the governing physical laws of the problem   . PINNs do this by embedding Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) into the loss function of a neural network using automatic differentiation. Fig. 8  shows the general structure of a PINN.

snippets: 2.2.4 Artificial neural networks Animals respond to the environment because of very small connected units called neurons in the nervous system. Like animals, artificial neural network imitates the behaviour of neurons and respond to the surroundings to achieve an optimal state. The artificial neurons, like the originals, process the input signals and then transmit them from one to another, thus traversing multiple intermediate hidden layers of connections to get the relevant output at the final layer. The known characteristics are fed into input nodes and mathematical operations are performed on them to get a final classification. The output of each artificial neuron is a non-linear function of the sum of its inputs. Similar to a person who learns from his experiences, the technique is trained to evaluate the parameters involved in mathematical operations so that the errors at the final stage can be minimized. As the learning proceeds, the weights with which these artificial neurons are connected to each other in different layers also vary. These weights are found out by using optimization methods. As the size of the network becomes very large, the complexity of the technique increases and is time-consuming. Moreover, efficient training of the network requires a large number of images. However, its ability to model any arbitrary, non-trivial distribution is of practical advantage. Different types of neural networks are being used currently [ 92 ,  93 ]. FNN classifier has been used in Refs. [ 66 ,  94-96 ]. The FNN is one of the simplest ANNs. In this network, the flow of information is unidirectional, from the input nodes, through the hidden nodes, and to the output nodes. It can classify separable non-linear patterns and can approximate any arbitrary continuous function. Various algorithms like Back Propagation algorithm, GA, PSO and ABC are used to train FNN but they easily end up in giving local optimum values of the parameters. Moreover, they suffer a drawback of high computational costs. FNN and RBF neural network have been used with the modified region growing involving both intensity and orientation constraint in Ref.    and gave satisfactory results. El-Dahshan et al. proposed a fast and robust hybrid intelligent machine learning technique in Ref.    for automatic detection of brain tumor. It is based on feedback pulse-coupled neural network for segmentation, DWT for feature extraction, the PCA for reducing the dimensionality of the wavelet coefficients and the feed forward back-propagation neural network to classify inputs into healthy or pathologically cases.

snippets: 5.2 Pattern recognition and machine learning algorithms Machine learning techniques are widely employed in a variety of disciplines for pattern identification and classification problems. Here are a few examples of machine learning algorithms used for pattern detection and classification: Support vector machines: SVM is a sophisticated binary classification technique. It selects the best hyperplane for separating data points of distinct classes with the greatest margin. Using kernel functions, SVM can handle both linear and nonlinear classification problems. Decision trees: Decision trees generate a hierarchical structure by recursively partitioning the feature space depending on feature values. They make judgements by traversing the routes that connect the root node to the nodes in the leaves, which indicate class labels. Decision trees may perform both regression and classification tasks and are interpretable. Random forests: Random forests of data are collective learning approaches that produce predictions by combining several decision trees. Each tree is trained on a randomly selected sample of the data, and the final prediction is made by majority vote or by aggregating the forecasts of multiple trees. Randomised forests are resistant to overfitting and can deal with data that is extremely dimensional. k-Nearest neighbours (k-NN): k-NN classifies data points in the feature space based on the class labels of those closest to them. It assigns a class label to a newly acquired point based on its k-nearest neighbours’ labels. k-NN is a basic and easy-to-use technique for multiclass classification jobs. Naive Bayes: A probabilistic method that implements Bayes’ theorem with an understanding of feature-independent. Given the feature values, it computes the likelihood of each class label and assigns the data point to the class with the greatest probability of occurring. Naive Bayes is a highly computationally effective method for dealing with data with high dimensions. Neural networks: In recent years, neural networks, particularly deep learning models, have received a lot of attention. They are made up of several layers of linked neurons that develop structures of representation from data. CNNs excel in the classification of images, but recurrent neural networks (RNNs) excel at sequence data. Deep learning models need a large quantity of labelled training data as well as computing resources   . Gradient boosting machines (GBM): GBM is an ensemble learning approach that sequentially combines poor students, often decision trees. It teaches each poor student to rectify the mistakes of the preceding ones, increasing total prediction accuracy.

Closely related to linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis tries to capture the quadratic relationship between the independent and dependent variables ( Hastie et al., 2009 ). It provides more powerful discriminant ability compared with the linear separation interface of two classes learned by LDA. 2.2 Artificial neural networks Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are techniques that were inspired by the brain and the way it learns and processes information. ANNs are frequently used to solve classification and regression problems in real world applications. Neural networks are composed of nodes and interconnections. Nodes usually have limited computation power. They simulate neurons by behaving like a switch, just as neurons will be activated only when sufficient neurotransmitter has accumulated. The density and complexity of the interconnections are the real source of a neural network’s computational power. Neural networks can be classified by their structures. In 1957 Rosenblatt proposed the first concrete neural network model, the perceptron ( Rosenblatt, 1958 ). A perceptron has only one layer; in essence it is a linear classifier. In 1960, Bryson and Ho proposed the multiple neural network and introduced the fundamental backpropagation algorithm for training a neural network ( Bryson and Ho, 1969 ). In theory, a three layer neural network can learn any complicated function. In 1982, the Hopfield network was proposed which has only one layer and all neurons are fully connected with each other ( Hopfield, 1982 ). Boltzmann machines can be seen as the stochastic, generative version of Hopfield networks ( Ackley et al., 1985 ). Boltzmann machines are able to solve difficult combinatorial problems and learn internal representations. The self-organizing map (SOM) was introduced around the same time ( Kohonen, 1982 ). It is a unique network which conducts unsupervised learning.

snippets: 1 Introduction In recent years, ML, especially DL, has increasingly drawn significant amounts of attention and has been widely applied in many different fields. Thanks to the combination of many layers of nonlinear functions, DL models show remarkable efficiency for numerous problems   , especially those with complex or unstructured data such as images, text, sound, or social network data. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been proven to improve efficiency significantly in various applications, including computer vision   , bioinformatics   , word processing   , social network data   , natural language processing   , information security   , healthcare   , economics, finance   , and many other applications   . The efficiency of DL models depends, to a large extent, on the amount of training data available and the computational capacity of the training server. The more data used to train DL models, the greater their accuracy   . For example, many mobile applications can achieve higher accuracy and create a better user experience by collecting enormous amounts of data from a large number of users   ; spam SMS filters   , voice recognition systems   , keyboard hinters, and spelling correctors    can also improve their performance with more data. However, in many cases, collecting and labeling data is relatively expensive and requires a great deal of expert demonstration. Furthermore, the resources to train DL models with such large amounts of data are not always easily available to individuals and small or medium-sized organizations because of the high cost   . For that reason, data outsourcing and distributed computation are essential. Computation services on cloud server systems allow users or organizations with insufficient resources to submit data in order to carry out complex computation processes such as DL training  , or use a model previously trained by the service server for prediction purposes based on the data submitted   . snippets: The need of large training datasets can be reconnected to the  curse of dimensionality  concept introduced in [ 39 ] explaining the exponential growth of learning complexity with the linear growth of dimensionality in classification approaches. Especially in civil engineering ML applications, this growth is not reflected by the volume of available datasets which, are often limited by confidentiality issues with the client. One of the possible consequences of small training dataset is overfitting. It means that the statistical model contains more parameters than can be justified by the data. Even if in specific circumstances the overfitting phenomena doesn't negatively affect or even increases the prediction performance of the algorithm [ 40 ], it will result in a poor prediction ability of the network in more general cases. Data augmentation [ 41–43 ] is the most common approach to tackle the issue of small datasets. It consists in minor geometric and/or appearance alteration of the images. The benefit is that, applying the same geometric alterations to the target mask, the data volume enlarges without any extra work. Dropout [ 44 ] is one of the regularization methods to avoid overfitting. Sometimes, it is also seen as an additional augmentation approach [ 24 ]. The value of its hyperparameter  ρ , representing the probability of disconnecting neurons at each training step, is usually set to 0.5 for crack detection [ 8 , 18 , 21 , 45 ]. Another very popular approach for the same problem is so called transfer learning. It represents the possibility to apply to the target task knowledge leveraged from a source task [ 46 ]. Avoiding overtraining with a cross validation approach [ 26 ] or avoiding overfitting by undercomputing [ 47 ] are two other solutions to face this problem. Finally, a less popular approach to reduce the risk of overfitting is ensemble learning. This approach consists in combining predictions from two or more models with statistics approaches [ 32 , 48 , 49 ]. The drawback of such an approach, especially for semantic segmentation, is the higher computational power required for both training and prediction phases. Apart from small datasets, another detrimental data related performance issue is  class imbalance  [ 50–52 ]. With this term we refer to the case when the number of samples belonging to one class (minority class) are outnumbered by the samples of another class (majority class).

snippets: 2.2.6 Deep learning Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that focuses on training artificial neural networks to learn and represent complex patterns and relationships in data. Inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain, deep learning involves the use of multiple layers, or “deep” architectures, to progressively learn hierarchical features from raw input data. Each layer in the network extracts higher-level features from the representations learned in the previous layer. Deep learning has revolutionized various domains, such as image recognition, natural language processing, and speech synthesis, achieving remarkable performance improvements compared to traditional machine learning techniques. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at image-related tasks by exploiting spatial hierarchies, while recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are adept at sequential data, like language ( Aggarwal, 2018 ). Deep learning models often require substantial amounts of labeled data and considerable computational resources, making them computationally intensive but capable of learning intricate patterns and representations. The use of deep architectures, in combination with techniques, such as regularization, optimization, and transfer learning, has enabled deep learning to excel across a wide range of applications and significantly advance the capabilities of machine learning systems ( Schmidhuber, 2015 ). 2.2.7 Neural networks Neural networks are computational models inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain's interconnected neurons. These networks consist of layers of interconnected nodes, or artificial neurons, which process and transform input data to produce output ( Aggarwal, 2018 ;  Du & Swamy, 2019 ). Each connection between neurons is associated with a weight, and these weights are learned from data during training. The architecture typically includes an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Information is fed forward through the layers, with each neuron performing a weighted sum of its inputs followed by a nonlinear activation function. This process allows neural networks to capture complex patterns and relationships in data that might be difficult for traditional algorithms. Various types of neural networks exist, such as feedforward neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) ( Ozturk, 2022 ) for image analysis, and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequential data processing. Neural networks have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in tasks like image recognition, language translation, and game playing, leading to their prominence in the fields of machine learning and artificial intelligence.

concept: Validation strategies in machine learning are crucial for ensuring unbiased model performance, with patient-wise validation being the most effective method to prevent data leakage. However, many studies fail to implement this, risking the integrity of their results.

The choice of validation methods significantly impacts the reliability of predictive models, with hold-out and k-fold cross-validation being the most commonly used techniques in stock market prediction studies.

Model selection is a critical process that involves choosing the best algorithm and hyperparameters to avoid overfitting and ensure good generalization on unseen data. Various techniques like cross-validation and grid search are employed to achieve this.

Accuracy and AUC are essential metrics for evaluating model performance, but they should not be directly compared. Variations in these metrics across studies highlight the importance of consistent methodologies and input parameters.
Feature importance analysis is vital for understanding model performance and can guide the selection of effective parameters for data collection, ultimately simplifying the modeling process.

The performance of AI models is influenced by data characteristics, preprocessing, and the integration of multiple methods, emphasizing the need for careful consideration of various factors when designing effective models.

The validation strategies employed in machine learning studies are crucial for ensuring the reliability of results, with patient-wise validation being the most effective in reducing bias and data leakage. However, a significant number of studies did not utilize this method, which raises concerns about the validity of their findings.

The most common validation techniques include hold-out, k-fold cross-validation, and leave-one-out cross-validation, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. The hold-out method is the most frequently used, but k-fold cross-validation offers a more comprehensive evaluation at the cost of increased computational effort.

Inter-patient variability poses a significant challenge in machine learning applications, as systems trained on limited or homogeneous data may not generalize well to diverse patient populations or varying conditions. This variability highlights the need for larger and more diverse datasets to improve model performance.

The lack of standardization in validation methods across studies complicates the comparison of results, as different approaches can introduce varying levels of bias and data leakage. This disparity underscores the importance of establishing consistent validation protocols in future research.

In the context of cybersecurity, particularly within the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), combining detection and prevention measures is essential for effective threat mitigation. Many studies focus solely on detection, which limits their effectiveness in addressing potential breaches.

Privacy-preserving techniques, such as blockchain-based solutions, are emerging as effective strategies for safeguarding sensitive data in various applications, including energy trading and healthcare. These methods enhance user privacy while maintaining operational efficiency and security.

snippets: 3.4 Validation Fig. 7 a  presents the validation strategy with respect to how data was split between the training set and the testing set. A patient-wise validation strategy, employed by 36 papers, implies that data collected from a single patient is not simultaneously included in the training set and the testing set, reducing bias. 37 papers (i.e. more than half) did not employ such a strategy, possibly containing information from a single patient in both the training and testing sets, or did not specify how such splitting was achieved which leaves them open to potential data leakage. Three different strategies were mainly used to split datapoints between training and testing sets. Hold-out , arguably the most common technique in the broader machine learning community, corresponds to separating a portion of the datapoints in a testing set at the beginning of the experiment in order to isolate it entirely from the training process, and was used 30 times in total, which makes it the most regularly used strategy. k -fold Cross-Validation (CV) ( k -CV) comes second, with 26 occurrences in total. This strategy consists in partitioning the datapoints into  k  different disjoint sets. An independent training procedure is then performed  k  times, each using a different set as testing data and the remaining  k  − 1 as training data. When performed correctly (i.e. ensuring that the training procedures are completely independent and isolating from each other) this has the benefit of evaluating the algorithm on all the data possible although at the expense of re-training the algorithm several times. Leave-one-out CV (LOOCV) is a specific case  k -CV for very small datasets, in which  k  is equal to the number of datapoints (or the number of patients, if the validation was done patient-wise) in the database. LOOCV is beneficial in that it also ensures that a maximum amount of data is present in the training set at any given time. LOOCV has been used 13 times. Two papers did not validate their method on a separated testing set, and one did not specify the validation method employed. Finally,  bootstrapping  refers to evaluation procedures in which the algorithm is trained once, but the effect of any individual datapoint can be isolated and removed from the model, thus allowing for said datapoint to be used in evaluating the reduced model.

snippets: 4.4 Inter-patient variability: the elephant in the room Small cohorts are problematic in ML because they limit the performance of predictive systems (several papers [ 35 , 49 , 54 , 60 , 62 ] stated lack of data as a limitation). Furthermore, the pathologies treated by DBS are heterogeneous causing a high inter-patient variability, on top of intra-patient variability (as the clinical state of the patients can fluctuate or because the recording conditions may vary). Therefore, a system trained on one patient or on one recording configuration is not likely to have good performance on another one, or later in time, which limits its prospective usability. The contribution of Khobragade et al. [ 40 ] illustrates this phenomenon well. They gathered surface electromyography and accelerometer data from two patients through several trials spread on different sessions, with at least a week between consecutive sessions. They did two experiments: the first one by training one model per patient and per session, therefore testing the model on trials of the same sessions. For the second one, they trained one model per patient, but trained the model on a set of sessions and tested it on other sessions. They obtained a perfect accuracy for the first experiment, but the median performance dropped to 46.15% for the second one. On the same extent, Rajpurohit et al. [ 21 ] reported results with a patient-specific feature normalization scheme (therefore not applicable prospectively), and with a patient-independent normalization scheme. Not surprisingly, the classification error rates of the patient-specific scheme are much lower (in the range of 0.0711 to 0.1353) than the patient-independent scheme error rates (in the range of 0.102 to 0.1979). The majority of the papers did not employ a patient-wise validation method [ 10 , 13–20 , 23–25 , 28 , 30 , 31 , 34 , 35 , 37–46 , 49 , 50 , 52 , 53 , 56 , 59 , 60 , 67 , 68 , 71 ]. A large number of those papers reported performance on a single patient, training a different model for each patient and validating it on that same patient. This is often because a singular patient has multiple signals and the model uses some for training and others for evaluation, treating the learning of a model as a form of calibration.

concept: Validation strategies in machine learning are crucial for ensuring unbiased model performance, with patient-wise validation being the most effective in reducing data leakage, yet many studies fail to implement this rigorously.

The hold-out method and k-fold cross-validation are the most commonly used validation techniques, but a significant number of studies do not specify their validation methods, raising concerns about the reliability of their results.

Hyperparameter tuning is essential for optimizing model performance, yet it remains underexplored, particularly in the context of imbalanced and overlapped datasets, where tailored adjustments could significantly enhance outcomes.

Specialized approaches that consider data characteristics, such as class overlap and imbalance, are necessary for improving classification results, yet many existing methods rely on default hyperparameter settings rather than empirical tuning.

The integration of data complexity and typology into algorithm design can lead to better performance, highlighting the need for more sophisticated methodologies that adapt to the unique challenges posed by specific datasets.

Future research should focus on developing comprehensive frameworks for hyperparameter tuning and validation methods that are sensitive to the nuances of imbalanced and overlapped data, ensuring more robust and reliable machine learning applications.

snippets: 3.4 Validation Fig. 7 a  presents the validation strategy with respect to how data was split between the training set and the testing set. A patient-wise validation strategy, employed by 36 papers, implies that data collected from a single patient is not simultaneously included in the training set and the testing set, reducing bias. 37 papers (i.e. more than half) did not employ such a strategy, possibly containing information from a single patient in both the training and testing sets, or did not specify how such splitting was achieved which leaves them open to potential data leakage. Three different strategies were mainly used to split datapoints between training and testing sets. Hold-out , arguably the most common technique in the broader machine learning community, corresponds to separating a portion of the datapoints in a testing set at the beginning of the experiment in order to isolate it entirely from the training process, and was used 30 times in total, which makes it the most regularly used strategy. k -fold Cross-Validation (CV) ( k -CV) comes second, with 26 occurrences in total. This strategy consists in partitioning the datapoints into  k  different disjoint sets. An independent training procedure is then performed  k  times, each using a different set as testing data and the remaining  k  − 1 as training data. When performed correctly (i.e. ensuring that the training procedures are completely independent and isolating from each other) this has the benefit of evaluating the algorithm on all the data possible although at the expense of re-training the algorithm several times. Leave-one-out CV (LOOCV) is a specific case  k -CV for very small datasets, in which  k  is equal to the number of datapoints (or the number of patients, if the validation was done patient-wise) in the database. LOOCV is beneficial in that it also ensures that a maximum amount of data is present in the training set at any given time. LOOCV has been used 13 times. Two papers did not validate their method on a separated testing set, and one did not specify the validation method employed. Finally,  bootstrapping  refers to evaluation procedures in which the algorithm is trained once, but the effect of any individual datapoint can be isolated and removed from the model, thus allowing for said datapoint to be used in evaluating the reduced model.
