snippets: 2 Traditional feature learning In this section, we focus on traditional feature learning algorithms, which belong to “shallow” models and aim to learn transformations of data that make it easier to extract useful information when building classifiers or other predictors. 17  Some manual feature engineering methods, such as image descriptors (e.g., scale-invariant feature transform or SIFT, 18  local binary patterns or LBP, 19  and histogram of oriented gradients or HOG, 20  and so on) and document statistics (e.g., term frequency-inverse document frequency or TF-IDF, 21  and so on), are not covered in this review. From the perspective of its formulation, an algorithm is generally considered to be linear or nonlinear, supervised or unsupervised, generative or discriminative, global or local. For example, PCA is a linear, unsupervised, generative and global feature learning method, while LDA is a linear, supervised, discriminative and global method. In this section, we adopt the taxonomy to categorize the feature learning algorithms as global ones or local ones. In general, global methods try to preserve the global information of data in the learned feature space, but local ones focus on preserving local similarity between data during learning the new representations. Moreover, we usually call locality-based feature learning as manifold learning, since it is to discover the manifold structure hidden in the high dimensional data. For instance, unlike PCA and LDA, LLE is a manifold learning algorithm. It is aimed to preserve the re-construction property within the neighborhood of each data point. Fig. 2  illustrates an example to show how LLE learns the 2D manifold structure of data from 3D observations. LLE can discover the nonlinear relationship between low-dimensional embeddings and high dimensional data. However, it is based on the assumption that the data are densely sampled. In the literature, van der Maaten, Postma and van den Herik provided a MATLAB toolbox for dimensionality reduction, which includes the codes of 34 feature learning algorithms. 22  Yan et al 23  introduced a general framework known as graph embedding to unify a large family of dimensionality reduction algorithms into one formulation.

snippets: 2.6.3 Feature selection As seen in Section  2.2.1 , there is not a unique feature that performs better than any other feature independently of the background and foreground properties because each feature has its strengths and weaknesses against each challenge. Thus, a way to take advantage of the properties of each feature is to perform feature selection. The aim is to use the best feature or the best combination of features on a per-pixel [ 335–340 ] or per-block [ 282 ] basis. A set of feature could be composed of  (1)  homogeneous features that are feature from the same category, and then the idea is to reinforce the reliability for the concerned type of features, or  (2)  heterogeneous features to complement the features each others [ 341 ]. Once the set of features is determined, ensemble learning methods such as the boosting classifier can be used for feature selection. Boosting algorithms usually generate a weighted linear combination of some weak classifiers that perform only a little better than random guess. So, weak classifiers can be learned from the feature values at a pixel and combined to perform better than the others alone. This combination produces a strong classifier. Thus, this method can effectively select different features at each pixel to distinguish foreground objects from the background. Extensions of this conventional algorithm are available in the form of on-line boosting algorithms [ 335–337 ] which use several classifier pools, and each pool contains several weak classifiers. Once an input image is given, each classifier pool selects the best classifier for the given image. The selected classifiers form a strong classifier group, and the final classification is performed using those strong classifiers. At the same time, each classifier pool selects the worst classifier as well. The worst classifier is replaced with a randomly selected classifier so that a better classifier can be included in the classifier pool. Instead of selecting the best classifier from each classifier pool as the previous method does, an improvement according to [ 282 ] selects several good classifiers from each pool. While the previous method replaces the worst classifier in each pool, instead this improvement replaces several bad classifiers. According to the literature in this area, feature selection has been less investigated in background modeling and foreground detection methods with only 9 papers.

snippets: However, when synergized with other strategies, such as oversampling or undersampling, it becomes conducive to addressing the challenges posed by imbalanced datasets. 5.2.11 Random Forest Random Forest (RF)    is an ensemble-based learning method tailored for classification and regression tasks. It synergizes multiple decision trees, crafting a model that is both robust and precise. Within RF, each tree undergoes training on a distinct subset of data, and at every tree node, a random feature subset serves as the split determinant. The ultimate prediction materializes either by averaging the tree outputs (in regression) or through a majority consensus (in classification). Such randomization fortifies the model against overfitting and heightens its stability. RFs are championed for their exceptional accuracy, adaptability, and capability to navigate extensive datasets riddled with missing entries and erratic features. They are equipped to manage both binary and multi-class classification scenarios, as well as regression challenges. One of RF’s strengths is its inherent resilience to CI. By weaving together numerous decision trees and amalgamating their verdicts, RF can diminish the repercussions of skewed class distributions and curtail any bias leaning towards the dominant class. RF’s architecture also enables it to spot anomalies within the dataset by scrutinizing individual tree behaviors, an attribute that is especially beneficial when the minority class encapsulates rare or atypical samples. However, while RF is adept at contending with CI, it is also resource-intensive. Furthermore, its potential inclination towards the majority class, given its predominance in the dataset, might skew the model’s sensitivity and specificity. Such biases could culminate in challenges when striving to accurately pinpoint the minority class. 5.2.12 Random Undersampling Boost RUSBoost    is an innovative algorithm that fuses Random Undersampling (RUS) with the boosting ensemble technique to adeptly manage CI in datasets. Boosting operates by sequentially constructing weak models, which are later amalgamated to give rise to a robust model. Within the framework of RUSBoost, the initial step involves undersampling the training dataset to equilibrate class distributions. Subsequently, using the boosting approach, weak models are successively developed on this balanced dataset.

snippets: High-dimensional datasets are a special case for random subspace-based ensembles. The technique mitigates the curse of high volume of data by choosing subsets of features at random, making it suitable for handling enormous feature counts. Random subspace sampling introduces diversity, which adds to the ensemble's resilience. The model is more likely to function successfully in a variety of circumstances and is less susceptible to changes in the input data   . The Rotation Forest (RoF) : The RotF is an ensemble learning method that belongs to the family of feature transformation-based ensemble classifiers. The key idea behind the RotF is to use feature transformation techniques to create diverse views of the input data   . In this manner it enhances the diversity among base classifiers by applying potential transformations to the input features. The transformation is applied to randomly selected subsets of features. This selection is also based on the concept of orthogonality. A variety of base classifiers are trained using various perspectives on the input data that were acquired throughout the transformation. The main goal is to use various feature subsets and transformations to create diverse base classifiers. Enhancing the ensemble's overall performance and resilience needs this diversity. The ensemble's ability to handle a variety of patterns and complexities increases as a result of its ability to capture multiple features of the incoming data. The individual predictions made by each base classifier are combined during the prediction phase. Classification by majority vote is a common technique. Because of the changes, the ensemble can effectively reduce its high volume and handle scenarios with a high number of features. Applying several changes adds diversity, which strengthens the ensemble's resilience. This improves generalization since the models are less susceptible to noise or unimportant features.

snippets: While AdaBoost minimizes potential for parallel computation due to its sequential nature, each classifier learned with wagging is independent, enabling parallel computation—a trait inherited by MultiBoost at the subcommittee level   . Random Subspace Method:  The Random Subspace Method (RSM) is a fusion technique introduced by Ho   . In RSM, adjustments are made to the training data, but these modifications occur within the feature space. Consequently, a random subspace of dimensionality r is derived from the original p-dimensional feature space. This results in a modified training set consisting of r-dimensional training objects. Classifiers are then constructed within these random subspaces and aggregated using simple majority voting in the final decision rule. Utilizing random subspaces for both classifier construction and aggregation can be advantageous. Specifically, when the number of training objects is relatively small compared to the data dimensionality, constructing classifiers in random subspaces can address the issue of small sample size. By reducing the subspace dimensionality while maintaining the same number of training objects, the relative training sample size increases. Moreover, in cases where data exhibit numerous redundant features, classifiers developed in random subspaces may outperform those constructed in the original feature space. Consequently, the combined decision of such classifiers may surpass that of a single classifier developed on the original training set in the complete feature space   . Rotation Forest (RoF):  Rotation Forest is an ensemble learning technique that uses feature extraction techniques to improve the accuracy and variety of individual base classifiers. It builds a collection of decision trees by using feature extraction and modification to produce a variety of training subsets. Every tree in the group receives training on a distinct rotated copy of the initial feature space. High variety among the classifiers is ensured by using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to choose subsets of features to accomplish the rotation randomly   . The provided set of features is first divided in a random fashion in subsets. It uses the training data to create a bootstrap sample for every feature subset. The PCA is then applied to every bootstrap sample of the feature subsets. The subset of characteristics is transformed using PCA into a group of uncorrelated principal components. In this stage, a rotation matrix for every feature subset is produced. To create a complete rotation matrix for all features in the initially supplied feature set, the rotation matrices from each subgroup are combined in the following step.

concept: Data preprocessing is crucial for enhancing the quality and representation of data before it is used in predictive models, particularly in fields like intrusion detection and big data analysis.
The majority of studies (23 out of 32) employed various data preprocessing techniques, indicating a strong recognition of its importance in improving model performance.

Data cleaning techniques were the most commonly used, focusing on handling missing data, eliminating outliers, and correcting inconsistencies, with linear interpolation being the most favored method for missing data.
Data reduction techniques, aimed at reducing dimensionality while preserving data integrity, were applied in 37.5% of the studies, with feature selection being more prevalent than feature extraction.
Data transformation techniques were also significant, with reframing and normalization being the most utilized methods, highlighting the need to prepare data in a suitable format for analysis.
The challenges posed by high dimensionality and data quality issues, such as noise and missing values, necessitate effective preprocessing methods to ensure reliable model training and analysis.
Advanced techniques like spatio-temporal regression and Kalman filters are recommended for sensor data, which often exhibit strong correlations that traditional methods may overlook.
The importance of addressing data imbalance is emphasized, as unbalanced datasets can skew model learning, particularly in scenarios where one class significantly outnumbers another.
Feature selection is a critical step in data preparation, with various methods available to improve model performance by reducing overfitting and enhancing interpretability.
Overall, a comprehensive approach to data preprocessing, incorporating cleaning, reduction, transformation, and addressing imbalance, is essential for developing robust predictive models.

snippets: Several data preprocessing techniques have been used before feeding data to the BGL prediction models: 23 papers out of 32 used data preprocessing techniques while nine papers did not specify if such methods have been applied. Data preprocessing techniques used in the selected studies can be categorized into three tasks: data cleaning, data reduction and data transformation. Table 6  shows the preprocessing tasks and techniques used by the selected studies as well as the datasets on which they were applied. Data cleaning:  These techniques aim to handle missing data, eliminate outliers, remove noise and correct inconsistencies. Data cleaning preprocessing techniques were used by 50% of the selected papers (16 out of 32) where missing data handling ranked first with 12 papers, followed by noise elimination with seven papers. Several missing data handling techniques have been used where imputation using linear interpolation was the most adopted in seven papers. Forward filling, filling with zeros and simple removal of rows with missing data were used twice each. The remaining missing data handling techniques were all used once each. With regard to noise elimination, simply removing outliers from the dataset was the most common noise elimination technique by defining thresholds and removing any rows with values out of the defined ranges. Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD), extreme value analysis, and moving average filter were all used once each. Data reduction:  This category of techniques intends to reduce the data dimensionality by selecting and extracting a minimum set of features to decrease the model computation time without losing the data integrity. Among the selected studies, 12 papers (37.5%) applied data reduction where feature selection was used by seven papers and feature extraction by six papers. Feature selection was performed using different techniques where correlation coefficient method was the most adopted in 3 papers followed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with 2 papers. Gini index, information gain, Lasso regression, PCA, Random Forest and Sequential backward selection (SBS) were all used once each. Concerning feature extraction, all the techniques were used once each. Data transformation:  The purpose of these techniques is to transform the data into a suitable form for mining and training the model. 40.625% of the selected studies (13 papers) used these techniques where reframing was used in nine studies, followed by normalization in six papers and categorical data encoding in one paper.

snippets: 4.2 Data preprocessing methods The representation and quality of the data is of primary importance in any data analysis process ( Pyle, 1999 ). Raw data usually contain noisy and unreliable data that can affect training and analysis. Moreover, datasets used in intrusion detection are characterized by high dimensionality, making it more difficult to discover knowledge during training. To build high-performance detectors requires efficient preprocessing. Fig. 4  summarizes the common data preprocessing methods used in intrusion detection, including data cleaning, imbalance learning, data transformation, feature selection, feature extraction, and Visualization ( RQ2(a) ). The above methods preprocess the data from different perspectives to enable the analysis model to better learn useful information from the data. In order to study the technical characteristics of different methods, we summarize their implementation principles and applications to answer  RQ2(b) . a ) Data cleaning Data cleaning corrects corrupt or inaccurate records. Quality criteria may include the following. • Validity. Data might have to be of a certain type, such as Boolean or numeric. • Accuracy. Data must conform to the situation. For example, outliers may exist due to the recording process. Accuracy is difficult to guarantee through data cleaning because real data sources are needed for validation. • Completeness. Some data may have unknown or missing values. Completeness issues are generally resolved through default values, setting zeros, or removal. • Uniformity. Inconsistency occurs when there are conflicts in a dataset. For example, a source IP may differ between two receivers. Fixing this type of problem requires the determination of which datum is most reliable. Data analysis based on means, standard deviations, or clustering algorithms can reveal errors, whose values can sometimes be set to a mean or other statistical measure. b ) Imbalanced learning A sample with different proportions of positive and negative cases will lead to a bias in the learning process toward the higher proportion. For example, in the extreme case of a dataset with 95 %  positive and 5 %  negative cases, the model will have no practical meaning. Since attacks tend to be sparse, datasets in intrusion detection are often unbalanced. The following methods may improve performance. • Sampling methods.

snippets: Traditional data cleaning techniques for conventional big data (e.g. data warehousing) do not take into account the strong spatial and temporal correlations typically present in sensor-based data types. Information about an event in sensor data is usually reflected in multiple measurement points due to overlapping areas of coverage. Thus, the inconsistency among multiple sensor measurements serves as an indicator for the data quality. Some useful approaches for data cleaning for sensor data have used techniques like spatio-temporal regression and Kalman filters   . The authors in    proposed three models to detect and identify erroneous data among inconsistent observations based on the inherent structure of various sensor measurements from a group of sensors. The first model used multivariate Gaussian model to explore the correlated data changes of a group of sensors. The second model used principal component analysis (PCA) to capture the sparse geometric relationship among sensors, and the third model used kernel functions to map the original data into a high dimensional feature space prior to using the PCA model (i.e. kernel PCA). Their results demonstrated good detection rates with limited false alarms. 3.3 Data integration, aggregation and representation The authors in    defined two types of sensor-based applications depending on the information that is needed at the sink: (1) functional – where only statistical summary values (e.g. maximum, average, median) are required, and (2) recoverable – where the full dataset is required. For functional applications, data integration and aggregation can be easily performed during the data collection and transmission process as part of a hierarchical data gathering tree. On the other hand, the challenges of recoverable applications pose more difficulty for data aggregation due to the lack of prior knowledge on the spatial data correlation structure. The recent work in    for a functional sensor application, proposed a data aggregation approach based on compressed sensing (CS). The authors showed that their CS scheme based on diffusion wavelets could achieve high fidelity recovery for aggregated sensor data while achieving significant energy savings. 3.4 Data modeling and analysis The aim of data modeling and analysis is to derive value from the big data system and discover new insight or knowledge through analytical and statistical methods. Fig. 3  shows some analytical/statistical methods used for big data systems. In this section, we will discuss some of the techniques, and point to the reviewed case studies in Section  2  when relevant. Recommender systems are arguably the defining analytic method for big data systems.

snippets: Data quality A common limitation we identify in literature is that of data quality, which can affect the performance, validity, and applicability of particular modelling approaches. Typical data quality issues include: missing values, incorrect values, inconsistent formatting, inconsistent reporting standards, or noise introduced into data from human or instrument errors. Some machine learning techniques may be robust to particular data quality issues, however their applicability in such cases depends on the type and severity of the issues. For example, clustering was often applied to noisy datasets, but not for datasets with missing values. This is because many similarity measures used in clustering algorithms are tolerant of small variations in the data, but cannot compute similarity where data is missing   . Other means of addressing data quality issues specific to AHRs include using ensemble-learning approaches and imputation algorithms for handling missing values    and class imbalance   .

concept: The combination of different models in Ensemble Reinforcement Learning (ERL) is a prevalent strategy that enhances structural diversity and predictive performance.
Both Machine Learning (ML) models and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) can be utilized in model combinations, with the choice depending on the specific problem and target solution.
Researchers often employ a mix of classical and state-of-the-art methods, including convolutional neural networks and gated recursive units, for prediction tasks.
The number of base learners typically ranges from two to three, although some studies integrate more than three models, demonstrating improved performance over baseline methods.
ERL can be categorized into parallel and sequential methods, with parallel approaches being more common in practice, allowing for simultaneous processing of models.
Combination learning aims to leverage the strengths of multiple models to enhance overall system performance, applicable in both supervised and unsupervised learning contexts.
Majority voting and weighted majority voting are common strategies for aggregating class-label outputs from multiple models, ensuring a robust final prediction.
Ensemble models effectively reduce bias and variance, leading to more accurate predictions compared to single models, with methods like bagging and boosting being widely used.
The choice of base classifiers in ensemble methods can include various classical models, such as support vector machines and decision trees, contributing to the ensemble's effectiveness.
Designing robust loss functions is essential for maintaining stable performance across different scenarios, particularly in complex decision-making environments.

snippets: 10.2.2 Combination learners Combination learning refers to the process of combining multiple models or learners to improve the overall performance of a machine-learning system. The goal of combination learning is to leverage the strengths of multiple models to compensate for their individual weaknesses, leading to a more accurate and robust prediction or classification. A combination learner is a type of machine-learning algorithm that combines the outputs of multiple base learners, which are usually simpler or weaker models, to form a more powerful or complex model. The combination learner can be used in both supervised and unsupervised learning problems. In supervised learning, combination learners are typically used for ensemble methods, such as random forests, boosting, or bagging, which combine the predictions of multiple base classifiers to improve classification accuracy or reduce overfitting. The base classifiers can be different types of algorithms, such as decision trees, support-vector machines, or neural networks. In unsupervised learning, combination learners are often used for clustering or anomaly-detection problems, where the goal is to identify hidden patterns or anomalies in the data. Ensemble-clustering methods, such as consensus  clustering or cluster-level ensemble methods, can be used to combine the results of multiple base-clustering algorithms to improve the clustering performance and robustness. A combination function tries to aggregate the outputs of learning models participating in the ensemble process. The outputs to be combined can be in class label form or continuous outputs. Depending on the type of output of the learning model, the combination function must be chosen. 10.2.2.1 Class-label combination To combine the class-label outputs of learning models, two simple strategies that can be used are  Majority voting  and  Weighted majority voting , as discussed below. 1. Majority voting : According to this technique, the ensemble chooses the class label with the most votes. That is, all the learning models have equal opportunities to choose their respective class labels (these are counted as votes), and the label with the most votes is chosen as the winner by the ensemble. For example, let us say we have ten learning models, and six learning models say that a particular instance, say  X 1  belongs to class A and four models say  X 1  belongs to class B. Then, the final output will be class A. This technique can have three different cases: (a) Case 1: All learning models agree unanimously without any conflicts in predicting a single class label. This is a  consensus voting  decision.

snippets: 11.6 Ensemble ML models Ensemble models combine the results from multiple learning algorithms to improve predictive performance. The result obtained using ensemble models is more accurate compared to the result from a single model. Factors such as noise, variance, and bias are responsible for the difference between the actual value and the value predicted by any ML model. Ensemble algorithms combine several ML models to form a new predictive model that reduces the bias and variance while improving the predictions. There are two methods of ensemble ML: homogenous ensemble learning where learners of the same style are aggregated and heterogeneous ensemble learning where learners of different styles are aggregated. In this work, heterogeneous ensemble learning models are implemented. Another way to categorize ensemble learning models is sequential and parallel ensemble models. In the case of sequential ensemble methods, the base learners are generated sequentially. It exploits the reliance on the various base learning algorithms. The aggregated performance can be accelerated by weighing iteratively mislabeled examples with the highest weight. In parallel ensemble models, base learners are produced in parallel. This harnesses independence between the base learners because the error can be drastically reduced by averaging. The first step defines the formulation of different classification/regression models using the same predetermined training dataset. Every base model is trained with a dissimilar subset of training data for each same algorithm or by using the identical split of training data with different base learning models. In this work, ensemble ML models for the same split of training data with different algorithms are used. The following ensemble algorithms are implemented in this work: MV, weighted-average voting (WAV), bagging, and gradient boosting. 11.6.1 Majority voting In the MV ensemble model, each base classifiers’ prediction for each instance of data is fed to the model; the prediction with the majority of votes is considered the final output of the model. Here, the model is free from any bias that might have occurred in any base learner model due to some of the attributes or feature subsets. Fig. 11.11  demonstrates the working of our MV ensemble model. The prediction by every ML algorithm for each instance is passed to the MV model; the model selects the prediction that has received the majority of votes. For the dataset under consideration, there are two labels, yes and no corresponding to 1 or 0. Here, the classifier  C t | x  is either 0 or 1 depending on whether our classifier  t  chooses  x .

concept: Deep Learning (DL) has made significant advancements in generative models, which can be divided into non-adversarial (e.g., VAEs, diffusion models) and adversarial types (e.g., GANs). These models generate images from random vectors, but understanding the latent variables at intermediate layers remains challenging.

Generative models excel in semi- and unsupervised learning tasks, successfully applied in areas like emotion recognition and disease diagnosis. However, they face complexity in computing joint and prior probabilities, which can lead to lower accuracy compared to discriminative models that focus on conditional probabilities.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been effectively utilized for anomaly detection in various domains, including power theft and network traffic. GANs, a recent technique, involve a generator and discriminator in a competitive framework to produce realistic data and improve anomaly detection.

Game theory has been applied to enhance steganalysis performance by balancing detection accuracy and efficiency, utilizing adversarial mechanisms to improve feature extraction and reduce interference from image content.

Adversarial-based methods in CNNs have shown superior performance in steganalysis, but they are vulnerable to adversarial examples. Game theoretical approaches have been proposed to optimize the interaction between steganographers and steganalysts, aiming to improve detection and deception capabilities.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are pivotal in data augmentation, particularly in image classification, by generating synthetic data that enhances model performance. They have also been adapted for tabular data and various applications, including intrusion detection and class imbalance problems.

snippets: DL has achieved a significant amount of progress in this area. DL generative models can be categorized into two types: non-adversarial and adversarial ones. The former includes variational auto-encoders (VAEs)   , GLO   , IMLE   , GLANN   , and diffusion models    while the latter includes the original GAN   , LSGAN   , WGAN   , StyleGAN   , etc. DL generative models take an arbitrary white Gaussian random vector as their input and generate an image of the target family via a DL generator (or decoder). All outputs at intermediate layers are latent variables. It is difficult to give them a physical meaning. There are preliminary efforts in the development of GL generative models, e.g., NITES   , TGHop   , Pager   , GENHOP   . GL generative models contains two modules: • Module 1: Fine-to-Coarse Image Analysis The dimension of color images of  N × N  pixels is  3 N 2 . As  N  becomes large, the diversity is too high to model with a reasonable mathematical model. To reduce the diversity, one straightforward idea is to partition one large image into non-overlapping smaller blocks, each of which has a significantly lower dimension. However, these blocks cannot be generated independently since they are correlated with each other. To take the block correlation into account, one can down-sample fine-resolution images to coarse-resolution ones and compute the residual image between interpolated coarse-resolution images and fine-resolution images. Then, to synthesize the fine-resolution images, the GL generative model only needs to model residual images as well as the coarse-resolution images. This process can be done recursively to get residual images at multiple resolutions as well as the coarsest-resolution images. This pipeline is called the fine-to-coarse image analysis. • Module 2: Coarse-to-Fine Image Synthesis Usually, the space formed by coarsest-resolution images is called the core subspace. A sample in the core subspace corresponds to a coarsest-resolution image. The core subspace was modeled using the independent component analysis (ICA) in    and the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) in   .

snippets: Generative models  generally work well at semi- or unsupervised learning tasks as they aim to model the distribution of individual classes. In the literature, generative models have been successfully applied in emotion recognition ( Schuller et al., 2003 ), and in several disease diagnosis tasks, such as heart disease diagnosis ( Pattekari and Parveen, 2012 ), depression detection ( Cummins et al., 2015 ), snore sound detection ( Dafna et al., 2011 ), to name but a few. The major disadvantage of generative models is that computing the joint probability and the prior probability is often more complex than computing the posterior probability directly. This added complexity might result in low accuracies when using generative models ( Ng and Jordan, 2001 ). Discriminative models Unlike generative models, discriminative ML models do not attempt to model an underlying probability distribution. Instead, they attempt to model the conditional probability  P ( Y | X ) by directly learning the regression line or boundary between classes. As discriminative models focus on directly learning their core objective, as opposed to modeling an entire probability distribution, they can often have higher accuracies, especially with limited training instances, when compared to generative models ( Ng and Jordan, 2001 ). Typical discriminative models in the digital health literature include support vector machines (SVMs) ( Smola and Schölkopf, 2004 ), decision trees ( Safavian and Landgrebe, 1991 ), K-nearest neighbors (KNNs) ( Kramer, 2013 ), and neural networks ( Goodfellow et al., 2016 ). Support vector machines  are a family of ML algorithms that learn a hard or soft decision boundary between classes by constructing a hyperplane or set of hyperplanes in a high-dimensional space ( Smola and Schölkopf, 2004 ). A key property of SVMs is that the learnt hyperplane can be expressed as the sum of a subset of training instances, known as the support vectors, that lie closest it. By representing the final model as a subset of training instances, SVMs are memory-efficient when compared to other ML models. The training procedure involves solving a quadratic optimization problem which maximizes the margin between two classes.

snippets: The deep CNN component helps in recognizing the nonperiodicity of power theft and the periodicity of normal power consumption based on 2-D representations. Janssens et al.    proposed CNN based feature learning model in rotating machinery using vibration data to autonomously learn essential features from the data when anomalies and faults occur. In   , evaluated various CNN models to detect network anomalies in traffic datasets. The various CNN models are shallow CNN, moderate CNN, and deep CNN. 6.2.5 Generative Adversarial Network Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is the most recent deep learning network technique. It consists of two cycles: generative network and discriminative network, where one network attempts to maximize the function value and the other minimizes it. The generator generates random samples from the noise in each adversarial round. GAN organizes an adversarial game among the discriminator model to differentiate between generated random noise and real data and generative model generating data to deceive the discriminator. i.e. GAN trains a generative network to develop noise and attempts to deceive the discriminator till it is unable to differentiate between real and noise samples. This dilemma is illustrated in  Fig. 12 . A commonly followed approach is to flip, rotate or randomly change the hue, saturation, brightness, and contrast of an image. This procedure is quite simple but has limited impact on generalisability compared to using GANs ( Shorten & Khoshgoftaar, 2019 ) as it does not introduce new synthetic training samples into the dataset. Sauber-Cole and Khoshgoftaar (2022)  provided an extensive survey of GANs for class imbalance, especially for tabular data. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) ( Creswell et al., 2018; Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) have revolutionised the area of image generation, as they can generate realistic images and videos ( Lu, Wu, Tai, & Tang, 2018 ). GANs consist of 2 major parts that include the generator and the discriminator. The generator learns to generate realistic data from a batch of samples. It produces samples with identical distribution to that of the original dataset, which act as negative examples for the discriminator. The discriminator’s role is to learn to distinguish synthetic data from real data. The advantage of GANs lies in their ability to generate diverse and quality synthetic data, which can be augmented to the original dataset for superior performance. Although GANs have been prominent for image-related tasks, they can also be used for tabular data. Sharma, Singh, and Chandra (2022)  developed a combination of GANs with SMOTE for addressing CI problems in tabular datasets. Ding, Chen, Dong, Fu and Cui (2022)  presented a KNN and GAN-based hybrid approach for intrusion detection.

concept: Deep Learning (DL) has made substantial advancements in generative models, which can be divided into non-adversarial (e.g., VAEs, diffusion models) and adversarial types (e.g., GANs, StyleGAN). These models utilize random vectors to generate images, with intermediate outputs as latent variables that lack clear physical interpretation.

Generative models are evolving, with GL generative models introducing a two-module approach: Fine-to-Coarse Image Analysis, which reduces image diversity by partitioning images into smaller blocks, and Coarse-to-Fine Image Synthesis, which models core subspaces for image generation.

Texture analysis in medical imaging, particularly in chest X-rays (CXR), is crucial for identifying disease indicators. It involves extracting features that can enhance machine learning algorithms for automated diagnosis, emphasizing the importance of effective feature extraction methods.
Various texture analysis techniques exist, including structural, statistical, model-based, and transform-based methods, each with its strengths and limitations in describing image textures.

Image synthesis technologies, particularly in brain imaging, aim to improve image quality and reduce costs. Deep learning methods like GANs and U-Nets are employed to enhance imaging speed and quality, addressing challenges like anisotropy and expensive equipment.
Super-resolution reconstruction using deep learning allows for generating high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs, facilitating faster imaging while maintaining quality.

Cross-modality image synthesis leverages deep learning to translate between different imaging modalities, such as converting label-free images to fluorescence images, often using unsupervised methods like CycleGAN to overcome the challenge of acquiring paired training data.

snippets: DL has achieved a significant amount of progress in this area. DL generative models can be categorized into two types: non-adversarial and adversarial ones. The former includes variational auto-encoders (VAEs)   , GLO   , IMLE   , GLANN   , and diffusion models    while the latter includes the original GAN   , LSGAN   , WGAN   , StyleGAN   , etc. DL generative models take an arbitrary white Gaussian random vector as their input and generate an image of the target family via a DL generator (or decoder). All outputs at intermediate layers are latent variables. It is difficult to give them a physical meaning. There are preliminary efforts in the development of GL generative models, e.g., NITES   , TGHop   , Pager   , GENHOP   . GL generative models contains two modules: • Module 1: Fine-to-Coarse Image Analysis The dimension of color images of  N × N  pixels is  3 N 2 . As  N  becomes large, the diversity is too high to model with a reasonable mathematical model. To reduce the diversity, one straightforward idea is to partition one large image into non-overlapping smaller blocks, each of which has a significantly lower dimension. However, these blocks cannot be generated independently since they are correlated with each other. To take the block correlation into account, one can down-sample fine-resolution images to coarse-resolution ones and compute the residual image between interpolated coarse-resolution images and fine-resolution images. Then, to synthesize the fine-resolution images, the GL generative model only needs to model residual images as well as the coarse-resolution images. This process can be done recursively to get residual images at multiple resolutions as well as the coarsest-resolution images. This pipeline is called the fine-to-coarse image analysis. • Module 2: Coarse-to-Fine Image Synthesis Usually, the space formed by coarsest-resolution images is called the core subspace. A sample in the core subspace corresponds to a coarsest-resolution image. The core subspace was modeled using the independent component analysis (ICA) in    and the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) in   .

snippets: 3.1 Texture analysis Texture analysis has been widely used to identify and quantify subtle patterns or abnormalities present in CXR image. By analyzing the texture of a medical image, distinguishing features that may be indicative of a disease can be identified, and used for diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of disease progression. These features can also be used to develop machine learning algorithms for automated diagnosis of medical conditions. The performance of machine learning algorithm greatly depends on the data features to be fed and learned by the algorithm. Traditional learning requires manual design of such feature extractors, and becomes more and more cumbersome for large-sized datasets. In this subsection we will discuss about various feature extraction and conventional machine learning approaches employed by existing systems for pneumoconiosis detection. Fig. 6  briefly illustrates the stepwise procedure employed by existing texture-based CAD systems for pneumoconiosis detection. 3.1.1 Feature analysis We broadly categorize the existing literature based on different textural analysis techniques used for feature analysis. By texture analysis, we mean a class of mathematical procedures and models that characterize the spatial variations within images as a means of extracting information ( Srinivasan et al., 2008 ;  Tuceryan et al., 1993 ). In digital image terminology, texture can be referred as an entity consisting of mutually related pixels and group of pixels ( Srinivasan et al., 2008 ;  Materka et al., 1998 ). Alternatively, textures are intricate visual patterns composed of entities, or sub patterns, that each have a characteristic  brightness ,  color ,  slope ,  size , etc. ( Materka et al., 1998 ). Texture analysis approaches are generally classified into  structural ,  statistical ,  model-based  and  transform-based  methods. ⁃ Structural  approaches ( Haralick, 1979 ;  Levine, 1985 ;  Bharati et al., 2004 ;  Ramola et al., 2020 ) describe a texture as the composition of well-defined primitives or texture elements. A primitive is either a pixel, a region, or any regular shape. The choice of a primitive and the probability of it being placed at a particular location can be a function of location or the primitives near the location. Structural methods provide good symbolic description of an image, but appear to be limited in practicality, as they are more suitable for textures with regular structures.

To make a robust system, Partial Least Square regression method was used to perform classification based on limited number of latent factors. 4  different classification cases were considered to investigate the efficacy of the system, the AUC for each case is specified in  Table 2 . 3.1.1.2 Co-occurrence Matrix Analysis Co-occurrence ( Tuceryan et al., 1993 ;  Materka et al., 1998 ;  Bharati et al., 2004 ;  Ramola et al., 2020 ;  Haralick, 1986 ;  Armi et al., 2019 ;  Haralick et al., 1973 ;  Zayed et al., 2015 ), a second-order statistical texture analysis method, is defined as the frequency with which a pair of pixels appear in an image along a given direction  θ  and distance  d . Unlike, histogram analysis, which only conveys information about the distribution of gray-level intensities, co-occurrence matrix provides critical information about the relative position of pixels with respect to each other in the texture. Let  δ = (θ, d)  be a displacement vector, then  P δ ( i , j )  represents the probability that pixels  i  and  j  have the same intensity, along a given direction  θ  and a distance  d  apart (in pixels). This probability takes the form of a matrix  P δ , with dimensions (i.e., rows and columns) equal to the number of discrete gray-level intensities in an image. If an image contains no texture, then the resulting co-occurrence matrix would be completely diagonal. As the local pixel intensity variations (i.e., image texture) increases, the off-diagonal values in matrix becomes larger. Since determining co-occurrence matrices  ∀ δ  requires an intensive amount of computation. Haralick et al. (1973)  computed only four co-occurrence matrices for  d = 1  and  θ = 0 ° , 45 ° , 90 ° , 135 ° , and describes that  14  features can be derived from each co-occurrence matrix. The textual and mathematical description of all the  14  features is illustrated in  Table 1 .

snippets: 3 Image synthesis Compared to other imaging tasks, mesoscale imaging of the brain requires expensive optical equipment, special fluorescent labeling materials, and complex computational processes, which are laborious and costly, usually taking several days or even weeks to complete   . In addition, due to diffraction of light, axial undersampling, and aberrations, existing imaging technologies suffer from imbalanced spatial resolution, also known as anisotropy, which manifests as more blurring in the axial direction   . To address the above issues, image synthesis technologies are used to obtain the desired target image with minimal cost, including super-resolution images and cross modal images ( Fig. 4 ). The key problem of this task is how to improve image quality while reducing the time and cost of mesoscale brain microscopy imaging. One solution to this is using deep learning methods such as the GAN    and U-Net    to assist imaging or simulate imaging to improve image quality, accelerate imaging speed, and reduce imaging costs. GAN and its variants are promising models for image synthesis, which have the powerful ability to approximate complex probability distributions of real images and thereby generate realistic images without manually simulating the imaging process. To assess and compare the performance of image synthesis algorithms, a quantitative evaluation is typically conducted across two key dimensions: imaging speed and image quality. Imaging speed is comprehensively evaluated by considering the algorithm’s execution time and the size of the processed image. As for image quality, commonly employed metrics for quantitative assessment include the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), root mean square error (RMSE), structural similarity index measure (SSIM)   , and full-width at half-maximum (FWHM). The first three metrics often require calculation with corresponding reference images to gauge the difference between the generated image and the target image, while FWHM reflects the relative resolution of the images. 3.1 Super-resolution reconstruction Due to expensive hardware, complex sample preparation and staining, the use of traditional super-resolution techniques for brain imaging is limited   . Therefore, deep learning methods are used to generate high-resolution images from corresponding low-resolution images without additional equipment. There are two main purposes of using deep learning for super-resolution reconstruction. One is to achieve faster imaging while ensuring image quality, and the other is to address the issue of anisotropy ( Table 2 ).

snippets: 3.2 Cross-modality image synthesis Light microscopy imaging can capture the dynamic characteristics of cells and tissues, but it requires fluorescent labeling to visualize specific cellular or molecular constructs, which may cause inaccuracies in experimental results due to the introduction of observation bias and interference with biological processes   . To avoid this, deep learning methods can be used to translate other microscopy imaging modalities such as label-free brightfield imaging with the least impact on the sample into specific fluorescence microscope images for brain research. Due to its ability to exploit and fuse features from images at multiple spatial scales by using skip connections between the encoding and decoding blocks, the U-Net architecture is widely used for image-to-image translation. Guo et al.    designed a multichannel 2.5D U-Net model for predicting fluorescence images from label-free images containing information of phase, retardance, and orientation. However, these methods generally train the models with paired data that is difficult to acquire in most cases. Therefore, to deal with these challenges, GAN and its variants, such as CycleGAN   , are used extensively for image translation, which allow unsupervised training of the model parameters without paired images. Chen et al.    proposed an unsupervised CycleGAN framework with cycle-consistency loss and structural similarity (SSIM)    loss to translate colorful microscopy with ultraviolet surface excitation (MUSE) images into H&E-stained images without using staining. Cycle-consistency loss is used to guarantee successful transformation between two modalities without using paired data for supervised learning and can be calculated by the average distance between the original image and the recovered image. Guo et al.    designed a multi neural network ensemble-learning framework including U-Net, CycleGAN, and SRResNet    to generate the same target image to increase the reliability of the results in the absence of unavailability of ground truth images. This method can achieve minimally-invasive deep-brain imaging with a simple microscope. Another important example of cross-modality image synthesis is using an annotated image, usually a binary image, to generate a real image to obtain paired data for training other deep learning models for brain image processing or analysis, especially in segmentation tasks that need pixel-level labels. These binary images can be randomly generated using prior knowledge or obtained from real images through segmentation algorithms.

snippets: 3.1.1 Data perturbation Data perturbation tries to run component learners with different sample subsets (e.g., bagging,  Breiman, 1996 ; boosting,  Freund and Schapire, 1997 ) or in distinct feature subspaces (e.g., random subspace,  Ho, 1998 ). In ensemble feature selection with data perturbation, different samplings of the original data are generated to construct different feature selectors, as described in  Fig. 2 . Several recent methods ( Davis et al., 2006; Bach, 2008; Meinshausen and Buhlmann, 2008; Abeel et al., 2010 ) fall into this category. These methods can be further distinguished according to the sampling method, the component feature selection algorithm and the rank aggregation method (see  Table 1 ). The combination of data sampling and ensemble learning for feature selection is probably the most intuitive idea to handle selection instability with respect to sampling variation. The superiority of such strategy has been verified both experimentally ( Davis et al., 2006; Abeel et al., 2010 ) and theoretically ( Bach, 2008; Meinshausen and Buhlmann, 2008 ). Interestingly, all methods listed in  Table 1  are based on the same aggregation scheme, i.e., linear combination. Note that it is also feasible to combine data perturbation with other complicated aggregation procedures such as those ones used in function perturbation (see next section).

Function perturbation is different from data perturbation in two perspectives: • It uses different feature selection algorithms rather than the same feature selection method. • It typically conducts local feature selection on the original data (without sampling). snippets: Beyond that, resampling and feature selection methods can all be done at the data-level, but in this study, given their importance for CSM development, both are further explored separately. According to  Fig. 7 , most methods were for data cleaning, followed by data transformation and data reduction methods, respectively. Table 5  addresses the specific steps taken. In the case of data cleaning, missing value replacement was often done by replacing missing data with the mean value of the corresponding attribute ( Wang et al., 2020 ;  Kokate and Chetty, 2021 ). Outliers were removed through different ways, including using KNN ( Armaki et al., 2017 ), and standard deviation outlier removal ( Munkhdalai et al., 2019 ). Djeundje et al. (2021)  filtered out data with negligible variance. As for data transformation, in most cases, data was normalized using the method of min-max normalization ( Kennedy et al., 2013 ;  Khashman, 2009 ;  Zhou et al., 2021 ;  Chen et al., 2020 ). Attribute selection was done either by merging underpopulated variables ( Djeundje et al., 2021 ) or transforming features into binary data ( Fenerich et al., 2020 ). Examples of discretization include Kononenko and Fayyad discretization criterions ( Ziemba et al., 2021 ). Finally, attribute subset selection for data reduction was done by removing highly correlated features ( Chen et al., 2020 ;  Ampoutolas et al., 2021 ), using k-Means Clustering ( Bao et al., 2019 ), and selecting attributes according to a bank's predefined risk assessment levels ( Li and Chen, 2021 ). These specific data reduction techniques are regarded as unsupervised feature selection methods so, given our greater interest in supervised learning, it's preferable to consider them at the data pre-processing stage. Still, it's evident that ML can contribute to improving data quality in the pre-processing stage ( Frénay and Verleysen, 2014 ), with different algorithms being used by authors to better prepare their data during the credit risk modelling process. 4.4 Feature selection In the era of Big Data, credit institutions have excess information about its customers. snippets: 3.4 Combination of models The ensemble of different types of models is a common and simple strategy in ERL. The combination of models can achieve structural diversity. These models can be either ML models or ANN models   . The structure of the model combination is determined according to the specific problem and the solution target. A single type or a combination of multiple types of models are both popular. For using only one type of model, ANNs with different depths can be considered. While other studies use different random initialization strategies    or ANN in different training stages   . Table 2  provides a summary of related work ensemble model combination strategies. There are three models mainly in relevant works, including ML models only, ANN models only, and ML&ANN models hybrid. The model selection process typically involves choosing from a range of classical or recently proposed methods that are specifically designed for addressing this type of task. For instance, when it comes to prediction tasks, most researchers will choose convolutional neural networks, gated recursive units, artificial neural networks (ANN), and other SOTA approaches in this domain   . Apart from determining the potential composition of ERL, it is also crucial to determine the number of base learners. In most studies, two or three single models are commonly employed. Besides, there exist some studies where more than three models have been integrated within the ERL framework   . Saadallah et al.   , Li et al.   , and Sharma et al.    are some examples in this regard. These studies have extensively demonstrated that employing a combination of strategies in ERL outperforms baseline methods as well as state-of-the-art ensemble learning techniques   . ERL can be divided into parallel ERL and sequential ERL according to the relationship between base learners in ERL. Figs. 7 and 8  give schematic diagrams of these two ERL methods. In most ERL studies, such as Liu et al.   , Schubert et al.   , and Shen et al.   , base learners are constructed in a parallel framework. These ML or ANN models are responsible for the same task. After each model processing, the final prediction result will be generated by a certain strategy.

concept: Overfitting is a critical issue in predictive modeling for smart cities and traffic flow, where models may learn noise instead of true patterns, leading to poor performance on unseen data.
The complexity of urban datasets, with numerous variables and inherent variability, exacerbates the risk of overfitting, particularly in traffic flow predictions.

Effective strategies to combat overfitting include regularization techniques (L1 and L2), cross-validation methods (like k-fold), feature selection, dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA), and ensemble learning approaches (e.g., random forests).
Regularization helps simplify models by penalizing complexity, while ensemble learning combines multiple models to enhance generalization and reduce variance.
The bias-variance trade-off is crucial; techniques like regularization and ensemble learning can help balance this trade-off, improving model accuracy and reliability.
Data augmentation through virtual sample generation can enhance model training by increasing the diversity of training data, which is essential in high-dimensional datasets.
Feature selection and extraction techniques are vital in managing high-dimensional data, helping to identify relevant features and reduce model complexity.
Collaboration among data scientists, domain experts, and stakeholders is essential for implementing these strategies effectively, ensuring robust predictive models for smart city applications.

snippets: 7.4 Overfitting Overfitting is a significant hurdle in the realm of predictive modeling of smart cities and traffic flow. It arises when a model captures irrelevant noise or fluctuations in the training data instead of the underlying patterns, leading to accurate performance on training data but inadequate generalization to new or unseen data. Overfitting can pose substantial challenges, especially in smart city contexts characterized by complex and diverse datasets, owing to the abundance of variables and features, exacerbated by the variability inherent in urban environments. Moreover, in traffic flow prediction, overfitting can occur when the model captures temporary patterns or anomalies rather than the fundamental traffic dynamics. Addressing overfitting is crucial for developing reliable predictive models that are essential for guiding decision-making in smart city planning and traffic management ( Santos & Papa, 2022 ). Overfitting, an undesirable trait in machine learning, arises when a model accurately predicts the training data but falters new data. Data scientists typically train machine learning models on established datasets before utilizing them for predictions. This dual challenge highlights the critical necessity of vigilant strategies to mitigate overfitting in predictive modeling applications, ensuring consistent and dependable performance in real-world settings. The problem of overfitting in the predictive modeling of smart cities and traffic flow can be addressed in several ways. First, regularization methods such as L1 and L2 regularization can be used to punish overly complex models and prefer simpler and more general models. Cross-validation approaches, such as k-fold cross-validation, help assess the predictive accuracy of a model on unknown data and detect early indications of overfitting warning signals. Techniques for feature selection and dimensionality reduction, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and prioritizing features based on importance, can assist in identifying relevant features while simplifying model complexity. Ensemble learning methods, such as random forests and gradient boosting, merge multiple models to enhance generalization and mitigate overfitting risks. Additionally, expanding the size and diversity of the training dataset can expose the model to a wider array of patterns, thereby reducing the chance of memorizing noise. Collaborative efforts among data scientists, domain experts, and stakeholders are crucial for effectively implementing these strategies and crafting robust predictive models tailored to smart city applications and traffic-management systems.

snippets: In a classification problem, there are two or more discrete classes. Each example belongs to one of these classes. In a large majority of classification problems, the class labeling of the input examples is specified. The main objective of a classification algorithm is to accurately predict class labels for previously unseen examples. Classification problems of this type where the input examples are labeled fall into the supervised learning category (see  Section 3 ). In contrast, unsupervised classification problems start with unlabeled input examples. The job of a classification algorithm in this case is to predict which examples belong to the same class. The interpretation of the classes in the unsupervised classification scenario is provided by human domain experts. Regression problems share the same problem structure as classification problems, with the key difference that the target values are no longer discrete labels. Measuring predictive performance : Prediction is the prime goal of machine learning algorithms in general. Therefore, the algorithms are evaluated in terms of their predictive performance. Several technical issues arise while measuring the predictive performance, which are referred to as  overfitting  and  underfitting . Consider a supervised classification problem, where a set of labeled examples are available in the input dataset. Following is a standard mechanism for applying a machine learning algorithm to the dataset. First, the input dataset is partitioned into three nonoverlapping subsets—training, validation, and test. The size of these three sets is a design choice. The  training set  is used during the  training phase  to help instantiate the parameters of the model so that the model predicts well. How well the model predicts is measured using the  validation set . The latter provides a set of examples that the algorithm has not seen during the training phase and is used to select a model that may not perform the best with respect to the training set but performs very well with respect to previously unseen examples. There is an important reason for measuring the accuracy of the model using the validation set instead of the training set. Imagine that the model does a perfect job predicting target values given feature vectors of examples in the training set. On the surface, it may seem like perfect learning. However, it could very well be the case that the model simply “memorized” the training examples. In that case, given a previously unseen example, the model will most likely perform poorly. This is known as  overfitting .

snippets: As a consequence, the final model will probably be less accurate due to the presence of noise, and it will be more complex, since non-real patterns may be modeled. In general, noise traits include attribute noise and class noise ( Zhu & Wu, 2004 ). • Attribute noise : Attribute noise has a certain impact on classification algorithms. Errors in attribute values in datasets will lead to incorrect rules. Attribute noise includes data errors caused by input errors, transmission errors, and operation errors of information values, and the level of attribute noise will affect data quality. Therefore, attribute noise here is different from attribute redundancy, or label noise after synthetic data augmentation. To better detect and correct the noise attribute data, some scholars started from the identification of noise and proposed some statistical methods to identify noise or outliers, such as average, standard deviation, constraint interval, statistical model, feature box, clustering, and other techniques are often used to smooth the noise data ( Ester et al., 1996; Ke et al., 2017; Van Hulse, Khoshgoftaar, & Huang, 2007 ). Yu, Huang, and Yin (2020)  proposed a double voting for attribute noise. Experimental results show that the proposed method can further improve the credit classification accuracy of sparse data with attribute noise. In addition, the problem of attribute noise is solved by integrating multiple classifiers, and good results are obtained in the literature ( Twala, 2010 ). • Label noise:  Label noise refers to misclassification or serious deviation in available data instances, and loss function modification with samples. The literature ( Frénay & Verleysen, 2013 ) used the machine learning method to validate the influence of attribute noise and label noise on the prediction results. The experimental results show that label noise is the main cause of poor prediction performance. Thus, the exploration of an effective and reliable class noise detection approach is necessary to improve the noise adaptability of credit evaluation models. The identification methods of label noise are constantly updated (e.g., isolation forest and bagging) ( Frénay & Verleysen, 2013; Sáez, Galar, Luengo, & Herrera, 2016 ).

snippets: The third challenge  is related to the complete understanding of the impact of label noise on the training and testing of machine learning models. One of the first papers to study this problem was published by  Angluin and Laird (1988) , who presented a theoretical investigation on how training is affected by symmetric label noise. The main conclusion was that the learning algorithm for a binary classification problem is robust to symmetric noise, as long as the label noise rate is less than 50%. Lachenbruch (1966)  studied the effect of symmetric label noise on binary classification problems, where effects become noticeable when noise rates in each class are different. The effects of label noise on normal discriminant and logistic regression are studied by  Michalek and Tripathi (1980)    and  Bi and Jeske (2010) . Uniform label noise also damages the generalization of a single-unit perceptron, as shown in ( Heskes, 2000 ). Furthermore, the robustness of  K  Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classifiers is shown to depend on the value of  K  and the noise rate, where larger noise rates depend on higher values for  K  ( Sánchez et al., 1997 ;  Wilson and Martinez, 2000 ). Before the advent of deep learning,  Nettleton et al. (2010) ;  Pechenizkiy et al. (2006)  studied the effect of label noise on naive Bayes, decision trees induced by C4.5, KNN, and support vector machine (SVM) classifiers, and results show that SVM tends to be less robust due to its reliance on support vectors and the feature interdependence assumption. The adaptive boosting algorithm (AdaBoost) also tends to be sensitive to label noise, as demonstrated by  Dietterich (2000) . Ensemble learning classifiers are also shown to be sensitive to high noise rate because models can severely disagree in some cases ( Ali and Pazzani, 1996 ). Spam filters can also overfit to the training samples with label noise because of their online update rules that quickly adapt to new spam ( Sculley and Cormack, 2008 ). Ever since deep learning models have become dominant in machine learning applications, with the groundbreaking paper by  Krizhevsky et al. (2012) , several researchers noticed that such models were particularly prone to overfit any complex function, even when the training set had corrupted labels ( Krause et al., 2016 ).

snippets: In particular,  Arpit et al. (2017)  show that higher label noise leads to slower convergence and poorer generalization to a test set that contains 100% clean label samples. Similarly,  Zhang et al. (2021a)  demonstrate that deep learning models can easily fit an entire training dataset with any rate of corrupted labels, which eventually resulted in poor generalizability on a clean test dataset. Although we understand the theory in some specific label noise problems ( Angluin and Laird, 1988 ), and the practical effect of different types and rates of label noise on many machine learning models ( Han et al., 2020b ;  Song et al., 2022 ), we still do not have comprehensive studies that can predict, for example, the performance gap caused by different types and combinations of label noise. Chapter  3  presents more details about theoretical aspects of the impact of label noise on the training and testing of machine learning models. The fourth challenge  involves the development and evaluation of techniques capable of making machine learning models robust to label noise (see  Fig. 1.9 ). The main strategies being developed in the field, which will be detailed in Chapter  4  are based on ( Cordeiro and Carneiro, 2020 ;  Frénay and Verleysen, 2014 ;  Han et al., 2020b ;  Song et al., 2022 ): 1) loss function design, 2) training algorithm development, 3) training data processing, and 4) model architecture planning. These techniques have been shown to provide robustness to several types of label noise, where even though the papers claim to be “robust to label noise”, they tend to focus only on the few benchmarks that the proposed method shows state-of-the-art results. Nevertheless, given the many different types of label noise, and the potentially large number of benchmarks presented in the first challenge, it is likely that some techniques are more adequate to particular types of label noise, but most papers fail to discuss such trade offs. Hence, it is difficult to confidently make a connection between label noise types and effective machine learning techniques. The fifth challenge  consists of estimating the noise rate and type(s) of label noise present in real-world datasets (see  Fig. 1.10 ). Such estimate involves the characterization of the whole noisy-label training set, which is a process that is not usually performed in machine learning.

snippets: 6 Challenges and discussions The aforementioned overview focused on the development of urban traffic state estimation, and most of the effort occurs under different missing state scenarios, different detector categories, different data type applications, and different methodologies. However, there are still some research deficiencies, which create an unprecedented opportunity to expand horizons and direct work in three challenging directions: challenges in changing missing research scenarios, the process of data fusion, and methodology application. These challenges are introduced in the following section. 6.1 Challenge 1: variations in different missing scenarios 6.1.1 Effect of different missing lengths and missing rates Different missing lengths and missing rates of traffic volume constitute different traffic estimation scenarios, as aforementioned in Section  2 . With an increase in missing traffic volume length, the method of missing volume imputation will be more complicated. For example, the longer traffic missing data length would cause the larger missing information of traffic dynamic fluctuation. Especially when the traffic volume on entire road segments are unknown, this estimation of traffic dynamic fluctuation based in time series presents a great challenge   . This missing volume estimation problem is equivalent to a long-term multi-step traffic flow forecasting problem   . Furthermore, the estimation difficulty will increase when missing rate rises, particularly in which missing states occur at multiple locations on a road segment. To address the difficulties caused by the different missing volume scenarios, two specific approaches have been proposed among the formulations of missing value estimation methods. First, when some road segments are missing point-wise and linear-wise volume, the missing volume can be interpolated based on neighbouring data or historical data which are correlated with missing object data. Some imputation methods can be employed to realize this goal by feature extraction   . Therefore, this kind of imputation method can be divided into statistical learning based methods (e.g., linear regression   , weighted regression method   , matrix decomposition   , compressive sensing   ), and the machine learning based method (e.g., ensemble learning theory   , neural network   , and Bayesian optimization   ). Each approach has its advantages and shortcomings. To improve the estimation accuracy, conducting scenario analysis and data pre-processing is crucial before determining the research method. Second, when the whole road segment lack traffic volume data, we need to estimate the missing volume by the correlation between the non-detection segment and other detection segments on the whole network.

snippets: 5.1.2 Data abnormality issue Influenced by extreme weather, traffic incidents, and other external environmental factors, traffic flow series may show an abnormal state ( Chen, Wu, et al., 2020 ), which has non-recurrent characteristics. In general training datasets, the sample ratio of normal data and abnormal data is normally unbalanced. The features of normal data usually dominate the features learned by the prediction model. However, it is more instructive for managers to learn and predict abnormal traffic flow. There are no keywords related to abnormal data in the keyword co-occurrence network (see  Fig. 11 ). Therefore, one of the future research opportunities is to adopt advanced AI technologies (e.g., data augmentation, and few-shot learning) to extract the abnormal data features of traffic flow. As shown in  Fig. 11 (a) and  Fig. 11 (b) (i.e., the node labeled “data fusion”), a few researchers (e.g.,  Choi & Chung, 2002; Soriguera & Robusté, 2011 ) have considered fusing heterogeneous data such as meteorological data, transportation network structure data, and points of interest to extract the spatiotemporal dependence features of traffic flow in the early years. However, heterogeneous data fusion research is still in its infancy and has not received sufficient attention in recent years (see  Fig. 11 ). In the process of heterogeneous data fusion, it is challenging to design an efficient data selection or data matching algorithm to coordinate the mapping relationship between traffic flow and other heterogeneous data. On the one hand, the granularity of traffic flow data collected by different types of traffic flow detectors is various.

snippets: 6.2.2 Data heterogeneity With the development of information technology, many emerging data can be applied to estimate the missing traffic volume of urban road networks, such as radar data, mobile data, probe GPS data   , online hailing data, and licence plate recognition data. The data application is introduced in the aforementioned section. Because of the heterogeneity of these emerging data, different data in the modelling process will produce large variances in estimation results. For example, comparing mobile phone data with taxi GPS data, both of them are viewed as probe detector data that are fused to other fixed detector data, taxi GPS data have more accurate positioning information than mobile phone data, and more accurate travel speed data can be obtained. However, due to the effect of the variance of travel demand from different areas, some areas with low travel demand rarely have taxi passing by, and the driving trajectory in these segments is sparse. Mobile phone data compensate the shortcomings of the sparse distribution of taxi data, and can have whole spatiotemporal coverage. However, limited by the influence of positioning accuracy and irregular positioning intervals, the accuracies of travel speed parameters from mobile phones are poor. Due to the differences in location accuracies and positioning intervals, the application of proposed estimation methods for different data types will not be consistent, and it is necessary to fully utilize of these unique data characteristics in the process of developing a volume estimation model. Generally, the problem of data heterogeneity is mainly considered from three aspects: data structure, data parameters, and data distribution. For different data structures, with the different market penetration rates of sample data, we need to calculate the minimum sample size by speed distribution. For the characteristic of the sparse distribution of trajectory data, it is necessary to consider fusion with other points of interest (POI) data. For different data parameters, we need to establish an integrated model for inferring other valuable traffic parameters by microscopic traffic flow diagrams    and fundamental network diagrams   . Furthermore, due to the difficulty of different data distributions, the adaptive transfer learning theory can be applied to address this problem   .
