snippets: 5.1.3 Heterogeneous data fusion issue Facing the complex and changeable traffic environment, it is difficult to accurately predict the future traffic flow only using the historical traffic flow data. As shown in  Fig. 11 (a) and  Fig. 11 (b) (i.e., the node labeled “data fusion”), a few researchers (e.g.,  Choi & Chung, 2002; Soriguera & Robusté, 2011 ) have considered fusing heterogeneous data such as meteorological data, transportation network structure data, and points of interest to extract the spatiotemporal dependence features of traffic flow in the early years. However, heterogeneous data fusion research is still in its infancy and has not received sufficient attention in recent years (see  Fig. 11 ). In the process of heterogeneous data fusion, it is challenging to design an efficient data selection or data matching algorithm to coordinate the mapping relationship between traffic flow and other heterogeneous data. On the one hand, the granularity of traffic flow data collected by different types of traffic flow detectors is various. For example, fixed detectors (e.g., radar, loop detector, and microwave) regularly collect traffic flow data of specific traffic stations, while probe sensors (e.g., GPS, connected vehicles, and mobile navigation) collect real-time trajectory data of different vehicles. As can be seen from  Fig. 11 (a) (e.g., red nodes at right) and  Fig. 11 (b) (e.g., blue nodes at the bottom left), the existing studies are still limited to the fusion of single-granularity data. Therefore, designing an effective method to match and fuse traffic data of different granularity, and accurately map the trajectory data to specific traffic stations is a research direction worth exploring. On the other hand, the development of social media can help people obtain timely information in specific areas, such as weather, traffic incidents, and entertainment activities. Although no papers related to multi-source data fusion have appeared on the two main paths in  Fig. 10 , a few studies ( Abdollahi, Khaleghi, & Yang, 2020; Essien, Petrounias, Sampaio, & Sampaio, 2021 ) in recent years have fully demonstrated the effectiveness of fusing traffic, weather, and event data to improve the accuracy of TFP.

snippets: 3.4 Validation Fig. 7 a  presents the validation strategy with respect to how data was split between the training set and the testing set. A patient-wise validation strategy, employed by 36 papers, implies that data collected from a single patient is not simultaneously included in the training set and the testing set, reducing bias. 37 papers (i.e. more than half) did not employ such a strategy, possibly containing information from a single patient in both the training and testing sets, or did not specify how such splitting was achieved which leaves them open to potential data leakage. Three different strategies were mainly used to split datapoints between training and testing sets. Hold-out , arguably the most common technique in the broader machine learning community, corresponds to separating a portion of the datapoints in a testing set at the beginning of the experiment in order to isolate it entirely from the training process, and was used 30 times in total, which makes it the most regularly used strategy. k -fold Cross-Validation (CV) ( k -CV) comes second, with 26 occurrences in total. This strategy consists in partitioning the datapoints into  k  different disjoint sets. An independent training procedure is then performed  k  times, each using a different set as testing data and the remaining  k  − 1 as training data. When performed correctly (i.e. ensuring that the training procedures are completely independent and isolating from each other) this has the benefit of evaluating the algorithm on all the data possible although at the expense of re-training the algorithm several times. Leave-one-out CV (LOOCV) is a specific case  k -CV for very small datasets, in which  k  is equal to the number of datapoints (or the number of patients, if the validation was done patient-wise) in the database. LOOCV is beneficial in that it also ensures that a maximum amount of data is present in the training set at any given time. LOOCV has been used 13 times. Two papers did not validate their method on a separated testing set, and one did not specify the validation method employed. Finally,  bootstrapping  refers to evaluation procedures in which the algorithm is trained once, but the effect of any individual datapoint can be isolated and removed from the model, thus allowing for said datapoint to be used in evaluating the reduced model.

snippets: Assessment Methods There are several methodologies to assess the prediction model performance but it is good to have the understanding that a perfect score (classification problem with  100% accuracy and regression problem with 0% error) is simply an unrealistic expectation. There will be inevitable error from data issues (inaccurate or incomplete data) or algorithm limitations. A good overall strategy prior to evaluation of the prediction model is to have a good baseline prediction model (good predictive models to start with include random forest or gradient boosting, see under ensemble learning) or simply try all the prediction models that you are familiar with (and then select the best one or few simple ones). The evaluation of a model with a test set of data (that the model has not seen before) can follow two methods: cross-validation or holdout method. In cross-validation, the original dataset is divided into  k  equal-sized subsets called folds, so that  k −1 subsets are used as the training dataset. In the holdout method, the master dataset is divided into training set, validation set (not always used), and test set (see the ML workflow section).

concept: Feature selection is a vital process in machine learning and data analysis that enhances model performance by identifying and retaining the most relevant features while discarding redundant or irrelevant ones.

Different feature selection techniques, such as filter-based, wrapper-based, and tree-based methods, each have unique advantages and disadvantages, impacting the effectiveness of the selected features.

Correlation-based feature selection, recursive feature elimination, and tree-based methods like random forests are effective strategies for determining feature importance and improving model accuracy.
The choice of features directly influences the efficiency of classification models, reducing computation time and improving overall performance.
Various feature selection strategies have been explored in research, with correlation-based algorithms showing modest improvements and the FAST algorithm outperforming others in specific contexts.

Dimensionality reduction techniques, while not the primary focus of all studies, can significantly enhance computational efficiency by minimizing the number of variables in datasets, particularly those with high redundancy or sparsity.

The integration of feature selection and dimensionality reduction is crucial for optimizing machine learning models, especially in complex datasets like those used in app usage analysis and patient encounter representations.

snippets: 27.3.3 Feature selection techniques The process of feature selection is crucial to machine learning and data analysis. It entails selecting the most important and useful components from a dataset while eliminating unnecessary or redundant information. In addition to increasing the effectiveness and accuracy of machine learning models, this approach helps to simplify and minimize the dimensionality of the data. Each method for feature selection has advantages and disadvantages of its own. Fig. 2  shows the broad classification of the feature selection techniques. A common method for selecting appropriate features from a dataset is filter-based feature selection. It involves inspecting each feature's characteristics independent of the target variable. This approach often ranks and selects the most informative characteristics using statistical methods or scoring criteria. Another technique for selecting features called “wrapper-based feature selection” includes assessing subsets of features based on how well they perform when applied to a particular machine learning algorithm. It approaches feature selection as a search problem, testing various feature combinations and ranking them using predetermined evaluation criteria. In tree-based feature selection, the algorithm builds ensemble models or decision trees using the dataset, taking different features into account at each split. A feature's significance is measured by how much it contributes to lowering impurities or enhancing the tree's or ensemble's ability to make predictions. The importance of a feature is determined by how frequently it is used for splitting and how much is the impurity or performance improvement. In the proposed work, correlation-based, recursive feature elimination, and tree-based feature selection are used, which are the subcategories of filter-based, wrapper-based, and embedded-based feature selection techniques. The statistical relation between each feature in the dataset and the target feature is measured using correlation-based feature selection. Low correlation features are eliminated while the most significant features with high correlation coefficients are kept. The RFE approach, which recursively eliminates the least significant features based on the performance of the model, is one of the well-known wrapper-based feature selection techniques. There exist several iterations, and in each of them, the features that are less important are eliminated. Random forest ensemble learning machine learning model is used to extract the important features for a tree-based feature selection technique. Random forest is constructed with the help of multiple decision trees, and the results of their predictions help to provide a robust measure of feature importance. In summary, feature selection is a critical stage in enhancing the effectiveness of machine learning models.

concept: Random forests (RF) are a powerful ensemble learning method used for both classification and regression tasks, leveraging multiple decision trees to improve prediction accuracy and robustness.
RF models are constructed by selecting random subsets of features to create diverse decision trees, which reduces correlation among trees and enhances generalization as more trees are added.

RF effectively handles high-dimensional data, identifies significant features, and is resistant to overfitting, making it suitable for various applications, including medical image classification and disease diagnosis.
While RF offers many advantages, its computational complexity can be a drawback, particularly with large datasets, though this can be mitigated through parallel processing and feature selection.
Ensemble learning techniques like stacking and concatenation combine multiple models to create stronger predictive capabilities, but they can also lead to overfitting if not managed carefully.

The ensemble process involves generating diverse models, pruning less effective ones, and integrating their predictions to enhance accuracy and robustness, with various methods available for model combination.
Overall, ensemble methods, including RF, bagging, and boosting, aim to improve model performance by leveraging the strengths of multiple learners, thus achieving better generalization and accuracy.

snippets: 4.2.2.1 Random forests Random forests are generally the most widely used bagging and ensemble learning models ( Breiman, 2001 ). Random forests use random decision trees as the base classifiers. In each iteration, the algorithm selects a random vector of features (i.e., a random subset of features) to construct a random tree. Therefore, the trees in the RF vary in nature and have a low correlation with each other. The generalization error of the ensemble decreases as the number of random trees increases. Although the performance of a random forest is extremely similar to boosting, it is simpler to tune and train. Therefore, it is the most widely used ensemble model by practitioners and researchers, as shown in  Fig. 4.1 .

snippets: 2.3.8 Random forests Random forests (RF) are widely employed in BIA as a ML algorithm for classification and regression tasks. They belong to the ensemble learning family, combining multiple decision trees (DT) to make predictions   . The RF algorithm trains multiple DT on different subclass of the training data, with each tree providing an independent prediction. The outcome is then obtained by adding the predicted results of all the forest’s trees. In classification tasks, this aggregation is typically achieved through majority voting, while in regression tasks, the predictions are averaged    ( Fig. 2.7 ). RF offer several advantages in BIA. They effectively handle high-dimensional feature spaces and identify significant features contributing to classification or regression tasks. Furthermore, they exhibit resistance to overfitting, as the aggregation of multiple DT reduces model variance. RF have been successfully applied to various BIA tasks, including image segmentation, classification of medical images, and disease diagnosis. They demonstrate high accuracy and robustness, even with noisy or incomplete data   . However, one potential limitation of RF lies in their computational complexity, especially for large datasets or high-dimensional feature spaces. Nonetheless, this limitation can be addressed by parallelizing the training process across multiple processors or utilizing feature selection techniques to reduce data dimensionality.

snippets: Many of the weak models (base models) used in boosting methods are highly adaptive, continuously fitting by giving more weight to observations in the dataset that were misinterpreted by the previous model ( Fig. 7 (b)). In many cases, this approach is effective in minimizing model bias and variability. It also allows for efficient handling of missing data. While this approach has many advantages, its real-time implementation is inherently complex, which can directly affect the behavior of the training algorithm. 5.6.4 Stacking Stacking (also known as stacking generalization) is a common machine learning technique that combines relevant knowledge from multiple standalone models to build a new model, called a metamodel   . In general, this method considers different weak learners, trains them simultaneously, integrates them, and optimizes the hyperparameters of the generated metamodel ( Fig. 7 (c)). The idea behind this approach is to combine a set of weak learners from which stronger learners (i.e., metamodels) are created for better performance. In ensemble learning theory, weak learners can be used as building blocks to create more complex models. In some cases, these weak models lack the robustness to perform well on their own due to high levels of bias and variance   . While the stacking method has many advantages (e.g., better predictive performance, more accurate data, better generalization, etc.), its main drawback is overfitting. That is, when too many predictors are used to make predictions about the same target, these predictors are subsequently fitted together to produce the final prediction. In addition, multilevel stacking models are expensive. 5.6.5 Concatenation Concatenation is one of the most widely used feature fusion techniques in machine learning that systematically combines multiple inputs into a single input   . The core idea of concatenation is to combine two or more output tensors (usually from different network layers) along the channel dimension. More specifically, two or more output tensors from different network layers can be processed with selected multivariate functions to integrate the outputs of multiple models. In this way, multiple data sources can be integrated into a common space. In practice, concatenation can be thought of as a stacking process. To illustrate, consider a CNN model with 128 channels in each of the two hidden layers.

snippets: A weak learner is a poor model, which still describes some crucial characteristic of the data. Hence, it is reasonable that combining over the appropriate collection of weak learners will generate a strong learner. Generally, there are two main principles producing ensemble models. First, combining models signifies a stronger model class than simply selecting one of them. Consequently, the weighted sum of predictions from a collection of models can achieve better performance than individual predictions since linear combinations of the models must produce a lower bias than any individual model. The predictions that the ensemble models are combined stay distinct since they are based on diverse assumptions, which cannot be easily merged, and they have various parameters with diverse estimates. In fact, ensemble models only enhance the model selection techniques when the models in the ensemble achieve various predictions (Clarke, Fokoue, & Zhang, 2009 Clarke, Foukoue, & Zhang, 2009). Two best-known ensemble algorithms are bagging and boosting.

snippets: The main goal for combining models is to improve their generalization ability, robustness, and increase result accuracy  [97–99] . An ensemble process ( Fig. 2.3 ) consists of 3 phases that are referred to as the overproduce-and-choose approach   . The first phase is  ensemble generation . In this phase, a set of models is generated. The focus is on models' diversity, which can be characterized as the degree of disagreement between the base models. Based on the number of induction algorithms that create the base models, there are two main ensemble model generation approaches: homogeneous    and heterogeneous   . The diversity of models in homogeneous ensemble can be achieved by manipulation of inputs of the single induction algorithm (data or parameters). The second phase is called  ensemble pruning . In this step, the set of previous generated models is pruned by removing some of the redundant or less accurate models. The goals of pruning are finding a small set of diverse models to achieve the maximum prediction accuracy and reducing costs without loss of accuracy (e.g. memory size or computational complexity caused by high number of models). There are several pruning approaches presented in the literature   , e.g. ranking, search-based and partitioning-based methods. The last phase is  ensemble integration  that applies various strategies to combine the results of models with respect to obtain more accurate final prediction results. The ensemble integration in regression is often defined as linear combination of given or calculated weights and predictions. There are several proposed combination methods producing weights for prediction models in ensemble. Some of them are very simple and produce uniform weights despite the prediction accuracy of the models, e.g. averaging methods. More complex methods consider the prediction error of the models based on actual or historical results. They assign weights in more dynamical way and can adapt to changes in data, e.g. error-based methods or generalized ensemble method that monitors correlations of models' errors. Other examples of advanced combination methods are stacking (stacked generalization), least squares regression or nature-inspired and evolutionary optimization algorithms, which try to minimize prediction error (e.g. MAPE, MAE, RMSE, etc.). concept: The Bias-Variance trade-off is a crucial concept in machine learning that highlights the balance between two types of errors: bias (error due to oversimplification) and variance (error due to overfitting).
High-bias models tend to underfit the data, failing to capture complex relationships, while high-variance models overfit, capturing noise instead of the underlying patterns.
The goal in machine learning is to achieve a model with low bias and low variance by selecting an appropriate level of complexity.
Learning curves can illustrate the bias-variance trade-off, showing how training and testing errors change with the amount of training data.
Techniques to manage the bias-variance trade-off include regularization, which limits model complexity, and ensemble learning, which combines multiple models to improve accuracy.

Addressing class imbalance in datasets can involve various strategies, such as over-sampling, under-sampling, and synthetic data generation techniques like SMOTE, which help improve model performance without increasing the risk of overfitting.
Advanced methods like easy-ensemble and balance-cascade can enhance model training by effectively utilizing majority class samples and reducing noise.
The use of evolutionary algorithms and active learning techniques can further optimize model performance on imbalanced datasets by refining sample selection and enhancing classifier sensitivity.

snippets: 7.1.3.1 Bias variance trade-off The Bias-Variance trade-off is a fundamental concept in machine learning that refers to the trade-off between two types of errors that can occur in a model: bias and variance. Bias is the error that occurs when a model is too simple to capture the complexity of the data, while variance is the error that occurs when a model is too complex and overfits the data. Bias refers to the error that is introduced by approximating a real-world problem with a simplified model. A high-bias model has a limited ability to represent complex relationships in the data. This often results in underfitting, where the model is unable to capture the important patterns in the data. For example, a linear regression model that is used to predict the price of a house may have a high bias if it assumes that the relationship between the price and the size of the house is linear, when in fact it may be more complex. Variance, on the other hand, refers to the error that is introduced by modelling the noise in the training data rather than the underlying patterns. A high variance model has too much flexibility and can fit the training data too closely, resulting in overfitting. Overfitting occurs when the model becomes too complex and captures the noise in the data, rather than the underlying patterns. For example, a decision tree that is used to predict the price of a house may have high variance if it is too deep, and it captures noise and random variations in the training data. The bias-variance trade-off states that there is a trade-off between these two types of errors, and it is important to find a balance between them. Models with high bias tend to have low variance, while models with low bias tend to have high variance. The goal of machine learning is to find a model that has low bias and low variance, which is achieved by selecting the right level of model complexity that is appropriate for the problem at hand. The bias-variance trade-off can be illustrated using a learning curve. A learning curve plots the training and testing error of a model as a function of the amount of training data. Initially, as the model is trained on a small amount of data, the training error and testing error are both high, indicating high bias and high variance. As more data is added, the training error decreases, indicating that the model is learning more about the data.

snippets: 3.1 Data diversity Data diversity-based ensemble methods use datasets with different sample distributions to train predictors. The conventional algorithms for data diversity are bootstrap aggregation (Bagging) and Boosting. 3.1.1 Use Bagging to generate data diversity The data diversity of Bagging is embodied in the bootstrap sampling phase. It repeatedly draws commensurate samples with replacement from the original training set, to obtain several sample sets. In Ref.   , a bagging reduced error pruning (REP) Tree model was proposed to forecast wind speed in the west of Turkey. The proposed ensemble learning model successfully improves forecasting accuracy. The obtained correlation coefficient between forecasting values and observed values is 0.8154. 3.1.2 Use Boosting to generate data diversity Boosting enhances multiple weak learners to build a stronger predictor. Adaptive boosting (AdaBoost) is a widely used representative algorithm of Boosting. It continuously trains the weak learners and changes the distribution of the training set according to the training performance. Samples with larger forecasting error will be allocated higher weights in the further training process. The weak learners are weighted integrated to obtain a strong learner with superior performance. The AdaBoost-ELM has been employed to achieve dynamic combination forecasting, which can get rid of the unstable results of ELM caused by random initialization   . Some variants of AdaBoost have also been utilized for wind energy forecasting, such as AdaBoost. MRT   , Modified AdaBoost. RT   , and TW-FE-Adaboost   . Unlike the AdaBoost, gradient boosting adopts the direction of gradient descent to correct the previous mistakes. The performance of gradient boosted regression (GBR) for wind energy prediction has been demonstrated to be more competitive than SVR   .

snippets: DL techniques in cybersecurity are advantageous because they can learn from large volumes of data and identify complex patterns that traditional approaches may overlook. However, much attention might be needed to ensure the effectiveness of the DL model and avoid potential biases or false positives in DT environments. 4.1.3 Rule mining and expert system modeling Typically, knowledge mining involves extracting insights, patterns, and relationships from large volumes of data   . An important part of knowledge mining is rule mining, which is used to find interesting relationships between variables in large datasets. Using discovered knowledge or rules and expert systems in cybersecurity modeling allows for enhanced threat detection and mitigation. In rule mining, patterns, and correlations are automatically discovered in vast datasets, which can be used to identify vulnerabilities and malicious behavior. Based on these rules, an expert system can be constructed that emulates the decision-making capabilities of human cybersecurity experts. To discover rules, Sarker et al.    explored a taxonomy of diverse methods such as knowledge-based approach,  i.e. , based on human expertise, data-driven approach,  i.e. , extracting insights or useful knowledge from data, and their ensembles. Different types of rules can be discovered depending on the data nature and the target cyber solution. For example, association rules    can be employed to identify a correlation between certain user behaviors and the likelihood of a security breach. Similarly, classification rules    can be used to identify the type of malware that is present on a network and to determine the appropriate action to take to mitigate the threat. In addition, fuzzy rules    and belief rules    based modeling can be used to handle uncertainty and imprecision in data. For instance, a fuzzy rule could be used to detect network traffic that is slightly anomalous but not necessarily indicative of a specific attack. Similarly, a belief rule could be used to determine the likelihood that a particular security event is a false positive, based on the level of confidence in the detection algorithm and other relevant factors. By using rule-based modeling, security analysts can detect and respond to threats more effectively and find the root cause of such threats for proactive solutions. Through continuous learning and adaptation, rule mining and expert systems enhance the resilience and security posture against evolving cyber threats. However, a balance between rule complexity and interpretability is crucial to effective cybersecurity decision-making.

Collaborative endeavors involving data scientists, domain specialists, and stakeholders are essential for crafting and implementing tailored remedies for high-dimensional challenges. This ensures the development of precise and scalable predictive modeling frameworks tailored for smart city applications and traffic management systems. 7.3 Data dependency Data dependency poses significant challenges in predictive modeling, particularly in areas such as smart cities and traffic management. Data dependency arises when a model’s ability to predict relies heavily on specific variables or features, which makes it more difficult to generalize to new data. This reliance can introduce biases and reduce the effectiveness of the model in real-world situations ( Kossmann, Papenbrock, & Naumann, 2022 ). Furthermore, data dependency complicates model validation and evaluation because the performance metrics may differ depending on the dataset used. Strong interdependencies among variables can obscure causal relationships, making it difficult to accurately interpret model outputs. Overcoming this challenge involves carefully considering feature engineering techniques and integrating domain knowledge to reduce the dependence on correlated variables. Additionally, ensemble learning methods such as bagging and boosting can mitigate the impact of data dependency by combining multiple models with different dependencies. Collaborative efforts among data scientists, domain experts, and stakeholders are essential for identifying and addressing data dependency issues and ensuring the development of reliable predictive modeling frameworks for smart city applications and traffic management systems. In computer science, data dependency occurs when a program statement refers to the data in the preceding statement. Dependence analysis, a technique in compiler theory, helps uncover data dependencies among statements or instructions, aiding in optimizing code execution and improving overall system performance. Altogether, the challenge of data dependency in predictive modeling can only be addressed through a combination of approaches. First, the use of advanced feature engineering methods significantly reduces reliance on some of the variables presented in data dependency. Thus, the features should be carefully selected and transformed to create an independent and diverse set of predictors. Second, the reduction in this effect through domain expertise contributes to this model. Finally, ensemble learning arguments such as bagging and boosting offer an effective way to combine models with different dependencies. Therefore, the robustness and generalization potential of the predictive model increased.

snippets: 7.4 Overfitting Overfitting is a significant hurdle in the realm of predictive modeling of smart cities and traffic flow. It arises when a model captures irrelevant noise or fluctuations in the training data instead of the underlying patterns, leading to accurate performance on training data but inadequate generalization to new or unseen data. Overfitting can pose substantial challenges, especially in smart city contexts characterized by complex and diverse datasets, owing to the abundance of variables and features, exacerbated by the variability inherent in urban environments. Moreover, in traffic flow prediction, overfitting can occur when the model captures temporary patterns or anomalies rather than the fundamental traffic dynamics. Addressing overfitting is crucial for developing reliable predictive models that are essential for guiding decision-making in smart city planning and traffic management ( Santos & Papa, 2022 ). Overfitting, an undesirable trait in machine learning, arises when a model accurately predicts the training data but falters new data. Data scientists typically train machine learning models on established datasets before utilizing them for predictions. This dual challenge highlights the critical necessity of vigilant strategies to mitigate overfitting in predictive modeling applications, ensuring consistent and dependable performance in real-world settings. The problem of overfitting in the predictive modeling of smart cities and traffic flow can be addressed in several ways. First, regularization methods such as L1 and L2 regularization can be used to punish overly complex models and prefer simpler and more general models. Cross-validation approaches, such as k-fold cross-validation, help assess the predictive accuracy of a model on unknown data and detect early indications of overfitting warning signals. Techniques for feature selection and dimensionality reduction, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and prioritizing features based on importance, can assist in identifying relevant features while simplifying model complexity. Ensemble learning methods, such as random forests and gradient boosting, merge multiple models to enhance generalization and mitigate overfitting risks. Additionally, expanding the size and diversity of the training dataset can expose the model to a wider array of patterns, thereby reducing the chance of memorizing noise. Collaborative efforts among data scientists, domain experts, and stakeholders are crucial for effectively implementing these strategies and crafting robust predictive models tailored to smart city applications and traffic-management systems.

Assuming, without any loss of generality, that the variance and cross-covariance of  z k s are  σ 2  and  ρ , respectively, we have (15.6) Var ( z k ) = σ 2 , Cov ( z k , z k ′ ) = ρ ; then Var ( z ¯ ) = σ 2 K + ( K − 1 ) ρ σ 2 K . Depending on  ρ , the variance of  z ¯  goes from  σ 2 K  to  σ 2  (under the assumption that  ρ > 0 , i.e., the estimators are not negatively correlated). In the current setting, since all the  K  estimators/learners share the same set of input data, they cannot be independent. However, by ensuring that  ρ  is as small as possible and increasing  K , one can make sure that the composed estimator  z ¯  will have the smallest possible variance. Several approaches may be used to ensure small  ρ , most of which are based on  randomly  dividing the input dimensions, data instances and/or other estimation/learning parameters into  K  subsets and constructing one estimator from each of these subsets   . The outputs of these estimators can then be considered to be random (or stochastic, in some sense) approximations of the ideal output with zero-bias and small variance. There is extensive empirical evidence for such strategies where the eventual  ensemble learner  will retain the discriminative power of the individual weak learners while reducing the apparent prediction variance   . We will use deep networks to construct an efficient weak learner, followed by presenting a systematic strategy to construct the ensemble – this overall learning procedure will correspond to the randomized deep network model.

snippets: From the perspective of data augmentation, the number of samples needs to be amplified (i.e., virtual sample generation). Virtual sample generation methods are mainly divided into two categories ( Zhang, Yu, Yin, & Lai, 2022 ): traditional mathematical statistics techniques (e.g., domain prior knowledge ( Bloch, Lauer, Colin, & Chamaillard, 2008 ), disturbance ( Li & Fang, 2009 ), interpolation ( Fernández, Garcia, Herrera, & Chawla, 2018 ), distribution ( Yang, Yu, Xie, & Zhang, 2011 )) and artificial intelligence algorithms (e.g., swarm intelligent optimization algorithm ( Chen, Zhu, He, & Yu, 2017 ), Traditional supervised learning methods ( Yu, Zhang, & Yin, 2022 ), and deep learning method ( Liu et al., 2019; Mancisidor, Kampffmeyer, Aas, & Jenssen, 2022 )). High dimensionality traits:  High dimensionality refers to a large number of attributes of data (e.g., dimension greater than 20 or 100 ( Yu, Yu, & Yu, 2021 )), which contains a large number of redundant and irrelevant features, affecting the accuracy and complexity of modeling. Processing techniques can be divided into two categories: feature selection and feature extraction. For the feature extraction method, the original data is transformed into a new feature space through projection mapping to extract new features, and the data sample is divided based on the new features. Such as principal component analysis (PCA) ( Yu, Yu, & Yu, 2021 ), Autoencoders ( Dastile et al., 2020 ),  t -NSE ( Mancisidor et al., 2022 ), etc. As for feature selection, its main purpose is to select the optimal feature subset in the original dataset, which mainly includes filters, wrappers, and embedded. Filters method is to use statistical and information theory models to calculate the relative importance of features, and then select features for modeling, such as relief ( Arora & Kaur, 2020 ), information gain ( Trivedi, 2020 ), and so on ( Guyon & Elisseeff, 2003 ). The wrappers feature selection algorithm fully considers the influence of different feature combinations on the results, and the feature selection step is connected with the model evaluation successively, which increases the complexity of the model.

concept: **Parallelization Methods**: The document outlines two primary methods for parallelizing computation: local training on multi-core machines and distributed training across multiple machines. Local training utilizes the cores of a single machine, while distributed training addresses the challenges of large datasets by spreading data or models across several machines.

**Deep Neural Networks**: The text explains the structure and training of deep neural networks, emphasizing the importance of parallelization in their training. It introduces inter-model parallelism, where different models are trained on the same dataset, and highlights the significance of ensemble methods in enhancing model performance.

**Ensemble Learning**: The document categorizes ensemble methods into iterative and parallel based ensembles. Iterative methods, like boosting, focus on sequential learning, while parallel methods, such as bagging, allow for simultaneous training of base classifiers, improving accuracy and reducing bias and variance.

**Knowledge Distillation (KD)**: KD methodologies are discussed, particularly progressive and online distillation. Progressive distillation involves a step-by-step knowledge transfer from a teacher model to a student model, while online distillation allows both models to learn simultaneously, enhancing adaptability and efficiency.

**Ensemble Model Construction**: The construction of ensemble models is detailed, emphasizing the importance of diversity among base learners and the aggregation of their outputs. The document distinguishes between dependent and independent frameworks for training base learners, with independent methods allowing for parallel processing.

**Generalization and Bias**: The concepts of generalization and bias in machine learning are introduced, highlighting the importance of ensemble learning in improving model performance by leveraging the strengths of multiple learners rather than relying on a single model.

Parallelization methods for computation can be categorized into local and distributed training, with local training utilizing multi-core processors on a single machine and distributed training addressing large datasets across multiple machines.

Local training can be executed through lengthy parallelization processes or batching systems, while distributed training can employ data parallelism (distributing data across machines) or model parallelism (distributing model components).

Deep neural networks, which mimic brain functions, can be trained using various parallelization methods, including inter-model parallelism, where different models with varying parameters are trained on the same dataset.

Collaborative training methods like co-training, co-teaching, and knowledge distillation enhance model performance by leveraging the strengths of multiple models, particularly in scenarios with noisy data.
Co-training involves training models on distinct data views, allowing them to improve each other's learning through shared predictions, as demonstrated in disease classification tasks.
Federated Learning (FL) decentralizes machine learning by training models across multiple devices without centralizing data, thus preserving privacy and enabling efficient model aggregation.

The FL framework includes clients monitoring IoT devices and a server coordinating the training process, utilizing aggregation algorithms like Mini-batch and Multi-epoch to update global model parameters.

Overall, these methodologies highlight the importance of parallelization and collaboration in enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of machine learning models, particularly in complex and large-scale applications.

snippets: 1.2.3 Parallelization Methods to Distribute Computation Across Multiple Machines The methodologies to perform parallelized or distributed computation on multi-core machines are given below. 1.2.3.1 Local Training Local training means that the data is being trained on a single machine which has multi-core processors. The entire datasets are loaded onto the same machine, the cores inside take care of the processing task. Multi-core machines can be used in two ways: • By loading multiple data in a single layer and processing them using the multi-core processor, which is a lengthy parallelization process; • By using a batching system to separate the datasets into many small batches and sending each batch to a core for processing. 1.2.3.2 Distributed Training When the datasets are so huge that they cannot be stored on a single system, distributed training resolves this problem. The data is stored across many machines in a distributed manner. Here, either the model or data can be distributed, which is discussed below. • In data parallelism, data is distributed across multiple machines. When the data set is large or its faster processing is required, data parallelism can be used. • In model parallelism, the model is typically too big to fit on a single  system. When a model is placed into a single machine, one model demands the output of another model. This forward and backward propagation establishes communication between the models from different machines in a serial fashion   . 1.2.4 Methods to Train Deep Neural Networks Using Parallelization Deep neural networks or deep artificial neural networks follow the structure of the actual brain and its functions. They use multiple layers of artificial neurons for classification and pattern recognition. Fig. 1.3  shows the structure of a non-deep neural network, having only one hidden layer, whereas  Fig. 1.4  depicts a deep neural network with three hidden layers. Networks having between 3 and 10 hidden layers are called very deep neural networks. There are four ways to parallelize neural network training. They are discussed in what follows. 1.2.4.1 Inter-Model Parallelism Generally, when inter-model parallelism is used, there are different models, and each model can have different parameters such as equation function, layer types, number of neurons per layer, etc. All three different model cases are trained with the same dataset. See  Fig. 1.5 .

snippets: A promising solution to avoid the complexities of estimating the noise transition matrix involves focusing on training with a subset of carefully selected samples. This approach aims to filter out clean instances from the noisy data for network training. In this context, collaborative methods via training two or more models leverages the cooperation between models for improving the performances of DL models. These methods encompass co-training, co-teaching, and knowledge distillation. 5.2.3.1 Co-training Co-training is a machine learning technique where two or more models are trained separately on distinct views of the data, and their predictions are used to enhance each other’s learning process. Zhou et al.    proposed a co-training approach to tune a single target network for disease classification. They pre-trained multiple reference networks to handle label uncertainty. To co-optimize the target network, they introduced a  Disentangled Distribution Learning (DDL)  strategy, which disentangle the multiple reference models’ predictions into a hard  Majority Confident Label (MCL)  vector (a pseudo cleaned ground-truth) and a soft  Description Degree Score (DDS)  vector. The MCL vector was computed by counting the number of networks giving positive and negative predictions for the corresponding disease label. The DDS vector was computed using the average over all the predictions. To optimize the target network, they used KL divergence based on the confidence-weighted relative entropy of the hard majority label vector with respect to the predictions of the target network. Moreover, they proposed  inter- and intra-instance consistency regularization  to enforce the target network to provide consistent predictions for images with similar medical findings. This involved using KNN smoothing modules and image augmentation. K  nearest neighbors of an image (the anchor image) were computed based on the fixed soft label distribution. Then, the target network was constrained to produce similar predictions for the anchor image and its  K  nearest neighbors. In addition, the anchor image was also augmented into different views and the target network was constrained to have the same prediction for these views. Experiments performed on chest X-ray and fundus image dataset, showed that the proposed approach is outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Xue et al.    proposed a  co-training with global and local representation learning framework . Two independent teacher–student networks were trained with different image augmentation and initialization strategies to ensure distinct weight parameters.

snippets: In this context of distributed training of detection models, it is important to discuss Federated Learning (FL), which consists of a strategy to form a global ML model from several local data-driven models   . This strategy decentralizes machine learning, eliminating the need to gather data on a single device. Instead, the model is trained through multiple iterations on different devices. FL is an ideal framework for aggregating distributed models, preserving privacy and allowing convergence to a distributed learning engine with precision close to that of a centralized implementation   . The framework architecture proposed by Rey et al.    is composed of clients that monitor IoT devices and a server that coordinates a Federated Learning process. The approach provides for intrusion detection through neural network models. Considering that IoT devices generally have limited resources and modest reliability, the clients responsible for training the models are not the devices to be protected, but other entities capable of collecting traffic from IoT devices present on the same network, such as fog nodes   . The server coordinates training efforts for federated customers and can be deployed in the cloud. It initializes the initial model weights and shares it with all clients, so each client starts with the same model. Client model parameters  k  are referred to as  w k  and global model parameters as  w . After receiving the updated template parameters from each client, i.e.  w k : ∀ k ∈ [ K ] , the server must aggregate them to form the new global template parameters  w . In the work, the authors used the aggregation function based on the mean, thus, the formula for the function is given by  w ≔ ∑ k = 1 K 1 K w k . Based on this function, the work also considers two aggregation algorithms, the Mini-batch and the Multi-epoch. In Mini-batch aggregation, the model is trained with a single mini-batch of data before sending it to the server for aggregation. After the aggregation done by the server, the client then receives the new aggregated global model, with which the training can continue. This process is repeated until a number of epochs over the complete training set are completed. On the other hand, in Multi-Epoch aggregation, the model is trained for all epochs at once before being sent to the server for aggregation. In addition, there are other steps that can be coordinated by the server. Data normalization can be performed directly on the combination of client training sets.

concept: Deep learning is a powerful subset of machine learning that utilizes artificial neural networks with multiple layers to learn complex patterns in data, significantly enhancing performance in areas like image recognition and natural language processing.
Neural networks, inspired by the human brain, consist of interconnected nodes that process data through layers, enabling the capture of intricate relationships that traditional algorithms may miss.

The deep-stacked ensemble classifier model employs multiple deep neural networks (DNNs) to extract features from raw data, utilizing activation functions like ReLU and sigmoid to optimize performance in binary classification tasks.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are specialized for image data, leveraging convolutional layers to extract spatial features, with notable architectures like U-Net for segmentation and ResNet for classification.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are designed for sequential data, maintaining context from previous inputs, but face challenges with long-term dependencies, leading to the development of advanced models like LSTM and GRU.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) analyze graph data by aggregating information from neighboring nodes, with models like Graph Convolutional Networks and Graph Attention Networks addressing various graph structures.
Parallelization methods in deep learning include local training on multi-core machines and distributed training across multiple systems, enhancing computational efficiency for large datasets.
Data parallelism and model parallelism are key strategies for distributing training tasks, allowing for faster processing and better resource utilization in deep learning models.

Recent advancements in cross-modality image matching involve optimizing batch normalization layers and classifiers to improve feature extraction and reduce modality discrepancies, showcasing the ongoing evolution in machine learning techniques.

snippets: 2.2.6 Deep learning Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that focuses on training artificial neural networks to learn and represent complex patterns and relationships in data. Inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain, deep learning involves the use of multiple layers, or “deep” architectures, to progressively learn hierarchical features from raw input data. Each layer in the network extracts higher-level features from the representations learned in the previous layer. Deep learning has revolutionized various domains, such as image recognition, natural language processing, and speech synthesis, achieving remarkable performance improvements compared to traditional machine learning techniques. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at image-related tasks by exploiting spatial hierarchies, while recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are adept at sequential data, like language ( Aggarwal, 2018 ). Deep learning models often require substantial amounts of labeled data and considerable computational resources, making them computationally intensive but capable of learning intricate patterns and representations. The use of deep architectures, in combination with techniques, such as regularization, optimization, and transfer learning, has enabled deep learning to excel across a wide range of applications and significantly advance the capabilities of machine learning systems ( Schmidhuber, 2015 ). 2.2.7 Neural networks Neural networks are computational models inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain's interconnected neurons. These networks consist of layers of interconnected nodes, or artificial neurons, which process and transform input data to produce output ( Aggarwal, 2018 ;  Du & Swamy, 2019 ). Each connection between neurons is associated with a weight, and these weights are learned from data during training. The architecture typically includes an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Information is fed forward through the layers, with each neuron performing a weighted sum of its inputs followed by a nonlinear activation function. This process allows neural networks to capture complex patterns and relationships in data that might be difficult for traditional algorithms. Various types of neural networks exist, such as feedforward neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) ( Ozturk, 2022 ) for image analysis, and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for sequential data processing. Neural networks have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in tasks like image recognition, language translation, and game playing, leading to their prominence in the fields of machine learning and artificial intelligence.

snippets: The structure of the proposed deep-stacked ensemble classifier is presented in the next subsection. 3.2 Deep-stacked ensemble classifier The classification model consists of four DNNs in the initial stage and is used for finding the features from the raw data and providing the metadata for further training. The multiple hidden layers in the DNN will help to extract suitable features from the input data. Each DNN consists of five layers including three hidden layer, as presented in  Fig. 2.3 . Though it  works in a feed-forward approach, the input data flow from the input layer to the output layer without forwarding back. The input gene data  D = { d 1 , d 2 , d 3 , … , d n }  is multiplied by the weight  W = { w 1 , w 2 , w 3 , … , w n } . The output  Y  of every layer after adding with bias  b  is represented by (2.1) Y = ( D ∗ W ) + b . The final output of the DNN  O  is obtained by passing the output of each layer  Y  through a nonlinear activation function and is represented by (2.2) O = f ( d · w ) = f ( ∑ i = 1 n d i w i ) , where  f  is the activation function, and  n  is each input gene feature. Two types of activation functions are used in the DNN. Rectified linear unit (ReLU) and sigmoid activation function are used in the hidden and output layer, respectively. ReLu is one of the most used activation functions in every deep learning model due to its properties of not activating all neurons at the same time and converting all negative input into zero. Also, it helps in accelerating the training performance compared with other activation functions [ 48 ]. Mathematically, it can be represented by (2.3) f ( d ) = max ( 0 , d ) , where  d  is the input data, and the output function  f ( d )  returns a value between 0 and 1. Though the proposed classification model is used for the binary classification problem, the Sigmoid activation function is used in the hidden layer. The output of this function lies between 0 and 1. It can be represented by (2.4) f ( d ) = 1 1 + e d . The detailed structure of each DNN including the number of layers and number of neurons in each layer is provided in  Fig. 2.3 .

snippets: 3.2.8 Convolutional neural networks CNNs are deep neural networks that are commonly used in structured data such as images. CNNs use a series of neural network layers to process images for different tasks, and the convolutional layers are a key design to leverage spatially correlated pixels to engineer task-specific features from images. Among various variants, U-Net [ 33 ] and ResNet [ 34 ] stand out as two of the most outstanding models. U-Net excels in image segmentation tasks, while ResNet is renowned for its deep architecture enabling advanced image classification. Notably, deep neural networks including CNNs, include a significant amount of learnable parameters (from millions to billions), thus requiring much more data for training for optimal performance and to avoid overfitting. 3.2.9 Recurrent neural networks RNNs are neural networks specially designed to process sequence data. The key feature of RNNs is their inherent ability to retain and utilize information from past inputs. As the model processes each element in a sequence, it incorporates relevant details from all preceding elements, allowing it to build and maintain a contextual understanding over time. However, RNNs often struggle to capture the dependency between two distant positions of a sequence, due to problems such as vanishing or exploding gradients. This has led to the development of more advanced variants like Long Short-Term Memory/LSTM [ 35 ] and Gated Recurrent Unit/GRU [ 36 ] networks, which are designed to better capture long-term dependencies. 3.2.10 Graph neural networks GNNs are powerful tools for analyzing graph data, a data structure representing the relations (edges) between a set of entities (nodes). The basic logic to obtain node representation in GNNs is to aggregate and transform feature information from the immediate neighbors of that node, effectively allowing the graph structure to be learned. Graph Convolutional Networks/GCNs [ 37 ] and Graph Attention Networks/GATs [ 38 ] represent significant improvements in GNNs. Graph Convolutional Networks are suitable in analyzing uniform graph structures, while Graph Attention Networks are optimal for graphs with non-uniform influence among neighbor nodes. However, challenges arise with GNNs in handling large-scale dense graphs, when the number of neighbors (adjacent or k-hop) grow exponentially, and in ensuring robustness against irregular graph structures.

snippets: 1.2.4.2 Data Parallelism The idea of data parallelism was brought up by Jeff Dean style as parameter averaging. We have three copies of the same model. We deploy the same model A over three different nodes, and a subset of the data is fed over the three identical models. The values of the parameters are sent to the parameter server and, after collecting all the parameters, they are averaged. Using the parameter server, the omega is synchronized. The neural networks can be trained in parallel in two ways, i.e., synchronously (by waiting for one complete iteration and  updating the value for omega) and asynchronously (by sending outdated parameters out of the network). But the amount of time taken for both methods is same, and the method choice is not a big issue here. See  Fig. 1.6 . To overcome the problems in data parallelism, task level parallelism has been introduced. Independent computation tasks are processed in parallel by using the conditional statements in GPUs. Task level parallelism can act without the help of data parallelism only to a certain extent, beyond which the GPU needs data parallelism for better efficiency. But the task level parallelism gives more flexibility and computation acceleration to the GPUs. 1.2.4.3 Intra-Model Parallelism Machine learning can leverage modern parallel data processing platforms like Hadoop and Spark in several ways. In this section, we will discuss how to scale machine learning with Hadoop or Spark. Three different ways of parallel processing can benefit machine learning. When thinking about parallel processing in the context of machine learning, what immediately jumps to our mind is data partitioning along with divide-and-conquer learning algorithms. However, as we will find out that data partitioning is not necessarily, the best way is to exploit parallel processing. There are other more fruitful areas   . See  Fig. 1.7 . 1.2.5 Parallelization Over Data, Function, Parameter and Prediction Scale The focus is on classical machine learning algorithms; moreover, we are only considering Hadoop and Spark for a parallel processing platform. 1.2.5.1 Data Partitioning With data partitioning and parallelism, the learning algorithm operates on each partition in parallel, and finally the results for each partition are stitched together. This is essentially the divide-and-conquer pattern. The critical assumption is that learning algorithms can be recast to execute in parallel.

snippets: Yin et al.    proposed a simple but efficient similarity inference to obtain the optimal intra- and cross-modality image matching. Zhang et al.    first used a local graph module to explore the potential relation of the different body parts and then used a global graph module to obtain contextual information across the two modalities for reducing the modality discrepancy. Feng et al.    first designed a homogeneous structured graph for an individual modality to learn identity-related features and then proposed a heterogeneous graph alignment module (HGAM) to achieve cross-modality alignment. Optimizing batch normalization layer:  The modality discrepancy can also be reduced by aligning feature distributions by optimizing those batch normalization layers in the parameter-shared networks. For example, Li et al.    proposed a modality batch normalization (MBN) layer, which normalized each modality sub-mini-batch to reduce the distribution gaps brought by batch normalization. Differently, Fu et al.    improved the performance of cross-modality matching by searching for the optimal separation scheme for batch normalization layers. Optimizing classifier:  The classifier forces VI-ReID models to extract those ID-discriminative modality-shared features. Considering that, some works try to optimize the classifier layer to better extract those ID-discriminative modality-shared features. For example, Ye et al.    suggested that learning cross-modality feature representations with a single modality-sharable classifier may lose discriminative information in different modalities. Therefore, they proposed a modality-aware collaborative (MAC) learning method to regularize the modality-sharable and modality-specific identity classifiers by utilizing the relationship between different classifiers. Later, a collaborative ensemble learning strategy was proposed in their extension work    to improve the performance by facilitating the knowledge transfer among different classifiers. Similarly, two modality-specific nearest neighbor classifiers were introduced in    to benefit the learning of the shared knowledge for cross-modality matching via preserving the same-modality and the cross-modality similarity. Tekeli et al.    proposed a novel distance based score layer, which preceded the loss function and gave higher scores for closer feature vectors and lower scores for distant feature vectors according to the distance metric.

concept: The training processes for ensemble methods can be categorized into two types: iterative based ensembles (like boosting) and parallel based ensembles (like bagging).
Boosting, particularly Adaboost, is the most widely used iterative ensemble method, focusing on misclassified samples to improve future classifiers.
Parallel based ensembles, such as bagging, allow for simultaneous training of classifiers, making them more efficient and popular in practical applications compared to iterative methods.

Bagging reduces overfitting by aggregating predictions from multiple models trained on different subsets of data, while boosting enhances model accuracy by iteratively focusing on difficult-to-classify instances.
The choice of base classifiers in ensemble models varies, with SVM, neural networks, and decision trees being the most commonly selected.
Recent advancements in ensemble techniques, including Neighborhood Balanced Bagging and online bagging, address class imbalance and memory constraints, respectively.
Overall, ensemble methods, whether iterative or parallel, leverage the strengths of multiple classifiers to improve predictive performance across various domains.

snippets: Note that the training process for the re-sampling based ensemble and bagging can be conducted in parallel, while boosting and some evolutionary based ensemble methods can only be trained using iterative processes. Therefore, in this study, we categorized the ensemble models into two categories, i.e. iterative based ensembles and parallel based ensembles. 3.2.1.1 Iterative based ensemble Boosting is the most common and most effective method for ensemble learning. We found 63 reviewed papers employed boosting in their ensemble framework, most of which were based on the first applicable boosting algorithm, Adaboost, proposed by  Freund and Schapire (1996) . The benefit of Adaboost is that samples that fail to be assigned to the correct class are given higher weights, which forces the future classifier to focus more on learning these failed classified samples. Adaboost has had several extensions: AdaBoost. M1, AdaBoost. M2, AdaBoost. MR and AdaBoost. MH ( Freund and Schapire, 1997 ;  Schapire and Singer, 1999 ); which were designed for solving multi-class and multi-label problems. Other typical iterative ensemble methods include Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) ( Friedman, 2001 ) and some evolutionary algorithm (EA) based ensemble algorithms. As mentioned in  Galar et al. (2012) , boosting algorithms are usually combined with cost-sensitive learning and re-sampling techniques. Table 4  lists some of the technical articles that have proposed novel iterative based ensemble algorithms. It can be seen that Adaboost and Adaboost. M2 have been the most popular iterative based ensemble schemes. Most ensemble models have considered cost-sensitive and re-sampling strategies. 3.2.1.2 Parallel based ensembles In this study, parallel based ensembles refer to ensemble models in which each base classifier can be trained in parallel. Parallel based ensemble schemes include bagging, re-sampling based ensembles and feature selection based ensembles. The basic framework for parallel ensemble methods is shown in  Fig. 5 , in which the dashed boxes and lines represent optional processes. Galar et al. (2012)  and  López et al. (2013)  suggested that bagging and the associated hybridizations with data preprocessing techniques have had good results compared with boosting. Through our research, it was found that parallel ensemble methods dominated two types of papers.

snippets: Neighborhood Balanced Bagging ( Błaszczyński and Stefanowski, 2015 ) incorporated the neighborhood information for generating the bagging samples for the class imbalance problems. Błaszczyński and Stefanowski (2015)  concluded that applying conventional diversification is more effective when applied at the last classification methods. Both roughly balanced Bagging and Neighborhood Balanced Bagging have not been explored in deep learning architectures. Thus, these approaches can be exploited to handle the class imbalance problems via deep ensemble models. The theoretical and experimental analysis of online bagging and boosting ( Oza, 2005 ) showed that the online bagging algorithm can achieve similar accuracy as the batch bagging algorithm with only a little more training time. However, online bagging is an option when all training samples cannot be loaded into the memory due to memory issues. Although ensembling may lead to increase in the computational complexity, but bagging possesses the property that it can be paralleled and can lead to effective reduction in the training time subject to the availability of hardware for running the parallel models. Since deep learning models have high training time, hence optimization of multiple deep models on different training bags is not a feasible option (see  Table 1 ). 4.2 Boosting Boosting technique is used in ensemble models for converting a weak learning model into a learning model with better generalization. Fig. 3  shows the diagram of the boosting technique. The techniques such as majority voting in case of classification problems or a linear combination of weak learners in the regression problems results in better prediction as compared to the single weak learner. Boosting methods like AdaBoost ( Freund and Schapire, 1996 ) and Gradient Boosting ( Friedman, 2001 ) have been used across different domains. AdaBoost uses a greedy technique for minimizing a convex surrogate function upper bounded by misclassification loss via augmentation, at each iteration, the current model with the appropriately weighted predictor. AdaBoost learns an effective ensemble classifier as it leverages the incorrectly classified sample at each stage of the learning. AdaBoost minimizes the exponential loss function while as the Gradient boosting generalized this framework to the arbitrary differential loss function. Boosting, also known as forward stagewise additive modeling, was originally proposed to improve the performance of the classification trees. It has been recently incorporated in the deep learning models to further improve their performance.

snippets: 3.5.3 Bagging, boosting and random forests Bagging, boosting and random forests are  ensemble learning algorithms . Their common property is that they generate ensembles of base classifiers and ensure their diversity by providing them with different sets of learning examples. Bagging. The term  bagging  is short for  bootstrap aggregating . Bootstrap ( Section 3.3.4 ) is a method for replication of learning examples when the learning set is small. In bagging, a series of different learning sets is generated. When the total number of learning examples is  n , each new learning set is generated by  n -times randomly (with replication) selecting an example from the original learning set. Some examples may therefore occur more than once, and some examples may not occur in a new learning set (on average, 36.8% of examples). Each newly generated learning set is used as an input to the learning algorithm. Thus we get a series of potentially different hypotheses that are used for predicting the value of a dependent variable by combining all generated hypotheses. Bagging excels especially when unstable base algorithms with high variance are used, such as decision or regression trees. Bagging is robust, as increasing the number of generated hypotheses does not lead to overfitting. Boosting. Boosting is a theoretically well-founded (see  Section 14.8.3 ) ensemble learning method. Its basic idea is to weight learning examples according to how difficult they are. It assumes that the base learning algorithm is able to deal with weighted learning examples. If this is not the case, weighted learning examples are simulated by sampling the learning set similarly as in bagging. The only difference is that the probability of selecting an example is not uniform, but proportional to its weight. Boosting requires several iterations of the learning process. In the first iteration the learning algorithm builds a hypothesis from equally weighted learning examples (each example’s weight is equal to 1). A hypothesis predicts the value of a dependent variable (the class label) for each learning example. Afterwards, all the weights are adjusted. For examples with correct predictions, weights are decreased, and for examples with incorrect predictions, weights are increased. The most frequently used approach for weighting of examples is as follows. Let  e  be the (normalized) hypothesis’ error on a particular learning example. The example’s weight is adjusted by multiplication with  e /(l − e ). Lesser errors therefore yield lesser weights.

concept: Knowledge Distillation (KD) is a method for transferring knowledge from a larger, complex teacher model to a smaller, efficient student model, enhancing the student's performance while reducing computational resources.
Progressive Distillation allows for a gradual transfer of knowledge, enabling the student model to learn simpler tasks first, which leads to better alignment and improved generalization.
Online Distillation involves simultaneous training of teacher and student models, allowing for adaptive learning and real-time knowledge transfer, which is beneficial in dynamic environments.
Self-Distillation is a variant of online distillation where a single model serves as both teacher and student, promoting efficient learning without the need for separate models.

Offline Distillation is efficient as it reduces computational burden by reusing a well-trained teacher model for multiple student models, but it lacks adaptability since the student cannot influence the teacher's learning.
Data Distillation focuses on creating high-fidelity data summaries that capture essential knowledge from datasets, optimizing model training and evaluation processes.
Feature Distillation emphasizes the transfer of internal feature representations rather than output probabilities, improving the student's performance by leveraging the teacher's learned features.

Various methodologies, such as dual KD and graph semantic guided networks, are being explored to address challenges like catastrophic forgetting and enhance specific applications like remote sensing imagery.

snippets: This method focuses on distilling discriminative information between sample pairs. 4.2 Training methodology KD involves various training methodologies to enhance the transfer of knowledge from teacher models to student models. These methodologies aim to improve the overall performance of the student model by introducing different strategies of training. Below are some key approaches within the domain of KD training methodology   . 4.2.1 Progressive distillation Progressive Distillation refers to a training methodology where knowledge is transferred in a step-by-step manner, rather than all at once. In this method, the teacher model gradually imparts knowledge to the student model by distilling progressively more complex layers   . The idea behind this approach is to let the student model handle simpler tasks first, and as its capacity improves, the more advanced knowledge from the teacher model is distilled. This helps in better alignment between the teacher and student models, leading to improved generalization and training stability, especially in scenarios where the student model is significantly smaller than the teacher   . For instance, In   , a progressive distillation method called PROD is introduced for dense retrieval tasks, applying progressive teacher and data distillation. This step-by-step approach prevents performance degradation that often occurs when a strong teacher model transfers knowledge to a smaller student model. Regularization helps avoid forgetting earlier knowledge, resulting in smaller student models outperforming larger ones. Similarly,    presents a progressive distillation framework for solving the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). Using curriculum learning, models are trained on increasingly complex instances, with smaller models teaching larger ones. This approach enhances both training efficiency and solution quality, outperforming traditional methods for large-scale TSP problems. 4.2.2 Online distillation Online Distillation is a dynamic approach where the teacher and student models are trained simultaneously, rather than pre-training the teacher model. In this methodology, both models learn in parallel, with the student continuously learning from the evolving teacher model   . This real-time distillation offers the advantage of adaptive learning, as the student model can align more closely with the teacher’s intermediate knowledge, leading to more efficient training in scenarios where data is streamed or training happens in real-time applications   . • Self-Distillation:  Self-Distillation is a specialized form of online distillation where a single model acts as both the teacher and the student.

snippets: Yu et al.    focus on incremental learning, introducing a dual KD method to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, which aligns with the incremental learning approach proposed by Xu et al.    and Xu et al.   , who use KD to enhance multimodal learning and hyperspectral image classification, respectively. Lastly, Zhou et al.    introduce a graph semantic guided network (GSGNet) for optical RS scene analysis, utilizing knowledge refinement to maintain high inference speed and contextual inference capability. Zhao et al.    propose a target detection model distillation framework that uses feature transition and label registration to improve the learning ability of lightweight networks in RS imagery, further contributing to the body of work on model distillation. 4.3.3 Data distillation Data distillation refers to techniques that aim to synthesize small, high-fidelity data summaries that capture the most important knowledge from a given dataset   . These distilled summaries are optimized to serve as effective substitutes for the original dataset in various data-usage applications such as model training, inference, and architecture search. The goal is to create a concise representation of the data that maintains its critical characteristics, allowing for faster and more efficient model training and evaluation   . Building on this concept, Zhang et al.    introduce a novel noisy label distillation method within an end-to-end teacher-student framework, which distills knowledge from labels across various noise levels. This approach exemplifies data distillation by effectively utilizing knowledge from noisy data to improve classification performance in RS image scene classification. Extending the application of data distillation, Zhao et al.    propose a pair-wise similarity KD method for RS image scene classification. By distilling discriminative information from a cumbersome model to a compact model, this study aims to maintain high accuracy while reducing model complexity, demonstrating another facet of data distillation. Furthermore, Yue et al.    contribute to this field with a self-supervised learning method that incorporates adaptive distillation for hyperspectral image classification. Their approach, which focuses on generating adaptive soft labels based on spatial–spectral similarity, underscores the importance of utilizing extensive unlabeled data in the data distillation process.
