snippets: 5.2 Sequential approaches in MER Sequential methodologies cater to MER scenarios where data is inherently sequential, such as speech and physiological signals, where understanding temporal patterns is essential for accurate emotion recognition. Sequential methodologies in MER heavily rely on RNN, LSTM, and GRU. These architectures are designed to process data over time, capturing the contextual information as it unfolds. For instance, in the realm of video-based emotion recognition, these methodologies can effectively analyze facial expressions and vocal changes over successive frames or audio samples. This ability to analyze emotional changes within a sequence makes them well-suited for capturing nuanced emotional shifts. Table 7  provides a compilation of sequential models in the field of MER spanning from 2019 to the present. These models harness the power of recurrent connections, endowed with inherent memory capabilities that facilitate context retention over time. This memory aspect enables them to detect subtle emotional changes present in sequential inputs. In the domain of audio-based emotion recognition, Yalamanchili et al.    introduced the Neural Network-based Blended Ensemble Learning (NNBEL) model. This model combines 1D-CNN, LSTM, and CapsuleNets architectures to effectively handle temporal and spatial cues in speech data. Their approach achieved an impressive accuracy of 95.3% on the RAVDESS dataset    and 94% on the IEMOCAP dataset   . Meanwhile, Chamishka et al.    proposed a novel strategy for detecting emotions in conversational audio data. They utilized Bag-of-Audio-Words (BoAW) based feature embeddings and an RNN model, enabling the capture of conversation context and individual party states for real-time emotion predictions. Their approach achieved a weighted average accuracy of 73.81% and an unweighted average accuracy of 73.32% on the IEMOCAP dataset   . Furthermore, Liu et al.    presented an approach that leverages the audio modality with a CNN featuring an Attentional Temporal Dynamic Activation (ATDA) module. This innovative approach captured both static and dynamic emotional features in speech. The model achieved accuracy rates of 75.1% on the IEMOCAP dataset and 41.7% on the MELD dataset   . Notably, the integration of LSTM and CNN models in    showcased enhanced performance compared to    specifically on the IEMOCAP dataset.

snippets: Error-Correcting Output Codes The simple methods discussed above are often very effective. Pairwise classification in particular can be a very useful technique. It has been found that it can in some cases improve accuracy even when the underlying learning algorithm, such as a decision tree learner, can deal with multiclass problems directly. This may be due to the fact that pairwise classification actually generates an ensemble of many classifiers. Ensemble learning is a well-known strategy for obtaining accurate classifiers, and we will discuss several ensemble learning methods in  Chapter 8 . It turns out that there are methods other than pairwise classification that can be used to generate an ensemble classifier by decomposing a multiclass problem into several two-class subtasks. The one we discuss next is based on error-correcting output codes. Two-class decompositions of multiclass problems can be viewed in terms of the so-called “output codes” they correspond to. Let us revisit the simple one-vs. -rest method to see what such codes look like. Consider a multiclass problem with four classes  a ,  b ,  c , and  d . The transformation can be visualized as illustrated in  Table 7.2(a) , where  yes  and  no  are mapped to 1 and 0, respectively. Each of the original class values is converted into a 4-bit code word, 1 bit per class, and the four classifiers predict the bits independently. Interpreting the classification process in terms of these code words, errors occur when the wrong binary bit receives the highest confidence. However, we do not have to use the particular code words shown. Indeed, there is no reason why each class must be represented by 4 bits. Look instead at the code of  Table 7.2(b) , where classes are represented by 7 bits. When applied to a dataset,  seven classifiers must be built instead of four. To see what that might buy, consider the classification of a particular instance. Suppose it belongs to class  a , and that the predictions of the individual classifiers are 1 0 1 1 1 1 1, respectively. Obviously, comparing this code word with those in  Table 7.2(b) , the second classifier has made a mistake: It predicted 0 instead of 1,  no  instead of  yes . Comparing the predicted bits with the code word associated with each class, the instance is clearly closer to  a  than to any other class.

snippets: With fewer than four classes it is hard to construct a really effective error-correcting code because good row separation and good column separation cannot  be achieved simultaneously. For example, with three classes there are only eight possible columns (2 3 ), four of which are complements of the other four. Moreover, columns with all zeroes or all ones provide no discrimination. This leaves just three possible columns, and the resulting code is not error correcting at all. (In fact, it is the standard “one-vs-rest” encoding.) If there are few classes, an exhaustive error-correcting code such as the one in  Table 8.2B  can be built. In an exhaustive code for  k  classes, the columns comprise every possible  k -bit string, except for complements and the trivial all-zero or all-one strings. Each code word contains 2 k– 1 –1 bits. The code is constructed as follows: the code word for the first class consists of all ones; that for the second class has 2 k– 2  zeroes followed by 2 k– 2 –1 ones; the third has 2 k– 3  zeroes followed by 2 k– 3  ones followed by 2 k– 3  zeroes followed by 2 k– 3 –1 ones; and so on. The  i th code word consists of alternating runs of 2 k–i  zeroes and ones, the last run being one short. With more classes, exhaustive codes are infeasible because the number of columns increases exponentially and too many classifiers have to be built. In that case more sophisticated methods are employed, which can build a code with good error-correcting properties from a smaller number of columns, or random codes are used. Error-correcting output codes do not work for local learning algorithms such as instance-based learners, which predict the class of an instance by looking at nearby training instances. In the case of a nearest-neighbor classifier, all output bits would be predicted using the same training instance. The problem can be circumvented by using different attribute subsets to predict each output bit, decorrelating the predictions.

snippets: The next step is segmentation, which can use the foreground (positive segmentation) or the background (negative segmentation). Segmentation results in connected components, which are often aligned with the particular elements of classification (e.g., objects). However, these components can be parts of objects or aggregates of objects depending on how well foreground and background are distinguishable and on the quality of the original images. For example, blurring can merge objects, and oversaturation can break up objects. Key-point detection is often an important next step in the image recognition problem. A common approach to image recognition currently is to use point clouds, which are, for example, produced by 3-D scanners when they are mapping the surfaces of scanned objects. In some ways, this is analogous to a Monte Carlo simulation, in which many events are accumulated and their statistics compared with a model. The point cloud is readily compared with a model of the object to be recognized. However, the key points to be detected need not be “randomly” distributed. They can instead be part of the model for the object [ Walk98 ], and as such recognition can be turned into an optimization (e.g., least-squared-error comparison) exercise. The object “recognized” is thereby the object whose model has the least squared error for the salient points. The approach just mentioned is confluent with the process of classification. For image classification, there are, not surprisingly, multiple factors to be considered. Among these are whether there are multiple images available including multiple perspectives or views on the object; whether the object has a specific, generic, or no representation in the training data; and whether a single process or multiple analytic processes should be used. Whatever the choice on these options, classification is a process that benefits from continually updated training data. The number of features that can be used for image classification is quite large, running the gamut from well gamut to saturation, chroma, intensity, texture, edges, and many other image features. An algorithm such as scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) can be used to determine the most salient features. The training data can be used to “reset” the image recognition process in several ways. First off, the new training data can be compared with the existing training data, and nonrelevant training data can be pruned (more on this topic in  Section 3.3 ).

snippets: Features also are usually considered together with other features. This may involve principal component approaches that “dissolve” features into a mixed solution, but it can also involve decision trees in which feature-based decisions are used to reach conclusions about the data. The tree branches are often based on the optimal reduction of entropy in the remaining data set. Feature-based decision trees are particularly useful for deriving classification and association rules: (a) Classification: if  j  and  k , then it belongs to Class  C . (b) Association: if  p  and  q , then it has attribute  A . For both of these, properly constructed tables allow the mapping of variables with attributes, features, categories, clusters, partitions, and classes, as appropriate. For our purposes, partitions are means of segmenting data based on  a priori  rules, while clusters are data segmentation rules learned  a posteriori . Partitions and clusters are integral to recognition, the topic of the next section. 1.7.7 Recognition Recognition is the assignment of data—usually compound data such as an image, a video, an audio clip, and a document—to a partition of the overall domain to which the data could possibly be assigned. Structured data will typically involve predefined and thus generally well-understood partitions in the data space, while unstructured data will typically require the generation of clusters. Classification is an advanced partition in which the partition is labeled and represented by categorization descriptives that allow it to be distinguished from other classes. Classes therefore provide both absolute and relative partitioning. Classes can be related to clusters, but they don’t have to be. Clusters need not be tagged and can be differentiated solely based on absolute and relative location within a domain. Thus, we can cluster solely based on a set of ranged values (multithresholding). We can follow clustering with the definition of classes, if we perform what I herein designate  attribute-based a posteriori construction  of classes (or, more simply, labeling). The example of image recognition is illustrative of a broader set of recognition approaches, and as such merits some discussion here. The first step in image recognition is often the binarization, or thresholding, step. The threshold distinguishes background (below threshold) from foreground (above threshold) and can be used more generally with any type of signal, image, or volume processing. In 1-D signal processing, for example, the DC level can be subtracted from the overall signal as a threshold.

snippets: 3 Application of machine learning in radiology 3.1 Segmentation Image segmentation is a necessary step in effective disease diagnosis and treatment in radiology imaging research. It helps clinicians to understand structural information and spatial anatomic relationships, however, it depends on the experience of clinicians and is very time-consuming [ 24 ]. Automatic classification methods are essential for improving diagnosis analysis and for the reproducibility of large-scale clinical studies. Table 2  summarizes segmentation applications with various machine learning techniques. 3.1.1 Brain segmentation Tree based methods are hot topics currently being investigated in the brain segmentation field. For example, Yoo et al. segmented multiple sclerosis lesions in multi-3D MR images from unsupervised features [ 88 ]. Features were extracted from T2-weighted and proton density MR images using a deep belief network, and a random forest was built for the final supervised classification. In order to improve the model performance from noisy training data and robustness against overfitting, Maier et al. proposed an extra tree forest to locate, segment and quantify sub-acute ischemic stroke lesions [ 89 ]. They used voxel-wise local features such as intensity, weighted local mean, local histogram and 2D center distance. However, their method can only deal with the T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted data sequences and high-quality images. Multimodal data from the same patient can provide extra useful information for diagnosis. Therefore, Mitra et al. proposed to use features from multimodal data to segment ischemic lesions, white matter and other secondary lesions. In their study, algorithms combined expectation maximization likelihood estimation and Bayesian-Markov random field to segment the probable lesion areas from FLAIR data then applied random forest on the multimodal data [ 90 ]. Neural networks and deep learning techniques are powerful tools in brain segmentation tasks. Si et al. proposed a semi-automatic method to classify the pixels of brain MRI into lesioned and healthy tissues by use of an artificial neural network with gray levels and statistical features as inputs [ 91 ]. The segmentation of early-brain tissues is more difficult than that of adult brains due to the lower tissue contrast [ 92 ], while multiple image modalities contain complementary information for insufficient tissue contrast [ 93 ].

snippets: In the DBSCAN algorithm, the data points can be identified as core points, boundary points, and noise points. For identification, two parameters are used: epsilon ( E p s ) and minimum points ( M i n P t s ). If a circle is drawn around a data point  p  with radius  E p s  and the circle encloses at least a  M i n P t s  number of data points, then it is called a core point. Otherwise, if  p  is enclosed in the circle of any other core point  q , then it is called a boundary point, else called a noise point. The idea is such that, all neighbor core points are kept in the same cluster along with their boundary points. Noise points are not included in any cluster. In this way, the clusters are formed based on density. In   , the authors proposed a modified version of the DBSCAN algorithm to cluster similar types of fingerprints, to find out related APs. K-means clustering:. k-means clustering is a common method to group instances from datasets into clusters. From a given dataset, initially,  k  random data points are selected and kept in separate  k  clusters. The data point in each cluster represents the centroid or mean value for that particular cluster   . Then, from the left-out data points, one is selected at a time and the distance from the mean value of each cluster is computed and the data point is kept in the closest cluster. In localization, received values from sensors are the data points and at the end, they are kept in  k  clusters. The training dataset values are labeled to their own cluster indicating a location, and each and every test data received from the sensor are checked for its closest cluster. However, parameter tuning, i.e. finding the optimal value of  k  is challenging. In   , researchers have used k-means clustering for IO detection on two types of datasets. At first, training and evaluation are done on an extracted portion of dataset (EPD) that achieves good accuracy, then training is done on EPD and for evaluation crowdsourced large data is used and degradation of performance is observed. Hierarchical clustering:. In the hierarchical clustering method, the data points of a dataset are grouped into clusters such that the clusters can be represented by a tree structure called a dendrogram   .

snippets: It is not as simple as getting a code that works and performs some tests; on the contrary, it is necessary to take great care of the experimental conditions to ensure that the obtained results are real. This is why we have devoted a major part of this article to the design of the experiment using machine learning techniques ( Hastie et al., 2009 ). From this point on, the most recent and most used techniques will be presented. The best results usually offered in the context of biomedical informatics and the state of the art in machine learning are The Support Vector Machines (SVMs), the large-scale Artificial Neural Networks (Deep Learning), the Random Forest or several different integration techniques; those techniques are increasing their relevance since the emergence of the -omics. Aforementioned techniques in particular are used in many different problems in biomedical informatics, ranging from medical image processing, clinical data analysis, exploitation of gene expression data or proteomics, etc. Support Vector Machines The SVMs are usually employed for classification problems, although there are variants available for regression and estimation tasks ( Burges, 1998 ). These algorithms are learning systems based on the studies of Vapnik in the Statistical Learning Theory field ( Vapnik, 1995; Chapelle and Vapnik, n.d.; Gunn, 1998 ). Initially the SVMs were developed to solve binary problems, where an input sample could be tagged with two possible values (true/false), but the algorithms evolved to allow multiclass classification. The SVM tries to find a linear optimal hyperplane which allows to make a distribution of the training data in two or more classes ( Cristianini and Shawe-Taylor, 2000 ). Thus, the samples belonging to the same class will be located in the same space limited by the hyperplane. Of course, in most problems there will be more than a hyperplane that allow us to make a separation of the samples. But only one of these will be the optimal hyperplane, that is, the hyperplane that maximizes the margin over all possible hyperplanes and the closest to the input samples. Based on the Vapnik studies, this hyperplane could be defined in terms of certain data from the training set called “support vectors,” that are those samples of each class closest to the hyperplane with maximum margin. However, in most of the real problems, a linear separation of the samples is not a valid approach because the examples are not linearly separable.

snippets: IMR is a crucial process in BIA that involves aligning multiple images for comparison and analysis. In BIA, several images of an identical individual are frequently acquired at various instances or utilizing various imaging modalities. IMR algorithms use various techniques such as feature detection and optimization to align images and enable accurate comparison. Image segmentation is another important technique used in BIA. Segmentation entails splitting an image into multiple section or segments to enable analysis and measurement. This technique has been utilized in multiple conditions, such as identifying tumors, measuring organ volumes, and quantifying tissue characteristics   . Image fusion involves combining multiple images of the same patient or tissue to create a composite image with improved resolution, contrast, or other characteristics. Image fusion algorithms use various techniques such as wavelet transforms and fuzzy logic to merge images and create a more detailed and informative representation. Image visualization is an essential part of BIA, as it enables healthcare professionals to interpret and communicate findings to patients and other stakeholders. Visualization techniques such as volume rendering and surface rendering are used to create three-dimensional representations of medical images, which can be used to visualize complex structures and abnormalities   . All these techniques empower professionals to diagnose quickly and precisely and improve patient outcomes by enabling earlier detection and treatment of diseases. With continued technological advancements, we can anticipate further breakthroughs to see further innovations in this field that will continue to drive progress in MI and analysis. 2.3.6 Intelligent machine learning techniques ML has become an increasingly important tool in BI, with applications ranging from image segmentation, registration, and classification to personalized medicine and drug discovery. ML has the potential to revolutionize BI, enabling more accurate diagnosis, more personalized treatment, and more efficient drug discovery. Some intelligent ML techniques used in BIA are given below. 2.3.7 Support vector machines Support vector machine (SVM) is a popular ML technique in BIA for classification and regression tasks. SVM operates by identifying an optimal hyperplane that separates input data into different classes or predicts continuous output variables   . In SVM, data are transformed into a higher-dimensional space, and the optimal hyperplane is determined by maximizing the margin between the closest data points of different classes. The goal of the SVM algorithm is to find the hyperplane that achieves maximum margin separation and minimizes classification error    ( Fig. 2.6 ). SVM offers several advantages in BIA.

Of course, in most problems there will be more than a hyperplane that allow us to make a separation of the samples.

snippets: Machine Classifiers In the context of machine learning, manifold learning mapping methods are preliminary feature extraction steps, after which pattern recognition and classifier algorithms are applied. Machine classifiers seek to identify to which of a set of categories (classes or subpopulations) a new observation belongs, on the basis of a training set. The training data set contains observations whose category (class) membership is known. The training set contains ‘ground truth’ as it is understood in the context of a given problem. The classifier seeks to predict the class of an unknown data set based on  known  properties that have been learned from the training data. Cellular images are large, complex, and dense sets of data. The complexity of cellular imaging is not only because of the high level of resolution but also because of the multiplicity of scales that are needed to represent a biological or pathological process. One of the challenges in approaching cellular imaging data is to choose classifier(s) that has the ability to deal with this complexity of data. The choice of classifier really has to do with a clear understanding of the image problem that is being approached. Some classifier algorithms are well suited for rapidly finding image similarities while others are better used for approaching the problem of predicting clinical or biological outcomes from image data. Machine classifier algorithms can be grouped into categories of algorithms supporting  supervised learning  versus those supporting  unsupervised  learning. In unsupervised learning, one deals with the problem of finding pertinent information from unlabeled data. Examples of unsupervised learning machine classifiers include artificial neural network, data clustering, expectation–maximization algorithm, self-organizing maps, radial basis function networks, generative topographic maps, and vector quantization. A supervised classifier algorithm, on the other hand, learns a task by inferring a function from training data. The training data have their objects labeled by an ‘expert’ as to class. A function predicting class assignment is generated from the training data and it is then generalized to other previously unseen data sets. There are over 20 supervised classifier algorithms and many more variations. Some common supervised classifiers are Bayesian networks, decision trees, gene expression programming, support vector machines, random forests, and ensembles of classifiers such as bootstrap aggregating (bagging) and boosting (meta-algorithm). Multiclassifier ensembles are powerful approaches to complex cellular imaging data such as that which resides in histopathology.

snippets: 5.2 Pattern recognition and machine learning algorithms Machine learning techniques are widely employed in a variety of disciplines for pattern identification and classification problems. Here are a few examples of machine learning algorithms used for pattern detection and classification: Support vector machines: SVM is a sophisticated binary classification technique. It selects the best hyperplane for separating data points of distinct classes with the greatest margin. Using kernel functions, SVM can handle both linear and nonlinear classification problems. Decision trees: Decision trees generate a hierarchical structure by recursively partitioning the feature space depending on feature values. They make judgements by traversing the routes that connect the root node to the nodes in the leaves, which indicate class labels. Decision trees may perform both regression and classification tasks and are interpretable. Random forests: Random forests of data are collective learning approaches that produce predictions by combining several decision trees. Each tree is trained on a randomly selected sample of the data, and the final prediction is made by majority vote or by aggregating the forecasts of multiple trees. Randomised forests are resistant to overfitting and can deal with data that is extremely dimensional. k-Nearest neighbours (k-NN): k-NN classifies data points in the feature space based on the class labels of those closest to them. It assigns a class label to a newly acquired point based on its k-nearest neighbours’ labels. k-NN is a basic and easy-to-use technique for multiclass classification jobs. Naive Bayes: A probabilistic method that implements Bayes’ theorem with an understanding of feature-independent. Given the feature values, it computes the likelihood of each class label and assigns the data point to the class with the greatest probability of occurring. Naive Bayes is a highly computationally effective method for dealing with data with high dimensions. Neural networks: In recent years, neural networks, particularly deep learning models, have received a lot of attention. They are made up of several layers of linked neurons that develop structures of representation from data. CNNs excel in the classification of images, but recurrent neural networks (RNNs) excel at sequence data. Deep learning models need a large quantity of labelled training data as well as computing resources   . Gradient boosting machines (GBM): GBM is an ensemble learning approach that sequentially combines poor students, often decision trees. It teaches each poor student to rectify the mistakes of the preceding ones, increasing total prediction accuracy.

snippets: 2 Machine learning in radiology In recent years, machine learning algorithms have become useful tools for the analysis of medical images in many radiology applications [ 15 , 23 ]. For example, machine learning algorithms can extract the useful information found within the details of medical images [ 24 ]. Thus, computer-aided systems based on machine learning help radiologists to make informed decisions while interpreting these images [ 15 ]. 2.1 Types of learning Depending on the utilization of labels in training data, there are three categories of machine learning algorithms: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and semi-supervised learning. Supervised-learning is the most common form in machine learning, and researchers widely use supervised-learning for classification and regression [ 26 ]. Data is usually collected and labeled in categories, as the purpose of supervised learning is to find an appropriate input-output function from training data, which generalizes well against the testing data. We can compute an objective function to measure the error between the desired pattern and the output score. In general, many scientific contributions focus on finding a suitable objective function with adjustable parameters. Contrariwise, in cases where labeled data sets are relatively rare or difficult to acquire, unsupervised learning can derive deductions from data without corresponding label information; the purpose of unsupervised learning is to discover the hidden structure or distribution of data [ 27 ]. Unsupervised learning approaches include clustering and blind signal separation techniques such as principal component analysis and independent component analysis. Lastly, semi-supervised learning lie between supervised learning and unsupervised-learning [ 28 , 29 ]. During the training phase, semi-supervised learning begins with a small set of labeled data and augments the training data size by gradually labeling unlabeled data. 2.2 Feature selection Feature extraction and representation is a crucial step in medical image processing. With the development of modern medical techniques, higher resolution and more features have become obtainable to feed the classifiers; however, this is an obstacle for machine learning techniques in achieving an optimal solution using high dimensional features. Significant interest exists in extracting and identifying reliable features from radiological images to improve classification performance [ 30 , 31 ]. Several methods exist for extraction of features from medical images including region-based, shape-based, texture-based, and bag-of-words features [ 32–38 ]. The performance of most image retrieval systems is dependent on the use of these features.

snippets: 3.1.1 Supervised learning There is extensive literature that leverages the combinations of the characteristics described earlier to train a supervised sentiment classification model [ 49 ]. In this research area we can roughly distinguish between the state of the art in two main fields (ie, baseline and ensemble models). Concerning the baseline models, several contributions have been provided in the last decade. Among the most recent approaches are those in [ 50–55 ]. Dhande and Patnaik [ 50 ] proposed a supervised machine learning approach that is able to combine naïve Bayes and neural network classifiers for sentiment categorization. In their investigation, they tried to overcome the attribute independence assumption underlying the naïve Bayes classifier by using a neural network to explicitly represent the dependencies among attributes (ie, words). The resulting naïve Bayes neural classifiers have been shown to be able to achieve promising accuracy with use of a simple unigram representation of user messages. Chikersal et al. [ 51 ] combine two main baseline approaches. The first one is a rule-based classifier that takes a decision about positive, negative, or unknown sentiment, using rules that are dependent on the occurrences of emoticons and opinion words in tweets (ie, lexicons). The second one, based on support vector machines, is trained on semantic, dependency, and sentiment lexicons to identify positive, negative, and neutral messages. The predictions provided by the two baseline approaches are subsequently combined to refine the support vector machine predictions. A further supervised approach based on sentiment lexicon construction was presented in [ 55 ]. The main goal is to deal with the problem of unavailability of labeled data by use of SentiWordNet [ 56 ]. The proposed framework, SWIMS (for “semisupervised subjective feature weighting and intelligent model selection”), starts by acquiring SentiWordNet as a labeled corpus to extract adjectives, verbs, adverbs, and nouns that are subjective. Then a new feature-weighting mechanism—based on the pointwise mutual information [ 57 ]—is used to finally train a supervised support vector machine for sentiment classification. Even though the traditional supervised learning approaches have addressed several sentiment analysis tasks, most of the recent literature is moving toward a different perspective of the problem. In particular, the current research direction is related to the definition of novel representation spaces, by means of word embeddings [ 58 ], for subsequent training of traditional learning models [ 52–54 ].

snippets: 5 Risk management Risk management of financial and non-financial companies refers to the evaluation, often in real time, of realistic data concerning the institution’s exposure to a certain source of risk and it is further concerned with statistics on trends that will influence that exposure in the future. While quantitative data is relevant and necessary for this, it must be complemented by qualitative information for informed decision-making, both in financial as well as non-financial institutions   . Risk management is addressed in terms of optimisation through metaheuristics for credit risk assessment and the resulting bankruptcy prediction. García et al.    provide a detailed review of developed systems and, to a less obvious extent, applications to the optimisation of trading rules in the financial markets. As depicted previously for portfolio management,  Table 5  presents the metaheuristic methodologies applied to the different subproblems of risk management. As before, the numbers inside each cell refer to the number of articles reviewed for each topic and methodology. From  Table 5 , several conclusions can be drawn. Firstly, GA are the preferred metaheuristics in risk management as well. Their popularity is expressed through the use in every single reviewed problem. Furthermore, PSO has also received widespread attention. Contrary to that, more exotic algorithms, such as harmony search, firefly algorithms, or bat algorithms were employed to a lesser extent. Secondly, it can be seen that bankruptcy prediction –as an advancement of credit risk analysis–, as well as optimisation of trading systems for foreign exchange (Forex) markets –as an advancement of optimisation in stock trading–, have received less attention in the literature and have been approached with fewer methodologies. They thus represent interesting future research lines. Thirdly, it becomes evident that hybridisation among metaheuristics or other optimisation methods is far more prevailing in risk management optimisation than in portfolio optimisation. Lastly, it is evident that relatively recently developed metaheuristics, such as IWO and honeybees mating optimisation (HBMO), have not been applied as comprehensively as well-established ones. 5.1 Credit risk assessment and optimisation Credit risk assessment is one of the most researched and recognised topics in the banking industry. VoxelMorph and PC-SwinMorph represent innovative approaches to medical image registration, with PC-SwinMorph achieving even higher Dice scores (0.812 for registration and 0.817 for segmentation) through a patch-based unsupervised learning method, indicating a trend towards more sophisticated and effective registration techniques.

Non-contextual methods for Re-ID are gaining traction, with a focus on passive techniques that rely on visual descriptors without learning-based approaches. This suggests a shift towards simpler, yet effective, methods in person re-identification tasks.

Medical image fusion techniques are diverse, ranging from pixel fusion methods to subspace and multi-scale methods. Each has its strengths and limitations, emphasizing the need for careful selection based on the specific requirements of the imaging task.

The integration of machine learning in radiology, particularly in segmentation, is crucial for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Techniques like tree-based methods and neural networks are proving effective in segmenting complex medical images, showcasing the potential of AI in healthcare.

The future of healthcare is leaning towards the fusion of multi-source data, including imaging and non-imaging data, to improve clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. This underscores the importance of developing connected systems that leverage deep learning for comprehensive data analysis.

The proposed ViT-V-Net network achieved a Dice score of 0.726 ± 0.130, which makes it superior to other state-of-the-art image registration methods. Deformable registration is an essential task in medical image analysis and has been a recent subject of interest to researchers. VoxelMorph is a medical image registration model proposed in [ 131 ]. The proposed framework formulates registration as a function based on CNN to map an input image pair to a deformation field that aligns these images. The training strategy is in two folds. The first part is an unsupervised setting that uses image intensities to maximize appearance matching based on the objective functions selected for the model. The second setting performs image segmentation on an auxiliary dataset. Fig. 7  is a depiction of moving images, fixed images, and warped images (columns 1–3). The resulting deformation field is in columns 4 and 5. The authors concluded that anatomical segmentations improve the registration performance with VoxelMorph in terms of Dice score while providing smooth deformations. The authors in [ 132 ] proposed a framework called Patch Contrastive Strategy with Shifted- window multi-head self-attention (PC-SwinMorph) for medical image registration and segmentation. The approach is a patch-based un-supervised learning method with a contrastive strategy that produces comprehensive orientation and richer feature representation. PC-SwinMorph, in its operation, makes non-overlap patches from input data [ 133 , 134 ] and is later fed into two weight-shared CNN encoders to generate patch representations. The 3D W-MSA and a 3D SW-MSA module are employed to refine and stitch the deformation field patches to obtain the entire deformation field. The proposed PC-SwinMorph achieves registration and segmentation Dice coefficient scores of 0.812 and 0.817, respectively. Fig. 8  is a visual representation of PC-SwinMorph and other state-of-the-art models. The rows show the three views from 3D volumes. The second column displays the ground truth (GT) results, while columns 3–6 display predicted segmentation from PC-SwinMorph and other unsupervised techniques.

snippets: With large camera networks, calibration of all cameras is not feasible. 4.2 Non-contextual methods Several approaches have been proposed that rely entirely on the analysis of visual descriptors and no external contextual information is incorporated to assist the correspondence process. These methods can be further classified as active and passive methods. Most of the recent research is focused on non-contextual methods. A popular classification within this class is based on whether single image ( single-shot ) or multiple images ( multi-shot ) are used to generate and compare the appearance descriptors. There are many different non-contextual techniques for Re-ID and in order to provide an overview of some of the more prominent approaches, a tabular summary is presented in  Table 1 . The approaches are distinguished based on the type of features used, single/multi-shot incorporation and the incorporation of false match rejection (novelty detection) in the matching framework. 4.2.1 Passive methods These methods deal with design of descriptive visual descriptors to characterize the person's appearance and compare these by computing similarity measures to achieve Re-ID. These methods are termed as passive as they do not rely on learning techniques, supervised or unsupervised, for descriptor extraction and matching. A color and shape features based appearance model from the detected blob is proposed in   . The blob is segmented into multiple polar bins and the color Gaussian model and edge pixels counts from each bin form the descriptor. A match is established using three similarity measures and the optimal match is the one that maximizes all the similarity measures. A spatiotemporal segmentation algorithm based on watershed segmentation and graph partitioning is used in    to detect stable spatiotemporal edges called edgels. The appearance of a person is a combination of color (hue and saturation) and edgel histograms and the intersection histogram is used to establish a match between observations. A non-surveillance application of person Re-ID was explored in   , where the objective was to find all occurrences of person in a sequence of photographs taken over a short period of time. A two step approach is adopted, where the first step, identifies different people that exists in the photographs by clustering frontal face detections. The clustering is based on 16-bin RGB histograms extracted from clothing.

snippets: 4 Medical image fusion As described in Section  2 , image fusion is the process that aims to produce a more representative image through merging the input images with each other. Various methods were proposed to perform the required fusion goal. Fig. 8  illustrates major classes of such methods while the upcoming subsections present a brief overview of each one. 4.1 Pixel fusion methods In these methods, simple pixel-by-pixel operations are used to perform the fusion task. These operations include simple arithmetic operators, such as addition, subtraction, division and multiplication as well as a minimum, maximum, median, and rank   . In addition, it includes sophisticated operators, such as the Markov Random Field (MRF) considered as a probabilistic model in which the local conditional probabilities are used to define such model. Li    introduced a detailed mathematical description of applying MRF in image analysis. Although this class of fusion methods is simple, it often faces certain limitations including contrast reduction of the image. Despite their limitations, these methods provide good results in some cases, such as whenever the input images have an overall high brightness and contrast   . 4.2 Subspace methods These methods are a collection of statistical techniques that remove the correlation between the input images. On other words, a high-dimensional input image is projected onto a lower dimensional space or subspace for the following reasons   : • Visualization: the reduction of the images’ dimensions helps in understanding the intrinsic structure of the input data. • Generalization: projecting the images in the lower dimensions allows for better generalization. • Computation: dealing with images in lower-dimensional spaces is faster and requires less memory than dealing with them in higher-dimensional spaces. • Model: representing the data in the lower dimensions can be used as a model in its right. Principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) are examples of the well-known subspace methods   . 4.3 Multi-scale methods Multi-scale also known as Multi-Resolution Analysis (MRA) of images consists of a collection of techniques that transform each input image  I ( k )  so that it can be represented in a multi-scale manner  y 0 ( k ) , y 1 ( k ) , … , y L ( k ) .

snippets: 3 Application of machine learning in radiology 3.1 Segmentation Image segmentation is a necessary step in effective disease diagnosis and treatment in radiology imaging research. It helps clinicians to understand structural information and spatial anatomic relationships, however, it depends on the experience of clinicians and is very time-consuming [ 24 ]. Automatic classification methods are essential for improving diagnosis analysis and for the reproducibility of large-scale clinical studies. Table 2  summarizes segmentation applications with various machine learning techniques. 3.1.1 Brain segmentation Tree based methods are hot topics currently being investigated in the brain segmentation field. For example, Yoo et al. segmented multiple sclerosis lesions in multi-3D MR images from unsupervised features [ 88 ]. Features were extracted from T2-weighted and proton density MR images using a deep belief network, and a random forest was built for the final supervised classification. In order to improve the model performance from noisy training data and robustness against overfitting, Maier et al. proposed an extra tree forest to locate, segment and quantify sub-acute ischemic stroke lesions [ 89 ]. They used voxel-wise local features such as intensity, weighted local mean, local histogram and 2D center distance. However, their method can only deal with the T1-weighted and diffusion-weighted data sequences and high-quality images. Multimodal data from the same patient can provide extra useful information for diagnosis. Therefore, Mitra et al. proposed to use features from multimodal data to segment ischemic lesions, white matter and other secondary lesions. In their study, algorithms combined expectation maximization likelihood estimation and Bayesian-Markov random field to segment the probable lesion areas from FLAIR data then applied random forest on the multimodal data [ 90 ]. Neural networks and deep learning techniques are powerful tools in brain segmentation tasks. Si et al. proposed a semi-automatic method to classify the pixels of brain MRI into lesioned and healthy tissues by use of an artificial neural network with gray levels and statistical features as inputs [ 91 ]. The segmentation of early-brain tissues is more difficult than that of adult brains due to the lower tissue contrast [ 92 ], while multiple image modalities contain complementary information for insufficient tissue contrast [ 93 ].

snippets: 3.2 Background, definitions, and notations The application of AI, particularly deep learning algorithms, is rapidly expanding and shows great potential to revolutionize healthcare. They are playing a significant role in the development of smart clinical decision support systems for disease diagnosis, prediction, prognosis, health management, and drug research and development. The development of computer-aided diagnostics (CAD) systems is crucial to support clinicians with a second diagnostic opinion for more accurate, fast, precise, and personalized care compared to the subjectivity and time-intensive procedures of manual diagnosis and handcrafted features. Significant research progress has been made in developing deep learning-based systems;  however, more focus has been placed on the development of CAD systems that are based on image data, including X-ray images, MRIs, CT scans, and ultrasound images, for image classification, segmentation, disease detection, and prediction tasks. The existing deep learning models consider pixel value information without data informing about the clinical context. Yet in practice, the healthcare community is now made up of multiple heterogeneous data sources and types, including contextual data from EHRs, structured laboratory data, imaging pixel data, unstructured narrative data, and sometimes temporal data. The sources of image pixel data are also increasing from emerging potentially medical imaging modalities like terahertz (THz), infrared, and microwave-based imaging techniques. Next-generation healthcare relies on synthesis of information and should improve clinical decision making, diagnostic accuracy, and patient outcomes through seamless fusion of imaging and nonimaging data for personalized care. Thus, the application of deep learning for processing and fusion of  multisource medical information will enable the development of connected and smart systems for next-generation healthcare systems. It is also significant to point out that the terms multisource and multimodal are used interchangeably to denote heterogeneous data/information acquired from heterogeneous sources or modalities. Also, the terms classification and prediction have been used to denote the deep learning-based processing tasks for classification and prediction. 3.2.1 Data fusion Data fusion is fostered by information theory and it is a methodology whereby disparate data sources or types are merged for creating an information state based on the complementarity of the data sources   .

snippets: The next step is segmentation, which can use the foreground (positive segmentation) or the background (negative segmentation). Segmentation results in connected components, which are often aligned with the particular elements of classification (e.g., objects). However, these components can be parts of objects or aggregates of objects depending on how well foreground and background are distinguishable and on the quality of the original images. For example, blurring can merge objects, and oversaturation can break up objects. Key-point detection is often an important next step in the image recognition problem. A common approach to image recognition currently is to use point clouds, which are, for example, produced by 3-D scanners when they are mapping the surfaces of scanned objects. In some ways, this is analogous to a Monte Carlo simulation, in which many events are accumulated and their statistics compared with a model. The point cloud is readily compared with a model of the object to be recognized. However, the key points to be detected need not be “randomly” distributed. They can instead be part of the model for the object [ Walk98 ], and as such recognition can be turned into an optimization (e.g., least-squared-error comparison) exercise. The object “recognized” is thereby the object whose model has the least squared error for the salient points. The approach just mentioned is confluent with the process of classification. For image classification, there are, not surprisingly, multiple factors to be considered. Among these are whether there are multiple images available including multiple perspectives or views on the object; whether the object has a specific, generic, or no representation in the training data; and whether a single process or multiple analytic processes should be used. Whatever the choice on these options, classification is a process that benefits from continually updated training data. The number of features that can be used for image classification is quite large, running the gamut from well gamut to saturation, chroma, intensity, texture, edges, and many other image features. An algorithm such as scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) can be used to determine the most salient features. The training data can be used to “reset” the image recognition process in several ways. First off, the new training data can be compared with the existing training data, and nonrelevant training data can be pruned (more on this topic in  Section 3.3 ).

snippets: IMR is a crucial process in BIA that involves aligning multiple images for comparison and analysis. In BIA, several images of an identical individual are frequently acquired at various instances or utilizing various imaging modalities. IMR algorithms use various techniques such as feature detection and optimization to align images and enable accurate comparison. Image segmentation is another important technique used in BIA. Segmentation entails splitting an image into multiple section or segments to enable analysis and measurement. This technique has been utilized in multiple conditions, such as identifying tumors, measuring organ volumes, and quantifying tissue characteristics   . Image fusion involves combining multiple images of the same patient or tissue to create a composite image with improved resolution, contrast, or other characteristics. Image fusion algorithms use various techniques such as wavelet transforms and fuzzy logic to merge images and create a more detailed and informative representation. Image visualization is an essential part of BIA, as it enables healthcare professionals to interpret and communicate findings to patients and other stakeholders. Visualization techniques such as volume rendering and surface rendering are used to create three-dimensional representations of medical images, which can be used to visualize complex structures and abnormalities   . All these techniques empower professionals to diagnose quickly and precisely and improve patient outcomes by enabling earlier detection and treatment of diseases. With continued technological advancements, we can anticipate further breakthroughs to see further innovations in this field that will continue to drive progress in MI and analysis. 2.3.6 Intelligent machine learning techniques ML has become an increasingly important tool in BI, with applications ranging from image segmentation, registration, and classification to personalized medicine and drug discovery. ML has the potential to revolutionize BI, enabling more accurate diagnosis, more personalized treatment, and more efficient drug discovery. Some intelligent ML techniques used in BIA are given below. 2.3.7 Support vector machines Support vector machine (SVM) is a popular ML technique in BIA for classification and regression tasks. SVM operates by identifying an optimal hyperplane that separates input data into different classes or predicts continuous output variables   . In SVM, data are transformed into a higher-dimensional space, and the optimal hyperplane is determined by maximizing the margin between the closest data points of different classes. The goal of the SVM algorithm is to find the hyperplane that achieves maximum margin separation and minimizes classification error    ( Fig. 2.6 ). SVM offers several advantages in BIA.

snippets: 5 Sentiment analysis 5.1 Sentiment analysis: Task description Sentiment Analysis, a pivotal field at the intersection of linguistics and computer science, involves the computational examination of textual data to discern and categorize the expressed sentiments. Analyze sentiment involves evaluating the emotional tone of a piece of text, that in the context of Information Disorder means identify content that may be deliberately crafted to evoke strong emotions, potentially leading to the spread of misinformation or manipulation. This task has grown remarkably recently, with several surveys analyzing the proposed approaches  [93–95] . Applications of sentiment analysis can be found in a variety of areas, the best known being social media  [96–98] , customer reviews   , and health care   . Beyond applications, several surveys were also conducted on more structural concepts such as aspect-based sentiment analysis  [103–105] , sequential transfer learning    and cross-lingual aspect   . Various initiatives have been put in place to obtain new methodologies to achieve greater accuracy and especially to contextualize the platform, language and all aspects that may be needed. In support of this, the various international competitions should be mentioned  [108–110] . 5.2 Sentiment analysis: Existing approaches The sentiment analysis classifiers can be classified into three categories: machine learning, deep learning, and ensemble learning. Machine learning classifiers, which encompass logistic regression, naive Bayes, and support vector machine, leverage mathematical models to make predictions about sentiment. On the other hand, deep learning classifiers, such as recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory (LSTM) models, employ artificial neural networks to generate forecasts about sentiment. Ensemble learning techniques combine multiple classifiers to enhance the performance of sentiment analysis. Focusing on the Machine Learning category, Alzyout et al.    conducted sentiment analysis about violence against women using various machine learning models. Their research demonstrated that SVM achieved the highest accuracy. In   , the authors aimed to develop a sentiment analyzer capable of classifying text polarity using five different classifiers and found that Naive Bayes performed the best. Numerous studies have been undertaken on deep learning   . In   , the authors utilized an MLP to conduct sentiment analysis on COVID-19-related Tweets.

snippets: 3.2 Literature survey This section discusses advancements of DSA by researchers in this field. The evolution of DSA is examined in relation to diverse types of sentiment analysis and framing survey queries (SQs) for systematic literature reviews. 3.2.1 Types of sentiment analysis Researchers have studied sentiment analysis over the years. Apart from traditional sentiment analysis, various modified versions are being explored. Some of these are as mentioned here: 3.2.1.1 Multi-aspect sentiment analysis It is among the emerging fields of sentiment analysis. It makes an attempt to analyze a variety of presumably related aspects that are usually discussed in a single review   . 3.2.1.2 Multiclass sentiment analysis Sentiment analysis and opinion mining for social media networking are the currently emerging research topics. The majority of research studies on automatic sentiment classification of text data gathered from microblogging websites and social media networks are directed to either be classified as binary (positive or negative) or ternary (positive, negative, or neutral). A revolutionary technique called multiclass sentiment analysis performs text categorization into several sentiment classes, rather than binary and ternary classification   . 3.2.1.3 Multidimensional sentiment analysis The two basic techniques for describing affect states are (1) categorical approach and (2) dimensional approach. The first depicts affect states using distinct binary classifications such as positive and negative. The second approach, in comparison to the category approach, portrays affective process states by using a continuous numerical value. VA space is largely explored in DSA. The valence shows the level of positive and negative sentiment, and the arousal reveals the level of calmness and excitement.  . 3.2.1.4 Multidomain sentiment analysis The task of sentiment analysis for multiple domains determines the polarity of any text/document by utilizing domain-specific characteristics. One of the primary issues, in this case, is determining the polarity of text data belonging to domains other than those utilized to create the opinion model   . 3.2.1.5 Multi-lingual sentiment analysis Most modern sentiment analysis techniques are confined to only English language. However, as the Internet spreads around the world, individuals are leaving comments in a diverse range of languages, mainly in regional languages. Sentiment analysis, particularly for a language, raises the possibility of ignoring valuable textual information written in plenty of other languages. These approaches have been designed to assess data in multiple languages   .

snippets: These hybrid models contribute to more accurate and stable forecasts, proving significant for investors and researchers in the field of financial markets. 4.3.8 Final analise Furthermore, it is possible to observe that most works rely on Deep Learning models, such as LSTM, CNN, GRU, and RNN. Regarding Machine Learning models, the main ones include MLP, Decision Tree, and SVM, while ARIMA and GARCH represent regression models. In the field of optimization, PSO and GA are the predominant approaches. Finally, among the decomposition models, EMD, EEMD, and CEEMDAN approaches stand out. The approach “Complete”, aims for the integration of time series decomposition, optimization, and machine learning models. It is acknowledged that this approach yields good results, but it is noteworthy for the increased computational cost, compromising its efficiency in online problem-solving. The second classification addresses “Decomposition”, demonstrating the operation of time series decomposition with machine learning approaches. This results in improved accuracy compared to a single model. However, sensitivity to outliers and the inability to capture seasonal patterns in financial data affect the decomposition task. The third classification is “Ensemble Learning”, where different models are used heterogeneously. There is a different perception of the algorithm regarding the problem, increasing the solution’s robustness and reducing overfitting. However, there are challenges, such as the increase in the number of base models, requiring proper hyperparameter tuning, which escalates the need for computational power and the difficulty in interpreting the models. Another approach involves the use of ensemble learning techniques in a homogeneous format, initially increasing accuracy and robustness, similar to the heterogeneous format. However, common errors are present as they share the same architecture, resulting in a decrease in robustness benefits for this type of problem-solving solution. The fourth classification is ‘Fuzzy’ which provides an appropriate treatment for noise in the financial time series (FTS). It allows for modeling smooth transitions between different states, useful for capturing long-term trends and patterns in financial markets. Additionally, it enables the accommodation of temporal variability, modeling temporal variations and present seasonality. However, in the case of abrupt changes in the environment, using Fuzzy theory to capture these modifications becomes challenging. This is due to its computationally intensive nature, stemming from the complexity involved in its modeling to handle financial data.

snippets: The study compares different forecasting models, encompassing statistical, machine learning, and deep learning techniques. Models such as ARIMA, hybrid ETS-ANN, and kNN are evaluated using daily financial market indices and price data. While predicting financial market fluctuations is challenging, with overall accuracy levels generally low, ARIMA and the hybrid ETS-ANN model perform better over longer periods, with both models demonstrating strong performance in most other sub-periods. Despite its moderate accuracy, the hybrid ETS-ANN model stands out as the most promising approach for financial time series forecasting, providing valuable insights for investment decisions   . In another study, a novel hybrid prediction method, the AR-ARCH-ANN model, is proposed to handle nonlinear and volatile real-world time series, especially those with heteroskedastic properties. This recurrent model incorporates conditional autoregressive heteroskedasticity and utilizes particle swarm optimization to train neural networks, increasing the likelihood of avoiding local minima traps   . Finally, the research by    aims to predict the performance of stock market indices using various machine learning techniques such as MLP, RNN, and ARIMA. The study compares these models with hybrid approaches, namely ARIMA-MLP and ARIMA-RNN, and analyzes their performance based on historical stock exchange data. Hybrid models like ARIMA-MLP and ARIMA-RNN demonstrate higher accuracy compared to single models, highlighting their potential in financial time series forecasting. The findings underscore the robustness and accuracy of these hybrid models across different stock markets, making them valuable tools for extrapolating financial market trends. In the study by   , new hybrid models are proposed for forecasting the closing prices of prominent indices, utilizing recurrent neural network-based models, including CNN-LSTM, GRU-CNN, and ensemble models. An innovative feature involving the average of the highest and lowest prices of stock market indices is introduced. Experimental results indicate that these models outperform traditional machine-learning models in various cases. In another research   , a financial time series prediction model based on a deep learning ensemble is introduced, combining a CNN, LSTM, and ARMA to effectively handle spatiotemporal data features and autocorrelation. The deep learning ensemble model demonstrates superior prediction accuracy and robustness compared to single benchmark models, highlighting its potential in financial time series forecasting.

snippets: Additionally, in the context of stock index and volatility forecasting, researchers explored the application of hybrid models incorporating financial variables   . The AWT-LSTM-ARMAX-FIEGARCH model, combining AWT, LSTM, and ARIMAX-GARCH models, showed significant improvements in stock index forecasting, especially for various time horizons, such as 1, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 60 days ahead. Similarly, the use of AWT and LSTM enhances the predictive accuracy of the HAR-RV model for stock volatility across various time horizons, especially for DJIA and IXIC. Additionally, another ensemble model combining EEMD, ARIMA, and Taylor expansion with a tracking differentiator was proposed for financial time series forecasting   . This approach decomposes financial time series into sub-series using EEMD and then uses ARIMA models to predict the linear part of each sub-series while employing Taylor expansion models to predict the nonlinear part. The hybrid model aggregates predictions from linear and nonlinear models, surpassing reference models in financial time series forecasting. The work of    aims to improve the accuracy and stability of financial phenomena forecasting. The CEEMD-PCA-LSTM model employs deep learning techniques and a complementary version of complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition (CEEMD) to predict stock markets, consistently outperforming reference models regarding predictive accuracy. Furthermore, a hybrid model proposed by    combines EWT, an algorithm enhanced by ABC, ELM neural networks, and the ARIMA model. This model is designed to denoise and analyze financial time series, demonstrating superior denoising capabilities and predictive performance. The study by    introduces a new hybrid deep learning model, CEEMDAN-DAE-LSTM, combining CEEMDAN with DAE and LSTM. CEEMDAN decomposition organizes stock index data into intrinsic mode functions, DAE removes redundant data, and extracts features at deeper levels. At the same time, LSTM networks predict stock returns for the next trading day. Similarly,    proposes a new framework that combines GRU with CEEMDAN to enhance the accuracy of stock index forecasts. snippets: Bagging algorithm The bagging algorithm is one of the most widely used ensemble learning algorithms   . It uses the voting mechanism to determine the final classification label. Bagging, also known as bootstrap aggregation, is a representative ensemble algorithm in parallel ensemble learning. An advantage of the bagging algorithm using out-of-package estimation is that it can adjust the training model in the training process of selecting basic weak classifiers, to reduce the risk of overfitting. A disadvantage is that some deviation is introduced in the process of the readoption of training samples, which may affect the final classification effect, so the algorithm is suitable for models with a small deviation. The core idea of the bagging algorithm is to train a learning algorithm for many rounds, and the training set of each round is composed of n samples that are randomly and quantitatively taken from the initial training set.  After training, a prediction function sequence is obtained, and finally, a new input value is discriminated by the way of voting of the prediction function. The main steps of bagging include building integration by copying and training multiple basic learning machines in the bootstrap sampling process of the original dataset. And then, the bagging algorithm selects the final output in the form of majority voting or average. Integrating multiple learning machines to enhance diversity can not only reduce the generalization error, but also ensure that the members of the set are as independent as possible.

snippets: 6.5.2 Bagging The bagging algorithm is also known as bootstrapping aggregating. It a set of meta-algorithms designed to enhance the stability and accuracy of weak classifiers. It augments the classification accuracy by generating an enhanced composite classifier and integrating the output of the learned classifier into a single prediction. Bootstrap aggregations and their variations, random forest, etc., are some of the popular bagging algorithms. Bagging differs from boosting by the truth that weak learners are structured in parallel form and a distinct detection scheme on each sub-ensemble can be applied before collection. In    proposed a collective contextual anomaly detection using a sliding window to identify anomalous energy consumption patterns. To enhance the capacity of anomaly detection, a bagging-based ensemble learning framework is implemented. The generic ensemble-based framework integrates pattern-based and prediction-based classifiers using majority voting. Wang et al.    proposed dynamic ensemble anomaly detection based on a one-class classifier. The pool of diverse one-class classifiers is trained using random subspace and bagging techniques. The proposed method uses adaptive KNN to determine the validation set.

snippets: 6.4 Bagging Bootstrap aggregating (bagging) is an ensemble learning technique widely used in ML to improve model performance and reduce variance. The main idea behind bagging is to create multiple models by training them on different random subsets of the training data. During the training phase, bootstrap sampling is performed, where data points are randomly selected with replacements to form each subset. These subsets are used to train individual models independently. When making predictions, bagging combines the predictions of all models, usually through voting (for  classification) or averaging (for regression), to arrive at a final prediction. Bagging reduces the risk of overfitting and increases the stability and accuracy of the overall model by reducing variance. It works well with high-variance algorithms like decision trees, creating a more robust and powerful ensemble model. Popular implementations of bagging include Random Forest for decision trees and Bagged Ensembles for other base models. Bagging has been proven effective in various domains, ranging from image recognition and sentiment analysis to financial forecasting and medical diagnostics ( Breiman, 1996 ).

In this way, the distribution of samples is changed. After combining the weak classifiers obtained from each iteration, a strong classifier with better performance can be obtained. For these strong classifiers, the features they use have good classification. The AdaBoost method has often been used in classification problems in the past few years. When designing the base classifier, the algorithm can select the classifier with the least error. snippets: 4.2.1 Boosting Boosting is “one of the most powerful learning ideas introduced in the last 20 years” ( Hastie et al., 2009 ). It is a family of dependent ensemble methods in which the learners are trained one at a time and seek to overcome the errors of the previous models using various strategies depending on the specific algorithm. Boosting algorithms can convert a set of weak learners into a strong learner. In simple words, a weak learner generates models that are slightly better than random guessing, whereas strong learners produce models that have a perfect or near optimal performance. The remaining part of this subsection briefly reviews some popular boosting methods whose interpretation methods are investigated in  Section 4.4 . 4.2.1.1 AdaBoost AdaBoost ( Freund & Schapire, 1997 ) is one of the most heavily used ensemble learning algorithms during the first decade after its creation. The name of the algorithm is derived from “adaptive boosting,” and it starts by assigning individual weights to the training samples, usually a uniform weight of  1 / n . For each iteration, the algorithm fits a new learner, computes the error, and updates each instance weight accordingly. Misclassified instances obtain increased weight values, whereas correctly classified instances obtain decreased weight values. Thus, the algorithm can focus on the most difficult training regions of  D . In addition, each weak learner receives a weight  α k  that is based on the accuracy of the model, which means that the weights do not need to add up to 1. With this strategy, the algorithm sequentially builds learners using different training data versions. 4.2.1.2 Gradient boosting machines GBMs have gained significant attention in the machine learning field in recent years ( Friedman, 2001 ). As is well known, boosting is equivalent to conducting a forward stagewise additive expansion using an exponential loss function ( Hastie et al., 2009 ). The strategy used is a greedy stagewise approach, in which there is an imperfect model at iteration  k  with the following form: H k ( x ) = H ( k − 1 ) ( x ) + β k h k ( x ) , where  α  is the weight given to the current trained model; thus, in this way, GBM improves the function  H k ( x )  by fitting a new model  h k ( x )  over the so-called pseudoresiduals.

snippets: 3.2 Ensemble learning Ensemble learning is the process in which multiple models or classifiers are combined to achieve higher performance than any of the models alone   . In this context, we use the idea of ensemble learning to combine the outputs of the three main classifiers into a fused vector that is used to train a final classifier, i.e., a feed-forward neural network. To combine this with representation learning, we use the output of the same classifiers trained on a different representation of the data generated by the SAE explained in the previous section. By training a neural network on the output of multiple classifiers, we essentially train that network to learn from the mistakes of these classifiers. Furthermore, utilizing SAE networks produces alternate representations of the data thereby enhancing the ability of the model to detect more complex patterns within the data thus increasing its attack classification performance.

snippets: 11.4.6 Ensemble learning Ensemble learning is the practice of scientifically producing and linking many models, such as classifiers or experts, to hold a precise computational intelligence problem. Ensemble learning is normally used to mend a model's presentation or lower the risk of an unintended poor model choice. Ensemble learning is also used for conveying a confidence level to the model's decision, selecting optimal structures, data fusion, incremental learning, nonstationary learning, and error correction.

snippets: 8.4.5 Ensemble learning Ensemble learning is an approach in which two or more models are fitted to the same data, and the predictions of each model are combined. Ensemble learning aims to achieve better performance with the ensemble of models than with any individual model. This requires deciding how to create the models used in the ensemble and how best to combine the predictions of the ensemble members. Ensemble learning is a useful approach to improving predictability and reducing the variance of stochastic learning algorithms, such as artificial neural networks. Some examples of popular ensemble learning algorithms are a weighted average, stacked generalization (stacking), and bootstrap aggregation (bagging); see also classification in  Fig. 8.1 .
